News.title: Trump hits out at ‘election fraud’ after Democrats ‘recruited candidate with same name’ to run in knife-edge election
News.content:
DIRTY POLITICS Trump hits out at ‘election fraud’ after Democrats ‘recruited candidate with same name’ to run in knife-edge election







Next

DONALD Trump has accused Democrats of “voter fraud at the highest level” just as Americans go to the polls.

A new New York Times report about the Midterm elections alleges that the Democrats sought out a same-name candidate for the upcoming crunch Alaska Senate seat.



Trump has demanded that the state change its ballot after the Democrats allegedly tried to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, according to a report.

“It was just determined that the Dumocrats in Alaska, despite their sworn statements to the contrary, put a man named Dan Sullivan on the Ballot in order to confuse the Public with respect to Highly Esteemed Senator Dan Sullivan,” he wrote on TruthSocial.



“This is Voter Fraud at the Highest Level, and the Dumocrat Candidate who was involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted.

“So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan. Nothing else will do!”

It was one of four posts about the alleged fraud that Trump shared on his account.

Two Dan Sullivans are running for the seat with Democrat Peltola poised for a upset, according to the polls.

But the new report alleges that Democratic staff have tried to stack the ballot in their favour using name confusion.

Staff members at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and on Peltola’s campaign spent months working to find such a candidate, the New York Times reported.



Mr. Sullivan has maintained that he entered the race of his own volition. The Peltola campaign and the D.S.C.C. denied any involvement in recruiting Sullivan for the ballot.

But the New York Times reported that a Peltola staffer was allegedly told to search for every Dan Sullivan in the state.

Other Alaskans with different names were also reportedly approached, apparently to add more options to the ballot and pull support from Sullivan, according to the outlet.



The whole operation involved secret journeys to remote communities and a mysterious Midwestern operative who pitched to would-be candidates at pubs, it was alleged in the report.

Eventually, they were reportedly able to get Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. into the race.

Trump confirmed that he personally ordered a lawsuit to stop Alaska from certifying election results if the Republicans lose there.

Reacting to the report, Trump accused the Democrats of cheating.

“They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it. That’s perjury,” he added.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Echoing the criticism, JD Vance also hit out, calling Peltola a “total crook” who tried to “rig” the senate race in her favour.

The Alaska contest has become one of the most closely watched Senate run-offs.

News.title: Armed robber wearing The Joker face paint threatened to stab workers trying to stop him stealing from Brit supermarket
News.content:
Next

AN armed robber with full Joker makeup terrorised frightened supermarket workers with a knife and threatened to stab them as he stole from the store.

Peter Braithwaite, 31, marched into Morrisons branch in Jarrow, Tyneside, on July 8 dressed entirely in black with his face painted as the twisted Batman villain.



Newcastle Crown Court heard how female workers intercepted the shoplifter as he attempted to push a trolley loaded with unpaid goods towards the exit.

Braithwaite simply winked at the women and instructed them to “speak to your manager” before a male security guard stepped in to help, prosecutor Kevin Wardlaw said.



Braithwaite was seen on CCTV with his face painted as the deranged criminal character, dressed all in black and carrying a black backpack.

Mr Wardlaw told the court that employees grabbed the trolley to halt his escape, prompting the masked man to draw a six-inch folding knife.



Wielding the weapon, the thief threatened to stab the terrified staff members, leaving the security guard convinced a violent assault was imminent.

Mr Wardlaw said: “The defendant had his face painted to resemble a Batman character, The Joker, and was seen pushing a trolley containing various groceries.

“The defendant was heard to make comments: ‘Do you want a bit? Do you want to get stabbed? Do you want to die?’ while pointing the knife towards staff and caused them to back away.”

Shocking shop CCTV footage captured the criminal fleeing the scene with the stolen groceries, wheeling the cart directly to his nearby home.



Confronted along the way by a neighbour who questioned his bizarre behaviour, Braithwaite offered no explanation and merely gave a “wide-eyed” stare.

Police officers quickly descended on the address, where they recovered both the bladed weapon and the stolen food.

Braithwaite, of Jarrow, pleaded guilty to robbery and was today handed a 40-month prison sentence.



The court heard the horrific ordeal has had a lasting impact on the victims.

One worker revealed they now suffer from severe panic and anxiety on the job.

The employee admitted that while tackling thieves never used to bother them, they now face “complete dread” when dealing with shoplifters.

The worker said: “I keep thinking about the moment when the offender with the painted face pulled a knife out and pointed it towards me asking if I wanted it.

“He looked so frightening, his eyes were bulging. I believed I was going to be stabbed.”



Sentencing him, Recorder Jamie Hill KC told Braithwaite: “This was a terrifying incident, essentially threatening to stab several people who were trying to do their job.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I realise you have come to understand and be remorseful about this and when you have spoken to professionals you may not have complete memory of exactly what you did, but I am sure those people who were there in Morrisons will never forget it.”

Defending the attacker, Robin Turton said his client suffers from mental health issues but is deeply remorseful and now fully grasps the severity of his actions.

News.title: Ukraine’s fate could be sealed by US midterms, Zelensky tells The Sun as Trump fights to avoid political bloodbath
News.content:
Next

PRESIDENT Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine’s fate could be sealed by the US midterm elections – as Donald Trump fights to avoid a political bloodbath.

The outcome of Tuesday’s elections will shape how much power the US President has for the rest of his term in office.



And according to the polls, the Republican Party is at risk of losing both the House of Representatives and the Senate amid a slump in Trump’s approval ratings.

If that happens, he will lose control of Congress and his ability to see through any future plans.



You can watch The Sun’s full explosive interview with President Zelensky here

Speaking to The Sun, Mr Zelensky tellingly said: “A lot of things now depend on American elections.



“The result will have an influence either way.

“And of course it will have influence on a lot of different things, including Ukraine, including the war in Ukraine, including the attitude to Russians and different deals with them.



“So I think that we will see. I don’t know, but changes are understandable.”

Mr Trump sparked fury last week after telling reporters at the White House: “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine.

“They haven’t been doing much.”

He delivered his comments just hours after one-year-old Angelina Mariukhna was killed by a drone whilst strapped in her pushchair at a park in Ukraine’s second city of Kharkiv.

Innocent Angelina’s teacher mum, Inna, 28, also died in the strike.



Mr Trump’s special envoy and golf-buddy Steve Witkoff fanned the flames further when he addressed Putin as ‘Sir’ during peace talks in St Petersburg and described him as ‘a humanitarian’.

Ukraine’s use of billionaire Elon Musk’s military-grade Starlink system was then restricted without warning – and saw thousands of drones used in the defence of Ukraine fall from the sky.

Inside his fortified presidential HQ, Mr Zelensky contrasted Mr Trump’s open desire to end the war and his cosying up to Putin.



Mr Zelensky – who has vowed not to agree a peace deal at any costs – said the US must stop sucking up to the Kremlin dictator and shift its position.

The wartime leader said: “We need more support.

“There is no pressure (on Russia). No strong signals from the United States mean that Putin is doing well.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“How about the condemnation? We don’t hear condemnation of aggression. We need it.

“If the United States, our strong partner, understands that Putin’s goal is to occupy us and to destroy us, they can’t be on Putin’s side.”

News.title: Moment taxi driver brawls with motorist in middle of busy street before ramming him with car in road rage attack
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a raging taxi driver brawls with a motorist in the middle of the street before ramming his car in a frenzied attack.

Hawkar Karimi, 37, was seen on dashcam footage embroiled in a brutal punch-up in the middle of busy Wavertree Road, in Edge Hill, Liverpool, Merseyside.



Mr Karimi was behind the unnamed man at a previous junction and “beeped his horn” at him because he missed a green light, a court heard.

The dad-of-one thought the man had been driving while using his mobile phone, Liverpool Crown Court heard.



The scuffle then erupted after the two men came into contact with Mr Karimi saying he wanted to sort things out “like a man” but had no intention of fighting.

The video – taken from the cabbie’s own dashcam – shows the men throwing punches at each other during 10 second road rage incident shortly after 7pm on September 13 last year.

At one point Mr Karimi falls to the ground as the man lands a punch to his head.

Moments later Mr Karimi is seen scrambling away as the main looms over him before getting back into his cab.



The taxi driver then launches into a minute-long car chase after the man, reaching speeds of up to 40 mph.

He chased him through a red light on a congested road and smashed into the back of him before they both turn down a narrow residential street.

As the car reaches the busy junction at Edge Lane, Mr Karimi crashes into the back of the man’s black Volkswagen for the second time.



The man quickly gets out of the car and runs from the scene before the taxi driver smashes into the back of the car again, making it hit a brick wall outside a furniture shop.

Mr Karimi was subsequently arrested at the scene.

The court was told that he chased the man as he didn’t want him to get away with hitting him.

Mr Karimi, who has no previous convictions, told the court he “regretted his behaviour”.

Matthew Cullen, defending Mr Karimi, told the court that the taxi driver was a “positively contributing” member of society.



Mr Cullen argued that the cabbie’s actions on the day did not show his “true character”.

Karimi had previously admitted one count of dangerous driving.

Judge Stuart Driver KC labelled Karimi’s driving as “disgraceful” before handing him a 12-month imprisonment suspended for a year last week.

He was also given 100 hours of unpaid work and a 12-month probation requirement.

Karimi was also banned from driving for 30 months and ordered to pay a £187 victim surcharge.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Under the Sentencing Act 2026 in March this year, any sentences of 12 months or less must be suspended in all but exceptional circumstances.

Judge Driver said he believed the cabbie should have gone to prison but said there were “no exceptional circumstances” for him to do so.

News.title: John Healey has delivered a Budget for just getting by, not getting on
News.content:
Next

WAS that it?

Last year, Labour gave us the Budget for Benefits Street.



This year, John Healey has delivered a Budget for just getting by, not getting on.

Under Labour, Britain is spending more on debt interest than on the Army and schools combined.



The benefits bill is going up by tens of billions of pounds. Next year, the tax burden will be the highest in our country’s history.

Healey resigned as Defence Secretary in June, because the government wouldn’t fund defence to three per cent of GDP.

Yet he couldn’t even find the cash in his Budget to hit the target he quit over!

Labour has made hiring more expensive with their jobs tax, energy more expensive with Net Zero policies, and mortgages more expensive with their excessive borrowing.

There is a better way. The Conservatives will cut government spending by over £70billion, including £36billion from the benefits bill.

We will use half that money to cut the deficit, so Britain doesn’t go bankrupt, and with the rest we will properly fund our defence and cut your taxes.



That is the Budget the Chancellor should have delivered.

The Budget he gave was simply not enough.

News.title: Budget exposes hollow promises behind Burnham’s radical plan to tackle cost of living crisis & get Britain working again
News.content:
Next

NOT so long ago, Andy Burnham stood outside No10 and promised a radical plan to tackle the cost of living crisis and get Britain working again.

What we got from his Chancellor was some timid tinkering worlds away from the PM’s lofty rhetoric.



Humdrum Healey’s biggest Budget giveaway — a £100 energy handout for the least well-off families — will be wiped out by a £276 increase in a typical household bill forecast for next year.

And, on the truly massive issues facing Britain, he simply bottled it.



This painfully cautious Budget did nothing to tackle any of the root causes of our economic woes. In fact, they are getting worse.

The welfare bill is forecast to skyrocket by £19billion this year to a staggering £353billion — equivalent to about 11 per cent of all Britain produces. In 2031/32 it hits a ruinous £431billion.

But all the Chancellor had to offer was the sound of cans being kicked down the road, insisting he must wait for some reviews into the benefits system to finish before any action can be taken.

Hard-working Brits are being taken to the cleaners to pay for it — with the tax burden headed to a peacetime high.

Healey’s freeze on thresholds will drag thousands more low earners into paying income tax and push others into higher tax bands.

Much of it will go on servicing the £3trillion national debt, with interest payments costing an extra £14billion this year.



Nor was there anything to show that Healey is serious about beefing up our depleted Armed Forces.

Just days ago, the Defence Secretary urged us to stockpile tinned food and water and prepare for war in 1,000 days, but there was no word from the Chancellor on how he will pay for his pledge to hit Nato spending targets by 2030.

To be fair, Healey did listen to The Sun by extending the fuel duty freeze.



But with global oil prices soaring, any relief at the pumps will soon be swallowed up.

Sneaky hikes in existing taxes proved irresistible to a Labour Party addicted to spending.

His short-sighted raid on landlords and savers will inevitably be passed straight down to tenants in the form of higher rents — or intensify the housing shortage by driving property owners out of the market.

Meanwhile, the five per cent rise in tax on gambling machines will cost yet more jobs and inflict yet another hammer blow to our ailing high street bookies.

This was meant to be a radical reset. It was a chance to show Labour understands the scale of our economic problems and has the guts to tackle them.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Instead we got more tax, more welfare, more debt and nothing to stimulate growth. Action on the great challenges of our times was simply postponed.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch summed it up perfectly, in just three words:

Is that it?

News.title: Thousands of jobs at risk as bookies slapped with new tax raid during Budget despite warnings it would hit high streets
News.content:
Next

THOUSANDS of high street jobs were put on the line yesterday as bookies were hit with another tax raid.

Chancellor John Healey pressed ahead with a fresh hike in gambling duties despite warnings it could force betting shops to close and leave town centres with empty premises.



But bookies were not the only ones in his Budget line of fire, with landlords, savers, banks and business owners facing bigger tax bills.

Mr Healey, who enjoyed a slice of cake in a cafe after his speech, defended the rises, saying: “I’ve made my choice at this Budget — asking a bit more of our banks to support ordinary people, raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street.”



The move sparked fury across the betting industry, which has already been battered by tax rises announced by Rachel Reeves when she was Chancellor last year.

The Sun’s Save Our Bets campaign has been leading the fight to protect betting shops and safeguard jobs.



Mr Healey announced Machine Games Duty on higher-stakes gambling machines would rise from 20 to 25 per cent from April next year, short of a feared 40 per cent rate.

But bosses fear the extra costs could still push betting shops over the edge.



Betting and Gaming Council chief executive Grainne Hurst said: “Every betting shop or casino closure means lost livelihoods, empty premises and another huge blow to our high streets.

“These venues will not simply be replaced, particularly in places already struggling to attract jobs and investment.

“The Chancellor has chosen a tax rise that will cost British jobs, close businesses and hollow out high streets, while handing an advantage to illegal operators.



“The Government cannot ignore the consequences of this decision.”

Another industry source slammed the move as “ideology on steroids pushed by donors, campaigners and Gordon Brown”.

Ex-PM Mr Brown has previously insisted the gambling industry is under-taxed.

The source added: “The PM used to back bookies, but now his Government is putting up gambling taxes yet again in the knowledge it will force hundreds to close.

“You can’t give people breathing space when they don’t have a job.”



The Chancellor said the extra tax would help fund a cut in business rates for high street firms.

He raised that threshold from £12,000 to £18,000, taking 70,000 businesses out of the system.

Elsewhere in today’s Budget…

More than 600 betting shops have closed since last year’s Budget, industry figures say, though not all were directly due to tax rises.

Last week, Flutter, which owns Paddy Power, Sky Bet and Betfair, announced plans to axe up to 1,400 UK and Ireland jobs, blaming tax increases announced last November.



Industry chiefs also fear squeezing licensed bookmakers will drive more punters towards illegal gambling websites.

Horse racing could suffer too, if betting shop closures reduce the money flowing into the sport.

Ladbrokes and Coral owner Entain yesterday revealed the latest increase would cost its UK and Ireland retail business around £25million a year.



Chief executive Stella David called it “another disappointing decision by the Government”.

She said: “The tax increases announced in November last year have already had detrimental consequences across the industry. These additional tax changes will further compound that damage and push more people into the growing illegal market.”

But the gambling industry was not alone in facing a bigger bill.

Britain’s banks were ordered to pay more, with a temporary increase from three to six per cent in the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge for 15 months from January.

The Chancellor said it would help pay for £100 energy payments to 20million households.



He told MPs yesterday: “Just as the British people helped support our banks 20 years ago, it is our banks that will help give families breathing space today.”

But there are concerns banks could eventually seek to recover some of the extra costs through less generous savings deals or more expensive lending.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said: “They are making the same mistake with banking that they made with oil and gas.



“Tax one of Britain’s flagship industries until they pack up and leave. The result? The country gets less money in tax.”

Landlords were also clobbered after Mr Healey increased income tax rates on property income by two percentage points from next April.

Basic-rate taxpayers will face a 24 per cent rate on taxable rental profits.

Higher-rate taxpayers will pay 44 per cent, and additional-rate taxpayers 49 per cent.

And tenants could end up footing the bill too, with the Office for Budget Responsibility warning landlords are likely to pass on higher taxes through raising rents in the long run.



The independent watchdog also warned Angela Rayner’s Employment Rights Act was likely to damage the economy, with higher costs and less flexibility for firms outweighing any boost to productivity.

Savers were also caught in the Chancellor’s sights, with tax rates on savings interest rising by two percentage points from next April.

The increase will affect those earning enough interest outside of tax-free accounts to exceed their savings allowances.

However, Mr Healey insisted 88 per cent of people would pay no more tax on their savings, and he ditched plans to cut the annual cash ISA allowance, keeping the tax-free limit at £20,000.

Some business owners also face a bigger bill when selling up, after the Chancellor halved the lifetime threshold for Business Asset Disposal Relief from £1million to £500,000. Mr Healey insisted three in four people claiming the relief would be unaffected.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

And people enjoying a staycation could face another hit to their wallets after regional mayors were handed powers to slap a tourist tax on overnight stays from 2028.

Hospitality bosses have previously warned the levy could add around £100 to the cost of a family’s two-week holiday in Britain.

News.title: Putin calls Elon Musk a ‘real genius’ after SpaceX boss ‘ordered Starshield blackout’ that left Ukraine defenceless
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin has hailed Elon Musk as a “real genius” after SpaceX cut Ukraine’s Starshield connection, plunging its air defences into darkness.

Desperate to develop a satellite internet network for Russia, the President has been taking notes from the billionaire.



“Elon Musk is a genius, a real genius,” the dictator said during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday.

“How many of these [low-orbit satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”



He added: “We are in close contact with our American partners, including Musk, because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order.”

Musk is yet to respond to Putin’s remarks.

Starlink uses a constellation of satellites that orbit far lower, reducing the signal travel time.

Ukraine has relied heavily on the system and its military version Starshield for battlefield operations, drone navigation and critical air defence.



But the government complained earlier this month of speed restrictions that even forced the cancellation of some major operations.

The issue of access has been a big hot potato that neither Musk nor the White House has been able to take control of properly.

Each accused the other of pulling the plug on the military-grade service that blindsided Ukraine.

It had been suggested that Donald Trump ordered the slowdown to show his anger with Volodymyr Zelensky.

Musk also blamed the US President, writing on X: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.



“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and POTUS.”

This added to the tensions between Trump and Zelensky, a relationship already strained by the reported deal on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

Last week, Trump confirmed he had asked Musk to “put it back”, having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.



Over the weekend, Ukraine said Starlink and Starshield were again ⁠fully functional, but the tech mogul accused the Ukrainian military of violating SpaceX‘s terms.

“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” he wrote on X.

“Ukraine[‘s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”

News.title: Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
News.content:
Millions of households will get Â£100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.

The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".

He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.

These include:

One-off Â£100 energy payment for people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" it

Gas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales, to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher bills

Extending the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel to July

Increasing minimum wage rates by 3.9% in April, although there will be no progress on narrowing the gap between rates for older and younger workers

Healey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.

News.title: I earn £30,000. I'm angry there was no fuel duty cut in the Budget
News.content:
Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.

He spends around Â£350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.

He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."

The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.

The only measure Dave wanted to see was a cut to fuel duty, and he was disappointed this didn't happen.

"I'm pretty angry, really. Nothing has been thrown my way," he says.

The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, and it will be frozen again, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."

News.title: Spain begins three days of mourning after train crash kills dozens
News.content:
Spain is beginning three days of mourning after at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured in one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history.

Emergency crews worked through the night under powerful floodlights to cut open metal carriages in the search for victims, with many of those killed in the crash still to be identified.

Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train on Wednesday morning.

Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said the "whole of Spain is grieving", adding that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense".

Hundreds of personnel have been deployed to the disaster site to assist with recovery efforts, according to Spain's interior ministry, with drones and helicopters being used to find victims and remove rubble.

The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, according to Spain's transport minister Ãscar Puente.

News.title: Family row over George Michael items up for auction - including Faith guitar
News.content:
Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.

She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.

"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.

"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."

The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.

The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.

In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.

Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".

It has an estimated price tag of between Â£60,000 and Â£120,000. Other less significant but more personal items have already exceeded their estimates.

A Filofax from the 1988 Faith tour with Siobhan's handwritten notes and annotations had a guide price of up to Â£600 and a current bid of Â£1,750.

Other items include a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.

The auction also includes the gold disc and platinum CD presented to her for sales milestones achieved by Michael's music.

"I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.

He said "she would never have consented" to the sale of these items, adding that the auction "breaks my heart".

"I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.

Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".

He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".

Bailey acknowledged that Belcher has a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

News.title: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
News.content:
Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site was once a rubbish dump but has been redeveloped and now protects 1,235 acres of mangroves.

The King walked along a new boardwalk through the wetlands to see the conservation work being done to protect this vulnerable, low lying island from climate change.

He met students carrying out field work in the wetland waters asking them about their exams and ambitions to be marine biologists.

"We've so been looking forward to this," said Joanne Smith, president of the Bahamas National Trust Council.

"We want more Bahamians to get involved in our national parks so they can use it to better themselvesâ¦ we are so pleased to have the King here, this is really significant for us."

Then it was on to the Junkanoo, where the King could be seen dancing alongside attendees dressed in feathered headdresses and bright costumes.

The history of the Junkanoo is not clear but it's believed it emerged out of the slave trade when enslaved men and women were given time off to mark Christmas.

A small protest near the parade, which had activists holding placards with the words "Pay us what you owe us", was moved on by the police.

The small group of protesters were from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.

The King acknowledged the "great suffering of the past" when he first arrived in the Bahamas, as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Noelle Nicholls, chair of the reparations committee, said :"We are demanding an apology for those crimes, and reparations for the harm that was done."

Nicholls said the protesters' presence "amidst the pomp and pageantry of the celebrations... are for us also a sombre occasion, because this is the King returning in a way that has still not atoned for the sins of the past."

The King has confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery at a major summit in Antigua next week.

News.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
News.content:
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.

Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."

"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.

"We will update the public when more information is available."

The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.

The information was put in a database named Icepick.

Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.

Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.

BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.

A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the groups work to hack DHS records.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.

Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.

The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.

Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.

A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."

Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.

In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.

Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.

Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.

Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement.

Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations, external, according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record.

News.title: Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters
News.content:
At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.

Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.

In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.

The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.

The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.

News.title: Weight-loss jab boom brings needles warning for recyclers
News.content:
The boom in injectable weight-loss drugs, such as Mounjaro and Wegovy, is leading to more used needles turning up at recycling centres, putting workers at risk of serious injury and infection, bosses say.

At a recycling plant in Coventry, I watched staff sorting rubbish on a fast-moving conveyor belt when a crushed yellow sharps container suddenly appeared among the waste.

"A resident has put this in a wheelie bin," explained supervisor Paul Pagett.

"It then gets crushed by the recycling vehicle and then it comes to us open and obviously we've got needles then falling out onto the line putting my guys at risk."

The sharps box should never have been there.

Used needles should be disposed of separately through dedicated clinical waste services. Instead, recycling bosses say they are increasingly finding them mixed in with household waste.

"There are safe disposal routes for needles but the worst place to put them is in your recycling," said Richard Dobbs, managing director of Sherborne Recycling.

"It ends up in facilities like ours where it will be touched by people and that's inherently unsafe."

News.title: Russell Brand tells trial sexual consent is 'fundamental'
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

Russell Brand has told the jury at his trial he believes sexual consent is "fundamental" and "more important than sex itself".

Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Brand said the allegations had been "deeply traumatic" and had a "devastating" impact on him.

The media personality gave evidence as his defence case began at his trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

Asked whether consent was important to him, he told the court: "Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself."

Brand told the court he had previously been "comfortable" allowing his fame to "facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong".

But asked by the prosecution whether he "needed and was prepared to go to any lengths", Brand replied: "Absolutely no."

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC suggested to Brand there were inconsistencies between his previous prepared police statement and what he told the jury.

"Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree," he replied. "Since these events occurred there's been escalating recollection.

"It's been a deeply traumatic episode of my life. I've focused on it at the expense of my marriage, my children and health.

"I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that."

He said: "I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.

"With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I've been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy."

He told the jury: "Regrettably I've had a lot of consensual sex, which I see has caused harm."

News.title: Mum of critically ill baby denied hospital food as she wasn't breastfeeding
News.content:
A first-time mum was denied hospital meals while her baby was "fighting for her life" because she was not breastfeeding.

Sophie Price, 22, was "shocked" when staff refused to give her a meal while her daughter Florence was being treated on a paediatric ward at Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen.

Despite giving birth in the hospital five days earlier, she was told she was no longer classed as a patient as she was not breastfeeding, so she would not be provided with meals.

Aneurin Bevan health board said it was "sorry to hear about Sophie's experience" and was "committed to supporting families throughout their child's stay".

"It was just an awful experience. I just needed a hot meal to keep going for my daughter," said Sophie, from Newport.

Her family said they spent more than Â£1,000 on food from the canteen and takeaway meals during their three-week stay at the hospital while Florence was treated.

News.title: NHS Western Isles prescribing weight loss drugs at triple the rate of other health boards
News.content:
Patients in the Western Isles are being prescribed drugs used for weight loss and diabetes at almost three times the rate of any other health board in Scotland.

A new report from the Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry (ABPI) found "significant variation" between Scotland's health boards prescribing new medicines, including drugs for heart attacks and strokes.

The biggest variation was seen in access to GLP-1 medication, which is widely used to treat type 2 diabetes but was approved for weight management in 2023.

NHS Western Isles said it was seeing "significant clinical benefit".

The ABPI said there were limitations to the data, but better planning could help overcome inequalities in access.

The Scottish government said it would "carefully consider" the findings of the report.

It said its health board reforms were intended to "improve equity of access to services and reduce the unwarranted variation and bureaucratic barriers we currently have in place".

These reforms include plans to reduce the number of mainland health boards from 14 to two, which leading doctors have opposed.

News.title: Huntingdon train attacker asked man 'do you want to die?', trial hears
News.content:
Train passengers fled "in sheer terror" from a knife attacker who asked one victim "do you want to die?", a trial has heard.

Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025. He is also accused of trying to kill three people in Peterborough the day before and then a boy at a London railway station.

Opening the prosecution case at Cambridge Crown Court, Christopher Paxton KC said that of those on the train "some stood tall, to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage".

Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder.

Williams is accused of attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett and Samir Zitouni on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on that Saturday evening.

He is also accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy and Dawid Taborski on a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on 31 October, and William Ogelby at Railworld car park in the city shortly afterwards.

Williams was then seen swigging from a bottle of alcohol outside Ritzy Barber Shop in Fletton in Peterborough, before going into the shop brandishing a knife.

The jury heard he then travelled to east London, where he stabbed a 17-year-old on a Docklands Light Railway train at Pontoon Dock in Silvertown in the early hours of 1 November.

During that attack, jurors were told a witness said she heard the defendant repeatedly say: "Are you trying to beef with the devil?"

News.title: Tommy Robinson guilty of harassing two Daily Mail journalists
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson has been convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.

A jury at Southwark Crown Court found the 43-year-old, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.

The case concerned Robinson's response to Daily Mail and Mail Online articles from August 2024, showing him on holiday in Cyprus while riots took place in England following the Southport murders.

The court had heard how Robinson, from Bedfordshire, used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, forcing them to employ security or leave home.

Robinson had denied the charges, saying he had "panicked" and had been "scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

He told the jury he felt the article had "endangered" his family by revealing they were staying in a hotel near Ayia Napa in Cyprus.

After the guilty verdicts, Frank Ferguson, the head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Robinson had "weaponised social media and subjected two journalists to a campaign of harassment which caused them serious fear of violence".â

Robinson was granted bail ahead of his sentencing, scheduled for 16 Decemberâ.

Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, or up to 14 years if the offence is racially or religiously aggravated.

News.title: 'My autistic son and I feel abandoned and failed by the system'
News.content:
A mother has said she feels her son has been "abandoned and is falling through cracks in the system" because of a lack of support for young adults with learning difficulties.

Cherrise Lanigan's son Callan has autism and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), as well as anxiety and other behavioural issues.

He recently turned 18 but cannot access adult disability services because of the way health trusts assess support needs using an IQ test. Cherisse believes it is a flawed system that is disadvantaging her son.

The Northern Health Trust has said it recognises the approach "can present significant challenges" for individuals and families who do not meet the eligibility criteria.

Cherrise, who lives with her son in Draperstown, County Londonderry, described his autism diagnosis as complex and said that he has "significant social and emotional support needs".

"My son's autism is so much more than his IQ, and he really struggles with the social aspects of being around people, but any help we had has now been taken away because of one test," she told BBC News NI.

"It just feels like he's being treated like he's not that important because without support, he's not going to make progress, so is he just expected to stay at home all his life?"

News.title: Terminally ill mum who can't talk, walk or dress herself refused Pip payment
News.content:
A terminally ill mum who has been given three years to live has been denied disability benefit despite being unable to eat, talk, dress or use the toilet independently.

Rachael Field, 56, from Rhondda Cynon Taf, who has tongue cancer, was first diagnosed six years ago.

She uses a feeding tube, has had her tongue and voice box removed, and had her windpipe reconstructed using chest tissue. Field also has mobility issues.

Earlier this year, she was denied Personal Independence Payment (Pip), to support people with disability-related extra costs.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it needed further evidence to complete the claim and was sorry for "any distress" to the family.

Field said she has had cancer four times in six years, and now cannot do anything for herself.

"I need help to wash, dress and use the bathroom. I can only walk a few steps with help. I cannot eat or drink, everything has to go through my feeding tube," she added.

News.title: Mum quits job as lawyer to voice Netflix cartoon
News.content:
A mum says she left her late-night legal career behind for voiceover work from home where she can care for her children.

Emily McGonagle started her working life as a lawyer in the capital, often finishing at 03:00, but started to question whether she could sustain it long term.

After having children, she decided to seek something "more flexible" than her daily commute from Colchester to Canary Wharf, and pivoted to voiceover work in 2019.

The 42-year-old voices eight characters for the children's television series Spike, which premiered on Netflix on 12 October and is its number one children's show on the site in the UK.

The cartoon began as a preschool animation on YouTube called Fire Spike!, which was about the adventures of a dragon and his friends.

It was created by a Lithuanian company called Bored Panda, founded in 2009.

When McGonagle joined the team, it had "less than 1,000 subscribers and minimal views".

It now has 1.25m subscribers and was the seventh most-watched Netflix show globally in its first week.

"It's insane," she said.

News.title: North Korea fires suspected ballistic missile towards sea off east coast, says South Korea
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

North Korea fired a ⁠projectile toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's Joint ⁠Chiefs of ​Staff ⁠said.

Japan's Coast Guard said the launched projectile could be a ballistic missile and had already fallen into the sea.

Japan's Defence Ministry ‌also said it had ‌detected a North Korean launch of a possible ⁠ballistic weapon, according to Yonhap News Agency.

North Korea last fired ballistic missiles on 12 October, amid heightened tension on the inter-Korean border over a mine blast that wounded South Korean soldiers last month.

Pyongyang ⁠has conducted missile tests on ‌more ​than 10 occasions ‌this year.

open image in gallery Propaganda messages at a North Korean village are seen in this picture taken from an observation deck in Gimpo, South Korea, October 26, 2026. REUTERS/Kim Hong-Ji ( Reuters )

North Korea has been under UN sanctions since 2006, aimed at halting Pyongyang's development of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles.

Earlier this month, South Korean president Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country's first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.

The 12 October missile ⁠launches appeared to be "a show of force in response to the successful test launch of our hypersonic missile, as well as an intentional demonstration of missile capabilities," a spokesperson for South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

North Korea also fired a ballistic missile on 3 October, with state media KCNA saying it was a hypersonic missile tested under the supervision of leader Kim Jong Un.

News.title: A lasting impression: How I got a Rembrandt tattoo that will last a lifetime
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Three years ago, I covered a story on Rembrandt van Rijn that left a lasting impression on me.

“The Poor Man's Rembrandt Project” brought together a group of tattoo artists who inked designs by the Dutch Golden Age master on visitors to his former home in Amsterdam, now a museum. I'd never even thought about getting a tattoo, but suddenly the idea appealed to me.

The 2023 pop-up at the Rembrandt House Museum was such a success that it is back for a second run this fall, and this week I went back to get another lasting impression. This time in ink.

It combines Rembrandt with another celebrated Dutch artist — tattooer Henk Schiffmacher, also known around the tattoo world as Hanky Panky.

“The poor man’s Rembrandt, I always liked that," Schiffmacher said. "Because that’s what we are. We supply something which lasts the rest of your days and goes with you into the grave.”

Schiffmacher has tattooed celebrities including the members of the Red Hot Chili Peppers and Lady Gaga. An internet search suggests he also inked Nirvana front man Kurt Cobain, but Schiffmacher says he can’t confirm that. A lot of rock stars passed through Amsterdam in the 1980s and ’90s and many of them stopped by.

I'm no rock star, but add my name to the list of happy Hanky Panky clients.

I'm sitting in a room of the museum, located inside the stately building where Rembrandt lived and worked on many of his greatest paintings. My left hand is resting on Schiffmacher's leg to keep my arm steady as his needle whirrs. After about a half hour and much less pain than I feared, it's done.

A surprised looking Rembrandt, his lips slightly pursed under his youthful mane of curly hair stares out of my arm. The design is based on an etching called “Self-Portrait with Beret, Wide-Eyed” and is dated 1630, when Rembrandt was still in his early 20s and lived in the university city of Leiden.

Painters like Rembrandt, “they’ve made beautiful and simple drawings — studies for their bigger work, and so it’s very tattooable,” Schiffmacher said.

That means that a Rembrandt-inspired artwork is now available for a tiny fraction of the eye-watering prices shelled out for a real painting by the man himself. Mine cost me 200 euros ($222).

I knew my arm was in good hands. Over a career spanning decades, Schiffmacher has inked countless biceps, triceps, legs, backs and other body parts. His designs have appeared on everything from the cover of Red Hot Chili Peppers album “Blood Sugar Sex Magik” to traditional blue-decorated Dutch Delft pottery and even a passenger jet operated by an international airline company.

Matt Lodder, a senior lecturer in art history at the University of Essex, said Schiffmacher is a highly respected member of the tattoo community not just for his ink work, but also his dedication to collecting historic artifacts and organizing early conventions that brought together like-minded artists long before tattooing went mainstream.

Back then, Schiffmacher was one of the few people “who cared about tattooing enough to make sure its visual, cultural heritage was kept and looked after and not chucked in the bin,” Lodder said.

Rembrandt House Museum director Milou Halbesma compares Schiffmacher to Rembrandt.

“I think they’re both very iconic people and they’re very iconic in their trade as well," she said. "And what I like so much about Henk Schiffmacher is that in Amsterdam he’s a total hero, everybody knows him, but he’s also world famous. And in a way Rembrandt is a real Amsterdam hero, but also world famous, actually larger than life.”

It's that combination that had me cycling across Amsterdam to get my first tattoo.

“Welcome to the world of the freaks,” Schiffmacher said as he put the finishing touches to the work and flashed me a broad smile dominated by his golden front teeth.

___

“The Poor Man's Rembrandt Project” runs through Nov. 7 at the Rembrandt House Museum. Tattoos range in price from 100-350 euros ($111-389).

News.title: Carney hosts EU leaders as Trump pushes Canada toward Europe, but membership label faces resistance
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prime Minister Mark Carney called Canada “the most European of non-European countries” early in U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war. Now, he’s hosting European leaders to pursue an unprecedented alliance, but the proposed EU “associate member” designation faces resistance even as the EU’s top official champions it.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will join Carney in Montreal on Thursday for a two-day summit aimed at deepening trade, defense and economic ties as Canada and Europe seek to reduce their dependence on Washington in a changing world order.

European Union officials who briefed reporters ahead of the summit said the proposed partnership could bring Canada closer to the bloc than any previous arrangement with a non-European country. But its structure and even its name remain unsettled, with some member states questioning the “associate member” designation proposed last month by von der Leyen.

Arriving in Montreal, von der Leyen showed no sign of abandoning the proposal, posting on social media that Europe wanted to bring Canada closer than ever before “as Associate Member of the EU.”

Anand Sundar, a special adviser at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France and Germany are among the countries unhappy with the designation and that it may not survive the summit.

Carney said Tuesday the summit would launch further negotiations over the next year.

“It doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians, young Canadians in terms of opportunities to study, work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities, Canadian researchers in terms of depths of opportunity, and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose.”

Carney has ruled out formally joining the EU, which would require Canada to align its laws and regulations with the bloc’s. Canadian officials said Canada would not assume the EU’s membership-related budget obligations, although it could contribute to specific programs. Carney has said any enhanced partnership would face a vote in Canada’s Parliament.

The summit puts Carney’s vision for a new global order to the test. At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January, he warned that the U.S.-led international order was breaking down and urged middle powers to unite against economic coercion.

Trump has suggested Canada’s proposed EU arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered it unfriendly. Asked Wednesday about possible retaliation, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the closer relationship was not directed against the United States but reflected longstanding shared interests.

An alliance without membership

The summit is expected to launch an “Alliance for the Future,” a framework for closer cooperation on trade, defense, critical minerals, technology and research. Von der Leyen said the alliance would help Canada and Europe respond together to a world of growing rivalries.

The proposed relationship could include regular meetings between Canadian ministers and European commissioners and expanded opportunities for students through the EU’s Erasmus+ program, which supports international study and educational exchanges.

European commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers will hold sector-specific meetings, beginning with a business forum Thursday before formal leaders’ talks Friday. Officials hope to develop the broader partnership for possible endorsement in 2027.

Tobias Gehrke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said the disagreement over terminology was unlikely to derail closer cooperation.

“There is no magic shortcut to rapidly reducing Europe’s and Canada’s reliance on the U.S. economy and military — not least since Washington might retaliate,” Gehrke said. “But the political window is now wide open to take a much bigger step than was previously conceivable.”

Canada’s longstanding European ties

Canada has long looked to Europe to reduce its dependence on its much larger southern neighbor.

“It was the idea of not being alone with the Americans that drove it,” said Robert Bothwell, a University of Toronto historian.

Carney has deep personal ties to Europe. The former Bank of Canada governor led the Bank of England from 2013 to 2020. He chose Paris and London for his first foreign trip as prime minister rather than Washington, a break with tradition. He said the countries reflected Canada’s founding Indigenous, French and British peoples.

Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, said Trump’s policies are accelerating Canada’s efforts to strengthen ties beyond the United States.

“The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong U.S. leadership and to act accordingly,” Béland said.

A changing world order reshapes economic and defense ties

Ottawa is reviewing plans to buy 72 additional American-made F-35 fighter jets and considering Sweden’s Saab Gripen as an alternative. Canada has committed to an initial 16 F-35s.

Canada is the only non-European country participating in the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($167-billion) SAFE defense procurement program, allowing Canadian companies to take part in joint European military purchases.

But deeper defense cooperation faces obstacles. Sundar said France is pushing for strict “Made in Europe” rules that could limit Canadian companies’ access to future EU defense spending, while Germany favors broader participation by countries outside the bloc. He said negotiations over the EU’s next seven-year budget could matter more to Canada than anything announced in Montreal.

The two sides already have a sweeping free trade agreement, known as CETA, that eliminated most tariffs. Most provisions have been in force since 2017, although some EU member states have yet to ratify it.

The United States accounted for 71.7% of Canada’s merchandise exports in 2025. Carney wants to double exports to other countries over the next decade.

Canada and the EU are pursuing closer cooperation on digital trade and critical minerals, including possible European Investment Bank financing. Canadian officials said Wednesday they were exploring ways to stabilize mineral prices and encourage investment.

Gehrke said Europe’s growing trade confrontation with China is driving demand for Canadian critical minerals. Canada has the resources and mining expertise Europe needs, while Europe offers industrial demand, technology and capital.

Sundar said the shifting international order presents Europe with an opportunity to become a more influential global power.

“Trump’s predatory behavior is allowing the EU to position itself as an alternative geopolitical anchor,” he said.

News.title: Four scenarios that could play out after Israel’s election as Netanyahu tries to cling onto power
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Israel appears headed for another impasse following Tuesday’s general election, with early counts leaving both prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a governing majority.

With roughly 85 per cent of votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, neither the incumbent’s right-wing religious bloc nor the broad coalition aligned behind Mr Eisenkot commanded the 61 seats required to form an administration in the 120-seat Knesset.

Because key parties have ruled out working with one another on ideological or personal grounds, political analysts note that forming an administration will require at least one faction to reverse its campaign commitments. In the absence of an agreement, Israeli law mandates a return to the ballot box.

Here are the four scenarios that could play out.

open image in gallery Netanyahu has fallen short of a majority ( Getty )

The prospect of a national unity government

In theory, one route out of the stalemate could be a grand coalition between Netanyahu’s Likud and Mr Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party.

However, Mr Eisenkot campaigned explicitly on unseating the long-serving prime minister. Addressing supporters in Tel Aviv early on Wednesday, the former military chief of staff reiterated his demand for Mr Netanyahu to retire from public life, citing a breakdown of public trust.

For Mr Netanyahu to attract centrist partners, he would likely need to cut ties with his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies. Yet in his own post-election address at Likud headquarters, Mr Netanyahu praised his traditional coalition partners and called for the swift establishment of a “strong right-wing government”.

Foreign policy developments could also alter domestic calculations. Prior to the vote, Israeli and US media outlets reported that Mr Netanyahu had discussed potential strikes on Iranian targets with the United States.

Observers note that a wider regional military conflict could generate domestic pressure on both leaders to form an emergency administration.

open image in gallery Gadi Eisenkot gestures as he addresses supporters at an election-night rally ( AFP/Getty )

An opposition alliance involving Arab parties

On the current numbers, the opposition bloc’s sole numerical path to 61 seats would require the backing of Arab-majority factions.

Arab parties emerged as one of the night’s most significant stories, buoyed by high voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel. Preliminary projections indicate the parties could secure a combined 19 seats.

The United Arab List (Ra’am) is on track for roughly seven seats, while the Joint List alliance is projected to win 12.

Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas has expressed an openness to join an opposition-led coalition, while Joint List representatives have suggested offering outside legislative support to block a right-wing government.

However, Mr Eisenkot and most Jewish opposition figures have repeatedly ruled out forming a cabinet dependent on Arab parties.

The Democrats leader Yair Golan remains the only prominent Jewish faction head publicly advocating cooperation with Arab parliamentarians, though policy differences over Gaza and West Bank administration would pose severe challenges to such an arrangement.

open image in gallery Mansour Abbas’s party Ra’am was buoyed by high turnout ( AFP/Getty )

Right-wing defections to Netanyahu

A third scenario involves Mr Netanyahu convincing hawkish opposition figures to cross the floor and join his coalition.

Attention has focused on former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who co-leads the Beyachad alliance, and Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman. Both share conservative views with Likud on national defence and regional policy.

However, both politicians campaigned directly on removing Mr Netanyahu from office. Furthermore, each has made the mandatory military conscription of ultra-Orthodox seminary students a core demand – a policy fiercely opposed by Mr Netanyahu’s long-standing ultra-Orthodox partners, Shas and United Torah Judaism.

While analysts have raised the theoretical possibility of Mr Bennett and Mr Lieberman replacing the ultra-Orthodox parties inside a restructured right-wing government, early seat totals suggest that configuration would still fall short of 61 seats.

The default path to a snap election

If coalition negotiations fail to produce a viable government within statutory deadlines, the default legal procedure is the dissolution of parliament and the scheduling of fresh elections.

Under Israeli basic law, an incumbent prime minister remains in office as head of an interim caretaker cabinet until a new government takes its oath.

Electoral analysts suggest that Likud strategists may see tactical advantages in a rerun. They argue that record Arab voter turnout might prove difficult to sustain if high participation yields no influence, while smaller right-wing factions that missed the 3.25 per cent electoral threshold could face pressure to consolidate behind larger parties.

Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five consecutive national elections due to identical parliamentary arithmetic, a pattern observers warn could easily repeat itself if party leaders maintain their current red lines.

News.title: Carabao Cup quarter-final draw LIVE: Fleetwood earn another home tie, Bradford to travel to Manchester City
News.content:
