World.title: Kalshi, cofounders hit with criminal charges in US state of Utah
World.content:
The charges come after a federal judge ruled that Utah could enforce its anti-gambling laws against prediction markets.

Share Kalshi, cofounders hit with criminal charges in US state of Utah on social media

The US state of Utah has announced criminal charges against popular prediction market Kalshi and its two cofounders, accusing the platform and its executives of illegally promoting online gambling.

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed the charges against Kalshi, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara on Wednesday, a day after US President Donald Trump’s administration sued the state to block its civil enforcement actions against the platform.

According to the criminal complaint filed in a Salt Lake City court, Kalshi facilitated an undercover law enforcement officer’s wagers on sports events, including games in the NFL.

The charges come after a federal judge in August ruled that Utah was entitled to enforce its stringent anti-gambling laws against online prediction markets, following a legal bid by Kalshi to block enforcement of the law.

The criminal complaint accuses the defendants of 12 counts of online gambling promotion, one count of general gambling promotion and one count of pattern of unlawful activity.

Kalshi and Brown’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Utah has some of the strictest prohibitions against gambling in the US, with its state constitution explicitly barring lawmakers from legalising the activity.

The charges mark an escalation in a showdown between US states and the Trump administration over the regulation of prediction markets.

On Tuesday, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a lawsuit seeking to block Utah’s enforcement actions against prediction markets, arguing that the platforms fall under federal jurisdiction.



The regulator announced the move after Utah last week filed a civil lawsuit accusing Kalshi of facilitating betting on sports, elections, politics and other outcomes in violation of anti-gambling laws.

Dozens of US states, led by both Republican and Democratic administrations, have argued that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission does not have the authority to regulate prediction markets.

Last month, the state of New Jersey asked the US Supreme Court to rule on whether state or federal authorities have jurisdiction over sports betting on prediction market platforms.

World.title: Rivals in Israel Election Strike Tone of Triumph, but Outcome Is Far From Clear
World.content:
Shira Shapiro, right, a candidate for the Yashar party, meeting with Gadi Eisenkot at a roadside bomb shelter where her son died during the Oct. 7 2023, attack, near Reim, Israel, earlier this month.

Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war.

The October 2023 assault looms large over this week’s vote. There are sharp divisions over who was to blame for failing to prevent the worst military, intelligence and policy disaster in Israel’s history.

About 1,200 civilians and soldiers were killed that day, according to the Israeli authorities, and roughly 250 were taken hostage to Gaza. Many of the family members of hostages held by Hamas rose to prominence as they campaigned for their loved ones in television interviews and at nationwide protests.

Most of them called for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take responsibility for the government’s failures of Oct. 7 and to prioritize negotiating the release of the hostages over continued fighting. Others supported Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government and urged it to keep up the military pressure on Hamas and Israel’s other enemies.

Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates with a chance to win a seat in Parliament:

Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it. As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.

Zvi Mor, the father of a released hostage, Eitan Mor, is running as a candidate for the far-right party Religious Zionism, headed by Bezalel Smotrich. While Eitan was in captivity, Mr. Mor, an educator, founded a forum of right-wing parents of hostages and soldiers who opposed making deals with Hamas and pushed for Israel to defeat the group militarily.

Omri Ronen, a reserve soldier, is running with the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. His grandmother, Nira Ronen, was killed in her home in Kfar Aza, one of the border communities worst hit in the October 2023 attack, along with her Filipina caregiver, Angelyn Aguirre. Before Oct. 7, Mr. Ronen had been one of the leaders of a grass-roots group of reservists protesting the government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary. He said in a recent television interview that Mr. Netanyahu, whom he called “Mr. Oct. 7,” must go. “The word responsibility has meaning,” he said.

Rafael Ben Shitrit, a former mayor of Beit Shean in northern Israel, is in Yisrael Beitenu, a right-wing opposition party led by Avigdor Liberman. Mr. Ben Shitrit used to belong to Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party, but abandoned it after his son, Staff Sgt. Elroy Ben Shitrit, was killed in battle on Oct. 7 near the Gaza border. He has been an advocate for an independent state inquiry into what went wrong that day. Mr. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry, and the opposition parties have pledged to establish one if they are elected.

Sharon Sharabi, also on Yisrael Beitenu’s list of candidates, is the brother of Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who was released from Gaza only to learn that his wife and two teenage daughters had been killed during the Oct. 7 attack. Another brother, Yossi Sharabi, was also taken hostage and killed after 100 days in captivity. Sharon Sharabi campaigned tirelessly for his brothers’ return. When Eli Sharabi was finally released, many Israelis were outraged over how emaciated he looked. “I was shocked,” Sharon said at the time. “I’d been told he would be thin, but I didn’t imagine how thin. It was extreme.”

Tali Gvili, running with Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, is the mother of Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, a member of a police counterterrorism unit who was shot and severely wounded in combat on Oct. 7 and then dragged into Gaza. His remains were recovered and returned to Israel in January 2026. The Gvili and Netanyahu families have become close, and the prime minister attended Sergeant Gvili’s state funeral, saying, “Our souls are bound with yours.”

Michal Hirsch Negri is running with Together, a joint slate led by right-wing politician Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid. Ms. Hirsch Negri’s son Maj. Roee Negri was killed fighting in Kibbutz Be’eri near the Gaza border on Oct. 7.

Maj. Shahar Varon, a commander in the reserves, is another Together candidate. He fought that day in Kfar Aza, another border community, and later went to fight in Gaza. He was wounded in battle, then went back into Gaza to fight again. “There is life before October 7th, and there is life after,” he wrote recently, adding, “Our government disappeared that morning — but our people showed up instead.”

World.title: Israel’s opposition may not be able to form a government, but it still could control Parliament.
World.content:
For decades, Israel’s Arab parties have been relegated to the margins of Israeli political life, often sitting on the sidelines while Jewish parties assembled a governing coalition in Parliament and picked a prime minister.

Heading into Israel’s pivotal election on Tuesday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned his supporters that the Arabs were “trying to steal the election,” though electoral officials said there were no reports of widespread irregularities. He repeatedly invoked the specter of Arab voters to galvanize his right-wing base, vowing to keep them out of power.

Mr. Netanyahu’s leading rival, Gadi Eisenkot, largely declined to answer whether he would partner with Arab parties if necessary to topple the Netanyahu government, though he said none met his conditions as potential allies.

But record turnout on Tuesday by supporters of the Arab parties looks to deliver them their largest vote totals in generations, possibly since Israel’s establishment 78 years ago.

Now, the Arab minority represents a political reality that cannot be ignored.

Turnout in the Arab community, which represents about 20 percent of Israeli citizens, appears to have translated into a stunning windfall of parliamentary seats — potentially as many as 19 combined between the two leading parties, Raam and the Joint List alliance. The Arab parties have 10 seats in the outgoing Parliament.

Israel’s future could turn in part on whether Mr. Eisenkot decides to take the political risks of partnering with them. Without their support, Mr. Eisenkot and his alliance will almost certainly fall short of the 61-seat majority required in the 120-seat Parliament to form a new government and end Mr. Netanyahu’s hold on power. Mr. Netanyahu’s alliance also looks to fall short of 61 seats.

Many Israeli Jews have long objected to building a governing coalition that relies on Arab party backing for a majority. Some say a Jewish state should be ruled exclusively by Jews. Some cite national security reasons, questioning whether Arab leaders who see themselves as part of the wider Palestinian people can be entrusted with crucial matters of state.

Those objections became even more acute after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and the subsequent rightward shift in Israeli politics. Both Raam and some members of the Joint List condemned the assault, although they have also been highly critical of how Israel has conducted its war against Hamas in Gaza.

The Arab parties for many years were themselves reluctant to join governments that oversaw the Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza. And turnout among Arab Israelis has traditionally been lower than Jewish turnout, reflecting doubts about their ability to influence national decision-making.

Raam, a socially conservative party with roots in Islamist politics, has achieved some acceptance in Israel’s mainstream by putting less emphasis on the cause of Palestinian statehood. But the Joint List, an alliance of three smaller parties that includes a joint Jewish-Arab leftist faction and a Palestinian nationalist faction, is seen as more antagonistic toward Zionism.

Initial election results show that the Joint List will be the significantly larger of the two in Parliament.

“Netanyahu knows that without the Arab parties, there’s no majority to unseat him. That’s why he incites against us,” said Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Joint List alliance in an interview. “The opposition should reject that incitement.”

He added: “The ball is now in Eisenkot’s court. Whoever wants to remove Netanyahu and change his policies — we are ready to cooperate to topple his government.”

Political analysts say the Joint List would be more likely to support Eisenkot from outside the governing coalition, for instance by agreeing to block any no-confidence votes. There is some precedent for this: In the 1990s, then Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin relied on Arab lawmakers to prevent the collapse of his own minority government.

Arab citizens, some of whom view themselves as both Israeli and Palestinian, experience a tension that can cut to the heart of daily life. Unlike Palestinians in the West Bank — who live under Israeli military rule — Arab Israelis can vote, and some have held high office, including on the country’s Supreme Court.

But they largely live in separate cities and towns from Jewish Israelis and retain tight familial and historical bonds with Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Many view themselves as second-class citizens in the Jewish state, saying they face discrimination in housing as well as neglect in receiving public services.

Before this year, the largest electoral success recorded by Arab parties was in 2020, when they secured 15 seats. And the first — and so far, only — time an independent Arab party joined the Israeli governing coalition was in 2021, when Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, joined Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals to unseat him in favor of a short-lived government.

Mr. Abbas has since worked to make his party more acceptable to Israeli Jews. He has recognized Israel’s Jewish character as a fact of life and publicly considered integrating Arabs into the country’s mandatory national service, in particular community service.

In a bold move during the election campaign, he named Jewish lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz — a former senior police officer and centrist Zionist — as the number two on the Raam candidate list.

But if exit polls and initial results are correct, Raam’s support would not be enough to give Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc a parliamentary majority. He would also have to rely on the Joint List to topple Mr. Netanyahu. While political analysts say that Mr. Eisenkot might be willing to bring Raam onboard, he would struggle to keep his bloc with him if he made common cause with the Joint List, even if he wanted to, because this could provoke too much political blowback from many Jewish voters.

“There’s a shift in Arab politics, an attempt to get closer to the Jewish Zionist mainstream. It’s just that the other side is not willing to do so,” said Thair Abu Rass, an expert on Israel’s Arab politics. “There’s no partner on the Jewish side to create an alternative reality.”

Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates with a chance to win a seat in Parliament:

Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it. As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.

Zvi Mor, the father of a released hostage, Eitan Mor, is running as a candidate for the far-right party Religious Zionism, headed by Bezalel Smotrich. While Eitan was in captivity, Mr. Mor, an educator, founded a forum of right-wing parents of hostages and soldiers who opposed making deals with Hamas and pushed for Israel to defeat the group militarily.

Omri Ronen, a reserve soldier, is running with the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. His grandmother, Nira Ronen, was killed in her home in Kfar Aza, one of the border communities worst hit in the October 2023 attack, along with her Filipina caregiver, Angelyn Aguirre. Before Oct. 7, Mr. Ronen had been one of the leaders of a grass-roots group of reservists protesting the government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary. He said in a recent television interview that Mr. Netanyahu, whom he called “Mr. Oct. 7,” must go. “The word responsibility has meaning,” he said.

Rafael Ben Shitrit, a former mayor of Beit Shean in northern Israel, is in Yisrael Beitenu, a right-wing opposition party led by Avigdor Liberman. Mr. Ben Shitrit used to belong to Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party, but abandoned it after his son, Staff Sgt. Elroy Ben Shitrit, was killed in battle on Oct. 7 near the Gaza border. He has been an advocate for an independent state inquiry into what went wrong that day. Mr. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry, and the opposition parties have pledged to establish one if they are elected.

Sharon Sharabi, also on Yisrael Beitenu’s list of candidates, is the brother of Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who was released from Gaza only to learn that his wife and two teenage daughters had been killed during the Oct. 7 attack. Another brother, Yossi Sharabi, was also taken hostage and killed after 100 days in captivity. Sharon Sharabi campaigned tirelessly for his brothers’ return. When Eli Sharabi was finally released, many Israelis were outraged over how emaciated he looked. “I was shocked,” Sharon said at the time. “I’d been told he would be thin, but I didn’t imagine how thin. It was extreme.”

Tali Gvili, running with Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, is the mother of Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, a member of a police counterterrorism unit who was shot and severely wounded in combat on Oct. 7 and then dragged into Gaza. His remains were recovered and returned to Israel in January 2026. The Gvili and Netanyahu families have become close, and the prime minister attended Sergeant Gvili’s state funeral, saying, “Our souls are bound with yours.”

Michal Hirsch Negri is running with Together, a joint slate led by right-wing politician Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid. Ms. Hirsch Negri’s son Maj. Roee Negri was killed fighting in Kibbutz Be’eri near the Gaza border on Oct. 7.

Maj. Shahar Varon, a commander in the reserves, is another Together candidate. He fought that day in Kfar Aza, another border community, and later went to fight in Gaza. He was wounded in battle, then went back into Gaza to fight again. “There is life before October 7th, and there is life after,” he wrote recently, adding, “Our government disappeared that morning — but our people showed up instead.”

World.title: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
World.content:
A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.

It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.

The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.

Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.

The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid, between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz.

The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente said.

He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.

Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.

The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.

Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."

One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.

Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.

World.title: Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster in Spain
World.content:
Some of the passengers were asleep, some had already started their working day on laptops - and others scrolled through their apps on their phones.

The journey was interrupted with an announcement that there was congestion on the tracks. This lasted a few minutes - for some, a bit longer for others.

Tangui Binier, 22, was in the Iryo train, the front carriage, number eight. His father was in number seven.

Their train was one of six to have been ordered to stop at 08:30. A few minutes later, "the train started speeding", Binier told the BBC, "then it came to a sudden halt".

Baffled, he looked out of the window and saw "wires on the left side come down, and then there being just a lot of smoke behind us."

Spanish journalist Roberto GÃ³mez was dozing on the high-speed Renfe train which had stopped more than 25km (16 miles) away from Binier's.

It was a brief stop. A few minutes later, the train began to move again, he explained, and then the crash happened.

He did not know that at 08:36 his train had been ordered to proceed with the journey and some 17 minutes later the "truly unbelievable" happened, Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente said.

"The impact was terrible," GÃ³mez told Onda Cero radio. "You can imagine, the carriage is completely destroyed. All the suitcases are all over the wrecked carriage."

GÃ³mez suffered only minor injuries but described another passenger falling on top of him and sustaining a deep gash on his head.

"We were able to help people who had suffered severe blows to their chest and ribs," he said.

Rafael Barcelo was in one of the worst-affected carriages. A bruise on his forehead makes him one of the lucky survivors. He was having a coffee at the time of the crash and "felt a huge impact".

"We were all thrown into the air," he told Reuters news agency at the site of the crash.

"I am reasonably OK, my friend is quite worse."

"I was travelling in coach seven, which is the one with more victims and the one most destroyed. I at least counted eight victims in that coach," he said, visibly shocked.

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro denies fleeing Brazil after landing in Miami
World.content:
Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida ended days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.

In a statement, Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ââas the good people of my own country".

"It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said. "I departed from a regime of exception so that I could become the leader my people deserve."

He called himself a victim of a coup d'Ã©tat and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family.

In the lengthy letter, he also repeated unsubstantiated allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.

On Wednesday, Trump declined to discuss the allegations made in Bolsonaro's letter.

"I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure," Trump said. He went on to add that he thought Bolsonaro "and his family were treated very unfairly".

After Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil's election, Lula won the second round by more than four million votes, which was attributed to significantly higher turnout, and swaying more undecided voters.

The result was confirmed by the president of Brazil's top electoral court, who was appointed by Bolsonaro's father, former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.

Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.

For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low-profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday, in addition to a criminal investigation that led to orders that his passports be turned into authorities.

But when he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline on Tuesday, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.

Speculation quickly grew that he'd left the country and Bolsonaro's lawyers said they had no idea where he was.

World.title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
World.content:
Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.

With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.

Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.

Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.

With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from groups including soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.

Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.

If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

World.title: How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios
World.content:
Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?

Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.

Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".

But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.

Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government" - remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.

One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.

This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.

World.title: Girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German wildlife park
World.content:
An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park.

She was inside an enclosure at the JohannismÃ¼hle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said.

They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".

The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured.

The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details.

The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx.

The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild.

It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit.

JohannismÃ¼hle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama.

The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe.

A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.

World.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
World.content:
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.

The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".

It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (Â£6,000) from $1,800.

Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.

The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.

The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.

Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.

The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.

Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day.

The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out.

"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed."

"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened."

Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".

Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.

"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia.

"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."

Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport.

World.title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
World.content:
The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.

The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.

Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.

The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment.

"Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.

Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

World.title: FEC approves ₦631.3 billion for nine road projects nationwide
World.content:
The Federal Executive Council (FEC) has approved approximately ₦631.3 billion for nine road infrastructure projects across Nigeria.

The Minister of Works, David Umahi, disclosed this after Wednesday’s FEC meeting presided over by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu at the State House, Abuja.

Mr Umahi said the projects would strengthen transportation networks, improve connectivity, and facilitate economic activities by constructing, reconstructing, and rehabilitating critical road corridors.

He said the approvals included reconstructing the 95-kilometre Etuke–Okeni–Ankpa–Otopa Road in Kogi, with a contract sum of N167 billion.

The council also approved N209 billion for reconstructing the 81.1-kilometre Ado–Ilawe–Ilumaba–Ikole Road in Ekiti, including a bridge.

Another ₦62 billion was approved for the Tungo–Karamti Road linking Adamawa and Taraba, with five bridges incorporated into the project.

Mr Umahi said FEC also approved N20.257 billion for an 18-kilometre road connecting Asiago to the Port Harcourt–Enugu Expressway.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

An additional N30 billion was earmarked for remedial works on deteriorated sections of the East–West Road.

The council also approved N11.33 billion for a road project the Abia Government previously undertook.

Mr Umahi said the approval followed the discontinuation of its funding arrangement under the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Ltd. tax-credit scheme.

He added that N28.218 billion was approved to rehabilitate a 17-kilometre section of the Sokoto–Illela Road, Route A1.

The minister also commended Mronubu for completing the first 118-kilometre section of the Abuja–Kaduna–Zaria Road.

He said the section was completed in 30 months, with 81 kilometres constructed using reinforced concrete pavement.

He added that work on the second section, covering 164 kilometres, was nearing completion, with only 16 kilometres remaining.

Mr Umahi further disclosed that the entire 375-kilometre Abuja–Kaduna–Zaria–Kano corridor would be equipped with solar-powered streetlights.

On the Lagos–Abidjan coastal highway, the minister said ministers from countries along the corridor would meet on Friday to discuss funding arrangements.

He said the highway comprises 79 kilometres in Nigeria, 89 kilometres in Togo, 576 kilometres in Ghana, 155 kilometres in Côte d’Ivoire and 128 kilometres in Benin Republic.

According to Mr Umahi, the proposed arrangement will involve the African Development Bank providing loans to participating countries to finance their respective sections.

He said the regional highway was intended to strengthen connectivity and facilitate trade among participating West African countries.

World.title: CBD COP17: Why African countries struggle to mobilise biodiversity funding – AfDB official
World.content:
African governments must demonstrate stronger commitment to biodiversity conservation by integrating it into national investment priorities and allocating resources for implementation, an official of the African Development Bank (AfDB) has said.

Arona Soumare, the bank’s Chief Climate Change and Green Growth Officer, made the call during a panel discussion on the sidelines of the ongoing 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.

The discussion, organised by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), was themed “From Commitments to Action: What Africa’s Seventh National Reports Reveal About Progress, Gaps and Opportunities for Delivering the Global Biodiversity Framework”.

Speaking on why African countries struggle to mobilise sufficient funding for biodiversity projects, Mr Soumare said many governments approach development financiers for other priorities, often treating biodiversity as an additional consideration rather than a central investment objective.

He said African countries must move beyond commitments under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and demonstrate their resolve through concrete investment decisions.

“Most of the time, African countries are not pushing the bank. There’s a big pool of projects we have met so far coming from the outsiders. You barely see an African country coming to us with a good and sound proposal on biodiversity,” he said.

According to him, governments frequently approach the bank for other development priorities, with biodiversity incorporated as a secondary component.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“This is an issue we have to face. If you are not able to, at country level, I don’t see any point coming to the other one and asking for something which is a priority for us, if you’re not willing to put our money on it,” he said.

Breaking financing silos

Mr Soumare identified the fragmentation of funding across development sectors as one of the major obstacles to biodiversity financing in Africa.

He explained that the bank works with countries through Country Strategy Papers, which guide discussions on national development priorities and determine the investments included in its portfolios.

He said biodiversity conservation should be integrated into these priorities rather than treated separately from infrastructure development, food security, livelihoods and other national objectives.

Citing Madagascar as an example, Mr Soumare said country allocations could support private-sector initiatives for national parks and help attract additional financing.

He also called for more flexible financing mechanisms to support both large-scale conservation programmes and smaller, community-led projects.

Although the bank provides funding opportunities for grassroots organisations, he said available resources remain inadequate to meet demand.

“When I have a call for proposals, I’ll be able to fund maybe three out of 10 applications I’m getting,” he said.

Mr Soumare advocated blended finance, which combines domestic resources with international funding, alongside green banks, green lines of credit and other financial intermediaries to channel investments into biodiversity conservation.

He also highlighted the potential of nature-related bonds to mobilise capital from financial markets, stressing the need for governments and development partners to strengthen the economic case for investing in ecosystems.

Regional cooperation

Speaking during the same discussion, Daniel Mukubi of the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development said inadequate financing remained a major constraint to implementing biodiversity commitments.

He noted that conservation efforts often competed with urgent national priorities, including food security, energy, infrastructure development and poverty reduction.

Mr Mukubi said regional cooperation could help countries overcome some implementation challenges by pooling expertise and strengthening institutional capacity.

He cited training involving technical experts from across the region to improve geographic information system (GIS) and biodiversity mapping capacities. These skills, he said, could support regional planning towards the global 30-by-30 conservation target.

The target seeks to conserve at least 30 per cent of the world’s land, inland waters, and coastal and marine areas by 2030.

World.title: Tinubu mourns veteran journalist, Mobolade Omonijo
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has expressed sadness over the death of Mobolade Omonijo, a distinguished journalist, political analyst, editor, and a respected clergyman.

President Tinubu expressed condolences to the Omonijo family, the media community, especially The Nation newspaper, and the Church of God.

The president described the late Omonijo as “a journalist of immense value whose contributions to the profession and the nation would be remembered for years to come.

“He distinguished himself in the various assignments entrusted to him throughout nearly four decades of meritorious service in journalism, earning a reputation for incisive analysis, professional integrity and a deep understanding of Nigeria’s political landscape.”

Until his passing, Mr Omonijo, a reverend, served on The Nation’s Editorial Board, where he authored several seminal commentaries on national affairs.

He previously served as political editor of The Nation and The Vanguard newspapers and also worked with The Economist, reflecting his professional experience and deep engagement with political and public affairs.

Beyond journalism, Mr Omonijo devoted himself to Christian ministry, serving as the Vicar of the Church of Pentecost in Dopemu, within the Diocese of Lagos West.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The president prayed for the departed’s soul to rest in peace and for succour for his family.

Bayo Onanuga

Special Adviser to the President

October 28, 2026

World.title: NPFL clubs demand answers over N15m sponsorship payout
World.content:
Some club chairmen in the Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) are demanding clarification over the distribution of sponsorship proceeds after receiving N15 million each from the league’s commercial partnership, PREMIUM TIMES has learnt.

In an exclusive interview with PREMIUM TIMES, one of the chairmen, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the payment fell short of what the clubs expected under an arrangement in which 60 per cent of sponsorship proceeds would go to the clubs, while 40 per cent would cover logistics and other expenses.

He said each club should receive at least N150 million for the season, based on the sharing arrangement, and that the chairmen wanted the league management to explain how the payments were calculated.

The concerns are expected to feature at a consultative meeting scheduled for Wednesday evening in Abuja between the NPFL management and the NPFL Club Owners Forum.

In a letter dated 28 October and addressed to the chairman of the club owners’ forum, the NPFL management confirmed that the meeting would hold at 7p.m. at Top Rank Galaxy Hotel, Jabi Utako, in Abuja.

The letter followed correspondence indicating that members of the club owners’ association intended to attend the engagement. It added that, as the league was not prepared to host an emergency congress, the club owners would bear their individual logistics costs.

The meeting comes after club representatives raised concerns about sponsorship receipts and payments at an earlier consultative meeting involving the NPFL management, GTI Asset Management and Trust Limited, the league’s strategic partner.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

‘We expected at least N150m per club’

The chairman told PREMIUM TIMES that the sponsorship agreement provided for 60 per cent of the proceeds to be shared among the clubs, with the remaining 40 per cent reserved for logistics and other expenses.

He questioned why the clubs had received only N15 million each despite the sponsorship deal announced by the league.

“From the partnership of $2.5 million, the agreement was 60 per cent would go to the clubs, while 40 per cent would go for logistics and everything,” he said.

He argued that the amount received so far did not reflect what the clubs expected under the arrangement.

The chairman said the clubs had previously received about N50 million per season under earlier arrangements, making the latest payment particularly disappointing to him.

He maintained that, based on the 60 per cent allocation to the clubs, each team should receive at least N150 million for the season. However, that figure represents his assessment of what the clubs should receive, rather than an independently verified amount stipulated in the sponsorship contract.

He also questioned how club owners had been represented in previous discussions, saying all chairmen should be involved in decisions affecting their financial interests.

Rather than relying on a few representatives, he said, the chairmen wanted to meet with the league management to seek clarification on the money received, the basis for the N15 million payment and the timing of subsequent disbursements.

The chairman said the clubs were expecting another tranche in November but wanted clearer information about the payment schedule and the amounts due to them.

Transparency concerns

The dispute follows a sponsorship consultative meeting held on 19 September involving representatives of the NPFL management, GTI and the club owners’ forum.

According to the report of that meeting circulated to club owners, GTI representative Nelson Ineh told participants that the company had received about $1 million from EuroMatch in connection with the league’s sponsorship.

The meeting resolved that each of the 20 participating clubs would receive N15 million from the sponsorship proceeds available at the time. It also called for greater transparency and communication about sponsorship receipts, payments to clubs and subsequent disbursements.

The report said the participants agreed that the NPFL management, GTI and club owners should continue working towards a sustainable financial framework for the league and its clubs.

The N15 million payment was therefore part of an earlier resolution on the distribution of available proceeds. However, the chairman who spoke to PREMIUM TIMES said some owners remained dissatisfied and wanted the league management to explain how the amount related to the broader revenue-sharing arrangement.

The NPFL announced a three-year title sponsorship agreement with EuroMatch in August, valued at $7.5 million, equivalent to $2.5 million per season.

At the unveiling on 26 August, the league’s chairman, Gbenga Elegbeleye, said 60 per cent of the sponsorship proceeds would go directly to the 20 participating clubs.

The agreement was presented as a means of improving the clubs’ finances and players’ welfare, including their ability to pay wages.

However, the total value of a multi-year sponsorship agreement is not necessarily the amount immediately available for distribution. The amount received by the league or its partners at a given time, and the schedule for subsequent payments, are relevant to how much can be disbursed.

The precise amount received under the deal to date, the detailed calculation of the clubs’ 60 per cent share and the schedule for further payments were not established in the information available to PREMIUM TIMES before publication.

More Questions

Beyond the sponsorship dispute, the chairman criticised the league’s handling of fixtures, saying the scheduling of matches did not always take account of the logistical challenges faced by clubs.

He said teams were expected to comply with dates fixed by the league even when travelling conditions or other circumstances made it difficult to arrive on time.

He cited an occasion when his team travelled for two days from Niger State to Katsina State but was still expected to play upon arrival.

The chairman argued that the league should consider clubs’ circumstances when deciding whether matches need to be rescheduled.

“If they can schedule our matches, so we feel if we have a reason for delaying a match, they should also consider us,” he said.

He called for better organisation and greater consideration of the challenges faced by clubs participating in the competition.

The meeting is expected to provide an opportunity for club owners to seek clarification on sponsorship receipts, the N15 million allocation and the timing and basis of subsequent payments.

World.title: Governor Lawal: The banker who won’t borrow, By Karen Ibrahim
World.content:
It is one of life’s ironies that Governor Dauda Lawal of Zamfara State, who spent many years in banking chasing deposits from federal and state governments and structuring credit facilities for their mega projects, would become a governor and choose to pursue his state’s development without taking commercial bank loans to finance his administration’s projects. How do his former colleagues in the banking industry view this remarkable change? Has Governor Lawal, like Saul on the road to Damascus, experienced a conversion that has made him deny the banks the very lucrative business he once helped facilitate? This is the fiscal paradox surrounding the former banker who now governs Zamfara State.

As Executive Director, Public Sector North, at First Bank of Nigeria, Lawal understood the business of chasing government deposits and packaging credit facilities from the other side of the table. That was his job. He dealt with state governments and public institutions, many of which depended on bank financing to meet their obligations and to execute major projects.Where would a bank be without mobilising deposits and extending credit? Yet, since assuming office in May 2023, Lawal has bluntly refused to finance projects with loans preferring to mobilize revenue, and expenditure discipline without compromising on quality.

Consider Gusau International Airport, a major infrastructure project built at a cost of about ₦75 billion, alongside the construction of roads, schools and hospitals. How has Lawal financed projects of such magnitude without resorting to bank borrowing? More importantly, what has his experience in banking taught him about the risks of public debt, the burden of debt servicing and the importance of fiscal discipline? While borrowing is not inherently wrong, its sustainability depends on the cost of credit, the government’s capacity to repay and the economic returns on the investments financed. Has Lawal’s banking experience shaped his approach to these considerations?

The question becomes even more compelling when his administration’s responsibilities are considered in their entirety. Since assuming office in May 2023, Governor Lawal has had to confront a huge infrastructure deficit, address insecurity, revitalize the public service which had been neglected and settled inherited financial obligations, including outstanding pension liabilities and salary arrears. These are competing demands on public resources, with each requiring sustained financial commitment and careful prioritisation.

In the security sector, Governor Lawal’s administration has invested heavily in strengthening the capacity of the security forces response to confront the terrorists, including the establishment of Community Protection Guards. In infrastructure, it has aggressively pursued road construction, urban renewal and the development of markets, including 70 kilometres of feeder roads and 40 new markets comprising approximately 4,000 shops. In education, the administration has worked to restore functionality to a system burdened by inherited obligations, including ₦1.4 billion in WAEC debts accumulated between 2018 and 2022, alongside other liabilities.

Under healthcare, the administration has moved beyond increased budgetary allocations to tangible projects and interventions, including the upgrading of Yariman Bakura Specialist Hospital, rehabilitation and equipping of primary healthcare centres across the state’s 147 wards, installation of solar power systems in health facilities, and recruitment of healthcare personnel. These interventions are backed by an increase in budgetary commitments, from ₦31.92 billion in 2024 to ₦64.12 billion in 2025 and ₦87.46 billion in 2026. Beyond healthcare, the Rescue Mission has also prioritised agricultural development, economic expansion and women’s empowerment through practical interventions designed to improve livelihoods, strengthen local enterprise and expand economic opportunities.

Beyond these sectoral investments, the administration has also addressed accumulated liabilities, including inherited pension and salary arrears. Settling these obligations while simultaneously financing new infrastructure and essential public services inevitably placed considerable pressure on the state’s finances. Without prudent management of its finances, the government would have resorted borrowing to meet its recurrent expenditure obligations, clear inherited liabilities and sustain new capital investments without compromising its capacity to deliver on other commitments.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

What, then, did Governor Lawal learn from decades in high-stakes banking about the dangers of borrowing? As the former Executive Director of Public Sector North at First Bank of Nigeria, he had had to deal with state financial distress from the lender’s vantage point—witnessing firsthand how aggressive borrowing leads to grueling loan reschedulings, squeezed cash flows, and suffocating servicing burdens. Today, that insider perspective has directly shaped his fiscal strategy: a strict commitment to living within the state’s actual means.

Zamfara State has clearly benefited from that professional experience. This underscores an important lesson about leadership: elections should not be determined solely by political affiliation, but by the competence, and the capacity of candidates to manage public resources responsibly. Governing a state requires more than political ambition; it demands the financial literacy to make difficult choices, the discipline to live within available means and the foresight to avoid decisions that will mortgage the future of the state.

Borrowing is not inherently flawed; when properly structured, loans serves as a catalyst for high-yield economic and social investments. The true test of fiscal leadership lies in debt affordability, long-term repayment sustainability, and whether the funded initiatives yielded results. For a state like Zamfara—confronting severe insecurity, infrastructure deficits, and massive inherited liabilities—the imperative is to meet urgent needs without triggering financial distress. Rather than relying on costly commercial banks loans, Governor Lawal’s administration has prioritized strategic partnerships with multilateral institutions. By leveraging concessionary, low-interest funding from bodies like the World Bank—such as the AGILE project to rehabilitate educational infrastructure, ACReSAL for agricultural and climate resilience, and RAAMP for rural road connectivity—the state secures capital tied directly to high-impact projects while preserving fiscal stability.

Fiscal discipline should not be measured solely by a government’s complete avoidance of debt, but by how prudently it manages its liabilities. Data from BudgIT’s State of States report provides compelling evidence of Zamfara’s debt reduction trajectory: total public debt dropped from ₦136.70 billion at the end of 2023 to ₦104.42 billion by December 2024—a significant 23.6% reduction, driven largely by a sharp decline in domestic obligations.

Furthermore, the administration clarified that the recorded ₦14.26 billion in borrowing does not represent new debt, but rather the outstanding from the

N20 billion bond issued by the previous administration specifically for the cargo airport project.

The funding behind Governor Lawal’s ambitious project portfolio reflects a fundamental shift in fiscal strategy, anchored by a dramatic expansion in Zamfara State’s Internally Generated Revenue (IGR). According to BudgIT data, IGR surged by approximately 240 percent—rising from ₦6.51 billion in 2022 to ₦22.16 billion in 2023—driven largely by personal income tax collections doubling to ₦12.18 billion. This upward trajectory propelled the state’s national IGR ranking from 36th to 26th while expanding total revenue from ₦87.68 billion to ₦144.95 billion over the same period. The IGR sustained further growth to approximately ₦25.46 billion in 2024.

Although Zamfara State’s revenue trajectory is improving, Governor Lawal’s determination is to break the state’s deep dependence on the Federation Account. His playbook extends beyond belt-tightening: it relies on attracting private capital into agriculture, manufacturing, and solid minerals, leveraged by strategic risk-sharing instruments from development institutions. The cornerstone of this strategy was signaled in July 2026 with the announcement of a $200 million private-sector lithium mining and processing project in Zurmi—an initiative designed to capture in-state value addition and create local employment rather than exporting raw ores. The investment holds genuine potential to diversify the economy and expand the tax base.

Governor Dauda Lawal’s fiscal approach offers a compelling blueprint for sub-national governance across Nigeria. The most credible assessment of his tenure thus far is that Zamfara State has achieved measurable progress in both revenue mobilization, debt reduction and project execution. Crucially, his strategy is not defined by a rigid refusal to borrow, but by a commitment to progressive self-reliance through disciplined spending, strategic concessionary financing, and high-return investments.

The seasoned banker has successfully bridged financial discipline and executive leadership. While he understands that money carries a cost, as a visionary governor he demonstrates something more: that public expenditure can yield tangible results, infrastructure can stimulate real economic activity, and essential state services can expand without burdening future generations with unsustainable debt.

World.title: Court to rule on Electoral Act provision on INEC’s power to review election results
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Abuja has fixed 8 December to deliver judgement in a suit challenging the power of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to review election results under the Electoral Act 2026.

Judge Muhammad Umar, on Tuesday, fixed the date after the parties adopted their respective filings and presented their final arguments.

The suit was filed on 24 August by Abuja School of Social and Political Thoughts, a Nigerian not-for-profit and intellectual forum advancing independent thinking on politics, law, economic policy, and media and culture and its director, Sam Amadi.

The plaintiffs sued the Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF), the National Assembly, the Senate, the House of Representatives, INEC and Nigeria’s 22 registered political parties, including the All Progressives Congress (APC), the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC).

They urged the court to strike down section 65(b) of the Electoral Act 2026, which empowers INEC to review, within seven days, the results declared by returning officers in violation of prescribed procedures.

Section 65 of the Act provides INEC “shall have the power, to within seven days, review the declaration and return where it receives report from its officials, and it is satisfied that a declaration or return may have been made —

“(a) under duress; or

“(b) knowingly and willfully contrary to the procedures prescribed under section 62 (4) – (8) of this Act.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Subsection (b), which centres on a return or declaration that intentionally violates prescribed procedures, is the part the plaintiffs’ suit contested.

The plaintiffs urged the court to hold that the said Section 65(b) of the Electoral Act interferes with, alters, or sets aside the declaration or result of an election made by the returning officer.

Disagreement over section 65(b)

At Tuesday’s hearing, the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Kemasuo­de Wodu, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), argued that section 65(b) of the Electoral Act constituted a threat to democracy and asked the court to declare the provision unconstitutional.

Responding, the lawyer for the National Assembly, the Senate and the House of Representatives, Williams Pius, urged the court to dismiss the suit, describing it as “incompetent and academic”.

Mr Pius maintained that the provision did not prevent aggrieved parties from approaching the courts “after INEC declared an election result”.

Similarly, INEC’s lawyer, Afam Osigwe, a SAN, who is the immediate past president of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), urged the court to dismiss the suit, as he maintained that setting aside the provision could allow a person who “obtained a position through fraud to benefit from that fraud”.

Also the lawyers representing APC, PDP, NDC, Action Democratic Party, Action People’s Party, African Action Congress, All Progressives Grand Alliance, Boot Party, National Rescue Movement, Youth Party and Social Democratic Party took their turns to oppose the suit and called on the court to dismiss it.

However, a handful of political parties comprising the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Action Alliance and National Democratic Party aligned with the plaintiffs’ position and asked the court to grant their prayers.

The AGF and about five of the 22 parties, including the New Nigeria People’s Party and Democratic Leadership Alliance, were not present at Tuesday’s hearing.

After hearing the submissions of those present, the court fixed 8 December for judgment.

Plaintiffs’ case

Mr Amadi and the Abuja School of Social and Political Thoughts asked the court to determine whether Section 65(b) of the Electoral Act 2026 is unconstitutional insofar as it empowers INEC to review results declared by returning officers for alleged non-compliance with Section 62(4)–(8).

They also questioned whether the provision conflicts with Sections 79, 119, 139, 184 and 285(1)–(5) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, and Section 134(1) of the Electoral Act 2026.

Section 134(1) provides that an election and its return “shall not be questioned in any manner other than by a Petition” before a competent tribunal or court. The plaintiffs argued that this provision should prevail because it directs challenges to election results through petitions.

Mr Amadi, who swore the supporting affidavit, maintained that INEC cannot alter or set aside a result once declared by a returning officer. He argued that only the appropriate election tribunal can challenge the declaration and cited Section 285(5) of the Constitution, which gives petitioners 21 days to file an election petition.

The plaintiffs further argued that neither the National Assembly nor the President can constitutionally empower INEC to interfere with such declarations. Citing Section 1(3) of the Constitution, they contended that section 65(b) is null and void to the extent of its inconsistency with the Constitution.

They warned that the power could cause “confusion, anarchy and a breakdown of law and order”.

Describing the suit as a public-interest action, the plaintiffs argued that the Act lacks safeguards against the “arbitrary exercise” of the power and does not require INEC to hear the declared winners before reviewing results. They urged the court to declare Section 65(b) unconstitutional.

Background

President Bola Tinubu assented to the Electoral Act 2026 on 18 February after the National Assembly amended the 2022 Act.

Under the legacy Electoral Act 2010, section 68 provided that a returning officer’s decision on scores and a candidate’s return was final, subject only to judicial review.

But this provision underwent significant change in section 65 of subsequent Electoral Act 2022 and the latest Electoral Act 2026.

READ ALSO: INEC speaks on suspicious photos in voter register

The 2022 Act provided for the finality of a returning officer’s decision on ballot validity and result declaration. It also preserves a limited power for INEC to review declarations and returns within seven days.

The 2026 Act retained INEC’s power of review but with a narrower provision focused only on the commission’s power to review a declaration or return where it is satisfied that the declaration was made under duress or knowingly and wilfully contrary to the collation procedures in section 62(4) – (8).

Section 65(a) covers declarations or returns potentially made under duress, while Section 65(b) concerns those allegedly made knowingly and wilfully contrary to Section 62(4)–(8).

That section requires electoral officers to verify accreditation figures and votes against polling-unit records and transmitted data, examine disputed or incorrect results, correct errors where necessary, and announce verified results.

With the general elections less than three months away, the disputed provision and its relevance to the upcoming poll will remain uncertain until the court reaches a decision and, possibly, final reviews by the appellate courts.

World.title: Viral Video: NAFDAC speaks on police demand for Reg Number from Zobo hawker
World.content:
A viral video circulating on Facebook shows police officers in Delta State questioning a Zobo hawker about the absence of a National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) registration number on the drink.

In the video, one officer is seen shaking a bottle of the drink and asking whether it has a NAFDAC registration number.

“This is ordinary Zobo. I am a content creator, and I will put it on Facebook,” a man who came to the hawker’s aid said.

“Put it (on Facebook),” a police operative responded.

Another officer, holding the drink, said: “As far as I am concerned, this thing is supposed to have a NAFDAC number. Does this thing have a NAFDAC number? As a police officer, don’t I have the right to ask?”

The confrontation attracted onlookers who gathered around the scene.

Zobo is a popular Nigerian beverage made from the dried calyces of the hibiscus plant. It can be prepared on its own or flavoured with ingredients such as pineapple, ginger, garlic and other spices.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Police defend officers

Bright Edafe, the police spokesperson in Delta, defended the officers, saying they were doing their duties.

Mr Edafe said he expected the press to condemn the content creator for chastising officers who were carrying out their responsibilities.

“The police officers are doing their jobs, but some carried cameras and asked police operatives why a drink should have a NAFDAC NUMBER,” he said.

He argued that products regulated by NAFDAC must comply with the agency’s requirements, questioning why anyone would challenge the need for a registration number on a consumable product.

He also cited the agency’s regulatory mandate, arguing that consumable products subject to NAFDAC regulation must meet the relevant requirements.

NAFDAC clarifies registration requirements

However, Christiana Obiazikwor, NAFDAC’s spokesperson, said the agency does not regulate Zobo sold in ordinary containers without packaging, sealing or labelling.

“If you produce Zobo without packaging it – putting a label, without sealing it. It is not under NAFDAC’s purview to regulate it. But when you now package, seal, and put a label, then it becomes under NAFDAC regulation. But if you just put ordinary Zobo in a container to sell, it is not under NAFDAC,” she said.

She compared the situation to cooking oil sold in open markets, explaining that it falls outside the agency’s regulatory mandate until it is packaged, sealed and labelled.

When briefed on the incident in Delta State, Ms Obiazikwor said: “It is supposed to have a NAFDAC number if it is packaged and labelled.”

A photograph of the drink shared on Facebook showed it in a labelled bottle.

NAFDAC’s clarification indicates that the product’s packaging and labelling are central to determining whether it falls under the agency’s regulatory requirements.

World.title: AU accredits Nigeria’s counter-terrorism centre for West Africa
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

The African Union (AU) has accredited Nigeria’s National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), under the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA), as a Regional Centre of Excellence in Counter Terrorism for West Africa and the Sahel.

The accreditation fulfils President Bola Tinubu’s vision, announced at the High-Level African Counter Terrorism Meeting held in Abuja in April 2024, to position the NCTC as a regional hub for intelligence sharing, operational coordination, specialised training and capacity building against terrorism and violent extremism.

A statement issued on Thursday by Abu Michael, Head of Strategic Communication at the NCTC, said the designation marked a significant milestone in Nigeria’s contribution to collective African security.

It said the recognition formally positioned the centre to support AU member states, particularly those in West Africa and the Sahel, through enhanced counter-terrorism cooperation and institutional capacity development.

According to the statement, the accreditation gives the NCTC an expanded regional mandate to provide specialised training, joint threat analysis, research, technical assistance, exchanges of lessons learned and other forms of counter-terrorism support.

The accreditation was announced on October 27, 2026, by the Acting Director of the African Union Counter Terrorism Centre (AUCTC), Dr Idriss Mounir Lallali, on behalf of the AU Commission’s Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security, at the conclusion of the African Lessons Learned Forum in Abuja.

Lallali said the recognition followed a rigorous assessment of the NCTC’s institutional capacity, governance, training programmes, analytical capabilities, coordination mechanisms and adherence to human rights and the rule of law.

He explained that the accreditation process began with the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between the AU and the NCTC in September 2025.

This was followed by a technical assessment mission conducted by the AUCTC in Abuja in December 2025, which produced an accreditation roadmap outlining the institutional standards required for recognition.

Since then, the NCTC has worked to strengthen its governance structures, develop training curricula and operational procedures, improve its analytical and coordination functions, and reinforce its commitment to human rights and the rule of law.

The statement said the successful completion of the accreditation requirements reflected the centre’s institutional development and the collaborative efforts of ONSA, NCTC leadership and personnel, as well as strategic partners.

Announcing the decision, Lallali said: “It is therefore my pleasure to announce that the African Union is accrediting the NCTC as an African Union Regional Centre of Excellence in Counter Terrorism.

“This decision will be conveyed formally to the Government of the Federal Republic of Nigeria through a Note Verbale. It will come from the Department of Political Affairs, Peace and Security, through the AUCTC.

“That Note will set out the terms of the accreditation: an initial period of three years, renewable, the regional responsibilities the Centre now takes on, and the commitments the African Union makes in return.”

Speaking at the event, the National Security Adviser, Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, represented by the NCTC National Coordinator, Major General Adamu Garba Laka, described the accreditation as both recognition of Nigeria’s progress and a responsibility to contribute more substantially to Africa’s collective security.

Ribadu said the development marked an important moment for Nigeria and the continent, while commending Tinubu for his leadership, political will and sustained investment in the country’s national security architecture.

He said the achievement advanced the administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda and fulfilled the President’s vision of positioning the NCTC to serve Nigeria, West Africa, the Sahel and the wider continent.

The NSA also commended the AU Commission and the AUCTC for their technical support and the rigorous accreditation process, particularly acknowledging Lallali’s role in the mapping, assessment and accreditation stages.

He specifically recognised Laka for his leadership and sustained efforts in driving the process to completion.

Ribadu also praised the centre’s officers and staff, Nigeria’s security and justice institutions, ministries, departments and agencies, civil society organisations, communities and international partners for their contributions.

He said the Federal Government and ONSA would continue to support the NCTC in meeting the demands of its expanded regional mandate through appropriate staffing, sustainable resources, institutional partnerships and continued compliance with accreditation standards.

World.title: ALTON urges states to scrap telecoms right-of-way fees
World.content:
Association says charges account for up to 60% of fibre deployment costs

By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja

The Association of Licensed Telecommunications Operators of Nigeria (ALTON) has urged state governments to abolish right-of-way charges on telecommunications infrastructure, warning that the fees account for up to 60 per cent of fibre-optic deployment costs in some states and discourage network expansion into underserved communities.

The association said scrapping the charges, particularly in rural areas and locations with limited commercial prospects, would lower infrastructure deployment costs, attract investment and help bridge Nigeria’s digital divide.

ALTON Chairman, Engr. Gbenga Adebayo, made the call on Tuesday on the sidelines of a plenary session sponsored by IHS Nigeria at the 2026 Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja.

Right-of-way charges are fees imposed for permission to access and use public or private land, roads and other designated spaces to install fibre-optic cables and related telecommunications infrastructure.

Adebayo said the high cost of obtaining right-of-way approvals had become a major obstacle to fibre deployment, making it difficult for operators to justify investments in communities where anticipated revenue might not cover infrastructure costs.

“Today, the cost of right-of-way amounts to a significant part of the cost of fibre deployment. For every one kilometre of fibre that you deploy, in some of the states, the cost of right-of-way can be as high as 50 to 60 per cent of the cost of deploying the entire infrastructure,” he said.

He called for legislation to make right-of-way access for telecommunications infrastructure free, particularly in rural communities and other areas where expected commercial returns were unlikely to attract private investment.

According to him, removing the charges would make network expansion more affordable and encourage operators to extend services to communities with poor or no connectivity.

The ALTON chairman also urged the government to introduce incentives for telecommunications companies investing in areas where infrastructure deployment costs exceeded the revenue they could reasonably expect to generate.

He said existing government intervention mechanisms, particularly the Universal Service Provision Fund (USPF), could be deployed more strategically to support network expansion in underserved locations.

“There are also intervention funds. We have the Universal Service Provision Fund, which is designed for special intervention in those areas that are lacking coverage,” Adebayo said.

He dismissed suggestions that telecommunications operators were unwilling to invest in rural communities, arguing that the challenge was largely economic and could be addressed through appropriate incentives and targeted government support.

Beyond expanding network coverage, Adebayo stressed the need for increased investment in fibre-optic cables, telecommunications sites and network capacity to improve service quality and prepare Nigeria for emerging technologies.

He said artificial intelligence (AI) depended not only on software and computing power but also on the telecommunications infrastructure needed to support reliable connectivity and the transmission of large volumes of data.

Describing telecommunications infrastructure as fundamental to the digital economy, he called for stronger investor participation to address the sector’s infrastructure needs and support Nigeria’s technological development.

Meanwhile, the Chairman of the Senate Committee on ICT and Cybersecurity, Shuaib Salisu, disclosed that the National Digital Economy and E-Government Bill had reached its third reading, expressing optimism that the National Assembly would pass it before the end of 2026.

Salisu said lawmakers were also working on cybersecurity reforms and reviewing the Data Protection Act to strengthen Nigeria’s digital governance framework.

He said the Federal Government’s planned 90,000-kilometre fibre-optic network would help extend connectivity to underserved communities and complement efforts to improve access to digital services.

The senator also identified the Three Million Technical Talent (3MTT) programme as a key initiative for developing the skilled workforce needed to support Nigeria’s growing digital economy.

He urged businesses and industry stakeholders to engage lawmakers early in the legislative process, saying such engagement would help ensure that proposed laws reflected industry realities and the requirements for attracting investment.

Also speaking at the summit, the Chargé d’Affaires of the United States Mission in Abuja, Jimmy Mauldin, called for stronger investment partnerships between Nigeria and the United States, stressing that cooperation should extend beyond trade to include job creation, technology transfer and support for local businesses.

Mauldin identified digital infrastructure, energy, manufacturing, agriculture, critical minerals and financial services as sectors offering significant opportunities for deeper economic collaboration between the two countries.

He said Nigeria’s large youthful population, growing technology sector and strategic position in West African commerce made it an attractive investment destination.

However, he stressed that predictable government policies, respect for contracts, efficient trade procedures and improved security were essential to sustaining investor confidence and attracting long-term capital.

“Capital is mobile. And it’s also important to remember that capital is very selective,” he said.
