World.title: Liberia Tells COP17 That Biodiversity Pledges Mean Little Without Money, Tools and Local Buy-In
World.content:
Dr. Yarkpawolo said Liberia stands with the African Group on four priorities. First, he wants global targets paired with real implementation support. He said reviews of progress should look not only at conservation results but also at whether developing nations were given the means to deliver

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

YEREVAN, Armenia – Liberia has told the global biodiversity summit in Armenia that wealthy nations must back their conservation promises with funding, technology and training, or the effort to halt nature’s decline will stall in the places that need help most.

The message came on Wednesday from Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo, head of Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency, who addressed the high-level segment of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. He spoke on behalf of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr.



Wildlife deaths as a warning

Dr. Yarkpawolo anchored his appeal in two recent cases at home. In Caldwell, a crocodile was killed by residents who feared for their safety. In Monrovia, a dolphin that had become stranded was reportedly killed on October 25, before fisheries officials could reach it.

He said the cases point to a shared failure: ordinary people have little guidance on handling dangerous or distressed animals, and the state lacks the means to respond quickly. The crocodile killing, he noted, reflected a real safety worry, while the dolphin’s death showed how thin the country’s emergency capacity is.

Protecting wildlife, he argued, cannot come at the expense of families’ security. Communities need to be equipped with knowledge and official backing so they never feel forced to choose between the two.

Four asks, aligned with the African Group

Dr. Yarkpawolo said Liberia stands with the African Group on four priorities. First, he wants global targets paired with real implementation support. He said reviews of progress should look not only at conservation results but also at whether developing nations were given the means to deliver.

Second, he called for biodiversity finance that is sufficient, predictable, timely and easy to reach. Liberia backs Africa’s push for a permanent financial mechanism answerable to the Conference of the Parties, with simpler application procedures and direct access for developing countries. Many African governments have complained that cumbersome funding rules slow projects and hamper responses to emerging threats.

Third, he pressed for stronger capacity and technology transfer. In Liberia, that would mean training wildlife emergency teams, expanding research and monitoring, equipping laboratories, and running public education campaigns in languages people actually speak.

Fourth, he urged fair sharing of the benefits drawn from biological resources, including digital sequence information, the genetic data increasingly used in research and commercial products. Liberia supports meaningful contributions from companies that use such data to the Cali Fund, a mechanism designed to channel benefits back to providers. Developing countries, Indigenous peoples and local communities, he said, should see real returns.

Dr. Yarkpawolo told delegates Liberia has already revised its national biodiversity targets and updated its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan to match the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the 2022 accord aimed at halting and reversing biodiversity loss. He described the changes as a base for better coordination among government bodies, conservation groups, communities and foreign partners.

Yet he cautioned that rewriting policy will achieve little without money and sustained follow-through.

Liberia holds large stretches of what remains of the Upper Guinean forest, along with wetlands, rivers, coastal zones and marine habitats that support livelihoods and provide vital services. Those assets are under pressure from habitat loss, overexploitation and uneven enforcement.

Conservation beyond the environment ministry

The EPA chief also urged governments to weave biodiversity into agriculture, fisheries, public health and national development plans, rather than leaving the job to environmental agencies alone. Conservation, he said, is tied to public safety, education and economic opportunity.

He asked COP17 to deliver outcomes that strengthen awareness programs, emergency response systems and income opportunities that give communities a reason to take part in protecting nature.

In closing, he called for information to reach people before fear drives them to destroy wildlife, for help to arrive before threatened animals are lost, and for conservation to offer tangible value to ordinary citizens. He ended with a short line of solidarity: Liberia stands with Africa for action, accessible financing and fairly shared benefits.

His speech adds to a wider African call at the Yerevan talks for a global framework that acknowledges developing countries’ financial limits and ensures that communities living closest to natural resources share in conservation gains. Negotiations and high-level meetings are continuing.

World.title: Liberia: Davis Urges Financing Reforms to Unlock Liberia’s MSME Potential
World.content:
AfDB Consultant Calls for Credit Guarantees, Technical Support and Market Access to Close $1.03 Billion Annual Financing Gap

By Charles G. Lamadine, contributing writer

MONROVIA — Dr. James Francis Davis, a senior international consultant for the African Development Bank (AfDB), has called for comprehensive financing reforms to help micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) overcome barriers to growth, create jobs and compete in regional markets.



Speaking at the 7th Prosperity Africa Conference in Monrovia, Dr. Davis delivered a lecture on “MSME Financing: The Financial Gap,” highlighting the challenges confronting small businesses in Liberia and across Africa.

The conference brought together policymakers, chambers of commerce, development partners and private-sector representatives to explore ways to translate trade and investment opportunities into sustainable economic growth and employment.

Dr. Davis emphasized that although MSMEs play a critical role in employment and economic development, many continue to struggle with limited access to affordable financing, high collateral requirements and short loan repayment periods.

He highlighted an estimated annual financing gap of US$1.03 billion for MSMEs in Liberia and a broader financing shortfall of more than US$209 billion for small businesses across Africa.

Beyond access to capital, Dr. Davis argued that sustainable business growth requires a comprehensive support system that combines financing with credit guarantees, technical assistance, mentorship and access to markets.

He stressed that financing alone is insufficient to help businesses expand, underscoring the need for policies and institutional arrangements that enable entrepreneurs to develop viable businesses and compete effectively.

Linking Local Businesses to Regional Markets

Dr. Davis also highlighted the potential of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to expand opportunities for Liberian businesses through regional trade and value chains.

He called for stronger economic cooperation among African countries, allowing businesses in different markets to specialize in supplying raw materials, processing products, providing logistics and delivering financial services.

For Liberia, he identified agriculture, light manufacturing, logistics, technology and tourism as sectors with significant potential to support enterprise development, attract investment and generate employment.

He stressed that improving MSME financing must go hand in hand with efforts to connect local businesses to regional supply chains and emerging commercial opportunities.

Youth Entrepreneurship Financing

Dr. Davis also linked the discussion to Liberia’s Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO), an initiative funded by the AfDB and the Government of Liberia that targets 30,000 youth-led businesses.

He highlighted the importance of the initiative’s approach of combining training, incubation and financing to prepare young entrepreneurs for sustainable business operations.

According to the presentation, equipping entrepreneurs with the necessary skills and business support before providing financing can help address weaknesses that undermine the success of grant-funded and other small-business support programs.

Dr. Davis further emphasized the importance of infrastructure investment, arguing that roads should be viewed not merely as transportation projects but as economic corridors capable of connecting producers to markets, reducing business costs and stimulating investment.

He called for stronger coordination among government institutions, chambers of commerce and development partners to ensure that investment commitments translate into tangible economic opportunities and jobs.

Call for Stronger Banking Partnerships

Dr. Davis commended the Liberia Chamber of Commerce for advocating greater opportunities for local businesses, while urging commercial banks to work with credit guarantee funds to make financing more accessible to MSMEs.

He identified high interest rates, demanding collateral requirements and short repayment periods as major constraints facing Liberian entrepreneurs.

Partnerships between commercial banks and guarantee institutions, he suggested, could help reduce lending risks and improve access to credit for businesses that lack sufficient collateral but demonstrate viable growth prospects.

His presentation, described as interactive and practical, aligned with the conference theme, “MSME Financing at the Africa Prosperity Conference for Sustainable Development: Policy Reforms, Innovation, and Opportunities.”

The discussions underscored the importance of addressing financing barriers as part of broader efforts to promote inclusive growth, strengthen private-sector development and expand opportunities for young entrepreneurs.

For Liberia, closing the MSME financing gap will require more than increased lending. It will also depend on coordinated policy reforms, stronger financial institutions, business development support and improved access to domestic and regional markets.

World.title: Liberia: After CBL Pay Shock, House Turns on Executives
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s House of Representatives has ordered a sweeping review of salaries and benefits across government, days after a rare public disclosure of a senior official’s pay reignited anger over the cost of running one of the world’s poorest countries.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

In a unanimous vote on Tuesday, the lower house of the national legislature instructed two of its committees, on Ways, Means and Finance and on Public Accounts, to examine the pay and perks of government officials and report back within two weeks. The motion was brought by Representative Alex S. Noah of Sinoe County.



Lawmakers argued that they are wrongly blamed for the country’s swollen wage bill, while ministers and the heads of state-owned enterprises earn far more.

The disclosure that lit the fuse

The vote came less than a week after Euphemia G.T. Swen-Monmia, President Joseph Boakai’s nominee for Deputy Governor for Economic Policy at the Central Bank of Liberia, appeared on October 22 before the Senate Committee on Banking and Currency for her confirmation hearing.

Asked about her pay, she did something Liberian officials rarely do: she gave the numbers. She testified that her monthly salary is US$9,000, that she receives around US$5,000 in cash benefits on top of that, and that her housing allowance should be about US$15,000. She has served in an acting capacity since August 12.

That amounts to roughly US$168,000 a year in salary and cash benefits before housing is counted. A civil servant on the government’s US$150 monthly minimum would need more than seven and a half years of uninterrupted work to earn what she receives in a single month.

Swen-Monmia is a career central banker who joined the bank in 2010 as a management trainee and rose to director of its Financial Markets Department. The controversy is not about her qualifications but about what her testimony revealed: pay at the top of Executive agencies is generous, and almost never made public.

No lawmaker cited her testimony by name during Tuesday’s debate. But the timing, and the focus of the two letters that triggered it, on officials earning more than US$5,000 a month, suggest the disclosure handed fresh ammunition to a chamber long cast as the main villain in Liberia’s debate over official pay.

‘We are suffering’

On the floor, several members described their own compensation as “peanuts” compared with Executive officials and argued the legislature deserves more because representatives serve larger numbers of constituents.

Representative Moima Briggs-Mensah of Bong County said a US$2,000 budget line meant for constituents’ school scholarships often never arrives, and that lawmakers lack the insurance enjoyed by Executive officials.

“We don’t even have Social Security benefits. We are suffering and people in the Executive are making mockery of us,” she said.

Representative Anthony Williams of Maryland County said lawmakers were being “falsely crucified” by the public while benefits such as fuel arrive months late.

“The Executive, especially SOEs are reaping the honey, while we are being falsely crucified,” he said, demanding that state enterprises disclose their gross and net pay and benefits to the House.

The numbers tell a different story

Lawmakers’ complaints sit uneasily with the figures. Senators earn US$8,000 a month each, according to the draft 2026 budget, and a bill to cut that to US$5,000, first introduced by Senator Abraham Darius Dillon in 2020, has stalled for years. In 2025, House members’ basic salary was put at roughly US$8,569 a month, with additional funding for security guards, drivers, cooks and other support staff.

The legislature as a whole has also grown more expensive. The draft 2026 budget gave lawmakers US$51.7 million, up from US$41.3 million in 2024.

That is in a West African nation of about 5.2 million people still rebuilding from 14 years of civil war that ended in 2003, whose national budget crossed US$1 billion for the first time this year. About half the population lives below the poverty line.

Meanwhile, front-line public servants struggle to get paid at all. Teachers’ U.S.-dollar pay has gone unpaid since October 2025, and nurses are demanding a monthly minimum of US$500.

A chamber in revolt

Tuesday’s vote follows weeks of turmoil inside the House over lawmakers’ own money. More than 40 members boycotted the legislature’s reopening session on October 9 in protest over unpaid benefits and allowances, including constituency visits, district projects, fuel and medical allowances. Calling themselves “Reformists,” they accused the chamber’s leadership of withholding benefits and legislative support funds.

The Senate faces its own scrutiny. A proposal from its Committee on Rules, Order and Administration, reported by FrontPageAfrica, seeks US$792,552 in the 2027 budget to raise salaries for 224 Senate staff, with some increases as high as 71 percent. The Senate has disputed the reporting and demanded a retraction; FrontPageAfrica stands by its story.

Two letters, two tones

The review was triggered by letters from two lawmakers who framed the problem very differently from their colleagues on the floor.

Representative Sumo Kollie Mulbah of Montserrado County asked the House to hold up the national budget until the Finance Ministry reports all salaries and benefits above US$5,000 a month for ministers, directors, county governors and commissioners. The central bank deputy governor’s testimony would place her nearly three times above that threshold.

Mulbah singled out housing allowances, fuel and phone-credit coupons, and overseas medical treatment on top of health insurance.

“While these elite benefits are sustained, critical national priorities like the increment of the minimum wage are continuously set aside,” he wrote.

Representative Musa Hassan Bility of Nimba County called for a special committee to review salaries, allowances, wasteful spending, duty-free privileges and tax exemptions across all branches of government, and insisted the legislature go first.

“We cannot continue to demand sacrifices from ordinary Liberians while protecting our own excessive privileges,” Bility wrote. “This must not be another selective exercise intended to embarrass particular officials for public applause.”

What to watch

The two-week deadline lands as the Executive prepares to send the 2027 budget to the legislature by October 31. The government projects total spending will fall to US$1.02 billion next year, meaning any gains for one group of officials will likely come at someone else’s expense.

The test is whether the committees follow Bility’s call to start with the legislature, or whether the review becomes, as he warned, a selective exercise aimed at the Executive. Liberians have heard promises of pay cuts before. A proposal to cut senators’ pay to US$5,000 has been on the table for six years without passing.

World.title: Liberia: Inside the Defense Bid to Overturn the Peter Bon Jallah Conviction
World.content:
A Liberian judge convicted a former national security aide of statutory rape and kidnapping but cleared him of gang rape. Four days later, his lawyers filed a motion arguing that the two halves of the ruling cannot both stand.

By Rodney D. Sieh

MONROVIA — When Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. delivered his verdict on Friday, October 23, he framed the case around three questions: whether the evidence supported a conviction for gang rape, for statutory rape, and for kidnapping. He answered no to the first and yes to the other two.



That split is now the battleground. On Tuesday, October 27, at 11:12 a.m., lawyers for Peter Bon Jallah, 63, a former special assistant to the director of Liberia’s National Security Agency (NSA), filed a motion for a new trial at Criminal Court “E” in Monrovia. The filing, received by Acting Clerk of Court Abraham Richards, asks the judge to set aside his own verdict.

The motion is the first formal test of a ruling that, by the court’s own record, states its conclusions on each charge without detailing how it weighed every witness and exhibit. That gap is what the defense is trying to exploit.

What the court decided

Jallah was arrested on January 7, 2026, after the mother of a 16-year-old boy complained to the police Women and Children Protection Section. The boy did paid chores at Jallah’s home.

A grand jury indicted Jallah and two unidentified men in February on charges of gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping. The indictment alleged abuse at Jallah’s home on November 29 and December 24, 2025. It also alleged that on January 1, 2026, Jallah lured the boy with an offer of football boots, drove him to a building off Camp Johnson Road in central Monrovia, and held him there for three days while he and two other men abused him.

The two other men were never brought before the court. Jallah, who has denied all the allegations, chose to be tried by a judge rather than a jury.

The court acquitted him of gang rape, finding the prosecution’s evidence insufficient. It convicted him of statutory rape and kidnapping. Jallah was remanded to Monrovia Central Prison pending a pre-sentence report from the Ministry of Justice’s Bureau of Probation Services. No sentence has been imposed.

The prosecution’s case

According to the written verdict, the prosecution called 13 regular witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses. The defense called eight witnesses, including Jallah, plus three subpoenaed witnesses from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, the mobile operator Orange Liberia and the John F. Kennedy Medical Center.

The state’s strongest scientific evidence came from Pascal Bavugirije of the Rwanda Forensic Institute, which analyzed exhibits after Liberia sent them abroad. He testified that DNA profiles from four clothing exhibits matched Jallah’s reference sample. Material collected from the alleged scene produced a mixed profile from unknown people that matched neither Jallah nor the boy.

The boy testified in August that he was assaulted three times, and the court admitted his police statement over defense objections. Investigators also told the court that phone records placed Jallah near one of the alleged scenes, contradicting his account that he had no contact with the boy.

The defense’s four arguments

The motion, signed by Counsellor G. Wiefueh Alfred Sayeh of the Law Offices of Sayeh & Sayeh, makes four main claims.

1. The kidnapping conviction contradicts the gang rape acquittal. The defense argues that the kidnapping charge rests on the alleged three-day confinement off Camp Johnson Road, the same episode at the heart of the gang rape charge. If the court found too little evidence that the gang rape happened there, the motion says, it cannot find that the boy was held there. It describes the conviction as “contrary to weight of the evidence.”

2. The court lacked jurisdiction over kidnapping. Criminal Court “E” is Liberia’s specialized court for sexual offenses. The motion argues it has no jurisdiction over kidnapping as a separate crime. This is a purely legal question, and if the judge or a higher court agrees, it could void that conviction regardless of the evidence.

3. Penetration was never proven. Under Liberia’s rape statute, penetration is an essential element. The defense points to three pieces of testimony:

* A JFK Medical Center doctor, called by the defense, testified that an examination under anesthesia shortly after the boy’s January rescue found no evidence of trauma. The hospital’s operative record lists the post-procedure diagnosis as “normal findings.” The motion says the prosecution offered no rebuttal.

* The Rwandan forensic examiner testified that DNA analysis cannot establish guilt or innocence and that his report did not show whether penetration occurred.

* A nurse examiner from the hospital’s One Stop Center for survivors of sexual violence, a prosecution witness, testified that she could not say the boy was not raped, adding that she was there only to report what she saw. The defense argues that statement does not prove rape and creates doubt that must favor the accused.

The motion goes further, accusing the judge of attributing the words “penetration” and “blunt object” to the nurse’s testimony when, it says, no witness used them.

1. The defendant did not get a fair trial. The motion alleges the judge remarked in open court that the prosecution was “asking weak questions.” It also says that after reviewing the defense’s Orange phone records, the judge on his own initiative subpoenaed Jallah’s records from a second carrier, Lonestar Cell MTN, over a defense objection that the court could not introduce evidence on the state’s behalf.

How strong are the arguments?

Each claim faces hurdles, and none has yet been tested by the prosecution’s response.

The medical findings do not settle the question on their own. Forensic medicine broadly recognizes that the absence of physical injury does not rule out sexual assault, particularly when an examination comes days after an alleged act. The prosecution can also point to the DNA findings and the boy’s testimony. A judge sitting without a jury is entitled to weigh credible testimony against an inconclusive medical record.

The kidnapping argument may be harder to dismiss. The acquittal on gang rape could reflect doubt about the two unidentified men rather than about the alleged confinement itself. Whether that distinction holds depends on reasoning the published verdict does not spell out.

The fair-trial complaint about the phone subpoena raises a recognized principle: a judge in an adversarial system is not supposed to build the prosecution’s case. How much weight the court gave those records is not clear from the verdict.

What happens next

Judge Wesseh must rule on the motion. If he denies it, the case moves to sentencing once the probation report arrives. The defense has already said it will appeal to the Supreme Court of Liberia, and the arguments in this motion offer a preview of that appeal.

The case has been closely watched in Liberia because of Jallah’s position close to the head of the country’s main intelligence agency, and because it tests how the courts handle sexual violence against children. It has already passed through two courtrooms, a failed prosecution bid to move the trial out of Monrovia, and a change of judge.

The Ministry of Justice, which prosecuted the case, had not filed a response to the motion as of Tuesday.

World.title: Liberian Activists Urge Freeze on New Mining Deals Until Decades-Old Law Is Rewritten
World.content:
A coalition of civil society groups says signing long-term contracts under Liberia’s 2000 mining law would lock in the weak oversight, lost revenue and pollution that have marked the sector for decades.

MONROVIA, Liberia — A coalition of civil society organizations in Liberia has called on the government to stop signing and ratifying new long-term mining contracts until the West African nation replaces its 26-year-old mining law.

The CSO Consortium on Minerals, Mining, and Inclusive Sustainable Development made the appeal on Monday, October 26, at a press conference in the capital. It urged President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the national legislature to impose a moratorium on new Mineral Development Agreements (MDAs) — the contracts, typically lasting 25 years or more, that set the terms under which large mining companies operate and that carry the force of law once lawmakers ratify them.



“We strongly believe that entering into new or additional long-term mineral development agreements under an outdated legal framework risk perpetuating existing governance weaknesses,” the coalition said.

Its members include the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia, Integrity Watch Liberia, the Sustainable Development Institute, Medica Liberia and ActionAid Liberia, among others.

Wealth that has not reached communities

Mining is central to Liberia’s economy. It accounts for about a fifth of gross domestic product and dominates exports, according to a March 2026 assessment by the Washington-based research group Forest Trends. Iron ore and gold are the main products.

Yet the coalition said decades of extraction have not delivered matching jobs, public services or development for the communities that host mines. It blamed weak enforcement, corruption, the export of unprocessed ore, poor transparency, environmental damage and the exclusion of local people from decisions.

The Forest Trends report reached similar conclusions. It found the government may be losing millions of dollars a year in uncollected mining revenue. Mining companies paid just over $844 million to the state between 2007 and 2023, according to figures from the Liberia Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (LEITI), the national arm of a global revenue-disclosure standard. Mining licenses now overlap more than two million hectares of forest in a country that holds about half of what remains of the Upper Guinean rainforest biodiversity hotspot.

A year of illegal mining and license violations

The call follows a year in which government inspectors repeatedly found companies mining outside the limits of their permits, or with no permit at all.

Liberia issues several tiers of mining license. Class C permits are reserved for Liberian citizens and allow only hand tools. Class B permits cover small commercial operations. Large industrial projects operate under MDAs.

In March, a committee of the House of Representatives suspended Hurine Mining Company in central Bong County after investigators found it had exceeded the limits of its Class B license.

In April, the Ministry of Mines and Energy closed JinXin Mining Company in Rivercess County for mining without a valid license on ground licensed to another firm. The ministry said JinXin had ignored an order in January to stop. Days later it shut Alex Gee Group of Companies in Grand Gedeh County, whose license had lapsed. Officers also dismantled an unlicensed site whose alleged Chinese operators fled before they arrived.

In June, officials in Gbarpolu County seized excavators working a Class C claim, where heavy machinery is banned. They also found Chinese nationals mining under another company’s license, outside its approved boundaries.

Mines and Energy Minister R. Matenokay Tingban has acknowledged that many small commercial license holders fail to account for the minerals they extract.

The problems are not new. In 2024, the then-minister sought legal advice on revoking licenses issued since 2018, citing letters from the presidency directing that license applications be routed through the Office of the President. In 2025, a ministry investigation found that two companies, Hamak Mining and its successor 79 Resources, had misrepresented their license status and owed the government more than $400,000 in fees.

Big miners under scrutiny

Concerns extend to the largest operators. An investigation by The Associated Press and The Gecko Project published this year found that Bea Mountain Mining Corporation, Liberia’s biggest gold producer, repeatedly leaked cyanide, arsenic and copper at levels the country’s Environmental Protection Agency said exceeded legal limits.

The investigation found the company failed to report a 2022 spill on time and had earlier blocked government inspectors from its laboratory. Bea Mountain exported more than $576 million worth of gold between July 2021 and December 2022.

Why the coalition wants a pause now

Liberia’s Minerals and Mining Law was enacted in 2000, before the country’s 14-year civil war had fully ended. Lawmakers opened public hearings on amendments in July. At those hearings, the Liberia Chamber of Mines, an industry body, warned that changes limited to small commercial licenses would not fix the sector’s deeper problems. It called for a full overhaul covering taxation, licensing, environmental protection and strategic minerals such as lithium, cobalt and rare earths.

In January, the legislature ratified an amendment to the contract of steelmaker ArcelorMittal, Liberia’s largest iron ore producer, extending it to 2050 with an option to renew for 25 more years. Some senators praised the deal as a model for renegotiating other contracts. Another senator abstained, citing the company’s record of unmet commitments to host communities.

For the coalition, that timeline is the core of the argument. Contracts signed under a law that government, industry and activists all describe as outdated will outlast any reform that follows.

What the activists want in a new law

The coalition drew up its proposals at a meeting with mining-affected communities on October 1 and refined them at an October 21 roundtable with government agencies, donors and companies. Its 10 recommendations include:

* Binding transparency rules for licensing, contracts and revenue, including public disclosure of who ultimately owns mining companies;

* Clear penalties for violations by companies and by officials, and legal remedies for affected communities;

* Enforceable benefit-sharing for communities, building on a 2018 land rights law;

* Requirements to process more ore locally and to prioritize Liberian workers and suppliers;

* Binding obligations for mine closure and land restoration;

* Measures to protect women, young people and people with disabilities, including against sexual exploitation and abuse in mining areas; and

* Tighter regulation of small-scale mining, including sand and quarry operations.

The coalition praised the Boakai government’s stated commitment to reform but said the new law “must go beyond updating existing provisions.”

The Ministry of Mines and Energy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Liberia: Grebo Leader Calls for Calm and Swift Probe Into Death of Samuel Gekor in Grand Gedeh
World.content:
MONROVIA – A prominent Liberian lawyer and leading figure in the Grebo community has called for calm and a swift investigation into the death of Samuel Gekor, a young Grebo man found dead on a cassava farm near Zwedru, the capital of southeastern Grand Gedeh County.

Gekor’s body was discovered in the Kanneh area of Electoral District Two after he had been missing for three days. The circumstances of his disappearance remain unclear.

Counsellor Kunkunyon Wleh Teh expressed deep sadness over Gekor’s death and extended condolences to his family and the wider Grebo community, one of Liberia’s major ethnic groups, concentrated largely in the country’s southeast.



Teh, a former student of Bishop Juwel High School in Zwedru, said he has spoken with Gekor’s family to offer his condolences and support.

While acknowledging the community’s grief, fear and frustration, and its legitimate demand for answers, Teh urged residents to remain calm, peaceful and law-abiding as the search for justice continues.

He called on the Liberia National Police and the Ministry of Justice to speed up the investigation, establish the facts surrounding the disappearance and death, and ensure that anyone found responsible is held accountable under the law. The family and the public, he said, deserve timely updates, transparency and credible answers.

“Every Liberian deserves the right to life, safety, and dignity, irrespective of tribe, county, or social standing. No family should be left without answers when a loved one dies under troubling circumstances,” Teh said.

He said the community’s responsibility at this moment is to stand with the family, promote peace and demand justice through lawful means, cautioning against letting grief and anger turn into actions that could endanger lives or deepen divisions.

“Justice must be pursued, truth must prevail, and peace must be preserved,” he said.

World.title: Investors, executives gather in Margibi as Liberia seeks new money for mining and energy
World.content:
MONROVIA – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai will open a two-day international mining and energy conference on Wednesday, as Liberia steps up efforts to attract foreign investment into the natural-resource sectors that underpin its economy.

The Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Expo (LIMEC 2026) runs October 28–29 at the Farmington Hotel in Margibi County, near Roberts International Airport outside Monrovia. Government officials, international investors, mining executives, energy developers and development partners are expected to attend.

Boakai is scheduled to deliver the keynote address, setting out his government’s plans for drawing investment and promoting responsible development of the country’s mineral resources.



Mining, chiefly iron ore and gold, is one of the West African nation’s main sources of export earnings, while chronic power shortages remain a major obstacle to industrial growth.

Held under the theme “Transforming Liberia’s Economy: Driving Development Through Sustainable Mining and Energy Investments,” the conference will feature panel discussions, presentations and exhibitions on investment opportunities in mineral exploration, production, renewable energy and related infrastructure.

Amara Kamara, president of the Liberia Chamber of Mines, said the gathering offers Liberia a chance to deepen ties with international investors, showcase its resources and build partnerships that could create jobs and drive growth.

He said the event’s value should go beyond investment promotion to opening doors for Liberian businesses, increasing local participation in the mining industry and ensuring that communities benefit from investments.

Kamara credited Mines and Energy Minister R. Matenokay Tingban and his ministry for coordinating with the Chamber of Mines and AME Trade Ltd., the international organizer, to stage the event.

Sponsors include Avesoro Resources, Mantrac Group, Huawei, CORICA Mining Services, Mansa Resources, Sarmin Metals, Westcrest Liberia, AGL Africa Global Logistics, the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC), the Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority (LPRA) and WBHO.

World.title: Pupils absconding classes over caterpillar harvesting
World.content:
A former educationist in Nseluka area in Katumba ward of Mungwi District has raised concerns over pupils who are absconding class in preference to caterpillar collection.

Edward Lombe described the trend as retrogressive and has since appealed to parents to stop their children from doing so.

Mr Lombe also called on traditional leaders to protect children from such abuse.

He disclosed that traditional leaders should work with schools to stop the trend.

” I know this is an economic activity which presents itself once in a year but allowing kids to miss classes is unacceptable,” he stated.

The Former Educationist said parents should not engage their school children in such activities at the expense of education.

One of the pupils, whose name has been withheld, said she was collecting caterpillars for sale during the common market locally known as ” Umunanda”.

She however, promised to continue with her education once the caterpillar collection is over.

And a check by a ZANIS crew this morning in the nearby bush behind Gibeon Adventist Secondary School found more than 15 children from nearby primary schools collecting caterpillars.

World.title: Government calls for targeted legal reforms- Mutti
World.content:
Government has called for targeted legal reforms to support the implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda and accelerate economic transformation.

speaking at the 2026 Association of Law Reform Agencies of Eastern and Southern Africa (ALRAESA) two days Conference in Lusaka, Speaker of the National Assembly, Nelly Mutti, said that the effective legal frameworks are essential to unlocking opportunities in agriculture, mining, energy and manufacturing.

“Laws and regulations must be aligned with national development priorities to promote investment, increase production, expand exports and create jobs,” she said.

Ms Mutti added that reforms should address regulatory barriers, improve the business environment and strengthen private sector participation.

She also stressed the need for evidence-based research and public consultation in the law reform process.

“The impact of recommendations should be measured by their contribution to economic activity, access to justice and improved livelihoods,” Ms Mutti said.

And Solicitor General, Marshal Muchende, says legal reforms are critical to translating Zambia’s economic policies into practical outcomes under the Government’s 2026–2030 Growth Zambia Agenda.

Mr Muchende said that laws must be responsive to national development priorities, including job creation, investment, regional trade and value addition.

He has called for stronger regional cooperation among law reform institutions to address cross-border challenges in trade, environmental protection, migration and digital governance.

Mr Muchende cited legislative changes supporting women’s representation in Parliament and the legal protection of free education as examples of how reforms can translate policy into enforceable rights.

“Law reform is essential to ensuring that Zambia moves beyond economic stabilisation towards accelerated growth and improved livelihoods,” Mr Muchende said.

Meanwhile, Commonwealth Association of Law Reform Agencies (CALRAS)has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening cooperation with regional law reform institutions to improve legal systems and share best practices.

CALRAS Vice-President and Malawi Law Commissioner, Rosemary Kumitsonyo, noted that collaboration between law reform agencies is essential for building institutional capacity and developing effective legal frameworks.

Ms Kumitsonyo said that the two associations share common objectives, including promoting law reform, exchanging expertise and encouraging regional and international cooperation.

She added that CALRAS works with the Commonwealth Secretariat to promote the role of law reform agencies and provide practical guidance on law reform methodology.

“Continued cooperation would provide opportunities for member institutions to address common challenges and strengthen law reform practices,” Ms Kumitsonyo said.

The conference, hosted by the Zambia Law Development Commission, is being held under the theme, “The Intersection Between Law Reform and National Development,” as the Commission marks 30 years of service.

World.title: Two juveniles appear for rape Case
World.content:
Two juveniles in conflict with the law have pleaded not guilty to a charge of rape, after appearing before the Chadiza Magistrate Court in Eastern Province.

The juveniles aged 14 and 16, who are pupils at a Day Secondary School in Chadiza District, appeared before Magistrate Fred Musaka.

Particulars of the offence are that on September 17, 2026, the duo jointly and whilst acting together allegedly had unlawful carnal knowledge of a woman aged 26, contrary to Section 132 of the Penal Code Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

Magistrate Musaka has adjourned the matter to October 30, 2026 for commencement of trial.

World.title: Illegal Structure Demolished in Mpika
World.content:
Mpika Town Council has demolished eleven illegal structures along the Great North Road near the Total filling station for contravening planning regulations.

‎The demolition exercise was conducted by the Council’s Planning Department and Council Police between 23:00 hours on October 24 and 01:00 hours on October 25, 2026.

The structures included clothing stalls, restaurants, alcohol outlets and other establishments erected without the requisite development approvals.

‎Mpika Town Council Public Relations Officer Mpundu Mushota says the owners of the affected properties had earlier been engaged and sensitised on the dangers of erecting structures in restricted areas.

Mr Mushota says the owners were also advised to halt construction and comply with planning regulations but disregarded the guidance, prompting the Council to demolish the structures.

‎He has urged members of the public to stop circulating what he describes as false information and accusing Council Chairperson Chola Chilumba of being responsible for the demolition exercise.

‎Mr Mushota said the exercise has attracted criticism on social media, with many people condemning the demolitions.

‎He has clarified that the Council operates through an established administrative hierarchy, with decisions and enforcement activities undertaken through the relevant departments and laid-down procedures.

‎Mr Mushota has further urged members of the public to obtain the necessary development approvals before commencing construction works and to avoid encroaching on road reserves, utility corridors and other protected areas.

‎He said the Council remains committed to enforcing the Regional and Urban Planning Act No. 3 of 2015 to ensure that developments within the district comply with approved planning standards and public safety requirements.

World.title: Eastern PS implores civil servants to rally behind the Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Eastern Province Permanent Secretary (PS) Paul Thole has called on civil servants and cooperating partners to ensure that President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda translates into tangible development and delivers real benefits to ordinary Zambians.

Speaking during the combined Second and Third Quarter Provincial Development Coordinating Committee (PDCC) meeting in Chipata, Mr Thole said the country must build on the economic gains recorded over the past five years to achieve economic expansion, create opportunities and improve people’s livelihoods.

Mr Thole said the Grow Zambia agenda is aimed at increasing production in key sectors, including agriculture, energy, tourism, mining and livestock, to drive economic growth and prosperity.

He explained that the agenda, anchored on the 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 targets, seeks to achieve 10 million tonnes of maize, 10,000 megawatts of electricity, five million tourist arrivals, three million tonnes each of copper and soya, one million tonnes each of wheat and sugar, and one billion United States dollars in beef exports.

The PS said achieving these targets should result in improved access to reliable electricity, increased agricultural production, higher household incomes, job creation and expanded infrastructure development.

“We are the key to the government achieving this agenda. Its success depends on how we work,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mr Thole has expressed concern over poor attendance and failure by some Cluster Advisory Group (CAG) members to submit reports during meetings.

He said the trend was undermining effective performance assessment and coordination of development programmes in the province.

Mr Thole noted that CAG and PDCC meetings were provided for under the law and served as important platforms for reviewing government performance and ensuring transparency in the implementation of development programmes.

“Failure to submit reports and attend both the CAG meetings and PDCC amounts to a refusal to work with the government. I urge you all to reflect and change your attitudes towards these important meetings,” he said.

He further called on all stakeholders to demonstrate commitment to their responsibilities and ensure that government policies and programmes deliver meaningful benefits to the people of Eastern Province.

Meanwhile, stakeholders attending the meeting raised concerns over the anticipated effects of El Niño on parts of central Eastern Province, highlighting the need for preparedness measures to mitigate its potential impact on communities and livelihoods.

Stakeholders called for the establishment of RTSA offices in Petauke and Lundazi districts to address concerns over rising motorcycle accidents and low registration rates, saying the offices would improve access to registration services and road safety sensitisation for riders in the districts and surrounding areas.

The issues raised underscored the importance of coordination among government institutions and other stakeholders in addressing local challenges and ensuring that development programmes respond to the needs of communities.

Eastern province Health Director Matthew Ng’ambi said concerted efforts are key to addressing the concerns and push the development agenda.

“I would say about 80 percent of accidents involving motorcycles happen in Chipata, and we have RTSA here, we have the Police. We need to do more. When you go to Chipata Central Hospital, you will see how much of a sorry sight it is, young people are losing limbs,” he worried.

World.title: MP calls for revival of folk music
World.content:
Saise Constituency Member of Parliament (MP), Remmy Sikazwe has called for the revival of traditional music in Mbala district.

Mr Sikazwe encouraged communities to establish cultural music groups to preserve and promote the Mambwe-Lungu heritage.

MP’s call follows the passing of musicians associated with the traditional hit song Palade, including Solo Kaselenga, whose deaths have left a gap in the local music scene.

He said there is a need for a new generation of musicians to carry forward the cultural legacy of the Mambwe‑Lungu people.

Mr Sikazwe emphasised that traditional music should reflect the community’s identity through the use of indigenous instruments, natural sounds and culturally significant songs.

“Traditional music is an important part of our identity, and we need to revive it by encouraging our people, especially the younger generation, to form cultural groups that will preserve and promote our Mambwe-Lungu heritage,” Mr Sikazwe said.

He has pledged to support groups committed to reviving traditional music and preserving traditional forms of entertainment.

Mr Sikazwe said traditional music will help safeguard cultural values, pass indigenous knowledge on to younger generations and showcase the history and traditions of the Mambwe-Lungu chiefdoms.

He added that the country’s ambition to attract more than five million tourists over the next five years presented an opportunity for Mbala district to promote its rich cultural heritage and stimulate local economic activity.

Mr Sikazwe notes that increased tourist arrivals will create opportunities for traditional musicians, dancers, and other local entrepreneurs if cultural activities were properly organised and promoted.

He has, therefore, called for concerted efforts to reorganise and strengthen Mambwe-Lungu cultural activities in anticipation of increased tourism.

Mr Sikazwe further stressed the importance of preserving indigenous traditions while creating opportunities for young people.

The proposed initiative will involve organising cultural performances, documenting traditional songs and instruments, and collaborating with traditional leaders and tourism stakeholders to ensure that the area’s cultural heritage is preserved and promoted.

World.title: Hichilema swears in 24 Cabinet ministers as Laura Miti and opposition leaders question 30-ministry government
World.content:
7Hichilema swears in 24 Cabinet ministers as Laura Miti and opposition leaders question 30-ministry government

President Hakainde Hichilema has appointed and sworn in 24 Cabinet ministers and ten provincial ministers at State House in Lusaka, putting most of his second-term government in place a day after the National Assembly approved his plan to raise the number of ministries to 30.

The appointments, made under Article 116(1) and Article 117(1) of the Constitution, fill new portfolios for Electricity, Petroleum, Industry, Trade and Exports, Skills and Higher Education, and Culture and Arts. They come as human rights activist Ms Laura Miti, Socialist Party president Dr Fred M’membe and the Citizens First party question why government is growing while programmes serving rural Zambians are under financial strain.

The biggest economic appointment went to Ms Brenda Tambatamba, who takes over the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development. She served as labour minister in the President’s first-term Cabinet and, before entering politics, worked as sustainability manager at Barrick’s Lumwana mine.

Ms Tambatamba now leads a sector the government wants to expand to three million metric tonnes of copper a year, close to triple current output.

The former Ministry of Energy, now split in two, is handed to two men who have both run it before. Mr Peter Kapala, energy minister from 2021 to 2024, heads the new Ministry of Electricity. Mr Makozo Chikote, who succeeded him in that role, takes the new Ministry of Petroleum.

Two familiar faces also return. Mr Felix Mutati, formerly in charge of technology, is back at the Ministry of Technology and Science, while former education minister Mr Douglas Syakalima leads the new Ministry of Skills and Higher Education. President Hichilema first nominated both to Parliament, and Speaker Nelly Mutti swore them in as Members before their appointment.

The new trade and industry structure goes to Dr Caroline Katotobwe at the Ministry of Trade and Exports and Mr Noel Nkoma, former board chairperson of the National Road Fund Agency, at the Ministry of Industry. Lackson Sichone takes Small and Medium Enterprise Development.

Ms Princess Kasune becomes Minister of Tourism, Chris Chibuye leads the new Ministry of Culture and Arts, and Likando Mufalali takes Youth and Sports.

Security portfolios went to Ambrose Lufuma at Defence and Dr Clement Andaleki at Home Affairs and Internal Security. Moses Moyo heads Agriculture, Olive Chibola takes Fisheries and Livestock, and Patrick Mucheleka leads the new Ministry of Lands.

Collins Nzovu moves to Infrastructure and Urban Development, while former Copperbelt Minister Elisha Matambo takes Water Development and Sanitation. Elvis Nkandu becomes Minister of Information and Media and Harry Kamboni takes Education.

Gift Sialubalo returns to Local Government and Rural Development. Jack Mwiimbu moves to Justice, Misheck Nyambose takes Labour and Social Security, and Sheal Mulyata heads Community Development and Social Services.

The list completes a Cabinet the Head of State began building in September, when he named Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane to Finance and National Planning, Mulambo Haimbe to Foreign Affairs, Dr Gilbert Siame to Green Economy and Environment and Prof Roma Chilengi to Health.

The schedule released on Wednesday names no minister for Housing or for Transport and Logistics.

In the provinces, Mwabashike Nkulukusa takes Central, Emmanuel Kasambo Copperbelt, Obvious Mwaliteta Lusaka and Lesley Mulwanda Luapula. Jairos Simbeye is Muchinga Minister, Wedden Chileshe takes Northern and Robert Lihefu North-Western.

Edgar Singombe goes to Southern Province, Kapelwa A. Mbangweta to Western and Yamikani Phiri to Eastern.

Addressing the new team after the swearing-in, Mr Hichilema told them to uphold the Constitution, respect the rule of law and serve every Zambian without discrimination. He said any minister who blocks or delays investment would be treated as guilty of bad behaviour in Cabinet.

The President said government must work inside the law, and amend it through Parliament where it stands in the way, rather than break it.

“We stay within the law. We operate within the law,” he said.

He singled out the Social Cash Transfer, the Farmer Input Support Programme and the Food Security Pack, directing that anyone who meets the criteria must receive support wherever they live. Mr Hichilema said he was aware of distortions in how social support had been distributed and had confronted those responsible.

He also told the ministers to keep Cabinet matters confidential and to uphold individual and collective responsibility, fairness, transparency and accountability.

The new structure cleared Parliament on Tuesday, when Vice-President Mutale Nalumango, Leader of Government Business, moved the motion to establish, merge and dissolve ministries. Five ministries were dissolved: Energy; Infrastructure, Housing and Urban Development; Commerce, Trade and Industry; Lands and Natural Resources; and Youth, Sport and Arts. Ten new ones replace them.

Mrs Nalumango told the House that changing energy demand required dedicated ministries for Electricity and Petroleum. The country needed “a ministry that will be looking at innovative ways of continuous generation and transmission,” she said.

She described Culture and Arts as an economic sector able to attract tourists and create jobs. Mr Mwiimbu, then speaking as Monze East Member of Parliament, backed the motion as consistent with the Grow Zambia Agenda, and a majority of lawmakers voted it through.

Outside the House, the reception was colder. Ms Miti said she was disappointed by the expansion and questioned why government was creating ministries for Petroleum, Industry and Culture while the Constituency Development Fund was reportedly facing reductions and the Food Reserve Agency could not buy all the maize farmers had on offer.

She mocked the scale of the restructuring.

“I am surprised there is no Ministry of Ministers,” Ms Miti said.

The activist said she wanted to know how rural voters, whom she credited with returning the government to office, would benefit, noting that the CDF and FRA had both been cut back.

Before the appointments, Ms Miti had urged the President to choose ministers focused on delivering services to rural Zambia rather than rewarding allies. She made a specific appeal on senior civil service posts, asking him “do not use the Permanent Secretary position to reward political friends.”

Dr M’membe said the move to 30 ministries showed the UPND administration was out of touch with the hardship ordinary Zambians face. The country needed a lean and efficient government, he said, and could be run with no more than ten Cabinet portfolios.

Party of National Unity and Progress leader Highvie Hamududu took the opposite view, defending the expansion and saying the additional cost of moving to 30 ministries was minimal.

Citizens First spokesperson Stanley Mhango said the restructuring would swell a public service wage bill he described as already bloated. He said government could not claim to be merging ministries while increasing their number.

“You merge to reduce wage bill, but you increase to blow the wage bill,” Mr Mhango said.

He warned that the wage bill, which he put at 51 per cent, could climb to between 55 and 60 per cent, leaving nothing for development. Mr Mhango also said 70 new constituencies had been created without funding, and that the changes were announced without public consultation.

President Hichilema wished all the ministers well as they took up their duties. Their first major test arrives on 6 November, when government presents the 2027 national budget, the first spending plan the expanded 30-ministry structure will have to fit inside.

World.title: Minister of Health commends local pharmaceuticals companies
World.content:
Minister of Health Professor, Roma Chilengi, has commended local pharmaceutical companies for investing in domestic production.

Professor Chilengi says the developments will create employment opportunities, strengthen the healthcare system and support the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

He said the investments demonstrate Zambia’s ambition to expand local manufacturing is achievable and is already translating into tangible results.

Professor Chilengi was speaking after an inspection tour of V.L. Health Net Services Limited and Medizam Healthcare Limited, local pharmaceutical companies.

He said the investments would also provide opportunities for graduates and future scientists to acquire practical skills and contribute to the country’s economic development.

Professor Chilengi further noted that increased local production would improve the availability of essential medical commodities within the country’s healthcare system.

Meanwhile, Professor Chilengi has announced that Zambia is expected to break ground for the construction of a cholera vaccine manufacturing facility this month, through a partnership between the Zambian and Chinese governments.

He said the Zambian Government, through the Industrial Development Corporation, IDC, would be the majority shareholder in the project.

Professor Chilengi said the initiative demonstrates the Government’s commitment to building local capacity in vaccine production, expressing optimism that Zambia would manufacture its first vaccine in the coming months.

And local Pharmaceutical companies have pledged to continue serving the people of Zambia by making quality healthcare services more accessible and affordable in line with the national vision.
