World.title: Senegal: Senegal's Youth Olympics' Welcome Should Include Everyone
World.content:
guest column

When the Olympic flame is lit in Dakar on October 31, Senegal will become the first African country to host an Olympic event. Nearly 3,000 athletes from 206 countries will compete at the Youth Olympics under the motto “Africa Welcomes, Dakar Celebrates.” Organizers have promised to greet them with teranga, a word that refers to the Senegalese tradition of hospitality, sharing and generosity.

On September 24, Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye told the UN General Assembly: “By welcoming the world’s youth, Senegal will be hosting much more than just a sporting competition.” He said hosting the Youth Olympic Games shows “our differences [are] a strength, our diversity a richness, and our common humanity the foundation of peace.”

These lofty values are, however, in stark contrast to a law adopted in March that provides for a 10-year maximum prison term for consensual same-sex conduct and punishes “promotion” of homosexuality, or financial or other support for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people and organizations.

A new Human Rights Watch report documents rights abuses under the amended law, including mass arrests, forced HIV testing, barriers to accessing legal representation, and degrading detention conditions.



Human rights defenders and lawyers said that the introduction of new offenses of “promotion” or “glorification” of homosexuality has led to fear and anxiety among legal professionals and contributed to an environment in which detainees struggle to secure legal representation.

The impact on LGBT people in Senegal has been devastating. A 22-year-old university student described children following him through his neighborhood singing a Wolof slur while adults looked on. “People started insulting me… I couldn’t even defend myself. I knew if I said something, they would all come after me. To come back home I had to wait until it is dark so no one would notice me,” he said.

Police and Gendarmerie have also tested detainees for HIV without consent, then used positive results to bring additional charges. Although a District court later dropped these charges, such practices have contributed to a broader climate of fear and mistrust around access to HIV-related services.

Health professionals said that the law and the arrests that followed had made people unwilling to seek needed care. “One-third no longer come in for appointments to seek HIV treatment,” a doctor in Dakar told Human Rights Watch. A psychologist at Cheikh Anta Diop University said campus consultations had tripled since March, many of them with young men experiencing severe anxiety, hypervigilance, withdrawal from social life, and obsessive behaviors driven by fear of being perceived and attacked as LGBT.

The new law also puts participants in the upcoming Dakar Youth Olympics, including athletes, staff, and fans -- both residents and visitors at risk.

Globally, many athletes are using the Olympic platform to champion inclusion and diversity, including on issues affecting LGBT people. Many have also openly supported their LGBT teammates, coaches, friends, and family members. At the most recent Winter Olympics in Milan a record 50 out LGBT athletes competed, reflecting that LGBT inclusion has become part of the contemporary Olympic movement.

Senegal’s new law also blatantly contradicts the Olympic Charter, which prohibits “discrimination of any kind” within the Olympic movement, explicitly including discrimination based on sexual orientation. Senegal’s government is a key member of the organizing committee for the Youth Olympics. As part of their agreement with the International Olympic Committee (IOC), Olympic hosts commit to prevent, investigate, and remedy human rights abuses related to the games.

The example of the 2021 Tokyo Olympics showed that the Olympic spirit can inspire governments to act positively on LGBT people’s rights. After promising to welcome the world with “omotenashi,” Japan’s tradition of hospitality, the Tokyo Metropolitan government adopted an anti-discrimination ordinance tied to the Games. A national bill protecting LGBT rights stalled in 2021, but two years later Japan passed its first national law on LGBT rights. Campaigners credit the Olympics with advancing efforts to protect LGBT people from discrimination.

Close 

President Faye has a landmark opportunity to follow Japan’s lead. As the Games open, he should make a public commitment that all participants, visitors and residents will be protected from discrimination and arbitrary arrest. He should order the release of those detained under the LGBT law and refer the law to the

Constitutional Council to review its alignment with the Senegalese Constitution and international human rights obligations.

The IOC should use its close working relationship with Senegal's government to call for action on the LGBT law before the games begin. Senegal can still reverse laws that expose its visitors, human rights defenders, journalists or lawyers to arbitrary arrest, harassment, violence, and discrimination.

One lasting legacy of the Youth Olympics that would be worth cheering is if the “teranga” welcome and safety can start with Senegal’s own citizens--no matter their sexual orientation or gender identity.

Larissa Kojoué is an LGBT rights researcher and Minky Worden is director of global initiatives, at Human Rights Watch.

World.title: Nigeria: Senator Questions Tinubu's Fresh Loan Request, Use of Previous Borrowings
World.content:
"The truth is that we have approved so much funds to be borrowed in the past... ," the senator said.

Anambra Central senator, Victor Umeh, has questioned the federal government's handling of previous loans, asking why contractors executing capital projects are still awaiting payment despite repeated borrowing approvals to fund projects.

Mr Umeh spoke on Channels Television's Politics Today on Tuesday in response to President Bola Tinubu's request for approval to borrow $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion.

He said the government has repeatedly framed borrowing as necessary to fund its budgets, yet it has failed to meet some of its financial obligations.



"The truth is that we have approved so much funds to be borrowed in the past, and on each occasion we've been told that this borrowing would be able to fund the budgets and these budgets have remained unfunded up till this day," he said.

Mr Umeh, who represents Anambra Central Senatorial District in the Nigerian Senate, noted that three budgets were running concurrently, while contractors handling capital projects had yet to receive payments.

"So if you borrow to finance a budget and you are not able to finance that budget, where has the money gone to? That is the question on the lips of everybody," he said.

He also said the latest borrowing request was likely to be approved, arguing that members of the ruling party would outnumber opposition lawmakers.

After reading the president's letter on Tuesday, Mr Akpabio referred the request to the Senate Committees on Local and Foreign Debts and Appropriations for further scrutiny. He directed the committees to report back within one week.

The senate is expected to take a decision on the request based on the recommendations of the committees.

But no loan request from the Tinubu administration has been rejected by the senate. All loan requests have had smooth sailing at the senate with minimal scrutiny.

Fresh borrowing

Mr Tinubu's request for fresh borrowings was contained in a letter read by Senate President Godswill Akpabio during plenary on Tuesday.

The president's letter sought approval to process external loans worth $20,517,755,901 and €1,045,083,643 under the 2026-2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan.

He explained that the funds would finance projects in infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare, education, water supply, security and employment generation, as well as financial management reforms.

According to the president, the projects were selected after technical and economic evaluations and are expected to contribute to the country's socio-economic development.

Close 

He said the borrowing was necessary to address Nigeria's infrastructure deficit and bridge the funding gap.

Mr Akpabio referred the request to the Senate committees on Local and Foreign Debts and Appropriations for consideration, directing them to report back within one week.

Previous borrowing approvals

The latest request follows other borrowing approvals granted by the National Assembly under the Tinubu administration.

In May, lawmakers approved a $516.3 million loan from Deutsche Bank AG for the construction of the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway.

The loan has a nine-year tenure, including a grace period of up to three years. Its interest rate is capped at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate plus 5.3 per cent annually. The facility is backed by insurance from the Islamic Corporation of Investment and Export Credit, the insurance arm of the Islamic Development Bank.

In March, the National Assembly approved a $6 billion external borrowing plan. The package included a $5 billion facility from First Abu Dhabi Bank to support the national budget and a $1 billion export finance facility arranged by Citibank for the rehabilitation of Tin Can Island Port and the Lagos Port Complex.

The latest request comes amid concerns over Nigeria's rising public debt and the cost of servicing government obligations.

The government maintains that borrowing is needed to finance infrastructure and other development projects. But Mr Umeh has questioned whether previous loans have translated into the funding of approved budgets and the payment of contractors.

World.title: Nigeria: Govt, Labour Congress Agree on Allowances, Arrears
World.content:
The Federal Government and the Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC, have reached an agreement on a series of measures to ease the economic difficulties facing workers, including a â¦70,000 transport intervention and the payment of 19 months' arrears owed health workers.

The resolutions were reached at a conciliation meeting held at the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment yesterday, following an earlier meeting convened on October 22.

The meetings were organised to address concerns raised by the NLC over the rising cost of living, the implementation of the National Minimum Wage, petroleum pump prices, workers' welfare and outstanding allowances.

The agreement was signed on behalf of the federal government by Dr. Muhammad Maigari Dingyadi,

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Minister of Labour and Employment; Timi Yakubu, Director-General, Budget; and Dr. Garba Abdul S. U., Permanent Secretary (SWO), Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, while

NLC president, Joe Ajaero, and National Secretary, JNPSNC, Olowoyo Gbenga, stood for labour.

Under the agreement, the federal government will provide a transport intervention of N70,000 across all levels for six months, beginning in November 2026.

The government also approved peculiar allowance with effect from May 1, 2026, while payment of the arrears is expected to begin in November and will be made in three equal monthly instalments.

In addition, the 19 months' outstanding allowances owed health workers is to be paid within three months, beginning in December 2026.

The meeting also agreed that the Minimum Wage Negotiation Committee would be constituted to commence work immediately.

However, the parties remained divided over the effective date for implementing the new minimum wage.

On the issue of tax relief for workers, the meeting resolved that the matter would be referred to the National Executive Council, as taxation is a statutory issue.

Meanwhile, the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security has submitted the list of beneficiaries and the cost implications of the proposed hazard allowance for agricultural officers to the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission for verification.

The verification is expected to be completed within two weeks, after which the commission will issue an implementation template.

Similarly, the NSIWC is expected to complete an updated assessment of the cost implications of the proposed CONHESS adjustment within three weeks.

Close 

The assessment will enable the Presidential Committee on Salaries to take a decision on the matter.

The federal government and NLC urged state and local governments to participate in the intervention process and implement the agreed measures.

The parties also agreed to reconvene after one month to review the level of implementation of the resolutions.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 28, 2026
World.content:
Ex-Wife of Zimbabwe's VP Chiwenga Freed After Seven-Year Trial Delay

Marry Mubaiwa, the former wife of Zimbabwean Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga, has been freed from remand after seven years on trial for allegedly attempting to impede his medical treatment in South Africa. A magistrate ruled that she had suffered mental, physical and financial prejudice due to delays in the proceedings after the State requested another postponement. Mubaiwa was accused of attempting to kill Chiwenga, while he was in hospital in Pretoria. The vice-president then went to China for four months of treatment. Her lawyer welcomed the decision but said it came too late, arguing that Mubaiwa's rights had been violated. Mubaiwa celebrated her release outside court, and said justice had been achieved and that she was proud of her lawyer. The State could still pursue a new trial.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigeria Inquiry Blames Overcrowding for 37 Detainee Deaths

An investigation into the deaths of 37 detainees in Nigeria's Niger State has found that severe overcrowding, poor ventilation, heat stress and dehydration caused acute respiratory failure. The detainees died in September while being held on suspicion of illegal mining. Investigators found that the mining sites were licensed. Fifty people had been held in a small cell without adequate water, sanitation or airflow, while officers allegedly ignored repeated calls for help. Adults and minors were detained together, and some detainees were held beyond lawful detention periods. Authorities have pledged to take legal action against those responsible, and the inquiry recommended compensation for bereaved families and survivors. The investigating committee also recommended $22,285 for each bereaved family and 10m naira for each survivor.

DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Surges Past 10,000 Cases

Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo have reportedly risen to 10,060, with 4,887 deaths since the outbreak was identified in mid-May. The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain its spread. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has described it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. Kenya has reported nine infections, including two deaths. Nigeria also confirmed an infection in a Swiss woman who had visited Uganda. Clinical trials are underway to assess potential antiviral treatments and whether existing Ebola vaccines can protect against the strain. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. It can cause fever, diarrhea, and, in some cases, bleeding.

Egypt Orders Closure of Independent News Website Mada Masr

An Egyptian court has ordered the closure of independent news website Mada Masr after convicting its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, of operating without a licence. Attalah was briefly detained and released after the outlet paid a fine of $53,400. The court also ordered the confiscation of its equipment. Mada Masr, founded in 2013, is one of Egypt's few remaining independent news outlets. It is known for its investigations into corruption, human rights abuses and the powerful role of the military in the country. Mada Masr plans to appeal the ruling, which has drawn condemnation from international press freedom and human rights organisations. The case has intensified concerns about growing restrictions on independent journalism in Egypt, where the outlet has faced years of legal challenges.

Thousands Flee Ethiopia Conflict into Kenya

Approximately 36,000 people have crossed from Ethiopia into Kenya to escape fighting around the border town of Moyale, according to the UN Refugee Agency. The displaced, many of them women and children, urgently need food, clean water, shelter, sanitation and healthcare. Kenya's human rights commission estimates that around 40,000 people have sought refuge in the area, placing pressure on temporary shelters and host communities. The conflict, which spread across seven districts in southern Oromia, followed tensions over a flag dispute and the killing of a 13-year-old girl. Authorities and humanitarian organisations have been urged to coordinate assistance and protect those fleeing the violence.

Close 

Over 100 Reportedly Killed in Sudan Market Drone Strike

More than 100 civilians were reportedly killed in a drone strike on Tangong Market in Nyala, South Darfur, amid escalating attacks across Sudan. The strike also injured numerous people and set parts of the market ablaze, according to reports. Separately, a drone attack on an electricity substation in Omdurman disrupted power supplies across parts of Khartoum, Omdurman and El Gezira, affecting several drinking water stations. The attacks are part of a wider escalation of assaults on markets and civilian infrastructure, with the UN Human Rights Office recording more than 306 deaths from drone strikes in the first three weeks of October. Calls have been made for a humanitarian truce and a permanent ceasefire.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Cases Top 10,000 in DR Congo Ebola Outbreak
World.content:
DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases and nearly 4,900 deaths. The outbreak involves a virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain its spread.

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo reported that Ebola cases had risen to 10,060, with 4,887 deaths since the outbreak was identified in mid-May.

The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has described it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

Where else have cases been reported?

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including two deaths, after a patient traveled from DR Congo through Uganda to the capital, Nairobi.

Nigeria also confirmed an infection in a Swiss woman, the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who fell ill after visiting Uganda. Authorities are investigating where she contracted the virus. She was evacuated to Switzerland.

Why is the outbreak difficult to contain?

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. It can cause fever, diarrhea and, in some cases, bleeding.

Early symptoms can resemble malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment.

The lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment against the Bundibugyo virus further complicates efforts to control the outbreak.

Are vaccines and treatments being tested?

Clinical trials of two antiviral treatment approaches have been underway since July.

Two further trials are investigating whether the Ervebo vaccine can protect against the Bundibugyo virus. The vaccine is currently approved and recommended only against Ebola virus, formerly known as Zaire ebolavirus.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Ethiopia: More Than 50 Detained After Burying Victims of Deadly Attacks On Orthodox Faithful in Ethiopia's Oromia
World.content:
Addis Abeba — More than 50 residents in Shirka Woreda, Southeast Zone (formerly Arsi zone) of Oromia region, have reportedly been detained after burying victims of recent attacks and assisting the wounded, residents told Addis Standard, raising concerns about a security crackdown in the aftermath of the killings.

The detention followed attacks by armed men in Chole and Birbo kebeles that left at least 48 people dead and more than 31 others injured, according to residents who spoke to Addis Standard. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Holy Synod subsequently reported that 60 Orthodox Christians were killed in attacks on 20 and 24 October across two woredas in Southeast Zone (formerly Arsi zone).

Hailu Adugna, head of the Oromia Regional State Communication Bureau, previously blamed an entity referred to as "Tsimdo" for the killings and destruction of property. He alleged that the group was seeking to divert government attention and escalate internal conflict but did not provide detailed information about the circumstances of the attacks or the response by security forces.

Attempts by Addis Standard to contact the regional communication bureau for further comment were unsuccessful.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A resident who requested anonymity said young people who participated in burials or helped transport and treat gunshot victims had been taken into custody. The resident, who was among those detained for 24 hours before being released, said searches and further arrests were continuing.

Although several women had been released, the source said more than a dozen people remained in detention at the time of their account. The grounds for the arrests remained unclear, but detainees were reportedly accused of being "threats to the country."

The resident said some of those arrested had been retrieving bodies or assisting injured people, including 22 gunshot victims. Two of the wounded subsequently died, the source added, while authorities continued searching for young people who had helped treat the injured.

At Tereta Chole Saint Raphael Church, 36 victims were buried on the day of the attack, and another body was buried there the following day, bringing the total buried at the site to 37, according to the resident. Three others were buried at Michael Church in Birbo, one at Kidane Mehret Church, while another person who was referred to Asella Hospital later died.

Another resident of Gobesa town said people who travelled to attend funerals, mourn relatives, or provide assistance were among those arrested, including individuals who had no involvement in the violence.

The resident said women mourning in the streets, some wearing traditional sashes, were also detained. Although some women had since been released, at least 50 people remained in custody at Gobesa Police Station, and roundups continued overnight, the resident alleged.

Those detained included relatives of people killed in the attacks, the source said, questioning why people were being arrested for mourning their dead or helping the wounded.

Residents also expressed fears of further violence, saying people were fleeing their homes with their belongings and livestock amid concerns that armed groups were advancing through the surrounding lowlands.

One resident said the violence in Tereta Chole had persisted since 2024, claiming that more than 200 people had been killed and over 5,000 households displaced from the woreda during that period. Addis Standard could not independently verify these figures.

Residents further alleged that authorities had been warned of a possible attack before 24 October but failed to take preventive measures. Addis Standard could not independently verify these claims.

On 26 October, Addis Standard reported that attacks in Chole and Birbo kebeles on 24 and 25 October had killed at least 48 people and injured more than 31 others. Residents described house-to-house killings, looting, and attacks involving heavy weapons.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Holy Synod subsequently said 60 Orthodox Christians had been killed in attacks on 20 and 24 October across two woredas in Arsi Zone. According to the Synod, 14 people were killed in Gora Silingo, Merti Woreda, on 20 October, while another 46 were killed in the Tereta, Chole, and Birbo areas of Shirka Woreda on 24 October.

The Synod called on government institutions to protect civilians, investigate the killings, and bring those responsible to justice. It also warned of escalating attacks, displacement, and property destruction affecting Orthodox Christian communities in Arsi and other parts of Ethiopia.

Part of a wider pattern of killing in Oromia's Arsi

The latest killings add up to years of attacks against civilians, particularly Orthodox Christian communities, in Arsi Zone of Oromia. Previous attacks have resulted in dozens of deaths, displacement and the destruction or looting of religious properties.

Between 30 May and 1 June 2026, armed attacks in remote farming communities around Teleta Gebriel in Aseko Woreda killed civilians, displaced hundreds of residents into surrounding forests and resulted in the burning of the historic Teleta Saint Gabriel Church and the looting of Kara Kuftena Medhane Alem Church, according to previous reporting by Addis Standard.

Close 

On 15 June, Abayneh Tebeqe, a priest serving at Gado Saint Mary Church in Shirka Woreda, was kidnapped from his farm in Mitana Gado and subsequently killed, according to reports published at the time.

Earlier attacks have also targeted civilians in the area. On 13 August 2024, an attack in Tijo village, Aseko Woreda, left six civilians dead, including a local priest, and three others injured, according to previous Addis Standard reporting. In November and December 2023, separate attacks in Shirka and surrounding areas reportedly killed more than three dozen people, with Orthodox Christian families and worshippers among those targeted.

In July 2026, the Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported that at least 432 civilians and four local militia members had been killed in targeted attacks across East Arsi since 2021/2022. The rights group documented killings, kidnappings for ransom and forced displacement, with Orthodox Christian communities disproportionately affected, according to its report.

The repeated attacks have prompted condemnations from religious leaders and councils, including calls for independent investigations, accountability and measures to protect civilians. Responsibility for these killings has remained elusive, with government officials previously attributing some attacks to the armed group they refer to as "OLF/Shene".

World.title: Africa: Ebola - Survivors Can Transmit Virus Through Sex, but Not Sweat or Saliva - WHO
World.content:
Patrick Otim, programme area manager for emergency response at the WHO Regional Office for Africa, explained the virus in a video answering questions.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) has explained that Ebola survivors may transmit the virus through sexual intercourse if it persists in their semen after recovery. In contrast, survivors who have met the criteria for discharge from treatment are not expected to transmit the virus through sweat or saliva.

Patrick Otim, programme area manager for emergency response at the WHO Regional Office for Africa, explained this in a video answering questions about the virus.

Mr Otim said male survivors should receive counselling on safer sex practices and access to condoms after discharge from treatment centres. He said they should undergo regular semen testing until they obtain two consecutive negative results.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Ebola virus after recovery and for patients with what we call a viral persistence can be transmitted through sexual intercourse," he said.

He explained that the virus could remain in certain parts of the body after clinical recovery, posing a risk of transmission through infected semen.

The WHO recommends that male survivors practise safer sex for 12 months in the absence of a semen-testing programme. Where testing is available, they should undergo regular testing until two consecutive negative results are obtained.

Sweat and saliva

Mr Otim said survivors who had recovered and been discharged from treatment centres could not transmit the virus through sweat or saliva because the virus would have been cleared from their blood.

He said patients were required to have two negative blood tests before discharge, adding that survivors who had met the discharge criteria could not transmit the virus through these fluids.

However, he warned that people who were still actively ill could transmit Ebola through sweat and other bodily fluids.

Outbreak raises concerns

The explanation comes amid an ongoing Ebola outbreak involving the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Kenya.

Nigeria confirmed an imported case on 20 October. The patient, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman living in Abuja, was evacuated to Switzerland with her husband on 26 October.

Although the WHO said Nigeria had no active confirmed cases after the evacuation, health authorities continued monitoring contacts and implementing containment measures.

Close 

In the DRC, the outbreak has recorded 10,060 confirmed cases and 4,887 deaths, according to figures released on Tuesday by the country's Ministry of Public Health.

World.title: Namibia: 'African Journalists Earn Below Basic Living Needs'
World.content:
A survey by the Federation of African Journalists (FAJ) has revealed that 61% of journalists in Africa earn below the minimum needed for basic living, raising concerns about the future of independent journalism and media freedom.

The 2026 report, released on Tuesday with support from Unesco, surveyed 1 586 journalists in 45 African countries, focusing on their working conditions, labour rights, safety, and media freedom.

The findings show significant economic insecurity, with 58% of respondents experiencing delayed salaries and 62% lacking written employment contracts. Additionally, 71% reported inadequate social protection, including no access to pensions or other benefits. Only 4% felt their salaries sufficiently covered essential living costs.

The report warns that poor working conditions threaten editorial independence, investigative reporting, and public accountability. Many journalists continue to work despite months without pay, relying on side jobs, loans and donor support to survive.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

It also found that 41% of respondents faced non-payment, 63% experienced editorial interference, and 57% encountered pressure to change stories.

According to the report, intimidation and political pressure impact media freedom, with 84% of respondents practising self-censorship due to fear of retaliation, dismissal, or other repercussions. Political interference was cited as the top threat to media freedom by 29% of respondents, followed by violence against journalists at 22% and restrictive laws at 18%.

The report further mentioned that safety concerns are prevalent, with 65% reporting threats or intimidation related to their work in the past three years. Only 17% said they always felt safe while reporting, while 55% felt rarely or never safe.

On the challenges faced by women journalists, 76% believe they face additional risks, including workplace discrimination, sexual harassment, online abuse, unequal pay, and exclusion from leadership roles. Meanwhile, 47% have considered leaving journalism due to low pay, insecurity, emotional exhaustion, and worsening conditions.

To address these issues, FAJ called for stronger labour protections, fair wages, written contracts, social security, collective bargaining, and improved safety measures. It also advocates for enhanced digital security training, legal assistance, and workplace policies to protect women journalists from harassment and discrimination.

The survey encompassed five African regions and included journalists from radio, television, print, online media, and other sectors.

Close 

FAJ cautions that these findings reflect broader trends rather than a statistically representative assessment of each country, as participation was voluntary.

- Nampa

World.title: Brewers win World Series for first time in franchise history with Game 5 victory over Rays
World.content:
For the first time in franchise history, the Milwaukee Brewers can call themselves World Series champions.

The Brewers couldn’t get the job done in seven games against the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1982 World Series, and it took them 44 years to get back to the Fall Classic this season.

In Game 5 against the Tampa Bay Bays, one night after getting walked off in the bottom of the 13th inning, the Brewers defeated their AL opponent, 4-1, to claim their title.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Game 4 was a suspenseful thriller, where it seemed like 22-year-old rookie Cooper Pratt would go down in World Series history after belting a top of the 13th solo homer to finally break a 2-2 tie.

But, facing a potential sweep at the hands of the Brewers, who did the same to the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS, the Rays strung together four straight singles in the bottom of the frame to walk off Game 4 and keep their season alive.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

In Game 5, the Brewers didn’t blink despite momentum swinging in the Rays’ favor ever so slightly.

Once again, it was Pratt, three years removed from playing high school baseball in Mississippi, coming through in the clutch with an RBI single in the top of the second inning off Drew Rasmussen, who made a start on short rest given the circumstances, to take a 1-0 lead.

Meanwhile, Jacob Misiorowski, the likely NL Cy Young winner, was dealing triple-digit fastballs the Rays couldn’t handle in the bottom frames. He went 5.2 innings before cramping in the bottom of the sixth inning forced manager Pat Murphy to finally go into his bullpen, which was exhausted in Game 4 due to extra innings. Misiorowski gave up just two hits and one walk, while striking out two.

The Milwaukee bullpen took over with run support, though, as David Hamilton shot an RBI single past a diving Rays defender in the top of the fifth, and two more runs would come across one inning later thanks to another RBI from Pratt on a sac fly and Williams Contreras roping a double to score Christian Yelich.

A 4-0 lead was just what the Brewers needed, as the bullpen continued to get its outs and the suspense this time was felt from Tampa Bay all the way to Wisconsin, where fans were inching closer toward a history-defining victory.

HISTORIC 5TH INNING AND MUCH MORE: BREWERS' WORLD SERIES GAME 3 BY THE NUMBERS

This was a team that had the best record in MLB this regular season at 103-59 despite having a payroll in the middle of the pack (19th overall at $146 million). World.title: Milwaukee Brewers defeat Tampa Bay Rays to claim first World Series title
World.content:
The Milwaukee Brewers’ 57-season wait for a World Series title ended Wednesday as their victory over Tampa Bay completed one of the most dominant postseason runs in MLB history.

Once closer Trevor Megill induced a soft ground ball for the last out and their 4-1 win over the Rays in Game 5 was final, the Brewers rushed up the steps of their dugout and onto the playing field at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida. The celebration had been in the making for more than half a century.

“This is one of the greatest moments of my life,” Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt said on Fox after the game. “Oh my gosh. It doesn’t even feel real. This is surreal.”

After having relocated from Seattle to Milwaukee and played for the first time as the Brewers in 1970, the team didn’t make the World Series until 1982, when it lost in seven games. It then waited 44 years to make its return to the Fall Classic.

Brewers starting pitcher Jacob Misiorowski celebrates after an out during Game 5. Daniel Shirey / MLB Photos via Getty

For a franchise starved for big moments, this year’s team supplied one after another.

The Brewers’ 12-2 postseason record is among the best since the MLB postseason format expanded in 1995 to include wild-card teams. The Brewers’ .857 winning percentage was just off the percentages produced by the 1999 New York Yankees and the 2005 Chicago White Sox, which each went 11-1 en route to their own titles.

“I don’t even have words,” star pitcher Jacob Misiorowski, who threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings of the clinching game, told Fox after the Game 5 win.

Milwaukee is MLB’s smallest market. Its payroll ranked only 19th out of 30 teams. In 12 postseason games, it trailed nine times. But the Brewers won seven of those games by finding ways to prevail in multiple ways. Milwaukee hit seven home runs in a National League Championship Series sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers yet took a 3-0 series lead on Tampa Bay while hitting just one homer. In Game 5, Milwaukee drove in runs using two singles, a sacrifice fly and a double.

Cooper Pratt and Brice Turang embrace after the Brewers defeated the Rays in Game 5. Carmen Mandato / Getty

Down to its final out in the bottom of the ninth inning, Tampa Bay got on the board when Chandler Simpson’s two-out double drove in Liam Hicks to trim the deficit to 4-1. With hard-throwing reliever Aaron Ashby waiting to relieve Megill in case he got into any more trouble, a soft grounder ended the game.

This was no fluke by a scrappy team that got hot at the right time. Milwaukee had the second-best record in baseball at July’s All-Star break and ultimately won an MLB-high and franchise-record 103 games. After it beat San Diego in the divisional round, it swept two-time reigning champion Los Angeles in the National League Championship Series. Even though the Dodgers’ payroll was more than double the Brewers’, Milwaukee scored 10 more runs over the sweep to secure a World Series berth against Tampa Bay.

William Contreras scores in the sixth inning. Rob Tringali / MLB Photos via Getty

The Rays were in some ways a mirror image of Milwaukee, another light-spending franchise looking to turn its regular-season success — the Rays had won the most games in the American League — into its first World Series victory.

“Best feeling ever,” Christian Yelich, the Brewers’ captain, said on the broadcast.

After one-run wins in the first two games of the World Series — including a Game 2 comeback in which Milwaukee fell behind 4-0 in the first inning — it won Game 3 in a 10-1 rout sparked by Christian Yelich’s stolen base in the fifth inning. When a challenge ruled Yelich safe at second base, Milwaukee proceeded to score eight runs with two outs, blowing the game open without ever hitting a home run.

Milwaukee’s championship run was possible thanks to a dependable core of players who spanned generations. Yelich, 34, and 33-year-old reliever Brandon Woodruff, whose save in Game 3 was his first appearance since July 4 because of injuries, were the only players remaining from a 2018 Brewers roster that was just one win away from that season’s World Series.

The Brewers' Jackson Chourio celebrates from the dugout. Daniel Shirey / MLB Photos via Getty

In the divisional round against San Diego, 20-year-old outfielder Jackson Chourio hit a late two-run homer that saved Milwaukee in its opening game of the postseason. Chourio then delivered a walk-off single to win the following game.

On the mound, Milwaukee constructed a feared rotation of arms starting with Misiorowski, the 24-year-old with blazing speed who made the All-Star Game as a rookie in 2025 after just five starts. For his encore, Misiorowski in 2026 led a pitching staff that allowed MLB’s second-lowest team ERA during the regular season. When he left games, a bullpen with arms just as nasty and hard-throwing as Misiorowski’s took over.

“This is just incredible,” Megill, on the mound for the final out, said after the win. “Ten-year-old me would be so proud.”

All of the pieces worked, all season. When the regular season ended, Milwaukee stood alone at the top of the standings.

And when the playoffs ended a month later, the Brewers were on top yet again. Their long wait for a title had ended.

World.title: RFK Jr. takes shortcut to make some unapproved peptides available for use
World.content:
The Department of Health and Human Services is giving compounding pharmacies a temporary green light to make six peptides while the agency continues to work on a formal rule change.

In a notice filed Wednesday, the agency said it would exercise “enforcement discretion,” meaning it will not take legal action against compounding pharmacies that make the six unapproved peptides. In practice, that means these pharmacies can start offering them now, even though the peptides aren’t yet on the Food and Drug Administration’s list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make.

The six peptides are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500.

They’ve been promoted online as treatments for everything from faster healing to younger-looking skin and a longer lifespan. None are approved by the FDA, and the agency’s own scientists concluded there is insufficient data to prove they are safe and effective.

The FDA said compounding pharmacies must certify the identity and purity of the compounds. They must also now report side effects, which was not previously mandated.

The move comes as a growing “gray market” has sprung up around peptides, where retailers sell them labeled “for research use only,” a legal workaround that lets them claim they aren’t meant for humans. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others have argued that allowing peptides to be compounded would move people away from this gray market and toward safer products.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, HHS is working to put prevention and patient safety at the center of health care—and that includes confronting the risks of black-market peptides,” Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said in a statement.

Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official who now leads the Center for Science in the Public Interest watchdog group, said the FDA was essentially “turning a blind eye” to widen access to drugs that have not been proven to work.

Compounding pharmacies generally may use only ingredients the FDA has added to an official list known as the bulk drugs substances list. Adding an ingredient requires the FDA to propose a rule, take public comment and issue a final rule, a process that can take several months.

The agency took a step toward that process in July, when an FDA advisory panel narrowly voted in favor of adding six peptides to the bulk list. The panel included six new appointees with ties to the peptide industry and another who is the son of a U.S. representative who has pushed Kennedy to make peptides more available. (During that meeting, some committee members expressed concerns that the recommendation could make it harder for the FDA to say no to other unapproved drugs in the future.)

On Tuesday and Wednesday, the FDA was scheduled to meet outside groups, including Medivant Healthcare, a compounding pharmacy that offers peptides, according to Reginfo.gov, a federal website that tracks government regulations.

Shabbir Safdar, executive director of the Partnership for Safe Medicines, which researches the dangers of counterfeit medicines, said both the enforcement discretion and upcoming rule change would expose Americans to “untested, dangerous substances.”

“Imagine what it means for the nation’s top drug regulator to announce they won’t enforce the laws on people making completely untested compounds and distributing them to the public,” Safdar said.

World.title: Manhunt grows for escaped murderer who may have left area where truck was ditched
World.content:
Jacob Morley, a convicted killer on the loose since Sunday, has no known connection to the small Illinois town where the truck he is accused of stealing was found, the police chief said Wednesday.

“What we have seen kind of leads us in the direction that he’s not still here. But that doesn’t mean that we’ve stopped looking,” Marion Police Chief David Fitts said.

Morley, 28, convicted of killing a co-worker in 2022, was serving a life sentence when he escaped from Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, sometime before 11:30 p.m. Sunday, officials there said.

Morley had stolen a work truck, and early Tuesday that truck was found behind a business in Marion, a town of around 16,000 that is around 100 miles north of Tiptonville, authorities in Marion and Tennessee said.

Security video captured Morley driving away in a flatbed truck.

There have been no reports in Marion of any other stolen vehicles, and there was no evidence around the truck that was found, Fitts said.

There have also been no confirmed sightings, he said.

“There’s really nowhere for him to go here where he wouldn’t be recognized. His face is all over the news,” Fitts said.

Morley has no known connection to Marion or southern Illinois, he said.

“Have no idea why he would come here, other than I-57 is a major interstate and it runs right through the middle of our town,” Fitts said. “And I don’t know, maybe he was low on gas and just pulled off. I don’t know.”

Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary after a trial in February 2025. He also pleaded guilty to theft of property.

He was accused of shooting Cody Birchfield in the back of the head in 2022, according to court documents. Birchfield’s body was found in a large metal box under Morley’s residence, the documents say.

Birchfield’s sister, Carrie Norman, said Wednesday that “it feels like a scary movie.”

The family, she said, “have to go back through the experience — once again. Once again, because you don’t know where he’s at, but you know what he’s capable of.”

Also Wednesday, the reward for information leading to Morley’s arrest increased from $2,500 to $15,000, a combined sum from the Tennessee governor’s office, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Marshals Service, the bureau said.

Fitts said he wished Morley had been caught, but he urged people not to take things into their own hands.

“This is really frustrating that we can’t find him. Somebody will eventually, I have no doubt in my mind. I wish it was us so we could catch him now,” Fitts said. “But, and I just want to let our people know that, again, don’t approach him. Call 911. We’ll handle it.”

Around 11:30 p.m. Sunday, prison staff members confirmed that Morley was unaccounted for and conducted an emergency count and search of the facility, the Tennessee Department of Correction said.

Security video showed Morley “breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform,” the department said.

The department has not given more details about how the escape occurred, which it said Wednesday is under investigation.

World.title: California judge denies Trump DOJ request to segregate alleged noncitizen ballots
World.content:
A federal judge in California on Wednesday refused the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots from individuals it alleges are noncitizens.

“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” U.S. District Judge David Carter wrote. “If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.”

What the administration was asking for, he wrote, “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”

He also questioned whether the government’s claims of over 20,000 noncitizen voters were accurate.

“Given the vagueness of Plaintiff’s descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiff’s process is credible,” Carter wrote, pointing to similar allegations the administration had made in a neighboring state.

“In Nevada, DHS initially identified up to 15,903 registered voters as noncitizens based on ‘high-confidence’ matches, but later reduced that number to 6,218, and then to 185 after conducting its manual review. Nevada officials later confirmed that all 185 individuals were citizens,” the judge wrote.

“Had Nevada officials accepted Plaintiff’s allegations there as true, 185 citizens would have been deprived of their vote. This Court will not deprive Californians who have met the requirements for voter registration of their fundamental right because of Plaintiff’s unfounded allegations.”

The Justice Department filed the suit Oct. 15, seeking a court order that the state “set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens” and not count them until their citizenship is confirmed.

The department said it had compiled “a list of over 20,000 names of people” the government “believes are likely non-citizens.”

Attorneys for the state countered that the government’s numbers are unreliable. In a July letter, it put the number of suspect voters at 190,000 and has refused to release information about how it has generated its lists.

“Where is the evidence?” an attorney representing California, Christina McCall, said at the hearing Tuesday, calling the government’s allegations “vague” and “not reliable.”

Another attorney for the state, Anne Bellows, told the judge “the stakes here are enormous,” arguing the government was trying to force California to initiate an unclear investigation into the citizenship of tens of thousands of people without any clear standards shortly before an election.

It “is a recipe for disenfranchisement,” Bellows said.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli told Carter: “We’re not telling California what they have to do. We’re telling them what they can’t do.”

Essayli said that once the state is made aware of potential noncitizens on its voter rolls, “they need to do something.”

“What they cannot do is do nothing and proceed to count the votes,” he said.

The judge said that if the government believes there is noncitizen voting, which is a crime, it should bring charges.

“Don’t you have the power of indictments?” Carter asked Essayli. “You brought 28 indictments,” he said, referring to a recent announcement by prosecutors of people who have been found to have voted illegally in California in recent years. “You may find others. You have the right to bring that indictment against them.”

“You’ve got a remedy, for goodness’ sakes,” Carter said. “Go out and indict.”

Essayli on Wednesday bashed the judge’s ruling and said an appeal is underway.

“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” he said in a statement. “The Solicitor General authorized an immediate appeal. We filed our Notice of Appeal and will immediately seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit.”

The Justice Department has already been to a federal appeals court once in the case. It filed a motion to expedite the case to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last week, after Carter did not act on its request to rule in the matter by Thursday.

The appeals court held an emergency hearing Sunday and ruled against the administration 2-1 on Monday.

The majority found it did not have jurisdiction because Carter had not yet ruled, but it found the government’s “claimed emergency” was at least partly “a self-constructed one.”

“At least part of the delay here is attributable to the United States’s own delay in filing suit,” Circuit Judge Mark Bennett wrote in the ruling.

“The United States has taken issue with California’s voter rolls since at least July 16, when it sent a letter to California’s secretary of state citing its ‘[p]reliminary’ analysis of California’s voter rolls. And neither California’s law permitting the processing of ballots twenty-nine days before an election, nor its law providing for the issuance of mail-in ballots to registered voters, is new,” he wrote.

Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in a concurring opinion that the government was asking the “court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike.”

The dissenting judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, wrote, “We should’ve granted the federal government relief — federal law precludes California from commingling ballots likely cast by aliens with legitimate ballots, because it encourages and induces illegal voting.”

World.title: Hayden Panettiere’s death is ruled accidental and police investigation is closed
World.content:
Actor Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled an accident and the case is now closed, police in South Carolina announced Wednesday.

“Based on the Medical Examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental,” Greenville police said, noting the investigation has concluded.

Panettiere, 36, the actor who starred in the shows “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was found unresponsive on Aug. 16 in a South Carolina apartment complex where she was staying.

Last month, the Greenville County Coroner’s Office ruled her death an accident caused by the toxic effects of multiple drugs: fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine.

The coroner said there were no signs of trauma that would have contributed to her death. Police also have said no signs of foul play were found during the initial response and investigation.

Panettiere, who had publicly discussed her struggle with addiction, had been in rehab just weeks before, according to the coroner’s report.

Panettiere’s on-again, off-again boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, was at the apartment complex at the time of her death. He showed police a “bag of medication” he said she was taking at the time, according to the police report.

After the coroner’s report was issued, Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, called her daughter a “fighter” who was “transparent with her addictions and her numerous rehab attempts show her resolve to live a healthy life.”

Vogel also said at the time that she had “never heard Hayden speak of fentanyl.”

The Drug Enforcement Administration was also investigating, a source familiar with the probe previously told NBC News. The agency typically looks into the narcotics involved in a case, how they were obtained and whether any laws were broken in procuring the drugs.

Panettiere entered Hollywood as a child actor and later carved her own path, starring in the films “Remember the Titans,” “Ice Princess” and “Bring It On: All or Nothing.”

In her memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” she detailed how her life began to spiral after she had a daughter with Ukrainian heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She began drinking heavily to cope with postpartum depression and Klitschko’s distance, she wrote in the book.

She checked into rehab and gave Klitschko custody of their child in 2018.

In the book, she also discussed grappling with pain and grief after her brother, Jansen Panettiere, died in 2023 from an undiagnosed heart condition.

If you or someone you know is struggling with a drug or substance abuse problem, call these numbers for help: The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s national helpline is 1-800-662-HELP (1-800-662-4357); the National Drug Helpline is 1-844-289-0879; and the American Addiction Centers’ hotline is (866) 464-3073.

World.title: Meet the Democrats trying to flip the script on gun rights: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Frank Thorp V and Ryan Nobles speak with Democratic candidates who are touting their gun credentials. Plus, Andrea Mitchell digs into President Donald Trump’s potential next moves on Iran.

— Adam Wollner

Meet the Democrats trying to flip the script on gun rights

By Frank Thorp V and Ryan Nobles

A group of Democratic candidates on the ballot next week are hoping to start a new conversation around guns as part of a strategy to win back rural voters in red-leaning areas.

Wisconsin’s 1st District: Democrat Mitchell Berman’s ads have portrayed him as a proud gun owner and hunter. One shows him fishing while wearing a handgun in a holster; another shows him skeet shooting with clay pigeons labeled “Data Centers.” After the target explodes in the air, his 6-year-old daughter yells, “Great shot, Dad!”

“That’s who I am,” Berman told NBC News. “When I go fishing up north — where I’m from we have wolves. We have — in spring trout season, we have bears that are coming out of their dens with cubs. We’ve even had a mountain lion on our trail camera. So, you know, when I go out into the woods, I carry a sidearm with me for protection.”

His race against GOP Rep. Bryan Steil was not expected to be close. President Donald Trump carried the district in 2020 and 2024, and Steil won re-election two years ago by 10 points. But polling has shown the race is within reach for Democrats.

Texas’ 15th District: Bobby Pulido, a Tejano singer-turned-Democratic congressional candidate, is not shy about his love for guns and hunting. He’s posted videos of him shooting a target a mile away, and his rec room is lined with the trophies he’s gathered on hunts. He even named his oldest son Remington.

“Listen, in the rural areas, firearms are a way of life,” Pulido told NBC News, saying that fundraisers in the Rio Grande Valley are more common at skeet shooting events than at golf courses.

Pulido is also running in an area that Trump won in the last two presidential elections. The district was redrawn earlier this year to make it more favorable for Republicans, but a shift in the Latino vote away from Trump mixed with a struggling economy has put Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz at risk of losing her bid for re-election.

Read more →

The big decision awaiting Trump after the midterms

Analysis by Andrea Mitchell

On the campaign trail, President Donald Trump has been confidently promising that oil prices will drop like a rock after the midterms — especially skyrocketing diesel fuel critical in farm states that could decide which party wins the Senate. Implicit is that he will attempt to do something decisive after next week to end the war against Iran and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

His not-so-subtle hints are backed up by new reporting in The Wall Street Journal and other publications that the U.S. has told Gulf partners it will resume intense, brief strikes against Iran after the midterms. And Israel’s hawkish Trump ally Benjamin Netanyahu has at least temporarily retained a caretaker role as prime minister while he and his rival, former Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, jockey for a majority. In Israel’s complex parliamentary system, a decisive outcome could take weeks or months, or even lead to another election.

That places Netanyahu in control of a potential resumption of the war, a position he had advocated for before Israelis went to the polls, according to The New York Times and other outlets. According to those reports, Israel’s military and intelligence leaders effectively vetoed that option, saying it would politicize their decision-making.

As flawed as Israel’s democracy has been in many respects, according to many of its own citizens and even many longtime U.S. supporters, it still has the virtue of a largely independent military. But in the U.S., critics fear that may not be the case with the civilian leadership of the military in the second Trump administration.

In past administrations in both political parties, secretaries of defense and their top deputies were usually experienced foreign policy or former military leaders, willing to offer independent opinions to the presidents they served in a formalized National Security Council interagency system. Conflicting options were debated in a deliberative process before they were presented to the commander in chief.

Yes, on occasion, chief executives were misled by false narratives, like those delivered during the Vietnam War by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara. Or, during the Iraq quagmire, when the chain of command was short-circuited by a powerful personality like President George W. Bush’s defense secretary, Donald Rumsfeld. Notably, Rumsfeld was forced out of his role the morning after Bush’s party got hammered in the 2006 midterms.

Now, whether his party wins or loses in next week’s midterms, Trump faces what could be the most consequential decision of his second term: whether to “finish the job” and resume attacking Iran.

Such a decision would fly in the faces of European leaders who counsel that renewed strikes would lead to higher oil prices and a potential economic downturn and not produce a more compliant regime in Tehran. At the same time, there is now a growing consensus in Riyadh and other Gulf capitals that they need to find some accommodation with Iran to get the regime to try to restrain its Houthi proxies, who threaten to become an existential threat to their economies.

The question for Trump is whether to follow the advice of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the former Fox News personality who has purged many of the Pentagon’s most experienced top generals and has privately advocated for resuming military action against Iran.

The hawks could be right that a weakened Iran could be felled by a decisive blow, though skeptics note that such a strategy has not yet proved successful. The U.S. and global economy — to say nothing of Trump’s legacy — may well depend on what he decides in the next few weeks.
