World.title: Argentina confirms Bolsonaro crossed via Iguazú before flying to Miami
World.content:
Argentina confirms Bolsonaro crossed via Iguazú before flying to Miami

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 14:50 UTC Full article

The migration agency’s statement does not say who organised the journey or mention any government involvement

Argentina’s government confirmed that Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated in Sunday’s presidential runoff and barred by a court from leaving Brazil, entered Argentina at Puerto Iguazú with his family before flying to the United States on a private plane. Bolsonaro landed on Wednesday morning at Opa-locka Executive Airport in Miami.

“The National Migration Directorate reports that at 22:50 on 27/10, citizens Flavio Nantes Bolsonaro, Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro entered through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge border crossing in Misiones province,” the agency said in a statement released at 2.01 a.m. on Wednesday. It added that they did so “with valid travel documents and without any legal impediment”. The bridge links Foz do Iguaçu with Puerto Iguazú, and Brazil does not check departures at that crossing, according to the newspaper La Nación.

On Tuesday morning, the migration agency had said it had no record of the senator entering, and presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier denied there had been any asylum request. The crossing took place that night. About 40 minutes later, the family boarded a Gulfstream G400 belonging to Argentine company Baires Fly, which had been waiting at Puerto Iguazú airport since Monday. The plane took off after midnight, made a refuelling stop in Guayaquil, Ecuador, and reached Miami at around 9.20 a.m. on Wednesday, according to Reuters. According to El País, citing the flight manifest, Bolsonaro travelled on his Italian passport, which Judge Alexandre de Moraes had also ordered him to surrender.

The migration agency’s statement does not say who organised the journey or mention any government involvement. Neither the presidency nor Baires Fly immediately responded to press inquiries. Argentine opposition lawmakers had asked the government on Tuesday to clarify whether Bolsonaro used Argentine territory to leave Brazil.

The senator is under investigation at the Supreme Federal Court for alleged money laundering and currency evasion together with a lawyer friend linked to betting companies; both deny wrongdoing. His term ends at the end of the year, when he will lose his parliamentary immunity. The US State Department has said it will grant visas to him and his family.

Javier Milei’s government, which backed Bolsonaro during the campaign, has not congratulated President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on his re-election. “There will be no statement,” it said.

World.title: Dozens killed as two high-speed trains collide in Spain
World.content:
Dozens killed as two high-speed trains collide in Spain

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 14:14 UTC Full article

The collision occurred shortly before 9 a.m. at kilometre 118 of the line

At least 68 people were killed on Wednesday when a Renfe AVE high-speed train ran into the back of an Iryo train that was stopped on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda station, in the province of Toledo, according to the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page. Another 58 people were hospitalised, 15 of them in very serious condition, and authorities fear the death toll will rise.

The collision occurred shortly before 9 a.m. at kilometre 118 of the line. According to García-Page, 24 of the dead were travelling in the lead carriage of the AVE and 44 on the Iryo train, two of whose carriages were destroyed. The Military Emergencies Unit deployed 200 personnel to search for people trapped in the wreckage, and medical helicopters flew the most seriously injured to hospitals in Toledo and Alcázar de San Juan.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that at around 8.30 a.m. the LZB control and safety system failed due to a communication fault in three computers, leaving a 63-kilometre stretch without it and automatically stopping six trains. The control centre of rail infrastructure manager Adif at Madrid’s Atocha station then took over and authorised the AVE to resume running normally, despite a red signal and with no speed restriction, according to the minister. The train travelled about 25 kilometres at close to 200 kilometres per hour before the impact. Puente added that the driver of another train corrected the controller, telling him the order should be to proceed “on sight”, at a maximum of 40 kilometres per hour.

“A rear-end collision on the Spanish network is truly implausible,” said Puente, who described the control centre’s decision as “inexplicable” and ruled out resigning for now. The Civil Guard and the Railway Accident Investigation Commission are questioning the operator who was managing traffic.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who travelled to the scene, declared three days of official mourning. “We will get to the bottom of this and, if there has been negligence, it will be known,” he said. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” he added, referring to the Adamuz crash in Córdoba, which killed 46 people in January. The high-speed line between Madrid and Andalusia remains suspended with no date for reopening, and the train drivers’ union Semaf kept in place a strike called for Thursday over rail safety.

World.title: Adderstone builds on the foundations of hangar success with new Stanley House contract
World.content:
Adderstone builds on the foundations of hangar success with new Stanley House contract

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 10:28 UTC Full article

M. Wallbank (Managing Director), G. Vatamanu (General Foreman) and Natasha Greenland (General Manager), Adderstone Co. (Falkland Islands) Ltd, outside the newly completed FIGAS hangar, Port Stanley.

Adderstone Construction (Falkland Islands) Limited, part of the Newcastle-headquartered property and construction group, has been awarded a further contract by the Falkland Islands Government, shortly after completing the redevelopment of the FIGAS aircraft hangar in Port Stanley.

The redevelopment gives the islands' air taxi service a hangar built for the long term, keeping communities connected to schools, farms and medical care.

Work is now underway on Adderstone's next Falkland Islands Government contract: upgrading residential amenities at Stanley House. Built in 1878, it is one of Stanley's oldest and most prestigious buildings, and since 1981 it has been where children from the islands' farms and settlements live while they attend secondary school. Children on remote farms,some more than 200 miles from Stanley, are taught at home by travelling teachers until secondary school age. At that point, many move to Stanley and board at Stanley House if their families live too far away to travel each day.

Both projects reflect Adderstone's growth strategy in the Falklands: long-term investment in the infrastructure and buildings that matter to island communities. Stanley House plays a role in island education every bit as vital to daily life as the hangar itself.

Martyn Wallbank, Managing Director of Adderstone's Falkland Islands division, said: “We see our relationship with the Falkland Islands Government as a lasting one, and it rests on doing what we say we'll do. We said we'd deliver on the hangar, and we have. We'll deliver Stanley House in exactly the same way.”

Colin Summers, Director of Public Works, Falkland Islands Government, said: “Adderstone delivered the hangar project on time and to the required standard, and that performance speaks for itself.

“We’re building a longer-term partnership with our delivery partners, including Adderstone, focussed on the essential infrastructure and upgrades that make a genuine difference to life on the islands.

“The FIGAS hangar and Stanley House are examples of that, and we hope there are many more in the future.”

Natasha Greenland, General Manager for Adderstone's Falkland Islands division, added: “I've lived here my whole life, and my family's been here for generations before me.

”That’s why both of these projects matter so much to me - and to families here. They’re about keeping islanders connected to each other, and now, giving children from across the islands a better place to call home while they get their education. That means the world to me, and it’s exactly why we’ll make sure we get this one right too.”

Adderstone's Falkland Islands division is part of a wider Group with operations across the UK and internationally, spanning affordable housing, civil engineering, construction, commercial property management and fit-out.

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil despite a court ban and the US will grant him a visa
World.content:
Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil despite a court ban and the US will grant him a visa

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 09:17 UTC Full article

A State Department official confirmed that visas would be issued for the senator and his family

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated on Sunday by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the presidential runoff, left Brazil with his wife and two daughters despite a Supreme Federal Court order barring him from leaving the country, and the US State Department confirmed it will grant them visas. According to the newspaper O Globo, he arrived in Miami on Tuesday night.

A State Department official confirmed that visas would be issued for the senator and his family, without specifying the type. Mexican lawyer Simón Levy, who is close to President Donald Trump, said Washington had authorised political asylum, which the US government has not confirmed. His brother Eduardo Bolsonaro lives in Florida, having moved to the United States in 2025, and faces a final arrest warrant in Brazil after being sentenced to four years and two months in prison for coercion in the case against their father.

Judge Alexandre de Moraes had given Bolsonaro 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering through online betting companies, which also involves a lawyer friend of the senator. The deadline expired at 11 a.m. on Tuesday and the Federal Police cancelled his ordinary and diplomatic passports. His exit route has not been officially confirmed. Argentina’s National Migration Directorate, after inspecting a private plane at Iguazú airport highlighted by the press, said its paperwork was in order and that no flight plan including the Bolsonaro family had been submitted. Argentine presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier said there had been no request for asylum.

On Monday, Bolsonaro had said he would hand over his passports and defend himself against “this farce”, and that his place was “beside the Brazilian people”. That same day, Supreme Court Judge Flávio Dino ordered the Federal Police to investigate possible foreign financing of his campaign, following complaints about contributions from Rockbridge Network, a network of US conservative donors founded by Vice President JD Vance, and alleged manipulation of social media algorithms. The senator is also under investigation over his links with banker Daniel Vorcaro, jailed over the Banco Master case.

“A citizen who sneaks out of his country must owe something. Leaving Brazil is shameful,” Lula said on Tuesday at a celebration of his 81st birthday. “He could have stayed here and shown that the accusations were not true,” he added.

Bolsonaro never formally recognised his defeat, although his Liberal Party accepted the result. His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also travelled to Florida after losing the 2022 election, two days before Lula’s inauguration, and stayed there until late March 2023. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 5, 2027.

World.title: Trump suggests Venezuela become the 51st US state and elect a governor
World.content:
Trump suggests Venezuela become the 51st US state and elect a governor

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 03:36 UTC Full article

“We’re bringing out a lot of oil for ourselves, a lot. It will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe someday soon it will become a prosperous 51st state. That’s possible,” Trump said

US President Donald Trump suggested on Tuesday that Venezuela become the 51st US state and that its citizens elect a governor instead of a president, at a rally at the port of Corpus Christi, Texas, where he announced the arrival of the first shipment of one million barrels of Venezuelan oil obtained under an agreement between Washington and Caracas.

“We’re bringing out a lot of oil for ourselves, a lot. It will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe someday soon it will become a prosperous 51st state. That’s possible,” Trump said, standing beside an oil tanker at an event backing Republican candidates a week before the November 3 midterm elections. “Let’s make it. Let’s make it the 51st state. And instead of a president, we’ll have an election for a governor. How about that? You know, they have a lot of oil.”

The president thanked Venezuela for a relationship he described as “very, very good” and presented the shipment as “a historic win that gives us control over a massive part of the world’s oil supply”. The crude, which Trump described as free, will be refined in Texas, including in Corpus Christi. “Billions and billions of dollars are now being invested by the biggest oil companies,” he added.

It is not the first time Trump has raised annexing Venezuela. In February he said it could become the 53rd state, after Canada and Greenland, and in August he shared a map of the country in the colours of the US flag with the caption “51st state”. Acting President Delcy Rodríguez has rejected the idea on several occasions; in July she said Venezuela has more than two centuries of sovereignty.

The remarks come amid close cooperation between the two governments. After the US military operation on January 3 that removed Nicolás Maduro from power, now jailed and on trial in New York, Washington recognised Rodríguez’s government, lifted sanctions on her and her brother, National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez, and in August sealed an oil agreement giving it majority control over a significant share of Venezuela’s reserves. The State Department has said that under the roadmap negotiated with the opposition, Rodríguez should leave the presidency vacant in 2027, although the presidential election still has no date.

The rally came two days after opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela after nearly ten months abroad. Trump said he hoped Machado “is safe”, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington had urged Rodríguez to allow her return. The acting president called the opposition leader’s arrival a “show”.

World.title: Latin America’s energy inflation reaches its highest level in a year
World.content:
Latin America’s energy inflation reaches its highest level in a year

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 03:30 UTC Full article

The study, based on data from the statistics institutes and central banks of member countries, shows energy inflation exceeded the previous high for the period, 8.03% in June

Annual energy inflation in Latin America and the Caribbean accelerated to 8.33% in August, its highest level in twelve months, and pressure on fuel prices continued in September and October, when diesel prices matched petrol for the first time, according to a report by the Latin American Energy Organization (OLADE) published by the Energy Report website.

The study, based on data from the statistics institutes and central banks of member countries, shows energy inflation exceeded the previous high for the period, 8.03% in June. Overall inflation in the region rose from 4.17% in July to 4.43% in August. The report links the acceleration to the resumption of hostilities between Iran and the United States in July, after a fragile ceasefire in June.

Diesel has risen faster than petrol. In August, its regional average price rose 2.5% to US$1.31 per litre, almost four times the increase in petrol, which rose 0.6% to US$1.38. In October, both fuels reached US$1.41 per litre, the highest level of the year. Since February, diesel has risen 26% compared with 18% for petrol, and the report expects it could overtake petrol in the coming weeks. Its rising cost has a particular impact on freight and passenger transport, farm machinery and the distribution of goods.

WTI crude averaged US$83.90 per barrel in August, US$97.31 in September and around US$98.29 in October. The report warns that the pass-through of crude prices to fuel is asymmetric: international increases are passed on quickly, while decreases are reflected with a delay or only partially, due to inventories, retail margins, taxes, subsidies and local price stabilisation mechanisms.

World.title: Trade negotiations between Mexico and India have officially started
World.content:
India and Mexico signed the Terms of Reference (ToR) for negotiations on a Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) on Monday, as the two nations seek to expand bilateral trade and investment.

Mexico’s Deputy Minister of Foreign Trade Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez Romano and India’s Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal signed the ToR, which sets out a roadmap for negotiations, during Agrawal’s official visit to Mexico.

The move advances an understanding reached by President Claudia Sheinbaum and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Canada in June 2025 to strengthen the bilateral partnership.

“India and Mexico are ready to turn untapped potential into tangible prosperity through balanced, ambitious and mutually beneficial negotiations,” the Indian Embassy wrote on the X social media site on Monday.

The proposed agreement includes key areas, such as market access for goods, rules of origin, customs procedures, trade facilitation, dispute settlement, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade and trade remedies.

Both countries are aiming to develop a “mutually beneficial and balanced PTA,” India’s Department of Commerce stated, emphasizing that Mexico is an important market for Indian exporters and investors.

Merchandise trade between India and Mexico totaled US$8.74 billion in 2024, with $5.73 billion in Indian exports and $3.01 billion in Mexican exports, resulting in a $2.72 billion trade differential, according to data from the Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics.

The development of a PTA will help expand bilateral trade, create business opportunities, boost investment flows and strengthen supply chains. Potential areas of cooperation include automobiles, chemicals, electronics, pharmaceuticals, agri-food, energy, critical minerals, medical devices and advanced manufacturing.

In a February meeting between Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and India’s Ambassador to Mexico Pankaj Sharma, the two officials also highlighted the need to foster greater cooperation in priority sectors such as science, technology and digitalization.

During the recent visit, Gutiérrez Romano and Agrawal discussed a potential Mexican business mission to India in the first quarter of 2027 to help identify commercial opportunities and further strengthen ties.

In 2024, India’s primary exports to Mexico included light vehicles, with a value of US $880 million, motorcycles ($390 million), base metals ($760 million), auto parts ($740 million), mechanical machinery ($460 million) and textiles and clothing ($410 million).

Meanwhile, Mexico’s main exports to India included crude petroleum oil ($1.7 billion), smartphones ($270 million), and gold ($170 million).

With reports from CNCV TV18

World.title: After its success in Mexico, Airbnb’s free medical stays will expand under a new funding model
World.content:
After a successful pilot year in Mexico, Airbnb will will allocate US $500 million over the next five years to expand its provision of free accommodations for people experiencing medical emergencies, natural disasters or domestic violence company CEO Brian Chesky announced on Tuesday.

Building on a new funding model similar to the one used in Mexico, the independent non-profit arm of the online rental platform, under the name Airbnb.org (rather than simply Airbnb), will establish a $500 million fund by contributing 10 cents of its own revenue for every stay booked on the platform, without increasing prices for travelers or reducing payments to hosts.

The dime per stay may not sound like much, but the cumulative effect is significant. “We tried to go as far as we could imagine,” said Chesky. “It’s a significant percentage of the company’s annual earnings.”

Airbnb.org has provided approximately 6,300 free nights in Mexico for various emergency situations, around 1,500 of which were for medical stays, according to Chesky.

The program also works with 20 non-profit organizations in Mexico, including Fundación IMSS, Ronald McDonald House Charities Mexico and Lilo Foundation Mexico, to meet the needs of families of patients requiring specialized care who must relocate to the capital, since almost 40% of the country’s specialized medical care facilities care oncentrated in Mexico City.

The program “was successful because the families were really satisfied with the service, and we felt there was enough demand to expand it,” said Chesky.

In May, Airbnb.org announced a $1.1 million contribution to expand its medical stay program in Mexico for three years. This was before the new 10 cents-per-stay fund.

The roots of Airbnb’s accommodations initiative go back to 2012, when a New York host offered her home to people displaced by Hurricane Sandy, encouraging other hosts around the world to do the same in subsequent disasters. Airbnb.org was formalized in 2020, and has had a globall reach even before the newly annunced initiative.

The new funding model launched on Tuesday is expected to serve more than 20 countries. The contributions will only apply to completed stays, not reservations canceled before check-in or to Airbnb Experiences or Services. The goal is to reach 1 million free nights per year for the next four or five years.

With reports from Expansión

World.title: Ebrard: More than US $8B in data center projects in the works
World.content:
Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Tuesday that companies have announced plans to invest more than US $8 billion in data center projects in Mexico.

Speaking to reporters after an event in Mexico City, Ebrard said that the planned data center projects are proceeding as expected.

Various companies have recently announced plans to build new data centers in Mexico.

They include Mexican company KIO, which announced it would invest up to $1.3 billion to develop a new data center in Querétaro, and U.S. company Cloud HQ, which plans to invest an estimated $4.8 billion to build six data centers and complementary infrastructure on a single site in Querétaro. The latter project is currently under development.

Querétaro is Mexico’s main data center hub, but it’s not the only state attracting investment in the booming sector.

The Guanajuato government said in September that the state had attracted $630 million in data center investment, while in New York earlier this month, Nuevo León Governor Samuel García said he had secured US $600 million in investment to develop industrial facilities, primarily data centers, in his state.

On Tuesday, Ebrard said that investment in data centers in Mexico will allow the country to strengthen its technological capabilities and its participation in the development of artificial intelligence.

“What we’re experiencing is an epochal shift and data centers are a significant part of that,” he said, referring to the rise of AI.

Ebrard acknowledged that the operation of data centers requires additional electricity infrastructure. He said that data center companies are working with the Federal Electricity Commission to ensure adequate power supply. Ebrard said that private investment in electricity projects related to data centers could reach around $400 million.

The economy minister also said that data center cooling systems use less water than they used to. He indicated that Mexican authorities are open to more data center investment in the country.

“I think we’re going to continue encouraging their installation and operation in our country,” Ebrard said.

For her part, President Claudia Sheinbaum said in August that Mexico needs data centers “to advance in artificial intelligence.”

But, she added, “Mexico does not necessarily have to be the data center [hub] for other parts of the world, because [their operation] requires high energy and water consumption.”

According to an Energy Ministry (SENER) report published in August, there were 170 data centers in operation in Mexico in 2023 and 200 in 2025. That number is projected to rise to 230 in 2027 and 243 in 2029.

“The sustained growth of this infrastructure is driven by the increase in data traffic, industrial digitization, and the expansion of cloud services,” SENER said in its report, titled “Energy Efficiency in Data Centers: Challenges, Trends and Opportunities.”

“Querétaro has established itself as the country’s leading hub, thanks to its geographic location, energy availability, and fiber-optic connectivity,” the ministry said.

“This development has spurred the creation of specialized technology parks and attracted foreign direct investment, primarily from U.S., European, and Asian companies. However, it has also created new challenges in terms of electricity capacity, water supply, and sustainable energy management, underscoring the need to incorporate energy efficiency into the planning and design of these facilities,” SENER said.

With reports from Milenio and Vanguardia Industrial

World.title: El Jalapeño: Uber to replace canceled Tulum flights with 22-hour drive in a Nissan Versa
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original articles here and here.

TULUM, Quintana Roo — In a bold display of logistical agility, ride-hailing giant Uber announced Friday that it will step in to replace canceled commercial airline routes to Tulum by dispatching drivers in 2018 Nissan Versas for direct, 22-hour interstate road trips from the United States.

The move comes after major carriers, including American Airlines, Aeroméxico and Volaris, announced reductions or pauses in service to Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport, leaving thousands of vacationers searching for alternative flight arrangements to the Quintana Roo resort town.

Under the company’s newly launched “UberLongHaul” tier, passengers stranded in hub cities like Miami, Charlotte or Atlanta can bypass commercial aviation entirely and hail a subcompact sedan straight to their beachside hotel lobby. The app automatically calculates toll fees, international border wait times and recommended driver shifts along the 1,400-mile highway route.

“While airlines are constrained by pilot shortages and complex airspace logistics, our driver-partners remain completely nimble,” said Uber regional strategy director Carlos Mendoza. “If a traveler in Florida needs to reach a wellness retreat in Quintana Roo, they shouldn’t be limited by flight schedules. They can simply tap a button and settle into a comfortable subcompact ride through a dozen or so picturesque states in the U.S. and Mexico.”

To accommodate long-haul passengers unused to multi-day highway commutes, participating drivers will provide onboard amenities including room-temperature bottled water, periodic air conditioning and head and neck pillows for sleeping.

Transportation experts have praised the initiative as a practical response to shifts in international transit patterns, noting that while jetliners face strict operational hurdles, a compact sedan can easily adapt to evolving travel demands provided passengers maintain patience through the long journey.

State tourism officials expressed optimism about the service integration, calling it a testament to modern flexibility. “Whether visitors arrive via direct flight or a multi-day highway ride-share, the important thing is that they get here,” said regional transit consultant Maria Gutierrez.

World.title: Mexico City opens investigation into fatal poisoning of dogs in Condesa
World.content:
Suspected poison hidden inside sausage at Parque España in Mexico City might have killed at least three dogs Tuesday, prompting a criminal investigation and warnings for pet owners in the capital’s Condesa neighborhood.

The Mexico City Attorney General’s Office opened an animal cruelty investigation after dogs became ill following walks in the 105-year-old park.

Residents reported four deaths, according to Uno TV, while Cuauhtémoc borough Mayor Alessandra Rojo de la Vega reported at least three, Infobae reported.

Police found a piece of longaniza, a seasoned sausage, containing a blue pill with white powder inside, La Crónica reported. However, authorities had not publicly identified the substance or established whether it was linked to the dogs’ illnesses.

Residents also reported finding suspected poisoned meat one block from Parque España, at the intersection of Avenida Veracruz and Calle Atlixco, La Crónica reported.

Excélsior reported that five dogs arrived at the Vetme veterinary hospital suffering from seizures, prompting staff to alert authorities. Three died and two remained hospitalized.

Among those that died was Rufián, a 4-year-old Irish setter-golden retriever mix.

“Three minutes after he arrived home, he started convulsing,” said Sofía Suárez, the dog’s owner and the mother of a 2-year-old.

“How am I going to tell my daughter that she doesn’t have a dog anymore? We’d go to the park every morning and every afternoon,” she said.

Two other dogs, a Belgian shepherd named Kiara and a small-breed dog named Siberia, remained hospitalized, Excélsior reported.

Their owner, Brenda Gómez Magaña, told the newspaper that blue capsules were recovered during a stomach lavage. Kiara appeared to be improving, while Siberia remained in serious condition.

Rojo de la Vega requested a review of surveillance footage and announced legal assistance for families filing complaints.

Investigators were collecting owners’ statements, examining evidence and seeking help from veterinary specialists. Excélsior reported Tuesday evening that authorities had collected nine pieces of evidence suspected of containing poison.

A neighborhood representative said the park would remain open, but its popular dog run and children’s areas would close pending cleanup. Residents wanted the entire park cleaned once prosecutors authorized the work.

Authorities began preventive patrols. Rojo de la Vega urged visitors to Parque España and nearby Parque México to prevent pets from eating anything off the ground and report information to investigators.

With reports from Infobae, Uno TV, Excélsior and La Crónica

World.title: Navy kills cartel operator Jesús ‘Chuy’ González, wanted by the US for $5M
World.content:
Jesús “Chuy” González Peñuelas, an alleged leader of the Guasave Cartel, is believed to have been killed during a clash with Mexican Navy personnel in Sinaloa on Monday, federal authorities said.

The death of González — a 56-year-old alleged drug trafficker who was wanted in the United States — was first reported by media outlets in Sinaloa.

In a social media post on Wednesday, the Navy Ministry (SEMAR) said that its personnel, in coordination with federal Security Ministry agents, “repelled an armed attack” near the community of Alfredo V. Bonfil, located in the municipality of Sinaloa in the state of the same name.

Personal naval de la @SEMAR_mx en coordinación con @SSPCMexico, repelió una agresión armada en inmediaciones de Alfredo V. Bonfil, #Sinaloa. Esta acción derivó de trabajos de inteligencia naval y como resultado se aseguraron 4 vehículos con reporte de robo, 3 armas largas, cargadores y municiones. Durante el enfrentamiento fallecieron 2 personas, cuya identidad podría corresponder a Jesús “N” (a) Chuy Peñuelas operador de 2do orden, solo por debajo de Fausto Isidro Meza Flores (a) Chapo Isidro, líder del Cartel de Guasave y Cesáreo “N”, quedando pendiente la confirmación pericial. Los indicios quedaron a disposición de la @FGRMexico para las investigaciones correspondientes. #Marina refrenda su compromiso de contribuir a la seguridad de la población, mediante la coordinación interinstitucional, con apego al marco legal y respeto a los derechos humanos. — SEMAR México (@SEMAR_mx) October 28, 2026

SEMAR said that two people died during the confrontation, adding that their “identities may correspond to” González and a man identified as Cesáreo “N”.

In a separate social media post, federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said that, “according to the available information,” González was one of the two people killed in the clash with military personnel on Monday.

SEMAR said that “expert confirmation” that González and Cesáreo “N” were the two people killed was “pending.”

Cesáreo “N” was identified in media reports as Cesáreo Peñuelas Ruiz, aka “El Profe” (The Teacher). He was reportedly González’s uncle.

The Navy Ministry said that its operation in the municipality of Sinaloa on Monday “stemmed from naval intelligence work.”

During the operation, four vehicles reported as stolen, three long guns, magazines and ammunition were seized, SEMAR said.

Who was Jesús ‘Chuy’ González Peñuelas?

According to SEMAR, González was the Guasave Cartel’s second-in-command, below only Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, aka “Chapo Isidro.”

The Guasave Cartel is also known as the Meza Flores Organization and Los Mazaltecos. It is based in the municipality of Guasave in northern Sinaloa.

While SEMAR and García Harfuch said on Wednesday that Gonzalez was a member of the Guasave Cartel, U.S. authorities have accused him of running his own drug trafficking organization.

In January 2024, the U.S. Department of State announced a reward of up to US $5 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction of González, saying at the time that he “reportedly leads an independent methamphetamine, marijuana, heroin, and cocaine distribution and production organization.”

The State Department noted that González had been indicted on international narcotics charges in the District of Colorado and the Southern District of California.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury said in May 2021 that González and his drug trafficking organization were “among the largest sources of raw opium gum and heroin in northern Mexico, and increasingly are a major distributor of fentanyl to U.S. markets.”

At that time, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control designated González and his drug trafficking organization as “significant foreign narcotics traffickers pursuant to the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act.”

The Department of the Treasury said that González oversaw “multiple heroin processing laboratories in Sinaloa” and that “the upper echelons” of his drug trafficking organization (DTO) hierarchy consisted of his family members.

“The González Peñuelas DTO cooperates with other DTOs within Mexico, including acting as an enforcement arm for the various Mexican DTO’s trafficking routes, and is aligned with Mexican drug kingpins Fausto Isidro Meza Flores and Rafael Caro Quintero, both of whom are subject to Treasury sanctions,” the department said on May 12, 2021.

With reports from Río Doce, EFE and El Financiero

World.title: Tropical Storm Vance heads toward Sinaloa, bringing more heavy rainfall to northwest Mexico
World.content:
Tropical Storm Vance continues to move northward off the coast of western Mexico and is projected to turn toward the coast of Sinaloa, where it could make landfall by the end of this week.

The U.S. National Hurricane Center forecasts that Vance will lose strength and become a post-tropical remnant low on Thursday, potentially approaching Sinaloa between Thursday and Friday. Landfall as a tropical storm is unlikely.

According to the National Meteorological Service, as of 12 p.m. today, Vance was located approximately 365 kilometers west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco, and 390 kilometers west-southwest of Punta Mita, Nayarit. The storm had sustained winds of 65 kilometers per hour, with gusts reaching up to 85 kilometers per hour and was heading north at a speed of 17 kilometers per hour.

A las 12:00h, la #TormentaTropical #Vance se localiza a 365 km al oeste-suroeste de Cabo Corrientes, #Jalisco, con vientos máximos sostenidos de 65 km/h y rachas de 85 km/h. Se desplaza hacia el nor-noroeste a 17 km/h. ⚠️ Para las próximas 24 horas se pronostican lluvias muy fuertes con puntuales intensas (75 a 150 mm) en Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco y Durango. En Colima, lluvias puntuales fuertes (25 a 50 mm). 🌬️ En la costa de Jalisco se esperan vientos de 30 a 40 km/h con rachas de 50 a 70 km/h y 🌊 oleaje de 2.5 a 3.5 metros. En las costas de Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, Nayarit y Colima, oleaje de 1.5 a 2.5 metros. 📲 Consulta solo fuentes oficiales: @conagua_clima y @CNPC_MX. — Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil (@CNPC_MX) October 28, 2026

Vance is expected to cause heavy rain across Mexico’s western states.

On Wednesday, rainfall totals of 75 to 150 millimeters are expected in central and southern Sinaloa, Nayarit, Durango, the southern tip of Baja California Sur and the coast of Jalisco.

The coastlines of Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, Nayarit and Colima could get hit with sustained winds of 20 to 30 kilometers per hour with gusts of 40 to 60 kilometers per hour and waves of 1.5 to 2.5 meters, while Jalisco could see waves of up to 3.5 meters.

In Baja California Sur, the Public Education Ministry (SEP) suspended all school activities for Wednesday in San José del Cabo and Cabo San Lucas. This suspension applies to all public and private educational institutions at every level.

Given the potential for rivers and streams to swell, authorities warned residents in affected states to avoid crossing watercourses or flooded areas, stay alert to weather advisories and follow the instructions provided by Civil Protection authorities.

With reports from López Dóriga

World.title: Jalisco governor details US $1.3B investment in Guadalajara’s water infrastructure: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

💧 Lemus announces “historic agreement” on Guadalajara water: Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus said the federal and state governments will invest 25 billion pesos (US $1.33 billion) in water infrastructure for the Guadalajara metropolitan area. The plan includes the construction of two new aqueducts: one from Lake Chapala (42 kilometers) to Guadalajara and one from the Calderón Reservoir to the San Gaspar treatment plant (31 kilometers). The federal government will contribute 14.5 billion pesos and Jalisco 10.2 billion pesos, with no new debt, privatization or water rate increases. Lemus said work “could” start next year and that the aqueducts should be finished by the end of 2028.

The plan includes the construction of two new aqueducts: one from Lake Chapala (42 kilometers) to Guadalajara and one from the Calderón Reservoir to the San Gaspar treatment plant (31 kilometers). The federal government will contribute 14.5 billion pesos and Jalisco 10.2 billion pesos, with no new debt, privatization or water rate increases. Lemus said work “could” start next year and that the aqueducts should be finished by the end of 2028. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 Sheinbaum says Mexico-U.S. trade talks have made “a lot” of progress: The president said Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard spoke this week with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick about whether a bilateral deal is “possible” before next Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. She conceded there are still unresolved issues, saying Mexico wants a “significant reduction” of U.S. Section 232 tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum.

The president said Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard spoke this week with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick about whether a bilateral deal is “possible” before next Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. She conceded there are still unresolved issues, saying Mexico wants a “significant reduction” of U.S. Section 232 tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum. 🇪🇸 Sheinbaum expresses solidarity with Spain after deadly train crash: Asked about the high-speed train collision near Toledo, which killed at least 68 people and injured more than 50, Sheinbaum said Mexico stands ready to help. She said she would ask Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco whether any Mexicans were affected.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The centerpiece of President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference was the announcement of a plan to address the long-running problem of water contamination in the metropolitan area of Guadalajara, Jalisco.

Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus said that the federal and state governments will contribute funds to the plan, which includes the construction of two new aqueducts.

Today’s announcement comes after thousands of Guadalajara residents demanded clean tap water at large protest marches earlier this month.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks about Mexico’s trade negotiations with the United States and her expression of solidarity with the people of Spain, where a train accident killed at least 68 people on Wednesday.

Jalisco governor announces ‘historic agreement’ to address water problems in Guadalajara

Lemus declared that it was “a historic day” for the metropolitan area of Guadalajara, Jalisco and “all of Mexico” given that the Jalisco and federal governments had reached “a historic agreement” to together invest 25 billion pesos (US $1.33 billion) in “the infrastructure necessary to supply quality water to families in the metropolitan area of Guadalajara.”

“The historic legacy that the federal government and the Jalisco government will leave will be to have solved the water problem for the next generations,” he said.

#Mañanera Lemus informó que Jalisco construirá una nueva red de colectores para evitar que el agua que viene de Chapala se contamine en la presa Las Pintas. Además, detectaron 150 descargas irregulares en el canal, que están siendo clausuradas, y sus responsables serán sancionados. 📹 Gobierno federal

https://t.co/uhCGj87YOO — REFORMA (@Reforma) October 28, 2026

As a result of the agreement, the federal government will build new aqueducts “for the people of Jalisco,” Lemus said.

He noted that the aqueducts will run between Lake Chapala and Guadalajara, and between the Calderón Reservoir and the San Gaspar water treatment plant, located in the metropolitan area of the state capital.

Lemus said that work on the new aqueducts “could” start next year. He said that the aqueducts are expected to be finished at the end of 2028.

Lemus told reporters that Guadalajara receives 60% of its water supply from Lake Chapala and a “significant part” of that water reaches the state capital via “an open canal built 70 years ago.”

That canal, he said, is “exposed to discharges of wastewater.”

“With the new aqueduct we will take less water from Chapala … and we’ll be able to use 100% of that water without it being contaminated in the journey [to Guadalajara] and without waste due to leaks or evaporation,” Lemus said.

The governor noted that the federal government will contribute 14.5 billion pesos to the 25-billion-peso water infrastructure plan — which includes various projects to complement the new aqueducts — while the Jalisco government will provide 10.2 billion pesos.

He said the investment will ensure that all residents of the metropolitan area of Guadalajara have clean water in the near future.

Lemus said that the state and federal money will be made available through “budget adjustments.”

“There will be no debt, … there will be no privatization and a very important thing is that there won’t be increases to water rates for the metropolitan area of Guadalajara,” he said.

According to information presented by National Water Commission chief Efraín Morales, the federal government will invest 9.3 billion pesos in the 42-kilometer-long aqueduct between Chapala and Guadalajara and 5.2 billion pesos in the 31-kilometer-long Calderón-San Gaspar aqueduct.

Could Mexico and the US reach a trade deal before the US midterms?

Sheinbaum told reporters that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard spoke to U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick about trade issues earlier this week. She said the officials looked at whether it was “possible” to reach a bilateral agreement before the U.S. midterm elections next Tuesday.

Sheinbaum said that a lot of progress has been made in Mexico’s trade talks with the U.S., but conceded that “there are still issues on which we haven’t yet reached an agreement.”

“We want a significant reduction of the [United States’ Section] 232 tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum,” she said.

“… We haven’t yet reached [an agreement on] what we consider important for Mexico, but there is very good dialogue, very good progress and a very good atmosphere in the communication,” Sheinbaum said.

Mexico and the United States have been seeking to resolve a range of trade-related issues following the U.S. government’s decision in July not to renew the USMCA free trade pact for an additional 16 years.

Both Sheinbaum and U.S. President Donald Trump said last week that Mexico and the U.S. were “very close” to reaching a deal.

Sheinbaum expresses ‘solidarity’ with the people of Spain after rail disaster near Toledo

A reporter asked the president about the deadly train crash near the central Spanish city of Toledo.

Sheinbaum expressed “solidarity” with the people of Spain and said that Mexico stood ready to help.

Video shows the immediate aftermath of a deadly high-speed train collision in central Spain on Wednesday that killed at least 64 people and injured 80 others, authorities said. The crash occurred in the province of Toledo when a high-speed train slammed into the back of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars. Both trains were traveling from Madrid to Seville, carrying a combined 544 passengers. The cause of the crash remains unknown. — CBS News (@CBSNews) October 28, 2026

As of 12 p.m. Mexico City time on Wednesday, 68 people were confirmed to have been killed in the accident, while more than 50 people were reported injured. The crash occurred when a high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped on the tracks.

Sheinbaum said she heard about the crash just before she began her Wednesday morning press conference. She said she would ask Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco whether any Mexicans were affected.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its condolences to the people and government of Spain in a social media post, but didn’t say whether any Mexicans had been killed or injured in the crash.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Latin American Pulse for Thursday, October 29, 2026

Brazil – Record Oil, Political Flight

The Senate voted 87 to five to admit 28 US Navy SEALs, who will train 87 Mexican naval special-forces personnel from 29 October 2026 to 15 April 2027. The official line is cooperation, while the debate at home is about sovereignty.

This is not just a security story. It is a test of how much US pressure Mexico can absorb without the president looking weak.

Chile – A Clásico Arrives Like a Cold Shower

Universidad Católica, a Santiago football club, drew 1-1 with Audax Italiano on 28 October. They face rivals Universidad de Chile in the Clásico, the big city derby, on Sunday 1 November.

The central bank held its policy rate at 4.5% again, and LATAM Airlines, the regional carrier, saw its shares fall 8.7% on Wednesday.For a foreigner living in Santiago, the frustration is palpable.The country is not falling apart; it is just stuck, and the Clásico now carries the weight of a small national mood.

Colombia – Crypto Booms as the State Asks Questions

Cryptocurrency transactions moved US$29.1 billion in the 12 months to June 2026. Stablecoins, crypto tied to the US dollar, account for about 48% of purchases on local platforms.

Many Colombians appear to be hedging against the local currency. That is a signal for any business weighing the peso.

For a foreigner doing business in Bogotá, the crypto volume is a reminder that the official economy and the parallel one now run side by side.

The Shared Mood

The continent is making a living from its old strengths: oil, copper, and now crypto. But the political floor is unsteady.

Washington is treating the region with a new kind of bluntness. Mexico feels it in the SEAL team vote.

Brazil feels it in the visa decision for a senator under court order. The reflex is not panic but a wary, defensive pride.

People are not expecting a sudden collapse. They are expecting to be squeezed from the north while their own leaders posture at home.

For a foreigner, the practical lesson is to bank the corporate profits but keep your personal plans flexible. The region is not becoming dangerous overnight; it is becoming harder to predict.

01 The pause that still tightens

The Fed did not move rates, but the message was hardly soft: activity was described as expanding at a “strong pace”, inflation remains elevated, and two officials wanted a hike. That combination explains the firmer 10-year Treasury yield at 5.021% and leaves investors paying more attention to the possibility of another increase than to a near-term cut.

For Latin America, the transmission is direct. A resilient US economy and high US yields support the dollar, raise the hurdle for Brazilian rate cuts and make a weaker real more likely if domestic fiscal concerns return.

02 AI’s golden glow meets the spreadsheet

The AI trade is broadening beyond US megacaps: South Korea’s KOSPI surged 6.6%, as chipmaker SK Hynix reported quarterly results. Yet the Nasdaq gained only 0.27% in New York, so sentiment still leans on strong earnings.

The same tension matters for emerging markets. Strong semiconductor demand can lift Asian exporters and commodity-linked currencies, but higher US yields can overpower that benefit for Brazil’s real and local assets.

This is the central tension for LatAm investors: global tech strength versus the dollar’s pull.

The morning data block is unusually dense. IGP-M and bank lending land early, meaning the first hour of B3’s session may be the most volatile as traders reprice interest-rate expectations in real time.

Vale’s earnings remain the corporate headline. Alongside Multiplan and Triunfo, today offers a cross-section of Brazil’s economy: commodities, domestic consumption and infrastructure financing.

04 Copom and the macro backdrop

The Selic question is the heart of every Brazilian asset decision right now. Investors are trying to judge how long the central bank will keep the rate at 13.75%.

Today’s IGP-M print matters because this index captures prices at the wholesale and construction stages — often an early warning for the official consumer inflation measure. Producer prices already ran hot on Tuesday: 4.34% year on year against a consensus of 2.7% and 2.5% previously (RT economic calendar, RT).

The US data flow added to the mood on Wednesday. The goods trade deficit widened to US$134.90 billion in September (consensus US$130.40 billion, previous US$132.07 billion), and US crude stocks fell 1.892 million barrels against an expected rise of 0.1 million, with stocks at Cushing, the Oklahoma oil-storage hub, down 0.624 million (RT economic calendar, RT).

The Copom meets on 3 and 4 November, so each data point can still shift the odds. A hot reading this morning could push local yields higher and weigh on the real.

05 Corporate stories to watch today

Vale’s results are the main event. The company’s iron-ore output and realised prices will be scrutinised against China’s uneven demand, while any commentary on dividends or buybacks could move the shares sharply.

Petrobras remains in the news because of the fuel-pricing debate in Brasília. Investors are watching whether the government will allow the state-controlled oil company to adjust fuel prices to international levels, a decision with direct consequences for margins and shareholder payouts.

Multiplan’s earnings offer a read on Brazilian consumers. Shopping-centre sales and rent growth indicate whether household spending is holding up despite higher borrowing costs.

Triunfo is the infrastructure angle. Its results reflect traffic volumes and the financial health of some of Brazil’s logistics and energy projects, which are sensitive to interest rates.

06 The levels to watch at the open

The Ibovespa’s prior-session low is the first line in the sand. If futures reclaim that level early, it signals that domestic buyers are willing to step in despite the political and fiscal noise. If not, the index may drift while traders wait for Vale’s numbers.

The USD/BRL pair matters more than usual because the real is the cleanest expression of foreign investors’ view on Brazilian risk. A break above the recent trading range would confirm that capital is leaving, while a quick retreat would suggest the previous session’s move was overdone.

Vale’s stock will set the tone for mining shares on Friday, once tonight’s results are known. A positive reaction to earnings could stabilise the Ibovespa even if banks and domestic consumption names stay weak.

For traders positioning before the bell, the practical watchlist is short: IGP-M, payrolls, bank lending and Vale’s earnings. Everything else is secondary until those four stories are known.

World.title: Sudan Accuses Ethiopia of Hosting Drones
World.content:
File photo, 2012. The Blue Nile Falls at Tis Issat near Bahir Dar, on the river at the centre of Ethiopia's dispute with Egypt. (Photo: Radosław Botev, CC BY 3.0 PL, via Wikimedia Commons)

Published Wednesday, 28 October, 11:30 p.m. ET (Thursday, 5:30 a.m. Port Sudan) · Source: Sudan Foreign and Information ministries, Rio Times reporting

Sudan has pointed a finger at its neighbour, and the charge could pull a second country into a war now in its fourth year. Officials in Port Sudan, the wartime seat of the government, say the drones that knocked out power stations this week took off from Ethiopia.

The accusation lands in the Sudan war, the fight between the army-led government and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group. Foreign Ministry undersecretary Muawiya Osman Khalid made it at a news conference on Wednesday, 28 October.

Key Facts What: Sudan says drones that hit its power sites took off from Ethiopian soil, including Bahir Dar airport.

Who: Muawiya Osman Khalid, Sudan’s Foreign Ministry undersecretary, made the charge. Ethiopia has not answered the latest claims.

Proof: Sudan showed drone fragments and flight-path data. Independent reporters could not verify them.

Next: Khalid says Sudan reserves the right to defend its territory. Watch for Ethiopia’s reply.

In plain English Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when the army and the RSF turned on each other. Ethiopia is Sudan’s eastern neighbour, and Sudan says its airspace is being used against it. Neither claim has been proven in public. Such accusations matter because they can widen a civil war into a regional one.

What Sudan Says Happened

At a news conference on Wednesday, 28 October, Sudanese officials from the defence, foreign affairs and information ministries laid out their case. They showed fragments of drones the army says it intercepted, plus flight-path data they say points to launch sites inside Ethiopia.

One site stood out: Bahir Dar airport, in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region. Sudan named the same airport in May, when it blamed launches from there for a drone aimed at Khartoum International Airport.

Khalid urged the international community not to overlook what he called Ethiopian-Emirati aggression against Sudan. He said Sudan reserves the right to defend its territory.

Railway yard in Atbara, northern Sudan. File photo. Photo: Bertramz, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Strikes Behind the Charge

Sudanese officials say a wave of drones hit electricity stations in recent days, including one at El Manaqil, in central Gezira state, on Wednesday that blacked out the town and nearby areas. Another was the Markhiyat station northwest of Omdurman, the city across the Nile from Khartoum.

They also reported attacks on fuel storage and a pipeline at Bashayer Port, an oil-export terminal on the Red Sea, and on hospitals, mosques and homes in several states. The government blames the RSF.

Our earlier reports tracked the pattern: drones hit the power grid in the capital earlier this week. Blackouts hit hospitals and homes first.

Why This Is Not New

Sudan recalled its ambassador to Ethiopia in early May after a drone was shot down near Khartoum International Airport. Sudan also accuses the United Arab Emirates (UAE), a Gulf state, of backing the RSF.

Ethiopia’s foreign ministry dismissed those earlier claims as baseless. No Ethiopian response to the latest charge was available at publication. The charge came the same day Sudan’s defence minister said more than 20 countries back the RSF.

What It Means for US Readers

Washington follows the war closely because it involves Red Sea shipping lanes, US-backed mediation and a humanitarian emergency. UN estimates put the number of people displaced at more than 13 million.

A confirmed Ethiopian role would test US relations with two governments at once and make a ceasefire harder to negotiate. An unproven charge still hardens positions, so diplomats will watch for independent evidence.

What Is Not Known

Nobody has independently verified the drone fragments or the flight-path data. It is unclear who operated the drones, how many were launched or what the casualty toll is.

Ethiopia has not confirmed or denied use of Bahir Dar airport this week. The UAE role Sudan alleges is also unproven.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Sudan accusing Ethiopia of?

Sudan says drones that struck its electricity stations and civilian sites took off from Ethiopian territory, including Bahir Dar airport. Ethiopia has not confirmed any role.

Has anyone verified Sudan’s evidence?

No. Sudan displayed drone fragments and flight-path data at a news conference on 28 October, but independent reporters could not confirm where the drones came from.

Sources: Sudan Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Information statements and news conference, 28 to 29 October 2026; UN humanitarian estimates for Sudan; Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements, May 2026.

Today’s Focus Gold held its ground on Wednesday after the US Federal Reserve (Fed), the US central bank, left interest rates unchanged. Spot gold ended near US$4,055 an ounce, roughly flat on the day, while the gold fund GLD closed 0.33% higher. Silver was weaker, slipping about 0.9% to US$53.92 an ounce. Mining shares did better than the metal, with the gold-miners fund GDX up 0.91%. The Fed’s decision was split: ten voters backed holding the target range at 3¾% to 4%, and two preferred a quarter-point rise. What matters today. Gold is priced in dollars and pays no interest, so a Fed that is split between holding and raising keeps pressure on the metal while the dollar and Treasury yields stay in focus.

01 The session in one read

Gold ended Wednesday close to where it began. Spot gold was near US$4,055 an ounce, down about 0.15%, while the GLD fund, which closes earlier in New York, rose 0.33% to US$373.51.

Silver fell about 0.86% to US$53.92, and the SLV fund lost 0.20% to US$49.06.

Mining shares were firmer than the metals: the GDX fund of gold miners gained 0.91% to US$83.95.

Assessment — Flat gold, a split Fed MEDIUM Gold’s move was within normal daily noise, and the fund and spot readings differed slightly because of closing times. Two Fed voters wanted a rate rise, which is a mild negative for non-yielding metals. The variable to watch is the 10-year US yield, which ended at 5.02%, and any shift in Fed language.

03 What moved it

The Fed was the main event. The decision came at 2:00 pm New York time, and the statement showed Governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, president of the Cleveland Fed, voting against the hold in favour of a rise.

The dollar index slipped 0.16% to 102.16, which helps dollar-priced gold, while the 10-year US Treasury yield rose to 5.02%, which weighs on it.

Other data from the RT economic calendar: the US goods trade deficit widened to US$134.9 billion, against US$130.4 billion expected. US crude stocks fell 1.892 million barrels, and stocks at Cushing, the Oklahoma oil hub, fell 0.624 million barrels.

04 The Latin American read

Mexico is the world’s largest silver producer, and Peru is among the top three. Pan American Silver, which mines in Mexico, Peru and Argentina, gained 0.70%.

The Mexican peso gained about 0.3% to 18.62 per dollar, a small help for local-currency costs at Mexican mines.

05 The names to watch

Newmont and Agnico Eagle are the largest US-listed gold producers in our basket, and both gained more than 1%. Hecla, a silver and gold miner, led with a 2.05% gain.

Barrick, which has big mines in the Dominican Republic and Argentina, fell 1.31% and lagged the group.

06 The outlook

Gold is likely to stay range-bound until the Fed gives a clearer signal. A move through US$4,100 would be a bullish sign; a fall below US$4,000 would be bearish.

Prediction markets give 52.5% to a dip to US$4,000 in October and 35.5% to a rise to US$4,100.

World.title: Wheat Fund Falls 1.03% as Soy Fund Slips 0.76% | Grains, Oct 28
World.content:
Grains — the daily wrap.

Oil — the daily wrap.

Key Facts The US Oil Fund (USO), a fund tracking WTI, the US crude benchmark, rose 1.64% to US$166.57 on Wednesday, October 28, and the Brent-based fund BNO gained 0.67%.

on Wednesday, October 28, and the Brent-based fund BNO gained 0.67%. US crude stocks fell 1.89 million barrels last week, when a small rise had been expected; gasoline stocks rose 3.87 million.

when a small rise had been expected; gasoline stocks rose 3.87 million. Ecopetrol rose 2.26% to US$17.68 and YPF 1.84% to US$49.34, while Brazil’s Petrobras fell 1.21% to US$22.03.

with WTI near US$102 a barrel. Prediction markets: Polymarket, a prediction market, puts 39.0% on WTI crude touching US$105 in October, as of 28 October 2026, 8:47 pm ET.

Today’s Focus Oil rose on Wednesday as US inventories shrank more than expected. The US Oil Fund, which tracks WTI crude futures, gained 1.64% to US$166.57. The US Energy Information Administration, the US government’s statistics agency, reported that commercial crude stocks fell 1.9 million barrels to 410.6 million barrels, while traders had expected a small rise. Latin American producers split. Colombia’s Ecopetrol and Argentina’s YPF rose, while Brazil’s Petrobras slipped. What matters today. Oil above US$100 a barrel raises petrol prices for American drivers and boosts the budgets of Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Guyana and Mexico, so crude moves ripple across the Americas.

01 The session in one read

WTI crude rose roughly 2% on Wednesday to about US$102 a barrel, and the USO fund closed at US$166.57, up 1.64%. The Brent fund BNO gained 0.67% to US$70.14.

Official weekly data supported prices. Commercial crude stocks fell by 1.9 million barrels to 410.6 million barrels, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).

Gasoline stocks rose by 3.9 million barrels to 209.2 million, which limited the gain.

Assessment — Tight crude, soft gasoline MEDIUM A crude draw when a build was expected, and a fall in distillates, support prices, but the large gasoline build is a sign of soft fuel demand. The mix explains why oil rose about 2% and not more. The variable to watch is next week’s gasoline data and any Gulf supply news, which could push prices either way.

The weekly inventory report was the main driver. A fall in crude and distillate stocks signals tight supply, while the gasoline build of 3.87 million barrels signals weaker demand.

The US Federal Reserve, the US central bank, held its rate at 3¾% to 4%, with two voters preferring a quarter-point rise, and the dollar index slipped 0.16%.

Colombia’s Ecopetrol gained 2.26%, and the COLCAP index was flat at −0.03%. Argentina’s YPF rose 1.84% and Vista Energy 1.03%, both tied to the Vaca Muerta shale field.

Mexico’s Pemex is not listed, and Guyana’s output is held by foreign partners, so neither has a direct listed proxy in our data.

Steel — the daily wrap.

Key Facts Gerdau, a Brazilian steelmaker, fell 3.01% in New York to US$4.51 on Wednesday, October 28.

on Wednesday, October 28. CSN, another Brazilian steel and mining group, plunged 7.55% to US$0.80 in the sharpest drop among Latin American steel names.

in the sharpest drop among Latin American steel names. Ternium, a Luxembourg-based steelmaker with main plants in Mexico, lost 1.39% to US$53.92 while US producers Nucor and Steel Dynamics gained 0.37% and 1.29%.

while US producers Nucor and Steel Dynamics gained 0.37% and 1.29%. The global steel ETF (SLX) slipped 0.12% to US$101.43 on very light trading volume.

Today’s Focus Latin American steelmakers fell on Wednesday while their US rivals gained. Gerdau lost 3.01%, Ternium 1.39% and CSN a heavy 7.55% in New York trading. Nucor, a major US steelmaker, rose 0.37% to US$271.79, and Steel Dynamics gained 1.29% to US$249.99. Steel is made from iron ore and scrap, and it is a barometer for building and manufacturing, so the split between Brazil and the United States is worth watching. What matters today. Brazil and Mexico sell steel into a US market that protects its own mills, so the gap between US gains and Latin American losses shows how exposed the region is to trade policy and to Brazil’s own sell-off.

01 The session in one read

Gerdau closed at US$4.51, down 3.01%, and CSN at US$0.80, down 7.55%. Ternium ended at US$53.92, down 1.39%.

The global steel fund SLX moved little, down 0.12% to US$101.43, but its trading volume was tiny, so the reading is weak.

Brazil’s Ibovespa fell 2.68% on Wednesday, so the Brazilian steelmakers fell with the market. We could not confirm company-specific news.

Assessment — Brazil’s market drives the drop MEDIUM Gerdau and CSN fell with Brazil’s stock market, while US steelmakers rose. That suggests the pressure is local and not a global steel story. The variable to watch is trade policy: any change in US tariffs on steel would affect Brazilian and Mexican exports quickly.

World.title: Flying to the US Soon? Every Passenger Must Sign a New Form From Nov. 3
World.content:
If you are flying to the United States after Tuesday, Nov. 3, you will have to sign a short health declaration before you board. Skip it and the airline will not let you on the plane. The rule applies whether the United States is your final stop or just a connection. A trip from San José to Madrid with a change of planes in Miami counts. So does a flight home to Toronto through Houston.

The requirement covers flights leaving at or after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Nov. 3. That is 10:59 p.m. the same night in Costa Rica, so a late departure from Juan Santamaría or Liberia that evening could be among the first affected. The form asks one thing. You confirm that you have not been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days before your flight. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ordered it on Oct. 22 to keep travelers who may have been exposed to Ebola from bringing the virus into the country.

The 21-day window is the longest time Ebola can incubate before symptoms appear. Anyone who left the DRC more than three weeks ago is past the point of risk. Never having been near the DRC does not get you out of signing. Every passenger has to sign, whatever their nationality, including U.S. citizens and green card holders.

Your airline collects the form. The CDC lets airlines take it on paper or digitally, and is urging them to build it into online check-in and their apps. Expect to see it at check-in or at the gate at your last airport before the United States. If you are unsure how your airline will handle it, check its website or app before you leave for the airport.

Each traveler needs their own form, so one signature cannot cover a whole family. A parent or guardian signs for children under 18. A relative or companion can sign for someone with a disability who cannot sign. Read it before you tick the box. The CDC warns that knowingly giving false information is a federal crime that can bring fines and prison time. Changing planes at an airport in the DRC counts as having been in the country, even if you never left the aircraft.

The declaration is not a test or a vaccine requirement, and it does not replace your passport, visa or ESTA. It applies only to air travel, so crossing into the United States by land or arriving by sea is not covered. The form sits on top of restrictions already in place. Since May, anyone who has been in the DRC within the past 21 days has been barred from boarding flights to the United States, and that bar was extended to U.S. citizens in July. Foreign nationals recently in the DRC, Uganda or South Sudan are also blocked from entering.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has killed about 4,700 people in Africa, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. The CDC says no cases linked to the outbreak have been reported in the United States and that the risk to the American public remains low.

The requirement is set to stay in place through Dec. 18 unless the CDC changes it sooner. That covers Thanksgiving and most of the December travel rush, so if you are flying north for the holidays, allow a few extra minutes at check-in.

World.title: El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo Qualifies for ATP Finals Despite Vienna Upset
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo and Croatian partner Mate Pavić have secured their place in the 2026 ATP Finals for the third consecutive year, although their preparations suffered a setback Wednesday when they lost their opening doubles match at the Vienna Open. The third-seeded pair fell 7-6 (8), 7-5 to Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo and Tomás Martín Etcheverry in a match lasting two hours and 27 minutes.

The result came just two days after the ATP confirmed that Arévalo and Pavić had earned one of the eight doubles spots at the season-ending championship in Turin, Italy.Despite the Vienna defeat, the qualification marks another successful season for the Salvadoran, who has established himself among the leading doubles players in professional tennis.

Arévalo and Pavić had recorded 39 tour-level victories together when their qualification was announced Monday. Their best result of the season came in June at Queen’s Club in London, where they defeated Finland’s Harri Heliövaara and Britain’s Henry Patten to capture their first title of 2026.

The pair also reached the Wimbledon doubles final in July but lost to Heliövaara and Patten in two tiebreaks. Additional runner-up finishes in Montreal, Monte-Carlo and Dubai helped them accumulate enough ranking points to qualify for Turin before the final tournaments of the regular season.

Wednesday’s result in Vienna was a notable upset. Cerúndolo and Etcheverry, better known for their singles careers, recovered from first-round singles defeats earlier in the week to eliminate one of the established doubles teams on the ATP Tour.The Argentines held their nerve in a closely contested opening set, winning the tiebreak 10-8 before securing the decisive break of serve in the second set.

For Arévalo, the larger objective remains the ATP Finals, where he and Pavić will attempt to improve on their runner-up finish in 2024. That year, the pair reached the championship match before losing to Germany’s Kevin Krawietz and Tim Pütz. They returned in 2025 but failed to advance beyond the group stage.

The Salvadoran and Croatian have been partners since the beginning of 2024. They won the French Open doubles championship that year and finished the season as the world’s top-ranked doubles team. Their return to Turin also extends Arévalo’s presence at the highest level of the sport, giving Central America another representative at one of professional tennis’s most exclusive events.

The 2026 ATP Finals will take place November 15–22 at the Inalpi Arena in Turin, bringing together the eight leading singles players and eight leading doubles teams based on their results throughout the season. With their qualification secured, Arévalo and Pavić can focus on preparing for another opportunity to win a season-ending championship that has so far eluded them.

World.title: Costa Rica Drops Bid to Join Pacific Trade Pact and Fires Its Trade Minister
World.content:
Today, President Laura Fernández removed Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos and ordered that Costa Rica not sign its accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, ending a four-year effort to join one of the world’s largest trade blocs.

The president said she had instructed the Foreign Trade Ministry (Comex) to share the full terms of the agreement with the sectors it would affect, and that the order was not carried out. She said the negotiators had declared the complete text confidential, so almost no one knew what it contained, whom it would benefit or whom it would harm.

She also said she could not put at risk the future of thousands of Costa Rican families who make their living from cattle ranching, dairy production and small and medium-scale fruit and vegetable farming. She ordered the accession file archived. The decision reverses a policy the government had defended and that she had included in her government plan.

Former president Rodrigo Chaves, now Minister of the Presidency and Minister of Finance, celebrated the conclusion of negotiations in early May as a major victory for the country. The CPTPP groups 12 economies: Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, Singapore, the United Kingdom and Vietnam.

The president acknowledged the agreement’s commercial value, citing access to a market of roughly 600 million consumers. Costa Rica formally applied to join in August 2022, and members agreed in November 2024 to open the accession process. According to Comex, the remaining steps after the May announcement were the legal review and drafting of the accession protocol, its signature and its submission to the Legislative Assembly.

Costa Rica had been expected to decide whether to sign at a meeting of members scheduled for Nov. 23 to 27. Trejos, who had been vice minister before taking over the ministry when the new administration began in May, defended the negotiation before lawmakers. Appearing before the Legislative Assembly’s Treasury Affairs Committee on Oct. 13, she said the process had been transparent and that the terms closed in May could not be renegotiated.

President Fernández met with representatives of the productive sectors on Oct. 9 in a session that lasted nearly seven hours. Afterward, she criticized the previous Comex administration for a lack of dialogue and transparency. Agricultural groups led the opposition. Ivannia Quesada of the National Chamber of Milk Producers said the agreement was not in the interest of the country or the national agricultural sector, citing import competition and the risk to domestic production and dairy jobs.

The Coffee Institute of Costa Rica, through Gustavo André Jiménez Elizondo, raised concerns about rules of origin and coffee traceability in a sector already under pressure from the strong local currency. Business groups had backed accession. Arturo Rosabal of the Chamber of Commerce said productivity gaps should be closed through improvements in production, while Rodney Salazar of the Costa Rican Chamber of Exporters (Crecex) supported the deal and acknowledged the concerns of agricultural producers.

The agreement also faced an uncertain path in the Legislative Assembly, where the National Liberation Party had said it would not support it under current conditions. Nogui Acosta, a lawmaker for the ruling Pueblo Soberano party, had defended an export-oriented trade policy and said the party would be watching for the signing.

The president said Comex will continue its work with support from the Agriculture and Economy ministries. She announced support for farmers who do not export, including a stronger Institutional Supply Program, run by the National Production Council, to increase government purchases from local producers, along with action against smuggling and illicit trade.

She did not give a budget or timeline for those measures, and the government did not immediately name a replacement for Trejos.

World.title: Thinking of Moving to Costa Rica? Put Puriscal at the Top of Your List
World.content:
Anyone who has lived in Costa Rica for a while knows the question. A friend, a relative or a stranger online is thinking about making the move and wants to know where to start looking. The usual answers come quickly: the beach towns of Guanacaste, Atenas, Grecia, Escazú. Those places all have their merits, but for a newcomer who wants mild weather, open space, real community and land that is still affordable, there is a better first stop. Put Puriscal at the top of the list.

Puriscal is a large and mostly rural area covering about 554 square kilometers in the southwest corner of San José province. It became a area in 1868, when it was separated from Escazú, and today it is divided into nine districts: Santiago, Mercedes Sur, Barbacoas, Grifo Alto, San Rafael, Candelarita, Desamparaditos, San Antonio and Chires. The 2011 census counted about 33,000 residents, and the population has grown since, spread across small towns, family farms and scattered hamlets. Santiago de Puriscal, the area seat, sits roughly 37 kilometers from downtown San José.

The first reason to look here is the climate

Much of the area lies between 800 and 1,400 meters above sea level, and Santiago sits at about 1,100 meters. Days are typically warm, in the mid 20s Celsius, while evenings are cool and breezy, the kind of weather that leaves windows open and air conditioning unnecessary. Puriscal has a dry season from December to April and a rainy season that runs roughly from May to November, when mornings are often bright and afternoon showers keep the hillsides deep green. For people coming from harsh winters or the humid heat of the coasts, it is hard to beat.

The second reason is the landscape

Puriscal is a place of ridges, river valleys and coffee and cattle land rolling west toward the Pacific. On clear days the hills seem to go on forever, and sunsets over the far ridgelines are part of ordinary evenings. It is the scenery that brings many people to Costa Rica, and here it is the view from the porch.

The third reason is the community

Puriscal has not been reshaped by tourism or large expat enclaves, and its towns still run on the rhythms of farming, church and family.
