Santiago has the supermarkets, banks, pharmacies, hardware stores and schools that cover daily needs, along with a weekly farmers market where local growers sell produce, cheese, eggs and coffee.

Its best known landmark is the former Catholic church in the center of town, a cross shaped building with 35 meter towers that was inaugurated in 1965 and closed after earthquakes damaged it in 1991. It was declared a national architectural heritage site in 2012 and remains a proud symbol of the town. Local traditions such as Puriscal’s food fairs bring residents together throughout the year.

The fourth reason is the land

While Escazú, Santa Ana, Ciudad Colón and Atenas have grown expensive, Puriscal remains more rural and generally more affordable. Buyers can still find larger lots, small farms and mountain parcels with long views and room for a garden, fruit trees or a few animals, at prices that would be difficult to match closer to the capital. Much of the land was historically used for coffee, sugarcane and cattle, and there is growing interest in agroforestry, small scale farming and ecotourism.

Nature rounds out the picture

La Cangreja National Park, in the Chires district near Mastatal, protects about 1,900 hectares of forest where the Central Valley meets the Pacific lowlands. More than 300 bird species have been recorded there, including scarlet macaws, toucans and trogons, along with coatis, agoutis, peccaries and poison dart frogs. Camera traps in the park have captured pumas, coyotes and deer, and the park is home to a tree found nowhere else on earth, named after the area itself.

Practical needs are covered too

The public health system operates a comprehensive health center, known as the CAIS, in Puriscal, which provides primary care and has also performed outpatient surgeries for Hospital San Juan de Dios, including hernia, gallbladder and some orthopedic procedures. For hospital care and specialists, residents turn to the major public hospitals in San José and the private hospitals in Escazú.

The best way to explore Puriscal is slowly

Spend a few days rather than an afternoon. Walk around Santiago, visit the farmers market, eat at a local soda and talk to the people selling vegetables and coffee. Drive out to the smaller districts such as San Antonio, Barbacoas and Mercedes Sur, where the views and the pace change from one ridge to the next, and save a morning for La Cangreja.

Consider renting before buying, and when a property catches your eye, confirm clean title, legal access, water availability and building permits before committing. A working knowledge of Spanish will make every step easier, since bilingual agents and contractors are fewer here than in Atenas or Escazú, and it opens the door to becoming part of the community rather than simply living next to it.

Not every newcomer will end up in Puriscal, and that is fine. But anyone serious about finding a home in Costa Rica owes it to themselves to see it first. The mild climate, the green hills, the wildlife, the farms and the friendly towns are what most people are looking for when they decide to move here. In Puriscal, they are all in one place.

World.title: Costa Rica Bus Crash Leaves Two Dead and Dozens Injured
World.content:
Two women died and seven other people were seriously injured Wednesday morning when a passenger bus overturned on Route 4 in Sarapiquí, Heredia, leaving dozens of passengers needing emergency medical attention. The accident occurred around 7:55 a.m. on October 28 in the community of Chiripa de Río Frío, near Horquetas de Sarapiquí. The bus overturned onto its side approximately 400 meters from the Palmitour restaurant, trapping several passengers inside.

The Costa Rican Red Cross confirmed that an elderly woman died at the scene. A second woman died while being transported by ambulance to the Hospital de Guápiles. Authorities had not released the victims’ identities. Emergency crews attended to 54 people following the crash. According to the Red Cross’s final assessment, seven were classified as critically injured, while another 32 required urgent medical attention. Thirteen people did not need to be taken to a hospital.

The scale of the accident prompted one of the region’s larger emergency responses in recent months. The Red Cross deployed approximately 29 ambulances and 70 emergency workers, including paramedics, doctors, nurses and rescue personnel. Firefighters arriving at the scene found the bus lying on its side, with passengers unable to escape. Four people were pinned inside the wreckage and had to be freed using specialized rescue equipment.

Firefighters also reported a fuel spill from the overturned vehicle, adding another hazard as rescue teams worked to reach the injured. Ambulances transported patients to medical facilities across northern and central Costa Rica, including clinics in Río Frío and Puerto Viejo de Sarapiquí, as well as hospitals in Guápiles, San Carlos and Heredia.

The emergency response involved teams from Heredia, Limón, Alajuela and San José, along with specialized rescue personnel from the Red Cross’s national emergency response division. The accident took place along Route 4, an important highway connecting communities in northern Costa Rica with the Route 32 corridor toward the Caribbean coast. The affected stretch passes through the Sarapiquí region, where buses provide transportation between rural communities and larger towns.

The cause of the crash remained unknown Wednesday afternoon. Authorities had not publicly established whether road conditions, mechanical problems or driver actions contributed to the accident. The Red Cross’s latest confirmed report placed the death toll at two, with seven other people in critical condition

World.title: Costa Rica Hospitals Overwhelmed as Patients Wait Up to Eight Days for Treatment
World.content:
Patients at several of Costa Rica’s largest public hospitals are waiting as long as eight days for a hospital bed, with overcrowded emergency departments forcing some people to spend days in chairs, wheelchairs and hallways while awaiting surgery or further treatment. A new internal audit by the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (the Caja), reveals serious overcrowding at Hospital México, Hospital Calderón Guardia and Hospital San Juan de Dios in San José.

Similar problems have been reported at regional hospitals in Heredia and Liberia, where patients and medical staff describe conditions that have become increasingly difficult to manage. The situation is particularly concerning because many of those waiting have already been examined by doctors and determined to need hospitalization. They are not simply waiting for an initial emergency room consultation.

Some require surgery, specialized procedures or continued treatment, but there are not enough available beds or medical specialists to move them out of emergency departments. At San Vicente de Paúl Hospital in Heredia, officials confirmed that 75 patients were waiting for admission to hospital wards on October 27. The average wait was seven days, although some patients had reportedly remained in the emergency department for as long as eight days.

At Calderón Guardia Hospital, the situation has become equally serious. Its emergency department has operated at approximately 200% of normal capacity, meaning the number of patients has reached roughly twice the space available to accommodate them. During a September inspection, auditors found around 40 patients waiting for hospital beds, another 13 awaiting specialized heart procedures and 13 more waiting for hip replacement surgery. By September 24, the number of patients waiting in the emergency department had climbed to 90.

Hospital administrators say these delays can have serious consequences, particularly for older patients and people suffering from conditions that require prompt treatment. A broken hip, for example, can lead to additional complications when surgery is delayed, while untreated abdominal emergencies can quickly become life-threatening.

Hospital México is experiencing similar problems. Its director reported that between 60 and 70 patients are waiting for hospitalization on a typical day, with approximately 80% having already been there the previous day. At San Juan de Dios Hospital, administrators say occupancy has remained at or above full capacity for extended periods. During a September inspection, 47 patients were waiting for inpatient beds while others remained hospitalized as they awaited specialized procedures.

The crisis extends well beyond the capital. At Enrique Baltodano Hospital in Liberia, Guanacaste, patients have described spending several days in metal chairs while waiting for surgery or a hospital bed. One patient reported waiting seven days, while others have reportedly resorted to lying on the floor because there were no suitable places to rest.

The conditions prompted complaints to Costa Rica’s Ombudsman’s Office, which encouraged affected patients and their families to formally report problems with the hospital’s emergency services. The CCSS has acknowledged the overcrowding in Liberia and introduced several temporary measures.

These include providing 20 reclining chairs to improve patients’ comfort and opening a nine-bed short-stay unit in Cañas for patients who need hospital treatment but do not require the services of a larger facility. However, the measures do not address all the underlying problems.

The internal audit identified a shortage of medical specialists, increased demand from accidents and serious illnesses, and difficulties arranging additional surgeries and specialized procedures outside normal working hours. Disagreements over the CCSS payment system for additional medical procedures have also complicated efforts to expand services.

Some doctors and technical staff have declined to participate under the revised payment arrangements, limiting the number of extra procedures hospitals can schedule. The growing number of patients arriving at emergency departments has placed additional pressure on a system already struggling with long waiting lists for surgery.

Across Costa Rica, approximately 211,650 surgical cases were on waiting lists, with nearly 60,000 concentrated at Hospital México, Calderón Guardia and San Juan de Dios. The audit warns that prolonged delays can increase the risk of avoidable complications and deaths when patients do not receive necessary treatment within the appropriate medical timeframe.

Hospital officials have attempted to reduce the pressure by prioritizing the most seriously ill patients, speeding up discharges when medically appropriate and transferring patients to other facilities when space is available. They are also encouraging residents with minor illnesses or non-emergency conditions to seek care at local clinics, health centers or EBAIS facilities rather than going directly to major hospital emergency departments.

However, people experiencing serious symptoms should still seek emergency medical attention immediately. For the hundreds of patients already waiting inside Costa Rica’s public hospitals, the immediate problem remains the same: even after doctors determine they need surgery or a hospital bed, the space and medical personnel required to continue their treatment may not be available.

The audit findings place additional pressure on the CCSS to find longer-term solutions to overcrowding, staffing shortages and treatment delays across the country’s public healthcare system.

World.title: Usher Returns to Costa Rica and Shares Photos of Guanacaste Getaway
World.content:
Eight-time Grammy Award winner Usher has returned to Costa Rica, spending several days enjoying the beaches, tropical scenery, and luxury resorts of Guanacaste before sharing highlights of his vacation with millions of social media followers. The American R&B star visited us from October 20 to 24 according to Costa Rica’s General Directorate of Migration and Foreigners. His trip took him to the Papagayo Peninsula, one of the best-known luxury tourism destinations.

Usher, whose hits include Yeah!, U Got It Bad, Burn, and My Boo, shared photographs and videos on Instagram showing how he spent his time along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast. The posts feature the singer enjoying sunsets over the ocean, playing golf, relaxing by the water, and taking part in outdoor adventures. In one photograph, he stands in the ocean with a woman as the sun sets behind them. Other images show him surrounded by Guanacaste’s tropical vegetation and coastal mountains.

He also shared footage of himself ziplining through the trees, dancing on the beach, and enjoying a swimming pool overlooking the surrounding landscape. During his visit, Usher reportedly stayed at Nekajui, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, an exclusive resort on the Papagayo Peninsula that opened in February 2025.

The property was the first Ritz-Carlton Reserve to open in Central and South America. Its rooms, suites, and villas offer views of the Pacific Ocean and the surrounding tropical dry forest. The resort also received international recognition in September 2026 when the Michelin Guide promoted it from two to three Michelin Keys, its highest distinction for hotels.

Nekajui was the only hotel in the Americas newly awarded three Michelin Keys in the 2026 selection. It joined Nayara Springs, located near La Fortuna and Arenal Volcano, as one of two Costa Rican hotels holding the distinction. The Papagayo Peninsula is also home to the Ocean Course, an 18-hole golf course designed by Arnold Palmer. The course overlooks the Pacific Ocean and Bahía de Culebra, offering golfers views of the coastline and surrounding forest.

Usher’s latest visit came shortly after his 48th birthday on October 14. No official reason for the trip has been announced. This was not the singer’s first vacation in Costa Rica as Usher previously visited during the 2012 holiday season, arriving on December 30 and departing on January 6, 2013, according to immigration records reported at the time.

During that trip, he celebrated New Year’s Eve at Dolce nightclub in Guachipelín, Escazú, surprising guests with his appearance. He traveled with family and friends, including music executive Scooter Braun, who shared photographs from their Costa Rican vacation. More than 13 years later, Usher’s return has once again brought international attention to Guanacaste, with his social media posts offering followers a look at the beaches, outdoor activities, and upscale resorts that have made the region a popular destination for international visitors.

World.title: Ruling Party Files Bill That Would Let Rodrigo Chaves Run Again in 2030
World.content:
Legislators from Costa Rica’s ruling Pueblo Soberano party filed a constitutional reform on Tuesday that would allow presidents to serve consecutive terms. Its backers said openly that the goal is to put former President Rodrigo Chaves back on the ballot in 2030. The bill, file number 25.867, was presented by legislator Osvaldo Artavia Carballo with the support of the Pueblo Soberano caucus. It would amend Article 132 of the Constitution and add a new Article 132 bis.

Under the proposal, a president could serve up to two consecutive four-year terms and would then have to wait four years before running again. The current rule bars anyone who has held the presidency from running until eight years have passed. José Miguel Villalobos, of Pueblo Soberano, said the reform is intended for Chaves because he is the only former president who could be elected again, according to statements reported Tuesday. Chaves governed from 2022 to 2026 and was succeeded by Laura Fernández, who won the presidency as the party’s candidate.

The ruling party holds 31 seats in the 57-member Legislative Assembly. A constitutional reform needs at least 38 votes, a two-thirds majority, so the bill cannot pass without opposition support. The process spans two legislative years. The bill must be read three times in the plenary, admitted for discussion by a simple majority and reviewed by a special commission, which has up to 20 business days to report.

It then needs two debates with at least 38 votes in the first legislative year, followed by a mandatory consultation with the Constitutional Chamber, known as the Sala IV. If it clears that stage, the president must include it in the State of the Nation address that opens the next legislative year, where it faces three more debates, again requiring 38 votes.

Opposition leaders rejected the proposal yesterday as Álvaro Ramírez, head of the National Liberation Party caucus, said the reform seeks to guarantee permanent immunity for a person who has much to answer for before the courts, and called it a distraction. Abril Gordienko, of the Social Christian Unity Party, said she doubted the ruling party could gather 38 votes in the next three and a half years. She compared the proposal to reelection models pursued by Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, Rafael Correa in Ecuador and Evo Morales in Bolivia.

José María Villalta, of the Broad Front, said his caucus could discuss reelection under normal conditions, but opposes it now because of what he described as signs of authoritarianism. The bill is not the first attempt this year. In February, then-independent legislator Leslye Bojorges filed a separate reform to allow one additional consecutive term. In July, Vice Minister of the Presidency Alejandro Barrantes acknowledged that the government did not have 38 votes for that measure.

The new bill cites a 2003 Sala IV ruling that annulled a 1969 constitutional ban on reelection. That decision allowed former President Óscar Arias to run again and win in 2006. The filing comes days after the Supreme Court elected Patricia Vargas as its president, completing a moment in which women lead all three branches of government amid ongoing tension between the executive and the judiciary.

The reform is at the very start of the legislative process and has no effect unless it clears every stage.

World.title: Why are police patrolling with flashing lights but no sirens?
World.content:
Why are police patrolling with flashing lights but no sirens?

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department has clarified that patrol vehicles operating with flashing lights in Belize City are not necessarily responding to emergencies, but may be using the lights to increase police visibility and make their presence known.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith addressed the practice during Wednesday’s police briefing after questions were raised about police vehicles travelling through the city at night with their emergency lights activated.

Smith explained that the objective is to make the presence of law enforcement more noticeable in communities as part of the department’s policing activities.

She noted that motorists should pay attention to the behaviour of police vehicles to determine whether an emergency response is underway.

According to Smith, when a police vehicle is travelling at a normal speed with flashing lights but without a siren or horn, motorists may continue conducting their lawful business.

However, when flashing lights are accompanied by a siren and horn, drivers should recognize that officers are responding to an emergency and take appropriate action to give way.

The clarification comes as police continue employing various measures to increase their visibility and strengthen crime prevention efforts across Belize City.

World.title: Police reject accusations of unlawful preventative detention, insist arrests are based on intelligence and investigations
World.content:
Police reject accusations of unlawful preventative detention, insist arrests are based on intelligence and investigations

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department has rejected allegations that officers are engaging in preventative detention, insisting that individuals are detained only when supported by investigative leads or intelligence.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith addressed the controversy during Wednesday’s police press briefing, responding to concerns raised by the Association of Defence Attorneys over what it describes as a pattern of arbitrary detentions.

As Breaking Belize News reported on Tuesday, the Association of Defence Attorneys has accused police of repeatedly detaining individuals without charges, raising concerns about the use of the Constitution’s 48-hour detention limit and restrictions on access to legal representation.

Smith maintained that preventative detention is not a practice employed by the department and acknowledged that detaining individuals without lawful justification would constitute an abuse of power.

She further argued that indiscriminately detaining people would represent a waste of police resources.

The Association of Defence Attorneys, in a statement dated October 22, raised concerns about repeated detention of individuals without charges, particularly in Belize City and San Ignacio.

Attorney Orson Elrington has argued that the Constitution’s 48-hour detention limit does not give police unrestricted authority to detain individuals without sufficient lawful grounds.

Responding to those allegations, Smith insisted that police detentions are supported by intelligence or concrete investigative leads and that individuals taken into custody are afforded their constitutional rights.

She also maintained that detained persons are provided with the required documentation outlining their rights while in police custody.

The controversy follows a landmark High Court ruling declaring the 2020 states of emergency unconstitutional, which has renewed scrutiny of the legal limits of police powers and the detention of suspected gang members.

Smith emphasized that the department would continue pursuing investigative leads and taking action to disrupt criminal activity, but insisted those efforts would remain within the law.

World.title: BEL chairman says new solar projects could save up to $28 million annually as utility races to reduce diesel dependence
World.content:
BEL chairman says new solar projects could save up to $28 million annually as utility races to reduce diesel dependence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) could save as much as $27 million to $28 million annually in electricity generation costs if several smaller solar projects are brought online as planned, Executive Chairman Lynn Young revealed during Wednesday’s virtual press conference.

Young said BEL is accelerating efforts to introduce additional solar generation as the company struggles with expensive diesel-powered electricity, reduced hydroelectric production and continued uncertainty over electricity imports from Mexico.

According to Young, BEL has already received Public Utilities Commission (PUC) approval for two solar projects and is seeking approval for a third. He expressed hope that one of the projects could begin supplying electricity by the end of December.

The chairman said electricity from the proposed solar facilities would cost approximately 13 Belize cents per kilowatt-hour, substantially less than the cost of diesel generation, which he estimated at approximately 75 cents to $1 per kilowatt-hour depending on the equipment being used.

Young explained that the new projects could allow BEL to reduce its dependence on expensive emergency generators and potentially discontinue some temporary diesel generation arrangements.

However, he acknowledged that solar power alone cannot resolve Belize’s electricity supply challenges because the country’s most expensive period for electricity purchases generally occurs between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m., when solar generation is unavailable.

Battery storage, he explained, is therefore essential to allowing electricity generated during daylight hours to be used during evening demand peaks.

Young said larger solar and battery projects are expected around 2028, although he warned that international supply-chain constraints, lengthy equipment delivery schedules and the complexity of electricity infrastructure development could cause further delays.

The comments come after Prime Minister John Briceño criticized delays affecting the World Bank-supported battery storage project, arguing that the setback had weakened Belize’s energy security.

The World Bank-backed Belize Energy Resilience and Sustainability Project, approved in January 2025, includes battery storage installations intended to improve electricity reliability and reduce system costs.

Separately, BEL has been pursuing major renewable energy investments, while the government has sought additional international financing. Earlier this month, BBN reported that Saudi Arabia’s finance minister had agreed to review a delayed US$77 million solar energy loan.

Young emphasized that large electricity projects can take several years to move from initial planning to completion because of financing negotiations, engineering designs, equipment procurement and construction requirements.

He said smaller solar projects are being prioritized precisely because they can be developed more quickly and provide earlier relief from the cost of diesel generation.

The chairman also disclosed that BEL has reduced its capital expenditure from approximately $100 million last year to around $70 million this year because of financial pressures.

That reduction has contributed to delays in the rollout of electric vehicle charging stations, although Young said BEL remains committed to supporting the country’s transition away from gasoline and diesel-powered transportation.

He maintained that bringing cheaper renewable electricity into the national grid remains the most effective long-term solution to BEL’s financial difficulties and the pressure on consumer electricity rates.

World.title: Nearly four years after guilty pleas, two men could face 17½ and 13 years for killing of police constable Osbourne Martinez
World.content:
Nearly four years after guilty pleas, two men could face 17½ and 13 years for killing of police constable Osbourne Martinez

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly four years after pleading guilty to manslaughter in the 2018 killing of Police Constable Osbourne Martinez, Tyrique Myles and Glen Lopez are finally moving closer to sentencing, with prosecutors and defense attorneys agreeing to recommend prison terms of 17 and a half years and 13 years, respectively.

The proposed sentences were presented before High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Wednesday, October 28, after the court accepted a plea agreement between the prosecution and defense. However, the judge has not yet decided whether to approve the recommended sentences.

Myles, 26, and Lopez, 29, pleaded guilty to manslaughter in November 2022 but have remained in prison awaiting sentencing for almost four years.

The case stems from the November 2, 2018 armed robbery at the Belcove Hotel on Regent Street West in Belize City, during which the 27-year-old police officer was fatally shot while responding to a robbery in progress.

According to the agreed facts presented in court, Myles was identified as the shooter, while Lopez participated in holding the hotel owner and employees at gunpoint and stealing cash, jewelry and cellular phones.

Crown Counsel Riis Cattouse outlined the aggravating factors considered in reaching the proposed sentences, including the use of firearms, the commission of another serious crime and the fact that Martinez was killed while carrying out his duties as a police officer.

The prosecution also acknowledged questions surrounding whether Myles intended to kill the officer when he discharged his firearm, while Lopez’s level of culpability was assessed as lower because he was not identified as the shooter.

Both men received proposed reductions for their guilty pleas, although the prosecution argued that neither qualified for the maximum one-third discount because their pleas were not entered at the earliest opportunity.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, the proceedings have suffered repeated delays, including difficulties locating the original agreed facts and completing the necessary sentencing documents.

Their third co-accused, Rayford Mejia, was convicted of murder in May 2023 following a full trial and subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment.

Justice Pilgrim has scheduled further proceedings for November 10, with mitigation submissions expected on November 19 before the court determines the appropriate sentences.

World.title: Gian Teck gets 3½ years for sex with 14-year-old girl after previous charge involving another 14-year-old was dropped in January; judge cites lack of remorse and risk of reoffending
World.content:
Gian Teck gets 3½ years for sex with 14-year-old girl after previous charge involving another 14-year-old was dropped in January; judge cites lack of remorse and risk of reoffending

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-two-year-old Gian Teck has been sentenced to three years, seven months and two days in prison for unlawful sexual intercourse with a 14-year-old girl after a High Court judge found that he showed little genuine remorse and presented a risk of reoffending.

Justice Nigel Pilgrim handed down the sentence on Wednesday, October 28, following Teck’s guilty plea earlier this month. The judge cited significant aggravating factors, including troubling statements Teck made during a Social Inquiry Report assessment in which he reportedly indicated that he saw no difference between having sexual intercourse with a minor and an adult.

The court also rejected Teck’s claim of genuine remorse, noting that although he had asked for forgiveness, his defense had challenged the victim’s credibility during the trial. Justice Pilgrim stressed that children must be protected, even from themselves, warning that adults who engage in sexual intercourse with minors should expect imprisonment.

“Adults are not to have sex with minors under the age of 16, period,” the judge declared.

Justice Pilgrim initially arrived at a five-year sentence after considering the circumstances of the offense and the aggravating factors. He subsequently reduced the sentence to four years after considering Teck’s previously clean record and positive character references. However, because Teck only pleaded guilty after the victim had testified, the judge granted a 10 percent reduction rather than the usual one-third discount for an early guilty plea.

After crediting Teck for seven days previously spent on remand, the final sentence was calculated at three years, seven months and two days, effective October 1, 2026.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Teck was 18 when he had sexual intercourse with the minor at his Belize City residence on June 5, 2023. He subsequently admitted to police that the encounter occurred but claimed he believed the girl was 15.

Teck also previously faced separate allegations involving another 14-year-old girl. That case was discontinued in January 2026 after the complainant declined to testify. Justice Candace Nanton cautioned at the time that the prosecution’s decision to enter a nolle prosequi did not amount to an acquittal and that the charges could be reinstated.

Teck was represented by attorney Javier Williams, while Crown Counsel Kirk Brown appeared for the prosecution.

World.title: Gunmen open fire on Belmopan residence reportedly linked to paralyzed street figure Ronlee Petillo; 19-year-old woman injured
World.content:
Gunmen open fire on Belmopan residence reportedly linked to paralyzed street figure Ronlee Petillo; 19-year-old woman injured

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a shooting at a residence in the Maya Mopan area of Belmopan believed to be associated with well-known street figure Ronlee Petillo, who was left paralyzed following a deadly shooting in March 2025.

The latest incident occurred shortly before 1:00 a.m. on Wednesday, October 28, when an unidentified gunman reportedly approached the residence, knocked on the door and identified himself as a police officer.

According to Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith, several individuals were inside the home when the man demanded that the door be opened. When the occupants refused, the house came under gunfire, resulting in injuries to 19-year-old Marcella Arzu.

Arzu was transported for medical attention and is listed in stable condition.

During Wednesday’s police briefing, Smith revealed that investigators do not believe Arzu was the intended target, but rather another individual residing at the property.

When questioned directly about whether the suspected target was Ronlee Petillo, Smith declined to confirm the information. She also refused to confirm whether the individual in question was paralyzed and uses a wheelchair.

Petillo, who has been associated with Belize City’s George Street gang, survived a deadly shooting along the Philip Goldson Highway in March 2025. The attack claimed the life of Joseph Lee Garcia and left several others injured.

Among the survivors was Shemar Faber, who subsequently died from his injuries in October 2025. At the time, BBN reported that Petillo had been left paraplegic as a result of the March shooting.

In the latest incident, police have identified two vehicles of interest through footage obtained from the Public Safety Monitoring Unit and are pursuing those leads as part of their investigation.

Smith also confirmed that police operations observed at the Maya Mopan residence following the shooting were connected to the ongoing investigation.

Police have not established a motive or officially identified the intended target.

World.title: Belizean artist Kenny Juice shot by two gunmen after leaving Queen Charlotte Street shop; Police suspect gang connection
World.content:
Belizean artist Kenny Juice shot by two gunmen after leaving Queen Charlotte Street shop; Police suspect gang connection

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police believe that the shooting of 26-year-old Belizean entertainer Kenroy Linares, popularly known as Kenny Juice, may be gang-related, although investigators have not established a definitive motive.

Linares was shot on Queen Charlotte Street in Belize City on Monday night, October 26, 2026.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith said officers patrolling the Yabra area heard gunshots at approximately 7:30 p.m. and subsequently received information from the police control room concerning a shooting on Queen Charlotte Street.

Investigations revealed that Linares had just exited a shop when two men approached him and opened fire, causing injuries.

He was transported for medical attention and was listed in stable condition, according to the latest information provided by police.

While investigators have not determined the exact circumstances that led to the attack, Smith indicated that the information gathered so far suggests a possible gang connection.

The shooting comes amid continued gun violence in Belize City, including an incident on Arlington Drive on Sunday night in which an 11-year-old girl was injured after a gunman opened fire on a group socializing outside a residence.

Police continue investigating the attack on Linares.

World.title: Two cops charged with extortion after detainee allegedly arranged $4,000 payment to be released from custody
World.content:
Two cops charged with extortion after detainee allegedly arranged $4,000 payment to be released from custody

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two members of the Belize Police Department, including a police sergeant, have been jointly charged with extortion following allegations that a detainee arranged a $4,000 payment to secure his release from police custody.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith confirmed during Wednesday’s police briefing that 48-year-old Police Sergeant Branston Peters and 40-year-old Police Constable Ociel Aguilar have been formally arrested and charged.

According to Smith, the charges stem from a complaint made by an individual who reported that, while detained by police on September 24, 2026, he arranged for $4,000 to be handed over in exchange for his release.

The allegation prompted a police investigation, which subsequently resulted in criminal charges being brought against both officers.

The charges come amid renewed scrutiny of alleged misconduct within law enforcement. On Monday, BBN reported that another police constable had been charged with the theft of more than $26,000 worth of government fuel.

Police have not disclosed the circumstances surrounding the complainant’s original detention or whether the alleged $4,000 payment was ultimately delivered.

Both officers now face criminal proceedings in connection with the allegations, which have not been proven in court.

World.title: WATCH: Holness hits back at Beenie Man after Hurricane Melissa relief comments
World.content:
This file photo shows Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness addressing a special press briefing at Jamaica House on Tuesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

ST ELIZABETH, Jamaica — Against the backdrop of criticism from dancehall veteran Beenie Man over the Government’s hurricane relief efforts, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness on Wednesday took a swipe at the artiste.

He said over $300 million of the Government’s $3.8 billion allocation to the health sector post Hurricane Melissa was spent to rebuild the Black River Hospital.

“[With] all the dignitaries… who are here, I thought to myself the Minister [of Health Dr Christopher Tufton] neglected to invite Beenie Man, because then he would see first-hand how the Government has been spending on the recovery,” Holness said on Wednesday during the reopening of the Black River Hospital.

Beenie Man criticised the Holness administration’s handling of millions of dollars in donations it received to assist Jamaicans devastated by the storm.

World.title: Holness points to sabotage
World.content:
A woman walks past these Hurricane Melissa-wrecked buildings in Black River, St Elizabeth, last Friday. Today marks the first anniversary of the Category 5 storm that inflicted heavy damage on sections of the island. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has signalled that changes are coming to the public sector as there are individuals deliberately delaying or derailing government programmes. As such, he said the country should prepare for a shake-up in how the public service operates.

Holness said he was increasingly concerned that some public officers were obstructing the Government’s plans, warning that it could no longer be “business as usual” as Jamaica continues to recover from Hurricane Melissa.

“I don’t usually speak in extreme terms, and there are some subjects that it is better not to speak about them. But more and more I’m coming to the conclusion that there are persons in the public sector who are determined to, again, to use the very harsh word, sabotage. And I don’t say it lightly, they delay, derail policies, programmes, and initiatives of the Government. I see you, [and] I’m preparing the country to expect these changes, as it cannot be business as usual,” he said.

The prime minister was speaking at a special press briefing at Jamaica House on Tuesday during which he outlined plans to reduce government spending and improve the delivery of public services as the country faces the continuing cost of hurricane recovery.

While announcing further spending restrictions, Holness said the Government would also examine how ministries, departments, agencies, and public bodies operate, with the aim of removing duplication, improving coordination, and speeding up decisions.

He indicated that personnel changes would form part of that process, particularly where leadership, capacity, or performance needed to be strengthened.

Holness said the changes were necessary to ensure that the public service could respond more effectively to the country’s needs, especially as the Government tries to move recovery projects forward while controlling expenditure.

“Government must be reset and reorganised to meet the needs of our country. Government must be frugal and disciplined in its use of public resources, agile in its decisions, and responsive to the people it serves,” he said.

The warning comes as the Government intensifies its efforts to redirect funds towards hurricane recovery, including an additional $9.65 billion for the Restoration of Owner and Occupant Family Shelter (ROOFS) programme.

Holness said the Government could not meet every demand without making difficult choices, and that savings would have to be found in some areas to finance higher-priority needs.

“If I have to find $9.65 billion for the ROOFS programme, some things will have to be cut elsewhere,” he said.

Among the measures announced on Tuesday was an immediate pause on the purchase of motor vehicles for public officials until March 31, 2027, alongside a review of Government property leases and restrictions on hotel retreats and end-of-year celebrations.

The measures build on a moratorium on non-essential official overseas travel announced last week, scheduled to remain in effect until March 31, 2027.

Holness said greater financial restraint must be matched by improvements in how public institutions work, arguing that Government leaders and senior officials must make priorities rather than attempt to satisfy every demand at once.

He said the Government would be expected to make changes to its systems and procedures, while warning that officials who delay or derail its programmes could not expect the existing arrangements to continue unchanged.

World.title: Sagicor delivers double boost to Melissa-hit schools
World.content:
Little London High School grade 11 student Alyssa Hinds (second right) presents a plaque of appreciation to Christopher Zacca (second left) — president and CEO of Sagicor Group Jamaica Limited, and chairman, Sagicor Foundation Jamaica — in recognition of the organisation’s support. Sharing in the moment are Latoya Harris Ghartey, executive director, National Education Trust; and Garfield James, principal, Little London High School.

SAGICOR Foundation Jamaica on Monday handed over restored facilities at two schools damaged by Hurricane Melissa last October and announced the allocation of an additional $30 million to support further school restoration.

The $30 million, the foundation explained, will build on the record $152 million raised through the 2026 Sagicor Sigma Corporate Run, which surpassed its $150-million fund-raising target.

“Last year, following the hurricane, Sagicor allocated $200 million to national recovery efforts, separate from and in addition to the funds raised through the Sagicor Sigma Corporate Run. I am pleased to share that $30 million of that allocation will support additional school projects, helping to fast-track restoration and return more children to safe, welcoming spaces,” Sagicor Group Jamaica President and CEO Christopher Zacca said during the handover at Little London High School in Westmoreland.

The foundation said that restoration works, at a combined value of approximately $50.4 million, have been completed at Little London High and Mayfield Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth.

Approximately $22.2 million was invested at Mayfield Primary and Infant School while approximately $28.2 million funded restoration and infrastructure works at Little London High School. The projects addressed priority sections damaged by the hurricane rather than complete school-wide refurbishments.

The two schools are among five selected to benefit from the 2026 run. Work at the remaining beneficiaries — Hopewell High, Green Pond High, and Salt Marsh Primary and Infant — is nearing completion, the foundation said in a news release.

The foundation also said it will work with the Ministry of Education and the National Education Trust (NET) to identify additional schools with the greatest need for restoration support.

On Monday, Zacca credited the public’s support for helping turn the fund-raising effort into completed improvements.

“The real value is a student focusing on a lesson instead of a leaking roof, a teacher working in a safe space, and parents sending their children to school with greater peace of mind. After the year these communities have endured, that stability means everything,” the release quoted Zacca.

“When we asked Jamaica to ‘Run for the West’, people answered the call. They registered, donated, volunteered and supported because they understood that getting our children back into safe and functional schools had to be part of the recovery of western Jamaica. Today, we can actually see what that generosity has accomplished. These improved spaces mean students and teachers can focus again on what matters most — teaching, learning and building a better future,” Zacca added.

Sagicor Foundation board member Brigette Azan said restoring schools is ultimately about protecting opportunity for Jamaica’s children.

“Education remains one of the greatest tools we have for creating opportunity. Not every child starts life with the same advantages or resources, but every child deserves the opportunity to learn, discover their talents, and fulfil their potential. That is why getting our students back into safe, welcoming schools matters so much,” Azan said.

Latoya Harris Ghartey, executive director of NET, said the completion of the projects demonstrates what can be achieved through purposeful partnerships centred on students and their education.

“When we first began this process, the priority was clear: identify the schools where the need was greatest and help get our children back into safe spaces where they could learn and thrive. NET was pleased to work with the Sagicor Foundation from those early stages, supporting the process of identifying the beneficiary schools and the areas requiring attention. Seeing the work completed at Mayfield Primary and Infant School and Little London High School is especially meaningful because, ultimately, this is about ensuring that the disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa does not become a lasting barrier to our children’s education,” Harris Ghartey said.

World.title: Kranium: A ‘glitch in the dancehall matrix’
World.content:
Kranium recently returned to New York for a performance at Sony Hall after a four-year absence.

“I am a glitch in the matrix.”

For Kranium, the statement is more than a catchphrase. It is his unapologetic assessment of a career that has challenged conventional thoughts about what it takes to establish oneself in dancehall, particularly the long-held assumption that an artiste must be physically based in Jamaica to remain connected to the culture and build a successful career.

Born in Jamaica, but based in New York, USA, for much of his professional journey, the Nobody Has to Know hitmaker has established an international presence while operating outside the island’s borders.

And while he is not seeking recognition for changing the game, he believes the evidence of his impact is already there.

“I don’t just feel that way; I know it for a fact,” Kranium told the Jamaica Observer when asked whether he considers himself among the artistes who helped change perceptions about where a dancehall career can be built.

“The facts and the history are there: I took dancehall music and cemented myself as a household name while living outside Jamaica. Unfortunately for those who withhold that information it is already written: Kranium is a glitch in the matrix,” he added.

It is a confident position, but one Kranium believes his body of work supports. Attributing his success to more than just overcoming geographical barriers, the entertainer shared that he has had to tap into his creativity while ensuring he remained authentically himself.

“I didn’t feel like I had to work twice as hard. What I had to do was create authentic, quality music and be real with myself,” he said.

That commitment to authenticity has helped Kranium to cultivate a catalogue that includes songs that have received gold and platinum certifications across three major markets.

For him, those milestones are both a measure of achievement and an incentive to keep pushing.

“Seeing them gives me more motivation to take things to the highest level at my own pace,” he said. “Most importantly, seeing them on my wall reminds me that I am a very talented artiste. It gives me all the validation I need.”

He also sees room for Jamaican music to compete more forcefully on the international stage, provided the ambition extends beyond simply being successful within the genre.

“Yes, I think we can compete at the highest level once we understand that we need to be the best in the school, not just the class,” he said, indicating that geography is not the defining factor in whether a song travels. He explained that the quality of the music and the way it is introduced to audiences matter more than an artiste’s physical location.

“I know how to make authentic music. Even if I were under a rock, if the song is a hit, it will take off with the right juggling,” he said. “I think you can still stay connected as long as you remain true to the culture and understand the importance of paying attention to the current state of dancehall.”

His comments take on added significance against the backdrop of his recent return to New York for a performance after a four-year absence.

The city has played a significant role in his development as an artiste, making the occasion more than another date on an international schedule. The timing also coincided with the anniversary of his first album, We Can, achieving gold certification, creating what he described as the right moment to reconnect with the market.

“Now was the right time to return because everything aligned — the anniversary of my first album, We Can, going gold and, most importantly, the fact that I hadn’t done a show there in four years,” he said.

For Kranium, the performance felt like a homecoming, and he approached it with the intention of making the night memorable for the audience. From the energy of the show to his choices of fellow performers, he was deliberate about how the experience unfolded.

“It felt like a homecoming. That’s why I worked so hard to make sure the show stayed active all night, right down to who I wanted to share the stage with,” he said.

The return also signals that he intends to maintain that connection without over-saturating the market. While he recognises the value of appearing regularly before an audience, he is mindful of the balance between being present and overdoing it.

“There’s a fine line between being in the market frequently and overdoing it. But, for sure, it won’t take that long for me to hold another event there,” he said.

World.title: NOT SO SWEET
World.content:
THE price of bread, biscuits, buns, and drinks could come under fresh pressure as Jamaican manufacturers face the prospect of paying more for refined sugar once a new refinery in Belize begins supplying the Caribbean market.

Major food and beverage producers, including Wisynco, Lasco and ice-cream maker Caribbean Cream, have raised concerns that changes to regional import arrangements could make it more expensive to buy the sugar used in products consumed by Jamaicans every day.

Manufacturers fear that once the Belize refinery begins supplying the region, they could lose the duty waivers that allow them to buy refined sugar from outside Caricom at world market prices. They would then have to weigh the Belize supplier’s price against the cost of overseas sugar carrying a 40 per cent import tariff.

Wisynco Group Chairman William Mahfood said the potential increase would affect businesses across food manufacturing, with consequences for consumer prices.

“Legally, we can’t really challenge it, so the only thing I think we can do is push the Government to lobby for a reduction in the CET,” Mahfood told the Jamaica Observer, referring to Caricom’s common external tariff.

He said Belizean suppliers had indicated that they were proposing a 40 per cent increase in refined sugar prices, arguing that the tariff protection would leave Jamaican manufacturers with little room to find a cheaper alternative.

“These trade regimes were not intended to have, you know, penalties, which is really what it is…,” Mahfood said. “It’s effectively like Jamaicans are being penalised so that an investor can put a refinery in Belize.”

Mahfood argued that reducing the tariff would allow manufacturers to continue buying sugar from other suppliers without facing the full 40 per cent duty.

“If the CET goes down, it changes the whole dynamic and it gives us the ability then to import refined sugar from wherever and we’ll pay the duty,” he said.

“It won’t have as significant an impact on the cost of the finished product as a 40 per cent price increase.”

An increase in the cost of sugar would not automatically produce an equivalent increase in the price of bread, biscuits or drinks. The effect would depend on how much sugar a product contains, other production costs and how much of the increase manufacturers and retailers pass on.

But the ingredient’s use across food and beverage manufacturing means the concern extends well beyond the three companies that spoke with the Business Observer.

Lasco’s James Rawle said the company had been discussing the matter with the Jamaica Manufacturers and Exporters Association (JMEA), but had received no formal notification about future sourcing arrangements.

“The major concern that Lasco has, you know, and I would imagine that this is shared by sugar users, is that we are all sourcing sugar on the world market at the world market price,” Rawle said.

He explained that waivers have allowed manufacturers to import refined sugar without paying the external tariff because regional producers have not been able to supply their requirements.

“We haven’t received anything like samples or anything like that from the proposed suppliers from Belize,” he added.

Asked whether the concern was about the inconvenience of changing suppliers, Rawle was direct.

“How it’s going to impact price.”

Caribbean Cream Chief Executive Officer Christopher Clarke raised similar concerns at the ice cream maker’s annual general meeting on Monday, saying additional approvals or changes to duty-free access could increase costs, extend purchasing lead times and complicate production planning.

“Our principal concern is whether changes in regional sourcing arrangements could limit our access to competitively priced sugar from alternate suppliers,” Clarke said during his presentation.

In the question-and-answer session, he added: “The concern is being forced to supply from one place, while right now, as it is now, we have the option to buy it from anywhere we want to.”

Caribbean Cream has not yet quantified the potential financial impact.

More than price

In an interview with the

Business Observer, JMEA representatives Kamesha Turner and technical consultant Joy Angulu said manufacturers also needed certainty about when the refinery would begin supplying them and time to test its sugar.

Turner said the changing timetable made purchasing decisions more difficult for businesses that arrange their supplies well in advance.

“The timeline for this refinery continues to be a moving target. So even that within itself creates some uncertainty for businesses,” she said.

During the interview, the JMEA representatives explained that obtaining samples was an essential part of preparing for a change in supply.

“The quality of your sugar will affect the quality of your product,” Angulu said, explaining that manufacturers would need to conduct product trials and stability testing.

The association said higher sugar costs could also weaken the competitiveness of Jamaican exports. Manufacturers selling overseas must compete with producers that may still have access to ingredients at lower world market prices.

“We can’t just look at Caricom as being a protectionist market because we’re now playing in a global landscape where we have to ensure that our products are competitive,” Turner said.

The association is working with Jamaican Government ministries on its position ahead of regional trade discussions.

“We are in dialogue with Foreign Affairs and Minister of Finance to put together the position,” Turner said.

The regional case

Caribbean Sugar Refinery (CSR) is being developed at the Santander complex in Belize to expand the region’s capacity to produce refined sugar.

The Caricom Private Sector Organization (CPSO), which supports the project and another refinery investment in Guyana, estimates that the region imported more than US$150 million worth of refined sugar from outside Caricom in 2024. It argues that processing more of the region’s raw sugar within the Caribbean would reduce dependence on external suppliers and strengthen regional production.

CSR has said regional refining capacity could improve supply stability and strengthen manufacturers’ ability to compete with producers outside Caricom.

In a September statement, the company said tariff waivers for refined white sugar would remain in place until April 1, 2027, allowing customers time to adjust while commissioning, quality assurance and distribution arrangements were completed. It said full commissioning was expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.

A report on an August stakeholder meeting, published in the Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica and VM Group’s September economic bulletin, said CSR intended to use the international London No. 5 refined sugar price as its reference, with logistics, payment terms and other commercial details negotiated with customers. The report also said the company was open to local warehousing and established distributors serving Jamaican buyers.

The JMEA said a proposed transition discussed with regional stakeholders would begin with manufacturers sourcing 30 per cent of their refined sugar regionally and 70 per cent from outside Caricom. The regional share would rise gradually to 70 per cent by the fifth year.

Those proportions remain a proposal. The association said they had been discussed at stakeholder meetings but had not yet been settled through Caricom’s Council for Trade and Economic Development (COTED), which makes decisions on tariff arrangements.

“So we’re not sure how they plan to move forward with that,” Angulu said.

World.title: ON THE BRINK
World.content:
Jamaican football superstar Khadija Shaw (Photo: AFP)

KHADIJA “Bunny” Shaw has long been one of Jamaica’s brightest stars. However, her historic achievement at the women’s Ballon d’Or has strengthened the belief that she deserves greater global recognition, with the dream of becoming the world’s best player closer than ever before.

Reggae Girlz superstar Shaw finished third in the Ballon d’Or Féminin rankings on Monday at the awards ceremony in London. She finished behind winner Alexia Putellas of Spain, who claimed her third hold on the award, while compatriot and former Barcelona teammate Ewa Pajor finished second.

Shaw, the only Jamaican and fourth non-European player to finish in the top three in the award’s history, had an incredible 2025/2026 season with Women’s Super League (WSL) and FA Cup champions Manchester City, where she finished with 35 goal contributions including 21 goals in 22 games to win her third-straight WSL golden boot.

The reigning WSL Player of the Season, Professional Footballers Association (PFA) Player of the Year and Football Writers Association (FWA) Footballer of the Year joined male superstars Erling Haaland and Kevin De Bruyne as the only Man City players to finish in the top three.

Women’s football writer with The Guardian in the UK, Tom Garry, told the Jamaica Observer that Shaw’s third-place finish shouldn’t be underestimated.

“The mere fact that she made the top three despite not playing Champions League football last season, said a lot about how revered she is and how immensely well-regarded she is across the world,” Garry said. “Almost every colleague I interact with in the media considers Shaw to be the best out-and-out central number nine in the world.”

Since joining City in 2021, Shaw has established herself among England’s elite, scoring 127 goals in 146 appearances in all competitions.

However, some in the sport believe she hasn’t received the level of recognition she deserves in the UK and wider Europe for her performances, particularly when compared with other top players.

Sports reporter and presenter with UK football outlets Hayters TV and FourFourTwo, Ayisha Gulati, who covered Monday’s Ballon d’Or ceremony, believes the lack of recognition is no fault of Shaw’s and expects that to change in the near future.

“I think there have been times when Bunny Shaw has been overlooked, although some of that comes down to the wider landscape of women’s football,” Gulati told the Observer. “Barcelona have been the dominant force in the women’s game in recent years, with global superstars like Alexia Putellas and Aitana Bonmatí attracting a lot of attention and dominating conversations about who the best players in the world are.”

“By comparison, Manchester City haven’t been competing in the Champions League in the same way, while Jamaica are not a leading nation in international football. Those factors can influence how much global exposure a player receives, regardless of their individual quality. But Shaw’s performances and the individual awards she has collected make it increasingly difficult to overlook her.”

Garry also believes Shaw warrants far greater appreciation on the international stage.

“I do think she is sometimes overlooked, and that is probably because so much emphasis is placed on performances at senior international level and especially at major international tournaments such as a World Cup and — through no fault of Bunny’s — that means the players who are part of more successful international teams are naturally getting more credit. That’s a shame, because Bunny and — for example, Ewa Pajor of Poland or Melchie Dumornay of Haiti — deserve more awards than they get.”

Shaw described being named the third-best player in the world as a “huge honour”. She finished 24th in the 2023 rankings before climbing to 15th in 2024.

Gulati and Garry believe her performances in Man City’s European campaign, along with her exploits at FIFA World Cup could be key to her bid to lift the prestigious golden ball.

“The Ballon d’Or is an individual award, but team success and performances in high-profile matches has a big influence on how players are perceived,” Gulati said “Manchester City must compete deep into the Champions League and delivering in those decisive knockout games would give Shaw an even bigger platform to showcase her ability. Internationally, Jamaica qualifying for and performing well at the next World Cup would also help, however, that is not entirely within her control and she can only do so much.”

Garry said, “Realistically, in 2027 she would either need to be part of a Champions League-winning side with Manchester City or a Jamaica side that goes into the latter stages of the Women’s World Cup, or perhaps if she was able to win the Golden Boot for the most goals at the World Cup, regardless of how far Jamaica progressed overall. The former will be very difficult because Barcelona are the heavy favourites for the Champions League.”

Next month, Shaw could cap off an already remarkable year by helping the Reggae Girlz secure a third-straight World Cup appearance when they battle Costa Rica in the quarter-finals of the Concacaf W Championship in Texas.

It will be the 50th senior cap for Shaw, who has 67 international goals to her name, including seven so far in 2026.

World.title: Main witness struggles to recall purpose of room at Kevin Smith’s church
World.content:
The lead attorney for murder accused Andre Ruddock jolted a key witness during cross-examination on Tuesday after he failed to explain the purpose of a room at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James, that was shown to him in photographs in the Home Circuit Court.

The witness was recalled to the stand to point out scenes in the photographs in the high-profile trial, and was seriously tested by defence attorney Anthony Williams, who was unrelenting in his questions.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 human sacrifice type killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner, whose throat was slashed, allegedly by the accused, who was said to be acting on instructions from his now deceased pastor Kevin Smith.

However, the attorney has insisted that the woman was killed by the pastor and that Ruddock was intimidated, threatened, and forced to say that he was the one responsible for cutting the woman’s throat.

The attorney accused the witness of covering up for the pastor.

During examination-in-chief by lead prosecutor Latoya Bernard, the witness was asked to explain what the room was used for.

However, he could not give a proper explanation.

Therefore, during during cross-examination, Williams tackled him heavily on the topic.

“When that image came up, the prosecutor asked you if you can remember what that is. Remember?” Williams asked.

“Yes I do,” the witness said.

“I observed you looking at the image for some time and you indicated to the prosecutor that you do not recall what that image is. Correct?” Williams asked.

The witness agreed that he in fact indicated that he did not recognise the area at the time.

Williams subsequently invited him to look at the image again.

The witness then said it was an area that was located beside a space that was used for storage.

“It is the area to the back beside where the storage would be. It has chairs and an altar,” he explained.

Williams then asked the witness to identify a grey object in a photo, which he confirmed to be a chair.

“Would you classify it as an executive type chair?” Williams asked.

The witness told the lawyer that he did not know what an executive chair was.

“Let me break it down. Would you classify it as a chair fitting for the pastor?” Williams asked, to which the witness explained that pastor Smith did not sit in those types of chairs.

“He had a custom-made chair,” the witness said.

Williams, then asked the witness what the room where the chair was located in was used for.

“It wasn’t used for anything specific. He just fixed up the area otherwise from the storage to the side,” the witness replied.

The attorney then asked: “In 2021, did you see persons in that room and before?”

“I don’t remember exactly when the room was fixed up, Sir, so I can’t tell you that I saw people in there doing anything, but I can recall seeing Mr Ruddock and [two other people] on that day. They were at the door of the room, Sir,” the witness replied.

That prompted the attorney to ask the witness if he was in fact an adjutant to the pastor.

The witness answered in the affirmative.

The lawyer then asked: “As an adjutant to the pastor, you did say that part of your duties was to comb his hair, brush his hair, and get him ready?”

The witness denied telling the court previously that he combed or brushed the pastor’s hair.

“I didn’t say comb or brush his hair, Sir. I did say sheer his head. Trim him,” the witness said.

“How long you had been an adjutant to pastor Smith?” Williams asked.

“If my mind serves me correctly, it would be from 2015 to 2021, six years,” the witness responded.

Williams then asked the witness that if, for six years he shaved the pastor’s head and was so close to him, how come the room, which appeared to be a meeting room, was unknown to him.

“As I stated to you, we moved to this location somewhere around 2019. This building was not built and completed until somewhere around 2020. It was not fully completed at that point in time after COVID-19. This room that you are looking at right there, Sir, that room I don’t want to assume, but if my mind serves me correctly it would have been done sometime late 2020 into 2021. There was no specific reason for that room,” the witness said.

The attorney proceeded to ask the witness what else he did apart from shave the pastor’s head.

“I helped him to get ready. I helped him to get dressed. I would help him put on his shoes. I would take his Bible and his bag and I would bring it to the pulpit or the altar and I would place it there,” the witness responded.

Williams, who seemed to be having a field day, the said: “The prosecutor asked you to look at that picture and you said you can’t recall, but suddenly you recall what that room was. What made you remember, within the space of a short time, what that room was?”

The witness replied: “Sir, by looking at the entrance to the storage area, I then realised what the area was. If I can go a little bit further, the reason why I did not remember in the moment what the area was is because there was a lot of shift around and changes done prior to an event that was held on the Saturday [October 16, 2021].”

Williams asked him if he would agree “that as someone who was very close to the pastor, in terms of getting him ready, putting on his shoes, taking his Bible and bag to the pulpit and shaving his hair, that you, in the capacity as an adjutant, you knew the various sections of the church, including that one?”

The witness replied: “Sir, as I stated previously, there were a lot of changes done to areas and there are areas that look identical in the sanctuary. Based on the set up, I couldn’t tell you where exactly it is.”

The trial continues today, when the main investigator is expected to testify from a remote location.

World.title: New power players at Elite
World.content:
Lewis founded the Ideal Group of Companies, which includes Ideal Betting Company Limited, Ideal Finance Corporation Ltd, Ideal Portfolio Services Co. Ltd, Ideal Securities Brokers Limited, Resource in Motion Ltd, Ideal Global Investment Company Limited, Ideal Group Corporation Ltd, Resource Assets Ltd, Donwis Limited, Children’s Health, Education and Wealth Foundation.

THE mystery surrounding the recent shake-up in ownership at Elite Diagnostic Limited has been partly cleared, with two St Lucia-registered companies emerging as its largest shareholders following weeks of heavy trading that raised questions about a possible takeover of the Junior Market-listed company.

Resource Assets Limited (RAL) and Navy Inc. now hold 49.80 per cent and 20.96 per cent, respectively, of Elite’s issued ordinary shares, according to a disclosure issued on Monday by the company’s secretary, Cube Corporate Support Limited. Together, the two companies account for 70.76 per cent of Elite’s issued shares, although neither has disclosed any arrangement to exercise control jointly.

RAL has been linked to Jamaican businessman and investor Donovan Lewis, whose investment interests extend across several companies listed on the Jamaica Stock Exchange. However, the latest disclosure does not independently identify Lewis as RAL’s beneficial owner.

The announcement follows several weeks of speculation over who had been acquiring large blocks of Elite shares after a series of transactions between July and October significantly altered the company’s ownership structure.

The transactions attracted attention earlier this month after Elite disclosed that a review of shareholder records showed a single investor holding more than 50 per cent of its issued ordinary shares between October 2 and 6. The holding subsequently fell to approximately 38 per cent, raising questions about whether the temporary majority position triggered an obligation to make a takeover offer to remaining shareholders.

Under the applicable takeover rules, an investor acquiring 50 per cent or more of a listed company’s voting shares may be required to make an offer to other shareholders unless an exemption applies.

Monday’s disclosure confirms that RAL held 49.80 per cent of Elite as at October 23, just below the 50 per cent threshold.

In response to enquiries from Elite, both RAL and Navy Inc indicated that they had acquired their shares as long-term investments and had no immediate intention of purchasing additional shares.

“It acquired its shares for long-term investment purposes and with a view to enhancing shareholder value,” the shareholders stated in their responses to the company.

Both entities also advised that they were not acting in concert with any other person concerning their Elite shareholdings and that their voting rights were not subject to any agreements.

Elite Diagnostic, which listed on the JSE Junior Market in February 2018, provides medical imaging services, including MRI, CT scans and X-rays. The company is chaired by Steven Gooden, while Marjorie Miller serves as general manager.

Lewis’S investment interests

The reported connection between RAL and Lewis has drawn attention to the businessman, who has built sizeable investments across several Jamaican listed companies.

Lewis, founder of the Ideal Group of Companies, has investment interests spanning banking, financial services, food manufacturing and distribution.

Through Resource in Motion Limited (RIM), he has accumulated significant holdings in GraceKennedy Limited and Salada Foods Jamaica Limited, according latest public data.

RIM holds 57.98 per cent of Salada Foods, while the original shareholding analysis places Lewis’ combined connected interest, including holdings through other companies and accounts, at 78.69 per cent.

His investment interests also extend to NCB Financial Group Limited, where the original analysis puts his combined holdings at 2.86 per cent. Lewis previously served on the board of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited between May 2002 and January 2011.

RIM has also increased its investment in Scotia Group Jamaica Limited, acquiring another 3,036,379 shares between May and July 2026. The transactions brought its reported holdings to 43,075,177 ordinary shares at the end of July.

Based on the revised acquisition consideration of J$75 per share being offered by Scotiabank Caribbean Holdings Limited, that holding would be valued at approximately J$3.23 billion.

The amount represents an estimate based on RIM’s last reported shareholding and does not establish its final entitlement under the transaction, which would depend on its holdings and the applicable terms of the offer.

While Lewis’ existing portfolio gives the reported RAL connection added significance, the extent of his interest in Elite cannot be independently established from the company’s latest shareholder disclosure alone.

Questions remain over Navy Inc

The identity of the beneficial owner of Navy Inc, Elite’s second-largest shareholder, also remains unclear.

According to information cited in the original shareholder analysis, Navy Inc was incorporated in St Lucia on November 7, 2024, with Foster Capital Inc serving as its registered agent.

Elite has not publicly identified the individuals ultimately controlling Navy Inc, although the company said it had sought information from its substantial shareholders regarding their holdings and intentions.

“The information above was provided to the Company by the shareholders concerned. The company has kept the Jamaica Stock Exchange and the Financial Services Commission informed of these matters,” Elite stated.

The unusual trading activity for the otherwise thinnly traded stock and limited information available to investors have also prompted public criticism.

Mayberry Group Limited Chairman Christopher Berry raised concerns on social media platform

X on October 12 about the movement of large blocks of Elite shares and what he regarded as information gaps affecting minority shareholders.

“Over 50 per cent of Elite has been sold, no takeover bid, stock exchange refusal to provide market [the] top 100 to market, information gaps, minority shareholders buying and selling without material information,” Berry wrote.

The concerns followed transactions involving several of Elite’s former major shareholders, including Excel Investments Inc, which had held 24.53 per cent of the company as at June 30, and NCB Capital Markets Limited, which had held 18.68 per cent.

Elite has maintained that it has kept both the JSE and the Financial Services Commission informed of the changes in shareholdings.

The company’s audited results for the financial year ended June 2026 showed revenue increasing two per cent to $867.29 million, while net profit declined 14 per cent to $27.60 million. The company has also been investing in new equipment and premises as part of efforts to expand its diagnostic services.

Elite’s annual report is due on October 28, while its first-quarter report is expected by November 14.

World.title: In the Middle East, the next front line is the narrative
World.content:
We live in an era where wars are fought not just on battlefields, but also on our screens, in our minds and through the narratives we are led to believe. Narratives are influencing perception while missiles destroy infrastructure. What happens when the war for truth becomes more dangerous than the actual battle itself? Who’s controlling the narrative?

Najla Al Midfa, researcher, TRENDS Research & Advisory

When wars end, the fighting over what they meant begins: who won, who was to blame and who can be trusted to keep the peace. These questions are settled less on the battlefield than on screens, in feeds and in group chats. For a Middle East emerging from the war that began on February 28, that contest may decide whether any new security order holds.

The region is now asking what comes after deterrence. That question brought policymakers, military leaders and researchers from the United States, Europe, Asia and the Gulf to the TRENDS 6th Annual Conference, held in Abu Dhabi and organized by TRENDS Global, in collaboration with its global offices. The answer cannot be measured only in missiles and alliances. Information resilience should be treated as security infrastructure, planned and funded like air defense, not managed as public relations.

What happens when the war for truth becomes more dangerous than the actual battle itself?

The struggle over perception can now matter as much as events on the ground. That is no longer hyperbole. In any crisis today, governments, media outlets, political movements and non-state groups compete in real time to define what is happening. Disinformation, coordinated propaganda and now content generated by artificial intelligence (AI) mean a false account can reach millions before an official one is drafted.

As former BBC correspondent Karen Allen put it at the conference, “Now in an instant, I’m able to influence millions of people,” and algorithm manipulation is what we are increasingly seeing.

This year’s war showed how real that is. Within days of the first U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, an AI-generated video of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa on fire, with crowds fleeing, was viewed tens of millions of times, according to BBC Verify. Fabricated images of damaged U.S. facilities in the Gulf spread just as fast, some posted by Iranian state-linked outlets. UAE Minister of State Noura Al Kaabi later described the attacks on the country as coming “from the sky and behind our screens.” Her government’s answer was to treat “fake news and misinformation as a security threat.”
