A more damaging false story was not a single video. It was the idea that the Gulf was a party to the war. The UAE did not want this war and said so. On March 3, Minister of State Reem Al Hashimy said the UAE did not “seek to expand the circle of confrontation,” that it had “repeatedly confirmed” its territory could not be used for any military operation against Iran, and that “returning to the negotiating table is the only rational way forward.” The attacks continued anyway. Reuters reported, citing UAE defense figures, that 186 ballistic missiles and 812 drones were fired at the country in the first days of the conflict.

Information resilience should be treated as security infrastructure, planned and funded like air defense, not managed as public relations.

Tehran sought to blur that record, framing strikes on Gulf cities as retaliation against American aggression. Its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, told NBC News that Iran had “not attacked our neighbors,” only “American bases,” and called the hotels hit in Dubai “collateral damage.” Countering that narrative does not require propaganda of our own. It requires putting the record in front of the world quickly and repeatedly: the UAE’s public calls for restraint before the war, its refusal to let its territory be used against Iran, and the hundreds of missiles and drones fired at it, most of which it shot down. Facts published fast, through verified channels, in Arabic, English and Farsi, are harder to bury than corrections issued too late.

Even after a war ends, the threats do not disappear; they simply take different forms. Ceasefires and reconstruction depend on public trust. If populations come to believe that the peace is a betrayal, or that a neighbor cannot be trusted, no deterrence framework or security pact will survive contact with domestic politics. Spoilers understand this. Their cheapest weapon is a story.

Seen from the Gulf, the lesson of recent years is that speed and credibility beat silence. Crisis communication is not a side function of security. When official channels inform the public quickly, consistently and honestly, rumors have less room to grow. When they hesitate, someone else fills the gap.

None of this is simple. Governments everywhere are still working out where countering disinformation ends and controlling speech begins, and that debate should stay open. But the common ground is wider than it looks: a society cannot be secure if it cannot tell what is true.

The harder test comes now. After a war, influence campaigns shift from shock to slow erosion: relitigating who was to blame, questioning whether Gulf governments can protect their people, and setting neighbors and communities against each other. Young connected audiences are the main target. They are also the best defense.

Protecting our societies from that influence does not mean closing them. It means official channels fast and credible enough that people turn to them first. It means platforms held to clear rules on labeling AI-generated conflict content, as X began to do in March. And it means a generation of young Emiratis and Gulf citizens equipped to verify what they see and able to tell the region’s story themselves rather than leaving it to others.

The harder test comes now. After a war, influence campaigns shift from shock to slow erosion.

This is not only a Gulf problem. The campaigns aimed at audiences in the Gulf also shape how Washington and Brussels understand the region. The UAE and its partners already work closely on defense and intelligence. Detecting and exposing cross-border influence operations belongs on that shared agenda as a joint effort between governments, platforms and researchers.

Diplomacy, investment, and deterrence will rebuild the region’s security. Whether that security holds will depend on something harder to measure: what people across the region believe about each other, and about who protects them. For the UAE, winning that argument with facts is not public relations. It is part of keeping the country safe.

Najla Al Midfa is an Emirati researcher at TRENDS Research & Advisory, a company under TRENDS Group. Her research focuses on geopolitics, international relations, economic diplomacy and regional security, with a particular interest in the UAE’s foreign policy and strategic partnerships. She holds a master’s degree in Global Affairs and Diplomatic Leadership from the Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy, where her thesis examined the UAE’s economic diplomacy through its Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement strategy.

World.title: Don’t turn a methane pause into a retreat
World.content:
Sixty investors, representing over €9.5 trillion in assets under management, have called for the EU Methane Regulation to be maintained and implemented as adopted. That statement pre-dated the Commission’s proposed one-year delay. Its central concern, however, is more relevant now: investors need a stable framework against which companies can plan, manage risk and allocate capital with confidence.

The regulation was designed with phased implementation. It gave companies, importers and national authorities time to prepare for stronger measurement, reporting and verification of methane emissions. It has helped bring methane from the margins into boardroom discussions, where it belongs.

Why methane matters to investors

For investors, methane performance can offer a useful view of how a company is run. It is an indicator of operational discipline, process safety and the quality of management oversight. By setting requirements for measurement, reporting and verification, the regulation can also improve the availability, consistency and reliability of methane data. That gives investors a stronger basis to compare companies and assess whether they are managing risks that could affect long-term value. Maintaining the regulation’s core provisions and avoiding any further delay would protect the progress already under way.

The EU’s position as a major oil and gas importer gives the Methane Regulation particular weight. Clear import requirements can improve the quality and comparability of emissions information across global supply chains. They can help create a more level playing field for companies supplying the European market, rather than allowing weak data or weaker controls to become a commercial advantage.

The choice is not between competitiveness, affordability and effective methane management. Europe can support all three.

This matters for competitiveness as well as climate-related financial risk. Energy affordability is a legitimate concern, particularly for businesses and households facing continued market volatility. But well-designed, practical rules can reward operational excellence, support informed investment decisions and give companies a clearer basis on which to plan, while implementation can be managed in ways that preserve market flexibility and limit unnecessary costs for consumers.

World.title: EU and Canada eye now-or-never window to Trump-proof their ties
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will join Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for two days of talks on trade, security, energy, education and the Arctic on Thursday.

The summit “is a very strong statement,” said Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada and EU Trade and Investment Association. “I don’t think there’s any feeling that this is going to be some discreet get-together.”

Canada is also looking to move before Europe’s politics shift. Ottawa wants changes to the partnership that will outlast Trump and Marine Le Pen, whose National Rally is polling ahead in France and has criticized the EU-Canada trade pact, CETA, said a Canadian diplomat. All the officials and diplomats in this article were granted anonymity to speak frankly about the summit preparations.

Avoiding Trump’s ire

Brussels and Ottawa are pushing to strengthen their relationship, including by cooperating more closely on trade and defense, international engagement and institutional links, according to a draft joint statement obtained by POLITICO.

In her September State of the Union speech, von der Leyen emphasized that the EU-Canada alliance is “not against anyone else.” Yet officials acknowledge that a stronger alliance risks triggering retaliation from Trump.

Von der Leyen, Costa and Carney “are fully aware that the eyes of the world are upon them,” said Camilleri.

World.title: Mark Carney isn’t the climate hero Europeans think
World.content:
Canada's prime minister used to be an eco-warrior. Now, not so much.

Ask European Union leaders what they think of Mark Carney’s climate credentials, and you’ll get a gushing response.

“We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her State of the Union speech last month, where the Canadian prime minister was the guest of honor.

“Canada and the EU are very, very like-minded,” the bloc’s climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, told POLITICO in an interview when asked about his hopes for climate collaboration between the two powers ahead of this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal.





But this rosy view sidesteps a less comfortable reality: Canada is a major fossil fuel producer whose climate ambitions fall far short of Europe’s.

And under Carney, those ambitions are weakening.

Last year, Canada produced more crude oil than any other country outside the big three producers, Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United States. Oil and gas are Canada’s biggest exports by far, and the industry lobby is an influential force in Ottawa.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at the Liberal National Convention in Montreal on Apr. 11, 2026. | Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images

In his previous life as a central banker, Carney was considered a climate champion. POLITICO even dubbed him an “eco warrior” in 2018. But since taking over as prime minister last year, he has weakened Canada’s climate policies at a rate few predicted, scrapping a national carbon tax and electric vehicle mandate and opening new oil and gas projects.

The list of climate laws Carney has watered down, repealed and canceled makes the EU’s own recent backtracking on green laws look minor. Some environmentalists argue it is comparable to U.S. President Donald Trump’s wholesale dismantling of environmental protections.

“The track the Carney government has taken on climate and environmental regulation has been a decisive move in the direction of the U.S.,” said Tim Gray, executive director of environmental non-profit Environment Defence. Carney, he said, “seems to be all in on fossil fuels.”





Keean Nembhard, a spokesperson for Canada’s Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, told POLITICO the Carney government is “committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero by 2050 by taking a pragmatic and durable approach.”

“This includes building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, and making significant investment in the low-carbon economy,” he said.

But Gray argued that Carney’s support for fossil fuels and weakening of environmental standards may complicate Canada’s attempts to forge closer ties with Europe, which has some of the world’s most stringent green laws.

Carney with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. | Pool photo by Oliver Matthys via Getty Images

Still, in Europe, Carney’s green image persists.

Last week, Belgian member of the European Parliament Saskia Bricmont gave expression to this faith in Carney’s commitment to climate issues when she called on him to lead a global push to put climate back on the agenda ahead of next month’s U.N. climate summit.

“Mr Carney … relaunch the fight against climate deregulation and for the restoration of biodiversity, and re-mobilize the international community around concrete, coordinated measures,” she said.

Carney’s green aura

Carney’s reputation as a climate champion is well earned. As governor of the Bank of England, he led a push among central bankers to take the economic risks of climate change seriously — memorably captured in his 2015 ‘Tragedy of the Horizon’ speech, in which he warned: “The catastrophic impacts of climate change will be felt beyond the traditional horizons of most actors.”

In 2021, after he’d left the Bank of England, he became a United Nations special envoy on climate action and finance and launched a net-zero financial alliance with some of the world’s biggest banks.

But things changed dramatically when Donald Trump took back the White House, and Carney replaced fellow Liberal Justin Trudeau as Canada’s prime minister in 2025. At the time, Trudeau and his Liberals had been way behind in the polls, battered by Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre’s attacks on his climate policies — in particular an unpopular consumer carbon tax.

Carney’s first act as prime minister was to scrap that tax.





Following his surprise victory in the elections that April, Carney set about promoting Canada as an “energy superpower.” To the dismay of environmental groups, he supported the “Pacific Link,” an oil pipeline costing tens of billions of dollars, designed to carry Alberta crude to Canada’s Pacific coast for export to Asia.

He then pushed for thawing relations with Beijing in January, a not-so-subtle pitch to find a new crude oil client that isn’t the U.S. Germany, rushing to replace its dependence on Russian energy, signed a long-term agreement in July to buy Canadian liquefied natural gas from a proposed port in British Columbia, despite backlash from environmental and indigenous groups.

He also scrapped laws on electric vehicle adoption, dropped plans for an emissions cap on oil and gas companies, watered down an existing industrial carbon price and introduced legislation to weaken environmental permitting rules for big infrastructure projects, which critics dubbed the “bulldoze nature bill.”

A landmark moment, according to Gray, came in November 2025, when Carney signed a memorandum of understanding with the government of Alberta, Canada’s biggest oil-producing province. That document, which promised to turn Canada into a “global energy superpower,” contained a string of promises to promote oil and gas and water down federal climate laws.

A view of the Canadian Natural Resources Limited Horizon oil sands project, north of the indigenous community of Fort McKay in Alberta on May 5, 2026. | Daphné Lemelin/AFP via Getty Images

So why the dramatic shift?

Carney, who has repeatedly positioned energy sovereignty as a bulwark against Trump’s economic aggression, offered his realpolitik response at an event in the heart of Alberta’s oil patch earlier this month.

“There’s a structural challenge of energy security and the existential challenge of climate change, and these challenges are forcing countries to think differently about where their energy comes from and on who they can rely on to supply it,” Carney said in Fort McMurray, Alberta on Oct. 1.

“Even under any plausible net zero scenario, the IEA [International Energy Agency] forecasts the world will still need tens of millions of barrels of crude a day. So the question is: who will emerge as the world’s trusted suppliers? It should be us. It must be Canada.”

Not black and white

Carney, to be sure, is no Trump. Unlike the U.S. president, he has retained his pro-climate rhetoric and promised to develop the country’s mining of critical minerals essential for the clean energy transition.

In May, he unveiled a national electricity strategy which aims to double Canada’s largely clean electricity grid by 2050 to meet soaring demand. “The path to net zero is electrification,” Carney said then.

In August, he announced C$10 billion in federal support for the Churchill Falls hydroelectric project in Newfoundland and Labrador, saying it will be the largest clean energy project in North America, capable of generating enough electricity to light up the equivalent of Canada’s three largest cities.





Nembhard, Environment Minster Dabrusin’s spokesperson, also pointed to new electricity transmission lines, electric vehicle subsidies and a C$2 billion plan to retrofit homes with heat pumps.

Canadian climate activist Alex Cool-Fergus said she does not think Carney “believes that oil and gas is the future,” but is simply being pragmatic about Canada’s economic reality.

“The electricity strategy that came out in May was incredibly important, and actually gives us a better idea of what his thinking is for the future,” she said.

Trudeau’s approach to climate change was “very much values-based, and it was about doing the right thing,” said Cool-Fergus. “I think that’s hit its limits. Carney’s approach makes more sense for the world of 2025-2026.”

The limits of the partnership

Hoekstra, the EU’s commissioner for climate, said he wants to deepen ties with Canada. “Given all the complications the world is facing, it is imperative to team up more closely with your closest partners,” he said. But he’s realistic about how far that relationship can go.

Hoekstra has ambitions of cementing the EU into a global network of economies with carbon pricing regimes. While he conceded nothing is “off the table,” he acknowledged linking the EU’s Emissions Trading System with Canada’s “quite different” version, which varies from province to province: “You’re talking about a completely different horizon, and that is not something we would attempt in the very short run.”





There are, however, other ways Hoekstra believes the EU and Canada can closely link on environmental issues.

“Doubling down, tripling down on electrification, on solar, on wind, on nuclear, on batteries,” he said, adding “that is one area that I think is potentially very fruitful for my portfolio.”

Another is critical raw materials, a key focus of this week’s summit.

Brussels is exploring ways for the European Investment Bank, the EU’s lending arm, to help finance the mining of Canadian mineral deposits that could supply the bloc with an alternative to Chinese-produced metals, with a framework agreement expected to be signed during the summit. Lithium, copper, nickel, and other key ingredients for electric vehicle batteries and clean energy technologies essential for decarbonizing Europe are abundant but often undeveloped all over Canada.

Carney at the Pomeroy Kananaskis Mountain Lodge in Kananaskis on June 17, 2025. | Geoff Robins/AFP via Getty Images

This week’s summit will also explore investing in infrastructure on Canada’s east coast to liquefy and ship Canadian gas to Europe, a move that could help the EU diversify its supply away from the U.S., which, along with Norway, has become Europe’s dominant supplier since it cut off Russian gas imports following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Many EU member countries will welcome success on these goals. But Gray warns that closer ties with Canada could lead to deeper penetration by the country’s powerful fossil fuel lobby, which he described as a “major, major force.”

“They’ll be spending time trying to make sure the alignment with the EU is in a direction that favors them,” he said.





The EU’s lack of oil and gas resources — and, by extension, the absence of a powerful fossil fuel lobby — has kept climate policy relatively bipartisan in the EU. Could inviting a fossil fuel “superpower” into the fold as an “associate member” change that?

“That would depend very much on what is an ‘associate member,’” Dutch Climate Minister Stientje van Veldhoven-van der Meer said.

World.title: Ukraine peace talks: 5 things to know about the chances of a deal
World.content:
What will they discuss?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the agenda for Abu Dhabi should first include initial steps toward de-escalation, such as prisoner swaps and ceasefires on energy infrastructure and for the Black Sea. There should also be a discussion among the technical negotiating teams of what format a future three-way meeting between leaders — Trump, Zelenskyy and Russia’s Vladimir Putin — should take, he told reporters this week.

When it comes to a final deal, one overriding question for Ukraine is what form of security guarantees it will get from Europe and the U.S., or potentially NATO. Zelenskyy won't want to accept anything he believes could leave Ukraine vulnerable to a future attack from Russia.

Putin is also likely to raise the need for security guarantees — for Russia — including limiting or potentially reversing NATO’s presence in the neighborhood.

Then there’s the question of territory. Zelenskyy’s view is that marking out any boundaries, temporarily or permanently, is something that can only be discussed at leader level. “No one else has the authority to do so,” he said Tuesday.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a press briefing at the Catshuis in the Hague on October 28, 2026. | Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP via Getty Images

Zelenskyy said during previous sets of negotiations over the past year, “as a compromise,” that Ukraine had been prepared to discuss the idea of a demilitarized “buffer zone” on both sides of the contact line in the Donbas region.

Similar ideas were proposed for other parts of Ukraine. Zelenskyy said his negotiators discussed these questions again with the Americans in recent weeks. “We are ready to discuss the issue of territories because the Russians keep wanting to discuss it and make it part of the agenda,” he said. But this would need to be at a leader-level meeting.

World.title: 5 takeaways from Andy Burnham’s first budget
World.content:
1) We’re in the holding pen

The chancellor’s big bazooka was to slap a much-anticipated tax rise on banks — but he surprised many by saying it will last only 15 months. It will raise less than £1 billion in its peak year.

It wasn’t the only temporary measure Healey unveiled on Wednesday. He extended existing cuts to fuel duty, a tax cut on household energy bills and a £2 cap on bus fares, but only until 2027. They will all need to be reviewed again before his next annual budget.

Likewise, some of Healey’s spending plans thin out after a few years, which suggests they may need topping up later. This applies even to the areas closest to Burnham’s heart. Budget documents suggest support to end rough sleeping will total £1.1 billion in the two years from April 2027 but only £270 million in the three years after that.

People pass through the Bank area of the City of London on May 29, 2024 in London. | Carl Court/Getty Images

There were plenty of changes, of course, such as to writing-down allowances, property income taxes and tax on savings. Whitehall will have to find more administration cuts while tax inspectors hunt down another £3.2 billion a year. But the Institute for Fiscal Studies, a non-partisan economic think tank, called it all a “hodgepodge” of “fiddly measures” that would do little to affect growth.

Many of the more fundamental decisions were kicked down the road. Healey has committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, but will only spell out how to fund it in a spending review at some point in 2027. Major reforms to the welfare system — spending on which is still rocketing — will only be decided after two reports by the Labour grandees Stephen Timms and Alan Milburn are published in November.

Healey published a “fiscal devolution roadmap” that spelled out a path to handing regional mayors full control of the business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, but this has an element of wait-and-see too.

World.title: EU lawmakers slam new border force powers to surveil social media
World.content:
After a 2019 monitoring tender with similar powers was revoked over criticism about privacy violations, Benifei said "the Commission now proposes copying ICE’s invasive online tracking,” referencing the much-criticized surveillance tactics of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.

Under the EU proposal, Frontex would set up an internal structure to monitor social media and report to the platform in question the content it says is facilitating illegal entry to EU countries. This comes as the Commission is seeking to double the agency's budget for the next seven years and vastly expand its powers to deport people.

The EU already has several structures that facilitate the exchange of information between civil society, social media platforms and authorities when it comes to disinformation campaigns or illegal content. These include a rapid response system on disinformation campaigns under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU's landmark law regulating digital platforms, as well as a recently established democratic resilience center.

Policing content

Brussels must tread a careful balance not to police individual pieces of content, especially given criticism from civil society activists that it is trying to become the arbiter of truth online. The legality of content is set by countries, which assign their authorities or civil society to monitor the platforms for problematic postings to be flagged to the platforms to be taken down.

Frontex would apply for trusted flagger status under the DSA, which gives priority to the content it flags to social media platforms. Entities that apply for this status have to demonstrate expertise and independence to a national authority, which grants them special status.

“The DSA’s trusted flagger program was never conceived for police forces to circumvent due process when assessing the legality of people’s online expression,” said Jan Penfrat, senior policy advisor at civil society group EDRi.

World.title: Spanish train disaster deals new blow to Sánchez’s long-shot election bid
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez, the Prime Minister of Spain near the scene of a train crash on October 28, 2026 near Los Yebenes. | Florencia Tan Jun/Getty Images

The deadly crash is undermining the prime minister’s central pitch to voters that his government is competent and bettering Spaniards’ everyday lives.

MADRID — A deadly train crash near the Spanish city of Toledo has prompted fresh questions about Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's management of public infrastructure weeks ahead of a snap election.

The cause of Wednesday's incident, in which at least 68 people were killed, has not yet been determined. But the disaster comes less than a year after another mass-casualty crash near the southern Spanish town of Adamuz. That catastrophe was attributed to poor maintenance, and it heightened scrutiny of Spain’s rail network and the left-wing government’s overall stewardship of public services.

World.title: Europe’s oil bill: EU pays €10bn more per month than in 2025
World.content:
European countries are paying far more for petroleum oil imports this year, following tensions in the Middle East in February 2026. Consumers are already facing higher petrol and diesel prices. Now, the EU’s import bill shows just how sharply costs have risen.

 

In the second quarter of 2026, the EU spent an average of €27.6 billion a month on petroleum oil imports, up 55.8% from €17.7 billion a month in 2025.

But the volume of oil imported barely changed. It rose by just 1.2%, from 36.3 million tonnes a month in 2025 to 36.7 million tonnes.

That means the EU paid €9.9 billion more a month.

The cost per tonne also rose, from €487 to €750 over the same period, returning to its 2022 peak.

Why is the bill rising?

The main reason is the rise in crude oil prices. “The monthly average of the Brent crude price in the second quarter of 2026 is 49.5% higher than the monthly average price of 2025 – a $34 per barrel increase,” Prof. Xiaoyi Mu from the University of Dundee told Euronews Business.

He noted that in 2025, around 20 million barrels of oil and oil products per day – approximately 20% of global daily consumption – were exported via the Strait of Hormuz. “When nearly 20% of world supply is cut, the price must rise to balance the market,” he said.

The cost per tonne tells the story. In the second quarter of 2026, the EU paid €750 for each tonne of imported petroleum oil. That was the second-highest level since 2021, just €2 below the peak recorded in the second quarter of 2022.

At the end of 2025, a tonne cost €435. The price rose to €498 in the first quarter of this year before jumping to €750 in the second quarter.

Szymon Kardas, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), emphasised that the war between the US, Israel and Iran had disrupted oil production and supplies to global markets, pushing prices higher.

“In some weeks, tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz returns to pre-war levels, only to fall again,” he told Euronews Business.

Kardas said such disruptions hit the EU hard because it was 90–95% dependent on oil imports from outside the bloc. According to Eurostat, this dependence stood at 96.6% in 2024.

Wolfgang Eichhammer, senior expert at the Institute for European Energy and Climate Policy (IEECP), agreed that tensions in the Middle East had the greatest impact, as supplies fell or became less secure. However, he said strong global demand also played a role, with Europe competing for oil with buyers in Asia, notably China.

The chart comparing import value and volume shows how the bill rose while the amount of oil imported remained broadly unchanged. In the second quarter of 2026, the EU spent €82.7 billion on petroleum oil imports, up from €50.3 billion a year earlier. Import volumes rose only slightly, from 105.2 million tonnes to 110.2 million tonnes.

The same pattern is evident over the past five years. Quarterly import volumes ranged from 105 million to 123 million tonnes, while the bill varied from €38 billion in early 2021 to €91.3 billion in 2022. It then fell to €47.8 billion at the end of 2025 before surging again.

Oil accounts for almost all of the rise in the EU’s energy import bill. In the second quarter of 2026, the EU spent €115.6 billion on energy imports, up from €81.4 billion in the same quarter of 2025. Petroleum oils accounted for €32.4 billion of the €34.2 billion increase, or 95%.

Spending on other energy products changed little. Gas imports rose by €1.6 billion and coal by €0.4 billion, while LNG imports fell slightly, by €0.2 billion.

Drivers pay more at the pump

European drivers have felt the impact at the pump. In the first week of January 2026, diesel cost an average of €1.54 a litre across the EU. Prices rose sharply from March, passing €2 a litre later that month and reaching €2.24 at the end of September. This was above the 2022 peak of €2.03. On 19 October, diesel stood at €2.14 a litre, 38% higher than at the start of the year.

Petrol followed a similar path. Its price rose from €1.60 a litre in early January to €2.10 at the end of September, also above its 2022 peak of €2.03. It has since fallen slightly to €1.99. Filling a 50-litre diesel tank now costs about €107, up from €77 in January.

Impact on households

Mu warned that as consumers spent more on filling their tanks, they would have less to spend on other things, such as food and other everyday goods.

“I would expect the prices of food, public transport and other everyday goods to increase as diesel is widely used in heavy transport and buses,” he added.

Kardas pointed out that the impact would vary across sectors. “Transport, heating, agriculture, and energy-intensive manufacturing will feel an immediate squeeze, passing higher freight, utility, and fossil fuels costs on to end consumers, whereas service-based industries will remain largely insulated,” he said.

How long will it last?

Experts do not expect oil import costs to fall soon. Asked whether costs would remain high in the coming months, Mu said: “Unfortunately yes, as we don’t see a practical way of ending the conflict.”

He also said higher shipping and insurance costs might not yet be fully reflected in the second-quarter bill but could push up costs in the third and fourth quarters.

Kardas expected costs linked to the conflict to “persist in the coming months and may well continue into 2027”.

Eichhammer is also of the view that there's a high risk of oil prices remaining high or rising further.

World.title: Sánchez pledges tough line on possible safety failures after Toledo train crash
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said that “the whole of Spain is in mourning” after a rail accident killed 68 people on Wednesday, expressing his solidarity with the victims’ families and the injured.

 

“Lives shattered, families broken,” he said, speaking about the consequences of the tragedy.

Sánchez stressed that the government’s overriding priority is to care for the victims and their relatives, to locate as many survivors as possible and to ensure they receive both practical and psychological support.

He also praised the work of the emergency and Civil Protection services, as well as the coordination between the authorities involved in the operation, including the regional government, the Toledo provincial council and the town councils of Toledo and Los Yébenes.

Another of the government’s main objectives, he said, is to clarify the circumstances of the accident. The Rail Accident Investigation Commission and the courts are working to determine the cause of the crash, while the Ministry of Transport is also trying to establish what happened.

One of Europe's deadliest train disasters this century has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's rail network after the transport minister reported an "error" and "inexplicable circumstances" that led to the crash.

Sánchez warned that the government would respond firmly if failures in the safety systems were confirmed.

In January, two high-speed trains collided in the southern region of Andalusia after one of them derailed and crossed onto the adjacent track, killing 46 people.

The investigation into that accident is ongoing, but the left-wing government faced heavy criticism over its management of Spain's railways.

Referring to the rail accident in Adamuz, Sánchez said it was “unacceptable” for two rail tragedies to occur in the same year, and pledged to work to restore public confidence in the safety of the rail system and in public transport.

The president of Castilla-La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, updated the death toll, which has now risen to 68. He also said health services have treated 53 people, 15 of them in a serious condition.

García-Page thanked the various administrations for their coordination, and the other regions for making their resources available to deal with the emergency.

Sánchez also announced three days of official mourning in Spain in memory of the victims.

He made the statement without taking questions from journalists.

World.title: Spain: Madrid mourns train crash victims as rescuers work through the night
World.content:
As night fell over the crash site near Urda, rescue teams continued working among the mangled carriages, using heavy cranes to lift sections of wreckage from the tracks. Footage shows a crane hoisting what appears to be part of a train's wheel assembly, while emergency workers search the damaged carriages under artificial lighting.

 

The disaster, which occurred when one train struck another that had stopped, is Spain's second deadly rail collision this year and one of Europe's deadliest railway accidents of the century.

In Madrid, dozens gathered outside City Hall in Cibeles Square for a minute of silence in memory of the victims. The tribute, organised by the Spanish Federation of Municipalities and Provinces, was attended by opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Mayor José Luis Martínez-Almeida and central government delegate Pilar Trinidad. But the gathering also became a protest against the government, with some participants holding placards reading "Corruption kills" and chanting for Transport Minister Óscar Puente to resign.

At least 68 people have died and more than 100 have been injured in a collision between two high-speed trains near Toledo, central Spain, on 28 October. Fifteen of the injured remain in critical condition.

World.title: Support for UN vote to end US embargo on Cuba falls to 30-year low
World.content:
The UN General Assembly has again called for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, but support for the resolution fell to its lowest level in more than 30 years.

 

The resolution, which has been put forward and approved almost every year since 1992, passed with 130 countries in favour, 17 against and 25 abstentions. That's the lowest level of support since 1995.

Last year, more than 160 countries backed the proposal. Germany, Italy and Latvia abstained for the first time in 34 years.

Several countries, including Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Morocco, Slovenia and Bosnia, voted against the resolution, many for the first time.

The resolution, while not legally binding, is seen as a reflection of international opinion. It calls for the lifting of the economic, trade and financial embargo against the island.

Cuban foreign minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla, left, speaks at United Nations headquarters, Wednesday. 28 October 2026. AP Photo/Seth Wenig

Renewed US pressure campaign against Cuba

The US embargo dates back to 1960, after Fidel Castro’s revolution and the nationalisation of US-owned property. Tensions between the US and Cuba are currently running high, with a renewed pressure campaign by Washington including restrictions on oil supplies and broad sanctions that have severely damaged Cuba's economy.

Just minutes before the vote took place in New York, US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz denied that Cuba was under a blockade and said "the plight of the Cuban people is exclusively the fault of this corrupt communist regime."

Ambassador Mike Waltz, US Representative to the United Nations, posts a video from the UN General Assembly on X, where he criticises the Cuban government

The Cuban government has in recent weeks accused the US of mounting a diplomatic offensive to pressure countries into withdrawing their support for the resolution.

Cuba's Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez accused Washington of seeking to "determine the nation's destiny" and "seize" its wealth.

Cuban foreign minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla holds up a photo of a medication while speaking at United Nations headquarters. 28 October 2026. AP Photo/Seth Wenig

There was also a heated confrontation between Rodríguez and Waltz, during which Rodríguez approached the US ambassador and accused him of lying, while Waltz shouted for him to back away.

During Tuesday's session, Waltz accused senior Cuban officials of enjoying luxury lifestyles while ordinary Cubans faced shortages. He held up pictures of Cuban leaders past and present, including President Miguel Díaz-Canel, wearing luxury watches, prompting members of the Cuban delegation to repeatedly bang on their desks in protest.

Writing on the social media platform X, Díaz-Canel accused the US of engaging in "gangster-like coercion."

Cuba's president Miguel Díaz-Canel Bermúdez celebrating the vote and criticising the US blockade in a post on X

"The world has once again spoken out overwhelmingly against the blockade, even despite the most blatant pressure and blackmail from the US to change the course of this vote," he wrote.

In January, President Trump threatened tariffs on countries supplying oil to Cuba, a move that has sharply reduced fuel deliveries and contributed to widespread power cuts and disruption to water, internet and telephone services.

US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz listens to speakers at UN headquarters. 28 October 2026. AP Photo/Seth Wenig

Cuba is continuing to face severe economic hardship, with widespread shortages of fuel and other essentials, frequent power cuts and disruption to basic services including water, internet and telephone networks.

World.title: Fed holds rates days before US midterms as two officials push for another hike
World.content:
The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, pausing after raising borrowing costs in September for the first time in three years.

 

However, policymakers were split 10-2, with Fed Governor Lisa Cook, whom US President Donald Trump is trying to remove, and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both voting for another quarter-point hike.

The decision came less than a week before Americans vote in the midterms, and with inflation at 3.7% and energy prices elevated, markets still expect the central bank to raise rates again in December.

The split marks a break from September, when the Fed's rate-setting committee voted unanimously for a hike.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who had also been tipped to vote for higher rates, backed the decision. Some economists had argued that dissents could even help Fed Chair Kevin Warsh by showing that there was still support on the committee for tighter monetary policy.

In its statement, the Fed said that "inflation remains elevated", adding that gathering more information would help it decide on the policy stance needed "to ensure a timely return of inflation" to its 2% target, and repeated that it "will deliver price stability".

The wording keeps the Fed's options open. In September, it said its hike would support a "timelier" return to its target.

FILE. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference in Washington, 16 Sept. 2026 AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein

The Fed also upgraded its view of the economy, saying activity was "expanding at a strong pace", compared with a "solid pace" in September, while uncertainty remained elevated "owing, in part, to geopolitical developments".

In June and July, the first two meetings Warsh chaired, it had pointed instead to "the conflict in the Middle East", and blamed above-target inflation partly on supply shocks in sectors "including energy".

Since September, it has dropped both references, becoming less specific about the Iran war in the statements.

As of the last hike, several senior officials have played down the urgency of moving again. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson pointed to a sharp rise in longer-term borrowing costs, while New York Fed President John Williams said there was "no need for urgency".

Cook's dissenting vote comes as US President Donald Trump presses ahead with his efforts to remove her over mortgage fraud allegations she denies. He has set up a three-person committee to recommend whether he has cause to fire Cook, who was appointed by former US President Joe Biden, and she is expected to appear before it next week.

In June, the Supreme Court halted a previous bid to oust her.

Inflation keeps the pressure on

The case for tighter policy has not gone away.

US consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, while core inflation, which strips out food and energy, climbed to 2.6%.

Petrol, which has cost more than $4 a gallon for the past three months, drove over half of September’s price increase, and diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon in late September.

Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell more than 6% on Monday as diplomacy over the Iran war gathered pace, and traded at around 111.75$ a barrel late on Wednesday, still far above the roughly $72 it fetched before the conflict began in late February.

Higher borrowing costs are already biting, with the average 30-year US mortgage rate hitting a three-year peak of 7.4% in early October.

Hiring has also slowed sharply, with employers adding just 29,000 jobs in September and unemployment rising to 4.2%, though the Fed said job gains had "kept pace with the workforce".

Yet the economy has held up.

It grew at an annualised 2.2% in the second quarter, and the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker points to 3.5% for the third.

What Warsh said

Speaking to reporters after the decision, Warsh largely repeated the Fed's statement, saying that "domestic spending has been resilient, productivity growth is strong and capital investment robust", but that "inflation remains elevated".

He said more information would help the committee decide on the policy stance needed "to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2% goal", adding that "the committee will deliver price stability."

Warsh has long opposed forward guidance, the practice of signalling future moves to the markets. Speaking in Bangkok earlier this month, he said "I don't prejudge meetings."

He also announced a shake-up of the calendar of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which sets US interest rates. The committee will keep meeting eight times a year, but from next autumn, some of those meetings will be dedicated to discussing strategy instead of setting rates.

"We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC, but in 2027 one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said.

He added that he expected "in 2028 we will have two meetings dedicated to discussions of strategy and six for setting policy", meaning the Fed will decide on rates seven times in 2027 and only six times in 2028, down from eight now.

After the decision, markets priced an 87.5% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's 8-9 December meeting, up from 73% on Tuesday, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool, which tracks interest rate futures.

Investors will also not have to wait long for their next clues.

On Thursday at 13:30 CET, the US publishes its first estimate of third-quarter growth and September data for the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index.

Attention then turns to Europe.

The European Central Bank announces its own decision on Thursday and is widely expected to hold its deposit rate at 2.5%, with France's bond market turmoil taking centre stage.

World.title: UEFA reschedules Europa League match amid planned French general strike
World.content:
A football match between Rennes and Greek side Olympiacos has been brought forward by a day due to a planned general strike in France next week.

 

The Europa League match was originally scheduled for Thursday 5 November, but will now be played a day earlier at 4:30 pm.

The decision was taken by UEFA after French unions called the general strike. European football's governing body said it had been informed by the French authorities that the usual security arrangements around the match in Rennes could not be guaranteed that day.

Kick-off has been set for 4:30 pm to avoid overlapping with the two Champions League games scheduled for 6:45 pm, Fenerbahçe against Liverpool and AEK Athens against Real Madrid.

Rennes fans furious

The timing has angered Rennes supporters. Romain, a 33-year-old Rennes fan, told Euronews: "A match at 4:30 pm on a Wednesday is not easy for everyone."

While he said he could make arrangements with his employer to attend the match, that is not the case for everyone. On the social media platform X, another supporter, Quentin, said he was "fuming with rage" at having "paid for a match [he] will not be able to attend".

Under the club's post announcing the change of date and kick-off time, numerous supporters expressed their anger, with some calling it a "disgrace" and others saying the decision showed a "lack of respect" towards fans.

Numerous matches postponed

French trade unions are calling for a general strike on 5 November as part of nationwide protests that began when students raised concerns about conditions in schools.

On Saturdays 17 and 24 October, nationwide demonstrations were organised. While "Act I" was marked by extensive damage and looting on the fringes of the marches, "Act II", a week later, saw fewer clashes, with authorised demonstrations largely taking place peacefully.

The protests have also affected France's domestic football championship. The Professional Football League (LFP) has already postponed several fixtures. The match between PSG and Olympique Lyonnais, initially scheduled for Sunday 25 October, was moved to the following day.

Further changes have already been announced in Ligue 1 this weekend as police and public authorities prepare for marches and demonstrations. OGC Nice will host Stade Rennais on Friday 30 October, Olympique Lyonnais will face Angers SCO on Sunday 1 November and FC Lorient will play Stade Brestois on Monday 2 November.

World.title: Egypt's mahrganat music: from the streets to five-star hotels
World.content:
Born in Egypt’s working-class neighbourhoods, mahraganat music is loud and raw, and these days it is practically impossible to escape. But for the artists behind it, mahraganat is more than just party music: they see it as the latest chapter in Egypt’s rich musical history.

Advertising

In this third episode of the season, we travel to the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to discover the origins of a genre that has become the soundtrack to urban life, despite receiving no official airtime.

Mahraganat evolved from shaabi: music by the people, for the people. Although it rose to prominence during the revolution of 2011–12, it has since become less overtly political.

It remains the music of happiness, partying, joy, and celebration.

Its fast rhythms and loud beats may be a far cry from the golden age of Egyptian music, but mahraganat has been on the scene since the early 2000s and it isn’t going anywhere, any time soon.

We trace its origins and evolution as we speak to one of the godfathers of the movement, his musical partner and a specialist in the genre.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora. Special thanks to Elisa Schouten for her contribution.

World.title: US: Department of Homeland Security data leak exposes details of more than 40,000 employees
World.content:
The leaked information reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel across several US security agencies. This follows recent data breaches involving the FBI and the Defense Department.

In the third major US government data leak in the past month, details on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including officials involved in surveillance, intelligence and undercover operations, were released on Wednesday by a nonprofit leak website.

Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the data was obtained by an entity calling itself "Department of Peace" and provided to the group and "journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew."

DHS said in a statement that it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The agency said it would provide further updates when more information became available.

Transparency group says releasing data justified

The leaked DHS data reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel from:

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

Customs and Border Protection (CBP)

US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)

the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)

​other DHS agencies

The data transparency group also provided a link to an online search tool that helps the public sift through the data.

Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the leak identifies "key personnel in DHS' ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," according to a statement on their website.

Best said the tool would "replace anonymity with accountability" and aid journalists as well as facilitate congressional oversight.

According to Reuters, the news agency called three DHS employees based on the data and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details.

DHS said in September that it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities," which are known to limit cooperation with federal authorities — as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration.

The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that the DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months.

Third serious data breach recently

This is the third major US government data breach in recent weeks:

Last week, the Defense Department faced a class-action lawsuit over a breach affecting millions of current and former military personnel

In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen data of thousands of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) employees.

World.title: EU countries block Canada's 'associate membership' plan
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wanted to give Canada a special status within the EU. But Germany and other member states have raised objections ahead of a summit in Montreal.

European Union member states have blocked a proposal by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to grant Canada a special status as an "associate member" of the bloc.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several other EU leaders pushed to remove the term from a draft declaration ahead of a two-day EU-Canada summit beginning Thursday in Montreal, according to diplomats cited by the dpa and AFP news agencies.

Instead, the revised document calls for a plan to establish "closer ties" between Canada and the EU without membership.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at the Chancellery in Berlin in August 2025 [FILE: August 26, 2025] Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

The declaration was approved by EU member states on Wednesday evening and is expected to be published on Friday, at the end of the summit.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen, European Council President Antonio Costa and several EU commissioners are attending the talks.

Why did EU countries oppose Canada's associate membership?

Von der Leyen first proposed making Canada the EU's first "associate member" in September during a speech attended by Carney.

Canada's PM welcomes EU associate membership idea To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, the proposal raised questions among member states because existing EU treaties do not provide for such a status.

Diplomats said several governments were concerned about the lack of clarity surrounding the proposed arrangement and insufficient consultation between the European Commission and EU member states.

Germany, France and Italy were among the countries that raised objections, although they broadly support closer cooperation with Canada.

Another concern was that the term "associate membership" had already been used in discussions about Ukraine's potential accession to the EU.

Merz had previously suggested such a status for Ukraine as an intermediate step toward full membership. Under his proposal, Kyiv could participate in EU summits and ministerial meetings without voting rights.

Von der Leyen, however, used the same term to describe a different arrangement for Canada, a country that does not have a legal path to EU membership.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada an "associate member" of the EU during a speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg in September [FILE: September 16, 2026] Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

An earlier draft of the summit declaration would have allowed Canada to participate in consultations on major EU political and regulatory initiatives as an associate member.

It also called for the full scope of the arrangement to be defined by the 2027 EU-Canada summit.

Carney, meanwhile, played down the dispute over the wording of the summit declaration.

He said the precise terminology mattered less than the practical benefits closer cooperation would bring to Canadians.

What will closer EU-Canada cooperation involve?

Despite the disagreement over terminology, both sides intend to significantly deepen their partnership.

The revised declaration focuses on an "Alliance for the Future," a term Carney has frequently used to describe relations between Canada and the EU.

The initiative aims to remove trade barriers, facilitate investment and secure supplies of critical raw materials, medicines and technologies during crises.

As Trump menaces, some think Canada should join the EU To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Both sides also want to strengthen cooperation on energy, climate protection, artificial intelligence, security and education.

Canada could gain broader access to EU programs covering research, education and defense.

A new economic council is planned to bring together businesses from both sides of the Atlantic.

The declaration also calls for a study into the feasibility of increasing Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe.

However, EU governments watered down several economic commitments in the original draft.

An explicit goal of deeper financial market integration was removed. Instead of promising preferential treatment in economic security measures, both sides now intend to limit potential negative effects on each other.

How has Donald Trump affected EU-Canada relations?

The push for closer ties comes amid growing uncertainty over relations with the United States under President Donald Trump.

Trade disputes, US tariffs and Trump's territorial claims have raised concerns in both Canada and Europe about Washington's reliability as a partner.

Both sides hope that closer cooperation will help reduce their dependence on other countries and strengthen their ability to pursue common interests.

How could Trump react to Canada-EU association plan? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump previously dismissed the idea of Canadian associate membership in the EU as ridiculous.

He also threatened consequences if the arrangement harmed US interests, warning that he could impose high tariffs or halt trade with Europe in several sectors.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in US, declares himself 'leader' of Brazil
World.content:
Flavio Bolsonaro declared himself the rightful leader of his country despite losing the presidential election runoff on Sunday. He and his family have fled to the US.

Brazilian right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro declared himself the rightful leader of Brazil after landing in Miami with his family on Wednesday.

Bolsonaro fled Brazil after the Supreme Court asked him to hand over his passports so he couldn't leave the country.

The right-wing senator had not conceded defeat in Sunday's presidential election to rival, President Luiz Inacio "Lula"da Silva.

Bolsonaro lost elections on Sunday and alleged irregularities. His party has acknowledged the results of Sunday's elections and international observers have observed it was fair. The chief of the Brazilian electoral authority said Wednesday that vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the country's laws and constitution.

The Bolsonaro's were escorted to a vehicle under cover of umbrellas Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/REUTERS

In an initial open letter posted to X, Bolsonaro declared himself the "elected president." He then deleted the version and updated it with another letter in which he said he was the rightful "leader" of Brazil.

Bolsonaro faces criminal investigations into alleged financial crimes before the country's Supreme Court. But he has cast those investigations as a political witch hunt against his family by left-leaning justices.

"I want to say, not only to my 60 million voters but to the Brazilian people, that I am the leader and that the criminals who stole Brazil’s election are part of a criminal organization that has established a ​tyranny," he said in the updated version.

Asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews about Bolsonaro's comments, US President Donald Trump declined to comment, reiterating earlier views on how it was "a very strange election."

The US State Department has said it will grant Bolsonaro and his family US visas.



Flavio Bolsonaro flees to the US from Brazil To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

When did Bolsonaro arrive and how did he reach Miami?

Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters were seen disembarking a Gulfstream G400 plane and heading into the Miami-Opa Locka airport on Wednesday morning.

Their journey across the Americas had captured regional attention.

The quartet first flew into Argentina late on Tuesday, then took a private jet to the Ecuadorian city of Guayaquil. From there, they continued to Miami, in Florida.

Bolsonaro would lose his immunity from prosecution in February when his term in the Senate ends. On Monday, he had said in an Instagram post that he had no intention of leaving the country and that he would "hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."

According to the AFP news agency, Bolsonaro also holds Italian citizenship and so was able to travel despite his Brazilian and diplomatic passports being canceled.

Bolsonaro's flights out of Brazil and towards Miami had been tracked overnight Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/REUTERS

Potential source of strain between Trump's US and Lula's Brazil

Bolsonaro's departure and his arrival in Florida — like his father Jair Bolsonaro before him after Brazil's previous presidential elections — could deepen a rift between the two most populous countries in the Americas.

During the election campaign, incumbent leftist President Lula had accused the Trump administration of colluding with the Bolsonaro family in a bid to help them return to power.

After the election results, Trump appeared to question the integrity of the vote, saying he thought the extension to voting times was a "very bad look." He had also alleged in the past that Jair Bolsonaro was the victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.

Bolsonaro senior is now in jail in Brazil on charges of leading a conspiracy designed to keep him in power despite defeat in 2022's presidential election.

Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
