World.title: How Contemporary Art Finds a Home in Small-Town China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019146/How Contemporary Art Finds a Home in Small-Town China
World.content:
The drive southwest from Hangzhou, the capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, takes about six hours. The highway passes through tunnel after tunnel, opening onto solar farms terraced into hillsides, villages with white walls and gray-tiled roofs, and transmission towers climbing the ridges. The last tunnel leads into a narrow valley, with clouds hanging low over the mountains.

This is Qingyuan County, which remains relatively remote despite its location in one of China’s richest provinces and improvements in transport infrastructure. Little known beyond its shiitake mushrooms and pencil manufacturing, the county moves to its own rhythm. I arrive at dusk, just as electric moped riders stream in from factories and workshops a few minutes outside town. Here, electric mopeds have a lane of their own. At traffic lights, riders cluster together, their helmets like a patch of colorful mushrooms, then move off as one when the light turns green.

Media portrayals of China often focus on modern metropolises or traditional villages, overlooking places like Qingyuan. Its urban center is a xiancheng, or county town, where schools, hospitals, shops, and cultural and government facilities serve both townspeople and residents of surrounding villages. Qingyuan County as a whole had 141,000 permanent residents in 2023. Across China, some 160 million people lived in similar county towns at the end of 2021. A 2022 national policy recognized their role in connecting cities and the countryside, calling for improved public services, including museums.

County towns have also been largely overlooked in China’s contemporary art scene. For more than a decade, Chinese artists and curators have been working beyond major cities like Beijing and Shanghai. Festivals such as Art Field Nanhai have brought installations to the countryside in the southern Guangdong province. The Bishan Project incorporated art into a “rural revitalization” initiative in a village in Zhejiang’s neighboring Anhui province. Anren, a historic town in the southwestern Sichuan province, hosted three editions of a contemporary art biennale.

These projects have expanded the reach of contemporary art in China. Yet artistic practices in county towns, where urban and rural life intersect, remain underreported. Another problem is the condescending language sometimes used in media coverage. For example, the term xiachen, literally “sinking,” is often used to describe cultural resources flowing from major cities to smaller communities, downplaying the role of local people in shaping art scenes.

The Art Museum of Pond Loach (AMPL) in Qingyuan offers a different perspective, showing how contemporary art institutions and smaller communities can shape one another.

Established in 2023, AMPL takes its name from a small, mud-burrowing freshwater fish. The museum draws on this image to describe its mission: immersing itself in the space between urban and rural life and engaging with the everyday experiences of county-town residents. It seeks to support what its director, Hu Dingyu, describes as “modest yet significant contemporary art.”

A Qingyuan native who left the county as a child and later studied and worked as a curator in the Netherlands, Hu has a complicated relationship with her hometown and resists portraying her return as a nostalgic homecoming or a search for her roots. Instead, she sought to establish a lasting institution where relationships among artists, museum staff, and local residents could develop over time.

That starts with the architecture. AMPL occupies two floors of a ceramics museum founded by a member of Hu’s family. Dedicated to celadon, a type of green-glazed ceramic with strong ties to Zhejiang, the museum shares a building with the local marriage registry and a library reading room.

Hu and her team carved out a space for contemporary art within this setting, and the contrast remains visible. Gray concrete walls, exposed rebar and pipes, and alarm fixtures sit alongside the polished glass cases displaying celadon downstairs. To me, these unfinished surfaces made the gallery feel like a work in progress, reflecting the artistic practices taking shape within and beyond its walls.

AMPL’s development resembles a process of grafting: artistic practices and networks formed elsewhere take root through encounters with local institutions, skills, and ways of life. These local conditions are not simply a backdrop. They are constantly evolving and actively shape what artists and the museum can do.

Indeed, AMPL’s curation, research, and public education programs are all centered around county-town life. It invites artists to spend time in Qingyuan and develop projects in collaboration with local people. Rather than focusing solely on the finished artworks, artists are encouraged to gain inspiration from everyday encounters, including those with local workers.

In one project, a modified “chariot” joined the evening moped traffic. In another, local shops and a long-vanished dance hall became subjects of an exhibition. The museum’s collaborations have also extended into classrooms. Working with artists, AMPL made recordings of contemporary art classes at Hangzhou’s China Academy of Art available to local high school teachers for use in their lessons. Together, these projects have brought artistic practice into familiar settings, from roads and shops to schools.

Local networks are equally important to AMPL’s day-to-day operations. Without a dedicated exhibition installation team, the museum relies on local welders, electricians, and other tradespeople recruited through personal contacts. Since the museum opened, workers who were initially unfamiliar with installing contemporary art have become regular collaborators. These relationships have become part of the museum’s infrastructure.

AMPL’s 2026 exhibition, “Factory Girl,” is perhaps the most convincing evidence of how contemporary art can take root — rather than “sink” — in county-towns. Featuring artist Zheng Que and curated by Nie Xiaoyi, the exhibition explores manufacturing in China’s counties through Zheng’s own experience. Beginning in 2023, she worked at a factory producing Christmas goods in Pan’an, another county in Zhejiang, and filmed herself on the job. Like Qingyuan’s pencils, the factory’s products connected local workers to consumers far beyond the county. Zheng herself was the “factory girl.”

According to Zheng, most workers were women from nearby villages, ranging in age from their 30s to their 70s and 80s. Many were retired and wanted something to keep them occupied. Coworkers were often also neighbors or relatives, connected through overlapping networks of family and acquaintances.

At the opening of “Factory Girl,” I met artists, curators, and other art professionals who had traveled from Shanghai and Hangzhou. Over dinner, we shared loach hotpot, a local specialty featuring the fish that gave AMPL its name, and shiitake mushrooms, all prepared by local residents.

Together, these activities suggest a more reciprocal relationship than the language of xiachen implies. At AMPL, the graft is both architectural and cultural. What matters is how the different elements come together: how space is shared, how local skills are put to use, and how relationships are sustained through repeated collaboration and practical adjustments.

Whether these connections can sustain AMPL in the long term remains uncertain. Resources and networks from major cities will continue to matter, but so will the museum’s ability to give artists time to develop work with local residents and maintain those relationships beyond individual exhibitions. For the graft to take hold, collaboration must become an ongoing practice, giving people in Qingyuan a role in shaping the museum’s future. More broadly, AMPL raises questions about how contemporary art can develop beyond China’s major cities, and the role smaller communities can play in shaping it.

(Header image: The installation “Zheng Que: Factory Girl,” Art Museum of Pond Loach, Qingyuan County, Zhejiang province, 2026. Photo by Luo Shunqi, Han Qian and Cao Danyang. All images courtesy of Jin Yu)

World.title: Are GCash’s P10 transfer fees here to stay?
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – GCash isn’t committing to further reducing its P10 bank transfer fee just yet.

At a media briefing following its historic October 20 stock market debut, Rappler asked executives of GCash parent Mynt how the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) new transfer fees rules would affect its revenues and whether keeping the P10 charge could hurt its competitiveness.

Jep Tang, Mynt’s head of capital markets and investor relations, clarified that BSP Circular No. 1238 does not require banks and e-wallets to offer free transfers. Rather, it requires a more reasonable pricing structure, with charges reflecting the actual costs of providing the service.

“We have a good working relationship with the regulators, and this discussion is still ongoing as to what level it should be moving forward,” Tang said.

Pressed on whether GCash could lose customers to banks offering free transfers, Tang pointed to the company’s diversified revenue streams.

“Our top payments use cases, there are five, and these five use cases account for 78% of our payment solutions revenue. And bank transfer fee is not one of them,” he said. “So, definitely, because we’ve reduced from P15 to P10, clearly that has been reduced. But what we’d like to highlight, and what we really want to see is that there will be more use cases because of these changes.” (READ: After the IPO party, GCash comes for 5-6 lending next)

After the briefing, Rappler asked Tang about the status of discussions with the BSP. He stated that they were ongoing, although he declined to speculate on what the outcome of such talks could be.

BSP Deputy Governor for Payments and Currency Management Mamerto Tangonan also confirmed to Rappler that the central bank is still continuing negotiations with the e-wallet giant.

“We’re discussing,” Tangonan told Rappler on October 22, declining to give a timeline on when a resolution might be reached.

How much is at stake?

The financial stakes are difficult to pin down, even with GCash now a publicly listed company.

According to GCash’s IPO prospectus, four revenue-generating services, GLoad, GBills, Pay Online, and offline payments, accounted for 78% of its payment solutions revenue in the first half of 2026. Express Send, its fifth flagship service, allows users to transfer money between GCash accounts for free. These are considered on-us transfers, compared with off-us transfers to other banks and e-wallets, for which GCash charges P10.

These off-us transfers fall under the remaining 22%, alongside cash-in services, remittances, disbursements, merchant services, and other businesses. GCash does not disclose how much revenue comes specifically from the P10 transfer fee.

Interestingly, the prospectus also acknowledges that further fee reductions could hurt its business. (READ: Why exactly did BPI make transfers free?)

“Compliance with BSP Circular No. 1238 may require us to modify our pricing mechanisms, including with respect to transfer fees for certain electronic payment transactions, which could reduce Payment Solutions revenues. While reduced transfer fees may drive increased transaction volumes and broader user adoption of the GCash App, there can be no assurance that any such increase will fully offset the resulting reduction in per-transaction fee revenues,” Mynt said in its propsectus.

Still an expensive convenience

Remember when Queen Máxima of the Netherlands visited the Philippines in 2024 as the United Nations’ special advocate for financial inclusion and asked a fisherman whether GCash was expensive?

He agreed, wishing there were no deductions from his transactions. The Dutch royal later met GCash CEO Martha Sazon at the company’s headquarters, although what they discussed remained behind closed doors.

After meeting the Queen, BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. likewise told reporters that he wanted to “know the cost structure” of digital payments and determine the right threshold for fee-free transactions.

Two years later, the BSP is still scrutinizing transfer fees charged by the country’s biggest e-wallets.

GCash and rival Maya both reduced their InstaPay fees from P15 to P10 in July, but stopped there. And while GCash is leaving its options open, Maya appears more inclined to keep charging.

In an earlier interview with Rappler, PLDT head of investor relations Jinggay Nograles described transfers as “one of the pillars of revenues” for Maya, which operates with a different cost structure from traditional banks.

“Maya needs to be a going concern,” Nograles said. “Looking at that particular revenue stream, it does make sense for Maya to keep that P10 fee.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Leak website releases data on thousands of US Homeland Security employees
World.content:
The leaked data is on more than 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees. DHS is aware of the potential breach and working to address it.

WASHINGTON, USA – The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said on Wednesday, October 28, it has released data on more than 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees, including details about officials working in sensitive fields such as surveillance and human intelligence.

DHS said in a statement it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” The agency said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public “when more information is available.”

The disclosure — which the nonprofit data transparency group says draws on information obtained by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” — is the third major government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.

In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the Defense Department was hit with a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.

The DHS data includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and other DHS component agencies.

Also included in the data were job titles and email groups, which, among other details, showed which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.

In a statement, Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the hacktivist and journalist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight. Crimew said her tool would provide “FOIA material for years to come!”

The Department of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction.”

The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.

Best’s statement said the Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta OKTA.O sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”

Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the entire data trove but it was able to match personal information about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs. Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.

In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations. – Rappler.com

World.title: Chagee’s new drinks use espresso shots, but with tea
World.content:
Whether it’s a cup of tea or a hit of caffeine, we all need that morning and midday energizer. As Chagee expands its Teaspresso lineup, you can now get your daily dose of both caffeine and tea in one drink.

We had the chance to try some of Chagee’s newly released Teaspresso drinks. Here’s what to expect from each one to help you find your next go-to order.

Frappe, Latte, Or Tea? Don’t worry, as Chagee has you covered. Each drink differs in its base: a milk base for your latte, a water base for your tea, and a blended one for your frappe. Despite their different profiles, they all share a shot of “teaspresso,” or in simple words, tea leaves that were extracted through an espresso-style brewing method, meaning you’re sure to get both flavors of tea and its extracted caffeine.

Teaspresso Frappe

One distinct change from the menu is their new Frappe-style drink. For a sweeter touch, the teaspresso blended in the drink gives a subtle hint of caffeine while highlighting the base of each flavor being either caramel or chocolate cookie. Topped with whipped cream, it finishes with a smooth, dessert-like texture that makes it feel like your needed sugar boost. It’s a good pick if you want something sweeter, yet balanced with the taste of tea and caffeine.

Teaspresso Pure Tea

To get a full experience of the Teaspresso, Chagee’s pure tea drink pairs a shot with a water base, making the tea stand as its core flavor. Compared to the others, this one places itself on the calmer side, focusing on the flavors of tea rather than added flavors or sugar. If you’re looking for a simple drink that’s not too sweet or plain, or simply in the mood for some tea, Teaspresso Pure Tea is the perfect choice.

Teaspresso Latte

Despite having no coffee, the Teaspresso latte had a faint yet distinguishable taste of caffeine. With a milk base and a shot of Teaspresso, it lands between something familiar to my go-to cafe latte in the morning and surprising given its gentle lift without tipping into a full coffee profile. For the coffee lovers, this is a nice middle ground for satisfying your daily caffeine while also getting a hint of tea.

Chagee’s new Teaspresso drinks brought different flavor profiles to their signature taste, assuring that whether you’re a tea or coffee person, or someone with a sweet tooth, you’re sure to find the right drink for you. Will you stick to your usual, or try something new on your next Chagee run? – Rappler.com

This piece was written by Rappler intern Sebastian Vincent U. Ngo. Basti is a multimedia creative storyteller who focuses on the everyday details that make ordinary moments feel special. He seeks stories and uses design, words, and motion to help people see the familiar in a new light.

World.title: The bee is strong: Jollibee eyes 1,500 more areas for expansion
World.content:
The fast-food giant sees more room to grow outside Metro Manila, while setting its sights on listing its international business in Hong Kong in 2027

MANILA, Philippines – The bee still has plenty of room to grow.

Fast-food giant Jollibee Foods Corporation (JFC) has identified more than 1,500 potential areas for expansion across the Philippines from 2027 to 2030, with most of these outside Metro Manila.

In a disclosure on Thursday, October 29, JFC said approximately 71% of these prospective markets are outside the capital region, where the company sees considerable room to grow its Jollibee, Mang Inasal, and Chowking brands.

The three brands already account for nearly 90% of its Philippine systemwide sales, with Jollibee alone contributing more than half at 62%.

But the 1,500 identified trade areas do not necessarily translate to 1,500 new stores.

The company has yet to disclose specific locations, investment requirements, or annual store-opening targets associated with its expansion plans. Actual openings will depend on site availability, commercial viability, and expected investment returns, JFC said.

The expansion outlook comes after JFC revised down its global store opening target for 2026 from 1,200 to 1,300 new stores to just 1,000 to 1,100 in its Q2 2026 updated full-year guidance.

JFC’s Philippine business reported 5.7% growth in systemwide sales during Q2 2026, while same-store sales, which measure performance at existing outlets, grew a more modest 1.3%.

Beyond opening new stores, JFC is also experimenting with different formats to improve sales.

The company reported that Mang Inasal’s eight drive-thru outlets operating as of the first half of 2026 generated average daily sales approximately 40% higher than those of its other stores.

Going global

Meanwhile, Jollibee has been happy to play part-time ambassador too.

When President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. visited Canada in July, he and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also made a stop at a Jollibee branch in Vancouver, where they mingled with customers and employees after their bilateral meetings.

PRESIDENTIAL VISIT. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. visit a Jollibee store in Vancouver on July 2, 2026 following a bilateral meeting between the two leaders. Photo from Presidential Communications Office

Two months later, British Trade Minister Anas Sarwar dropped by a Jollibee store in Bonifacio Global City during the first visit by a UK trade minister to the Philippines in nine years. He met JFC founder Tony Tan Caktiong, sampled the menu, and even received a Jollibee Funko Pop dressed in a Barong Tagalog.

MABUHAY! UK Trade Minister Anas Sarwar (second from left) and British Ambassador Sarah Hulton (second from right) meet Jollibee founder Tony Tan Caktiong (center) and executive William Tan Untiong (right) at a Jollibee store in BGC on September 23, 2026. Photo from Jollibee.

The bee, it seems, is becoming quite the fixture in international relations.

And its international ambitions extend to the stock market.

JFC is preparing to spin off its international operations into a separately listed company, Jollibee Foods Corporation International (JFCI), with Hong Kong selected as its proposed listing venue instead of the United States, as originally planned.

Under the proposed restructuring, the Philippine business would remain listed on the Philippine Stock Exchange, while investors would be able to hold shares in a separately traded international company.

JFC is looking at a potential listing by late 2027, although it clarified on October 20 that reports of a Q3 2027 listing target were premature. The transaction remains subject to restructuring, market conditions, and regulatory approvals.

As of the first half of 2026, JFC operated 3,516 stores in the Philippines and another 7,251 internationally. – Rappler.com

World.title: What’s at stake for Trump in Israel’s deadlocked election?
World.content:
TRUMP AND NETANYAHU. US President Donald Trump welcomes Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the entrance of the White House in Washington, DC, USA, April 7, 2025.

The outcome will have implications for US-Israeli relations, which have been dominated by the joint fight against Iran, stalled Gaza peace efforts and signs of eroding US public support for Israel

WASHINGTON, USA – With Israel’s election yielding no clear winner, President Donald Trump could face prolonged uncertainty over who will lead Washington’s closest Middle East ally as he confronts challenges from Iran and Gaza across the region.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc secured the most seats in Israel’s parliament but still lost its parliamentary majority on Tuesday, October 27, despite Trump having endorsed him against a rival alliance of parties led by hawkish former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.

While Netanyahu seemed in a stronger position, neither side was projected to have an outright path to form a new government after Israel’s first election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

The stage appeared to be set for a period of painstaking coalition bargaining – or possibly another election – while Netanyahu remains in power in a caretaker capacity.

The outcome will have implications for US-Israeli relations, which have been dominated by the joint fight against Iran, stalled Gaza peace efforts and signs of eroding US public support for Israel.

The uncertainty comes at a sensitive moment for Trump, when he and Netanyahu have threatened to join in another round of attacks against Iran.

“Israeli politics can be messy,” said Aaron David Miller, a former Middle East adviser in Democratic and Republican administrations. From the US perspective, he said, “it would be good to get some clarity, but that’s easier said than done.”

Which outcome would Trump prefer?

Netanyahu – a consummate political survivor who has had a close but sometimes turbulent relationship with Trump dating back decades – may have survived again. He is the longest-serving Israeli prime minister and the only one the US president has ever worked with.

Eisenkot, who projected an image as a ⁠political outsider and security-minded former general during the campaign, has seen his governing chances dimmed but not extinguished. He is not known to have ever met Trump.

Some analysts say creation of a broad unity government keeping Netanyahu in power might serve Trump’s interest in a politically stable Israeli partner. But neither side has shown a willingness to take that path.

Asked whether he was going to get involved in an effort to form a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump told Axios on Wednesday he hadn’t thought about it, adding: “I will take a look.”

What does the election mean for the war with Iran?

Topping the list is how Trump might engage with Israel in the war against Iran, which has rocked the Middle East. The eight-month-old conflict has disrupted global energy supplies, pushed up US gasoline prices and driven down his approval ratings, imperiling his Republicans’ control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.

Trump, in his October 18 endorsement, insisted he wanted Netanyahu to remain in power to help him soon “finish the job” against Iran. The president said overnight that Netanyahu, who outperformed pre-election polls, had done “very well” and that his backing had boosted the Israeli leader.

Trump has repeatedly signaled that the US and Israel could restart attacks on Iran after the midterms, with some critics, including in Israel, suggesting Netanyahu might see it as a way to bolster his political standing as caretaker prime minister.

Jonathan Panikoff, a former deputy US national intelligence officer on the Middle East, said any future Israeli leadership would likely be on the same page as Trump if he decides to escalate from the current stalemate with Israel’s regional arch-foe.

“It’s hard to imagine any real daylight between them on that point,” said Panikoff, now at the Atlantic Council think tank in Washington.

Where Netanyahu and many Israelis have sometimes differed with Trump is when he has offered concessions in now-stalled negotiations with the Islamic Republic.

What are the implications for Gaza peace efforts?

No matter how Israel’s next government shapes up, there is little reason to believe there will be any sweeping shift in tough policies toward the Palestinians.

This doesn’t bode well for breaking the diplomatic deadlock between Israel and Hamas and fully implementing Trump’s Gaza peace plan following the war there. Israel, in response to the militants’ deadly cross-border attack, leveled much of the enclave and killed tens of thousands of Palestinians.

Administration officials have privately expressed frustration over what they see as intransigence by Netanyahu, who has insisted that Hamas must first disarm.

Eisenkot, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, stressed his military credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically during the election campaign. He has vowed to break with Netanyahu’s far-right coalition allies, but not with the hawkish approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. – Rappler.com

World.title: Netanyahu set to remain caretaker after inconclusive Israeli election
World.content:
UN ADDRESS. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu holds up a Starlink device as he addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 24, 2026.

While a caretaker government faces some constraints, experts say it retains powers, including over the war with Iran

JERUSALEM, Israel – Benjamin Netanyahu looked set to remain Israel’s caretaker prime minister after unexpectedly strong backing among Jewish voters left his opponents little apparent prospect of unseating him, despite his right-wing bloc losing its parliamentary majority.

With nearly 86% of votes tallied on Wednesday, Israel’s three main broadcasters projected Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties would win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, well ahead of the 48 for rival Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc.

Parties representing Arab Israelis were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot little realistic path to power without their broad backing, which many Jewish political leaders reject.

The results could still change as counting continued, but Eisenkot’s bloc of anti-Netanyahu parties, ranging from the center-left to the hard right, had fallen short of pre-election polls that forecast a tight race.

Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister during any coalition negotiations and potentially until another election next year. While a caretaker government faces some constraints, experts say it retains powers, including over the war with Iran.

Guy Lurie, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, said a caretaker government formally had the same powers as a regular government, but also “a duty of restraint” and less discretion in some areas.

Security fight sharpens

Netanyahu, addressing his Likud party’s faithful after 3 am (0100 GMT), called for the formation of “a strong, right-wing national government.”

He highlighted Israel’s military successes and raised the prospect of renewed joint military action against Iran alongside his ally, US President Donald Trump, saying the two countries had a “singular historical opportunity” to remove what he called the Iranian threat “once and for all.”

Trump, who had urged Israeli voters to keep Netanyahu in power so the two leaders could “finish the job” in Iran, said Netanyahu had done “very well” and claimed his endorsement had “helped him a lot.”

Israel’s high-turnout vote was brushed aside by some in the rest of the Middle East.

In Tehran, banners with images of slain Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei reminded Iranians of US and Israeli strikes launched in February which kicked off the war. Just to the right was a poster of late Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, who was killed on Netanyahu’s orders in Lebanon.

“I genuinely see the possibility of attack,” said 50-year-old Iranian citizen Abdollah Karimi.

Frustration was also palpable in Egypt, the first Arab country to make peace with Israel in 1979.

Outhman Selim, a 62-year-old lawyer, said his hopes that a Netanyahu defeat would steer the country away from the far right had been dashed.

Eisenkot acknowledged that Netanyahu remained caretaker prime minister but warned that he might use security for political ends.

“I call on the heads of the security establishment and the civil service: Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people’s trust,” he said. “Stand firm in the face of any attempt to challenge you.”

Netanyahu’s office has previously rejected accusations that he is using the Iran conflict for political gain and did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

The prospect of a caretaker government without a parliamentary majority weighed on Israeli markets. The shekel ILS= currency weakened around 1.6% to 3.10 to the US dollar. Tel Aviv’s key benchmark stock indexes fell more than 3%.

Decisive shift in Israeli politics

The result underscored the rightward shift among Israeli Jews during Netanyahu’s years as the country’s dominant political figure. The center-left that dominated Israel for the first half of its history has been reduced to a small fringe.

Nearly all Jewish parties now share Netanyahu’s rejection of an eventual independent Palestinian state, the basis of internationally endorsed peace efforts since the 1990s.

The election was Israel’s first since Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages in attacks on October 7, 2023, that plunged the country into wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

The war in Gaza, which flattened the territory and killed 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities, has left Israel increasingly isolated on the world stage.

Netanyahu himself is wanted by the International Criminal Court in The Hague on war crimes charges he calls absurd, and faces corruption charges in Israel that he dismisses as an establishment plot.

Turnout reached 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades, and was particularly high among Israelis of Palestinian descent, who make up more than a fifth of the population. Many were motivated by what they see as open racism from Netanyahu’s cabinet, which includes a party leader convicted of inciting racial hatred against Arabs.

The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released. “We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Joint List candidate Faten Gattas.

The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu relied on one small Arab party, but Eisenkot’s underperformance means the opposition would now need backing from the Joint List itself. Most Jewish leaders have shunned formal alliances with Arab parties since Israel’s founding. – Rappler.com

World.title: China’s Monroe Doctrine and Its Strategic Blunder in Myanmar
World.content:
The United States has its Monroe Doctrine, which asserts American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere, placing Latin America within its sphere of influence. Over the past three decades, China’s rapid economic growth and military expansion have transformed it from a regional power into a global superpower. It is therefore unsurprising that Beijing would seek to establish a similar sphere of influence over neighboring Southeast Asian countries.

Myanmar holds particular strategic importance for China. Through Rakhine State, Beijing can access the Indian Ocean, bypassing the strategically vulnerable Strait of Malacca during a crisis. Myanmar also possesses substantial deposits of rare earth elements essential to modern technologies. Furthermore, the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) is one of the six major economic corridors under China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

Yet in pursuing these geopolitical objectives, China appears to be missing the forest for the trees. Its decision to prop up Myanmar’s military junta at the expense of democratic forces represents a serious strategic miscalculation—a bet on the wrong horse. Following a widely discredited sham election, the junta has attempted to rebrand itself as a civilian government under former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing, with a ruling party dominated by military officers and loyalists. Such a regime is ill-equipped to deliver what China needs: a stable, secure and predictable neighbor capable of supporting its long-term economic ambitions through the BRI and its broader maritime strategy.

The culprit behind an unstable neighbor

Since the 2021 military coup, Myanmar has become increasingly unstable, while ethnic resistance organizations (EROs) have expanded their territorial control. Ironically, many resources and infrastructure projects China hopes to develop now lie in territories controlled by EROs and People’s Defense Forces (PDFs). Rare earth deposits are concentrated in Kachin State, where the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO) exercises substantial control. The Chinese-backed Kyaukphyu deep-sea port, a strategic gateway to the Indian Ocean, lies in Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army (AA) has established extensive territorial control. Significant stretches of the China-Myanmar gas pipeline also pass through areas where resistance forces operate in Magway and Mandalay regions.

So far, PDFs and EROs have shown considerable restraint in refraining from attacking these strategic assets. This reflects, in part, their desire to earn Beijing’s goodwill and demonstrate their ability to safeguard Chinese investments.

An unreliable partner turning to criminality

Myanmar’s economy has deteriorated sharply under the weight of military expenditure, corruption, nepotism and mismanagement. The junta is in no position to fulfill its commitments under numerous bilateral economic agreements with China, particularly because it cannot guarantee security in project areas. Worse, the regime has allowed scam centers to proliferate, with some military officers reportedly maintaining close ties to the warlords operating them. Many centers, particularly in northern Shan State, have targeted Chinese citizens. Despite repeated requests from Beijing, the military failed to take effective action.

Operation 1027, launched by an alliance of ethnic armed organizations, proceeded with Beijing’s tacit approval after the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) framed it partly as a campaign against scam operations. Among those subsequently handed over to China was Bai Suocheng, a former lawmaker from the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party.

Beyond its inability to provide stability and security, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime is hardly a trustworthy ally. He has repeatedly sought to balance competing powers against one another and could readily turn against China if doing so served his interests. His efforts to court Western goodwill were evident in a recent TIME magazine interview, a low-profile U.S. delegation visit to Naypyitaw in September and the expensive hiring of Washington-based lobbying firms to advocate on its behalf.

Previously, Min Aung Hlaing courted Russia to counterbalance China’s influence, only to turn back toward Beijing when Moscow could not meet his needs. Beijing should think twice before entrusting its long-term strategic interests to a regime whose loyalty is conditional and whose survival is increasingly uncertain.

Why the opposition is a more reliable partner

Many EROs have concluded that genuine autonomy, security, and prosperity are unattainable under military-dominated rule. They increasingly see their future in a federal democratic union. For decades, these organizations understood that none could defeat the military alone. They also recognize that their battlefield successes since 2021 would have been far more difficult without the nationwide Spring Revolution, which fundamentally transformed the country’s political landscape.

This convergence of ethnic resistance and the broader pro-democracy movement has created an unprecedented opportunity. In March 2026, the movement took a significant step forward with the formation of the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF). It brings together influential resistance actors, including the KIO, KNU, CNF, Karenni National Progressive Party (KNPP), Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), and National Unity Government (NUG). A few months later, the federal units of Sagaing, Mandalay, and Magway joined the initiative.

The SCEF combines political leadership and military coordination within a common framework. It seeks not merely to defeat the junta but also to lay the institutional foundations for a future federal state. For China, this emerging coalition offers an alternative to continued dependence on a weakening military regime.

The assumption that China cannot tolerate a flourishing democracy in its neighborhood oversimplifies Beijing’s strategic interests and Southeast Asia’s political realities. China already maintains important economic and diplomatic relationships with democracies such as Japan, South Korea and India. Myanmar is comparatively small, and any government emerging from the current conflict will have compelling geographic and economic reasons to maintain constructive relations with its powerful neighbor. A federal democratic Myanmar has no inherent reason to be antagonistic toward Beijing.

Myanmar’s democratic forces are also learning that the West is unlikely to sustain its strategic attention. The Trump administration included Myanmar among the countries subject to a full travel ban, while its dismantling of USAID disrupted American assistance. Washington’s reported attempts to reengage clandestinely with the junta have further frustrated the democratic movement.

In contrast, the NUG has adopted a pragmatic approach toward Beijing. Its 10-point Position on China, released on January 1, 2024, explicitly commits to safeguarding Chinese investments and cooperating with China against online scams and human trafficking. Democratic forces thus recognize the importance of maintaining a workable relationship with their powerful neighbor.

A strategic opening for Beijing

China’s ambition to achieve national rejuvenation and modernization by the centenary of the People’s Republic of China in 2049 requires long-term strategic thinking rather than short-term political expediency.

By recalibrating its Myanmar policy, Beijing has a rare opportunity to earn the goodwill of the Myanmar people at a pivotal moment. Supporting a political settlement that recognizes the aspirations of ethnic nationalities and democratic forces would not undermine China’s interests. On the contrary, it could help establish the stability, security, and predictability Beijing has long sought.

China should therefore engage constructively with the SCEF and other credible democratic stakeholders rather than continue to prop up a failing junta. Such engagement could protect Chinese investments, improve regional stability and strengthen Beijing’s international standing.

The underlying principle of a Chinese Monroe Doctrine—a regional sphere of influence shaped by strategic interests—is understandable as a geopolitical ambition. But achieving that ambition requires choosing partners wisely. If China wants to secure its long-term interests in Myanmar, supporting the forces capable of building a stable federal democratic union would be a far more prudent investment than backing a military regime marked by declining territorial control, economic mismanagement and uncertain loyalty.

Than N. Oo is a co-founder of advocacy group Free Myanmar and writes frequently about Myanmar’s political developments.

World.title: Nationalist Regime Supporters Turn Against China Over Northern Shan
World.content:
Staunchly nationalist supporters of the Myanmar military are growing wary of the regime’s increasing dependency on China on all fronts, voicing rare criticism of the way Chinese money and influence are being allowed to shape their country.

It was the question of northern Shan State that finally galvanized this resentment among the pro-military crowd.

Many nationalists believe that China enabled Operation 1027, the offensive by an alliance of three ethnic armed groups that dealt a serious blow to the Myanmar military in 2023-24. They staged protests at the time accusing Beijing of interference, and the sentiment has recently resurfaced over what they see as the “Sinicization” of borderlands that the regime has lost in northern Shan.

“We accept them making investment in our country. But supplying arms and funds to ethnic armed groups to capture towns and interfering in our government is unacceptable,” a nationalist told The Irrawaddy. “Public opinion must be voiced openly.”

The renewed criticism comes after the Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—an ethnic coalition comprising the Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the Shan Nationalities League for Democracy (SNLD), and a Shan militia group—issued a statement on Oct. 23 accusing Kokang’s Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) of imposing Chinese language in schools, granting land rights to foreigners, and erasing local traditions in territories it seized during Operation 1027. The MNDAA swiftly rejected the allegations as unfounded.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and the stability of the China–Myanmar border.

Ta’ang civil society groups similarly condemned the MNDAA in April after it seized Kutkai Township, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

At the peak of Operation 1027, China pressured armed groups to agree ceasefires with the regime in northern Shan, but since then has allowed them to consolidate their quasi-autonomous administrations there rather than handing back all the territory they had gained to the regime.

No other armed group has been able to consolidate administrative control as rapidly as the MNDAA, which analysts say would be impossible without Beijing’s backing.

Regime supporters were initially silent about this perceived Sinicization, but started to voice concerns when exiled independent media widely covered Chinese border encroachment in northern Shan areas controlled by the MNDAA. The regime warned domestic outlets not to publish stories that could damage bilateral ties, but the concerns persisted.

The pot seems to have boiled over when Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun in mid-October recommended “high-level autonomy” for ethnic monitories. His remark was interpreted in different ways across Myanmar’s political circles, stirring debate over China’s intentions.

Along Myanmar’s eastern frontier, three armed groups are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, the others being the United Wa State Army (UWSA) and the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA). The latter two have upheld ceasefires with the Myanmar military for nearly four decades, and in return they exercise de-facto autonomy in their fiefdoms, serving as effective buffers that insulate China from Myanmar’s instability.

Under the 2008 Constitution, the MNDAA’s Kokang—with a population of fewer than 200,000—is a self‑administered zone, but that covers only Laukkai and Kongyan townships east of the Salween River. But after Operation 1027, the MNDAA reorganized both that original enclave and newly captured areas into four districts: Laukkai, Kutkai, Hsenwi, and Monekoe. Governance in these territories increasingly mirrors administrative practices seen in Beijing, raising alarm not only among staunch nationalists but also among some lawmakers.

“We don’t like it when a powerful neighbor interferes in our sovereignty,” one MP remarked. But he admitted, “The Myanmar government is not in a position to shut out China. We don’t have that strength, and we are deteriorating in every aspect.”

Democracy activists, for their part, accuse Beijing of propping up the military since the coup, reaping political and economic benefits. The exiled leader of the Democratic Party for a New Society, Hnin Hnin Hmwe, said the regime itself is starting to worry about its over-reliance on China.

“China has pushed its interests so far that even the regime is beginning to feel constrained,” she said. “At the same time, China maintains ties with revolutionary forces. China is shrewd to keep the balance.”

World.title: Resistance Forces Inflict Heavy Losses on Regime Troops in Indaw
World.content:
A Myanmar junta offensive to reclaim territory in Sagaing Region’s Indaw Township near the Kachin State border has suffered heavy losses in resistance ambushes, resistance sources said.

Dozens of junta troops were killed and many, including a tactical commander, were reportedly captured by pro-democracy forces.

Troops from two regime Tactical Commands advancing south from Indaw town toward Wuntho and Tigyaing were ambushed by resistance forces on October 4. According to reports, the regime units buried the bodies of dead soldiers in local villages, and one Tactical Command lost contact with its base.

The regime retook control of Indaw town and the Mandalay-Myitkyina road from resistance forces at the end of April. However, it is still conducting clearance operations in the area.

On October 4, roughly 700 troops from Indaw, led by Colonel Kyaw Win Tun, deputy commander of the 33rd Light Infantry Division (LID), advanced south and split into two Tactical Commands: Tactical Command 331, led by Col. Myo Thein, and Tactical Command 332, led by Col. Kyaw San Win.

Both were ambushed by resistance forces, sparking fierce clashes and prompting the regime to bomb the area from the air, Indaw Revolution (IR), a local news information page, reported on Monday.

IR reported that locals found the bodies of 50 regime soldiers near Nanthe Village and cremated them on October 23. Other soldiers’ bodies were spotted near villages on the Indaw-Tigyaing road, it said.

“Eyewitnesses reported over 50 dead bodies. More than 20 [regime soldiers] surrendered, and it is initially understood that a tactical commander was among them,” a source close to the resistance forces told The Irrawaddy.

Intense clashes were reported between regime troops and resistance groups—including the civilian National Unity Government’s People’s Defense Force (PDF), the Kachin Independence Army, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front and allied groups—on October 25 and 26.

Zin Yaw, a military defector and military analyst, told The Irrawaddy that both Tactical Commands had suffered heavy losses.

“Tactical Command 332 led by Col. Kyaw San Win lost communication with the base for 48 hours,” Zin Yaw said.

The troops led by Col. Kyaw San Win advanced along the Indaw-Tigyaing road and ended up near Ma Au Kone Village, which is 23 km south of Indaw town.

According to the reports, some regime soldiers were captured by or voluntarily surrendered to resistance forces.

However, The Irrawaddy couldn’t independently verify the situation, and there has been no official statement from resistance forces or the regime yet.

Madaya Myohman force, which is under the command of the Mandalay PDF and is believed to have taken part in the ambushes, stated that the regime’s 33rd LID faced heavy losses on Monday.

The clashes and bombing in the area forced residents of at least 35 villages in Indaw and Wuntho townships to flee their homes, according to a source close to the resistance.

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Applications Plunge at Thai CI Centers Amid Boycott
World.content:
The number of Myanmar migrant workers applying for Certificates of Identity (CI) in Thailand has dropped sharply in the past few days following the launch of a social media campaign against the CI process, according to migrant groups and agents.

The Myanmar regime opened five Thai hubs on October 14, offering migrant workers CI required for residency and work. In exchange, workers must comply with a new Labor Ministry mandate to remit 25 percent of their wages through official channels and pay 2 percent annual tax.

The number of registered Myanmar workers in Thailand rose to nearly 3 million as of November 2025, but a significant population remains undocumented.

Many migrants say that as low-wage workers they can barely afford CI application fees, while the regime’s mandatory 6,000-baht remittance rule adds an extra layer of cost.

Labor activists say the boycott is also being driven by reluctance to legitimize the regime or help fund its ongoing military attacks on civilians.

Migrants launched the online campaign on Oct. 18, calling on the Thai government to grant them residency-work permits without CI documents.

Regime Labour Minister Maung Myint slammed the campaign on Oct. 20, insisting the new process was meant to ease CI registration for workers in Thailand. He claimed that around 1,500 workers had used the new centres in the first few days. However, migrant workers groups and agents said applications have plunged as the campaign gains momentum.

“Very few workers are applying for the CI,” Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee, which assists migrants, told The Irrawaddy on Tuesday.

“Normally, the CI centre in Samut Sakhon alone receives over 1,000 CI applications daily,” he said, adding that the hub has gone quiet in the past few days.

He estimated that at least 500,000 workers are due to apply for their CI, but few are showing up at centers.

Labor activists said workers were also delaying CI renewal because of the cost.

“Migrants’ income levels vary,” Naing Aung Aung of the Arkan Worker Organization in Thailand told The Irrawaddy. “Some took loans to pay for passport and visa issuance. They don’t have extra savings.”

He said the regime’s remittance scheme is unviable given it can easily be bypassed by bribing corrupt officials. Applicants can secure a CI without evidence of remittance for a fee of 1,500 baht, according to labor activists and agents.

Experts note the new policy benefits the cash-strapped regime while piling financial burdens on low-paid workers and cutting remittance lifelines for their families at home. They argue that instead of restrictions and punishment, workers should be offered incentives to remit money through official channels.

Under the current scheme, Myanmar workers lose at least 5,000 kyats for every 100 baht they remit via regime-endorsed channels. While official channels offer 125 kyat per baht, informal markets offer upwards of 130.

The Labour Ministry continues to push the new scheme, projecting that 2026 inflows will match last year’s total of US$ 5.6 billion. Annual remittances have more than doubled since 2019, driven by the mass emigration of workers escaping the turmoil and economic collapse that followed the 2021 coup.

World.title: Hostage Diplomacy: How the Myanmar Junta Is Weaponizing Jailed Aung San Suu Kyi
World.content:
As the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s November summit approaches, the Myanmar junta—desperate for international recognition—has made a series of minor concessions regarding access to jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Highlighting the regime’s ongoing atrocities against civilians, observers and anti-regime groups have warned that the regime’s moves are merely a ploy to win resumption of full participation in ASEAN and ease international pressure.

Since the 2021 coup, the Myanmar regime has been barred from attending high-level ASEAN summits for failing to comply with the bloc’s peace plan, which calls for the immediate cessation of violence against civilians and the opening of a dialogue among all concerned groups, among other things.

Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to meet with ICRC representatives in Naypyitaw on August 3, and to receive books and a diplomatic letter from King Charles on October 19. The jailed Nobel Peace Prize laureate was also permitted to talk with her youngest son, Kim Aris, on October 22, for the first time in the five years since her arrest.

Domestic and regional observers warn that the regime has started using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to gain access to the bloc’s upcoming summit.

“The regime led by the sham president Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to scam the world by using hostage diplomacy,” said Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma.

She cited another recent instance of hostage diplomacy, in which the junta jailed 78 Filipino trafficking victims who had escaped from scam centers. Instead of repatriating them, the regime used the victims as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Maria Teresa Lazaro, the Philippine foreign secretary, who was forced to request the release of her compatriots during a visit to Naypyitaw in January, then thank the internationally-isolated regime for freeing the jailed Philippine nationals.

An ASEAN humanitarian delegation led by the bloc’s special envoy Maria Teresa Lazaro is scheduled to visit Myanmar for two days starting Wednesday.

The tactic was used again with the detention of U.S. citizen Adam Castillo, which allowed the regime to secure engagement with the U.S, Stothard said. A delegation of U.S. officials visited Naypyitaw to secure Castillo’s release.

“The regime continues to use its hostage diplomacy by … dangling Aung San Suu Kyi to secure normalization of relations with ASEAN,” she said. “ASEAN and the international community shouldn’t be easily scammed this way. They shouldn’t be normalizing relations with a gangster who is the architect of genocide and war crimes.”

Thailand welcomed the U.S. engagement with the regime and expected discussions to be held at the upcoming ASEAN summit in Manila on how to proceed with the Myanmar issue, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told media on Friday.

The minister, who is working to improve relations between ASEAN and the military regime, commented that the regime’s granting of permission for Aung San Suu Kyi and her son to speak represented a positive development.

Further evidence of the regime’s concerted effort to secure ASEAN’s recognition and support can be seen in Naypyitaw’s recent decision to form an ASEAN Affairs Committee to communicate and cooperate with the bloc.

Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, who chairs the committee, said it was formed to foster additional channels of engagement with ASEAN. The regime is currently engaging regional neighbors on a country-by-country basis according to priority levels, he added.

Coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been engaging with the U.S., and in recent months has visited ASEAN members Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

David Gum Awng, deputy foreign affairs minister of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), told The Irrawaddy he shares the view that the regime is using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to secure Min Aung Hlaing’s attendance at the upcoming ASEAN summit.

“Civilian leader Daw Aung San Suu Kyi is entirely innocent and is merely a political hostage unjustly detained by the regime for political reasons. Allowing her to receive books and gifts sent by King Charles and permitting a 20-minute phone call with her son is purely a political transaction by the regime,” he said.

He said the regime’s recent moves are a political ploy, despite some ASEAN member countries’ characterization of them as a positive development, and warned that “ASEAN needs to see this reality.”

Mon Mon Myat, lecturer at the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, remarked that the junta’s apparent relaxation regarding access to the jailed civilian leader “might include hopes of being allowed to attend the ASEAN summit. It appears they urgently need both international recognition and assistance. On the other hand, they might be pushing for this out of fear of becoming more isolated on the international stage if the ICJ ruling comes out later this year.” The International Court of Justice is considering a genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over the military’s persecution of the Rohingya minority in Rakhine State.

The regime’s charm offensive may be having some effect. Former Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said in an exclusive interview with Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should assist in Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN. For the time being, however, ASEAN as a bloc is upholding its summit ban, citing the failure to honor its peace plan. Known as the Five-Point Consensus, the plan established over five years ago in Jakarta includes calls for an immediate end to violence and the holding of dialogues. Both coup president Min Aung Hlaing and his rubber-stamp parliament have formally rejected the plan. Meanwhile, the regime continues its five-year campaign of airstrikes, shelling and village burnings.

The NUG’s David Gum Awng said ASEAN must clearly and decisively call out the regime’s total failure to implement the peace plan. He warned that bilateral engagement with the junta by individual member states is emboldening the regime’s war crimes against civilians, rather than applying necessary pressure.

“While ASEAN member states may have different views on the country’s crisis, there must be definite consequences if the junta fails to comply with the agreements. Without clear repercussions for their defiance, the regime has absolutely no incentive to cooperate,” he added.

Citing the junta’s ongoing attacks on civilian targets, Stothard noted that hostage diplomacy is a smokescreen for the regime’s continued brutality against its own people.

“ASEAN and the international community should not be engaging or dancing with a regime that has turned Burma into a transnational crime hub, created the worst humanitarian crisis in the region, and will negatively impact ASEAN for years to come,” Stothard said.

World.title: The Fatal Flaw in China’s Myanmar Policy is Economic Collapse
World.content:
While Beijing’s military‑centric approach — backed by its “three bottom lines” — defines China’s Myanmar policy, the ground reality shows that civil war is not the only source of instability. Alongside the widening conflict, Myanmar’s foundations are being shaken by a deepening economic crisis with historical echoes. The collapse of General Ne Win’s Burma Socialist Programme Party regime four decades ago was not triggered by battlefield defeat, but by economic breakdown — a reminder that today’s regime faces the same danger.

Deepening economic crisis

When Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited in August 2024, the junta was facing not only military setbacks but also severe inflation marked by surging commodity prices. Thanks to Chinese financial assistance, inflation eased after his trip and the kyat stabilized at around 4,000 per US dollar. But it plunged again after military-staged elections early this year and now hovers near 4,600 per dollar.

Starved of hard currency, the junta restricted imports and choked off border trade. The cost of fuel and cooking oil surged, followed by staples such as rice, eggs, and onions, as well as household electronics and medicines. Vehicle prices soared, and black markets reemerged. Domestic manufacturing, agriculture, and livestock industries — reliant on imported technology, seeds, feed, fertilizers, and medicines — were hit hard, while foreign investment also dwindled.

As the kyat weakens, commodity prices are surging again and shortages are widespread. This is not merely a policy miscalculation: the junta channels all foreign currency into military spending, compounding the economic crisis. Without an end to war, the economic crisis cannot be fixed.

Corrupt state apparatus

Another major issue is systemic corruption in the bureaucracy. Graft grew steadily under military rule from 1988 to 2010 but was restrained somewhat by public oversight during the 2010–2020 reform period. But since the 2021 coup, the entire machinery of government — from Min Aung Hlaing and the top brass down to the lowest ranks — have exploited power for personal gain.

Legal restrictions and licensing requirements have become tollbooths for bribery. Payment is required for import permits, ID cards, passports and the right to travel at home or abroad. Importers routinely pay bribes, while ordinary people face extortion by soldiers and police on the streets. This endemic corruption has also facilitated the boom in narcotics production and online fraud gangs.

Narcotics and online scams

Myanmar is among the world’s largest producers of heroin, methamphetamine, and synthetic drugs, with output now rising annually as officials, soldiers and police turn a blind eye in exchange for bribes.

Online scam syndicates previously confined to borderlands are now spreading inland. Evidence from Karen State and northern Shan’s Kokang shows that gangs are relocating under the protection of military‑linked MPs, administrators, border guards, police, and senior officials. Even as criminal syndicates elsewhere in northern Shan are dismantled, Muse—the only border town Naypyitaw still controls thanks to China—remains an online scam hub, highlighting the regime’s complicity in cyber-fraud.

In other words, the economic crisis is not a standalone problem, but deeply intertwined with systemic corruption, narcotics production, and scams.

Poverty and social collapse

Illicit revenues from narcotics and scam syndicates have flooded Myanmar, fueling inflation and driving property values to unsustainable heights. Ordinary citizens are bearing the brunt as the country’s economic crisis deepens. Chinese loans cannot solve this problem.

The persistent civil war, combined with entrenched corruption and criminality, rampant inflation, and worsening shortages, has created a dire situation. While a handful of elites hoard wealth, most of the population struggles to afford basic food, leaving Myanmar society fractured and unstable.

A UNDP report released on October 8 revealed that one in three Myanmar citizens — over 17 million people — are already experiencing multidimensional poverty, with another 19 million at risk. In total, about 37 million people, or 68 percent of the population, are either poor or vulnerable to poverty.

Years of conflict, displacement, economic collapse, and climate shocks have devastated housing, healthcare, education, and livelihoods, worsening deprivation.

China’s other Myanmar headaches

Beyond these crises, China must also reckon with four other problems.

First is anti‑China sentiment — which is rising not only among resistance forces but also within the regime itself. Resistance anger is fueled by Beijing’s support for a failing military regime, not hostility toward Chinese people.

For the regime, however, anti‑China sentiment remains a core worldview. In times of political, economic, or military crisis, the Myanmar military often resorts to Burman nationalism, routinely stoking anti‑China and anti‑Muslim prejudice. In this way, it diverted public anger over rice shortages in 1967 by orchestrating anti‑Chinese riots. Today, the regime sponsors ultranationalist groups such as Ma Ba Tha to sustain this narrative.

Propping up the regime offers China no protection from Naypyitaw’s deep-seated disdain. This hostility is not incidental but fundamental; Beijing will be forced to confront it again and again no matter how much support it provides.

Second, the regime’s corrupt apparatus continues to protect online scam syndicates, undermining China’s efforts to suppress them.

Third, the regime has closed key border trade gates including Muse and Chinshwehaw once worth billions annually to China. At a time when Chinese goods are cheaper than Japanese or Western equivalents, the border-trade shutdown is a major loss. Meanwhile, talk of opening trade routes with India has alarm bells ringing in Beijing.

Fourth, the regime is seeking to reestablish relations with the United States. While China might accept restoration of normal diplomatic ties, anything deeper would be difficult for Beijing to tolerate given its red line over Western engagement with ethnic armed groups.

‘Three bottom lines’ collapse

China’s policy goal is stability in Myanmar. But by betting on the Myanmar military to deliver it, Beijing has tethered itself to failure. The regime’s reliance on force over negotiations, corruption over the rule of law, entanglement with narcotics and scams—coupled with economic breakdown—guarantee perpetual instability.

Despite Beijing’s support, Myanmar remains mired in conflict and crisis. The “three bottom lines” have not been upheld: civil strife is intensifying, ASEAN engagement is faltering, and international powers are finding new entry points.

China’s core objective — stability in Myanmar — remains unfulfilled.

World.title: Malaysia to Seek Clarification Over Reports of Detained Myanmar Returnees
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR—Malaysia will seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country are being held in military detention, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said on Monday.

Malaysia in late September sent back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals as it launched a scheme that rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.

Kuala Lumpur said the group agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centers amid an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

Myanmar pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.

Mohamad told parliament on Monday that Malaysia’s charge d’affaires in Myanmar would investigate the allegations and learn the condition of those reportedly detained.

“If there is news that the 300 people are still being detained, we will ask the Myanmar government to explain to us,” he told parliament in response to a lawmaker’s question.

“We will ask the Myanmar government to ensure that the assurances it gave us are honored,” he added.

Myanmar news outlet the Democratic Voice of Burma reported on Thursday that more than 400 ethnic Rakhine residents who returned from Malaysia earlier this month “remain in military custody” after arriving in Yangon.

They were among a group of 1,476 returnees who arrived by ship outside Yangon, the first of 5,000 that Kuala Lumpur says Myanmar agreed to take back amid the anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

An additional 3,524 people are expected to be repatriated in a second phase.

The UN has warned conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.

Myanmar’s coup leader turned president Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since the putsch, but Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants earlier this month.

During the visit, Min Aung Hlaing said migrants from his country held in Malaysian detention centers will be returned home “as soon as possible”.

“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” he told a joint news conference with Anwar.

The opaque repatriation scheme has been criticized by rights monitors, some fearing ethnic Rohingya may be sent back to a country where they have experienced persecution that rights experts say amounted to genocide.

World.title: How Career Priorities Reveal Gender Inequality in Kazakhstan’s Families
World.content:
ASTANA – A woman receives a long-awaited promotion, but accepting it means moving to another city. Her husband has a career of his own. Whose job should take priority?

Workplace inequality is often measured in hiring, promotions and pay. Yet some of the decisions that shape women’s careers are made far from the office, within families where professional ambitions do not always carry equal weight.

For many couples in Kazakhstan, the answer still favors the man, according to a recent analysis of nationwide survey data examining how families navigate competing professional ambitions. The analysis, by Aigul Zabirova, a professor and chief research fellow at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies (KazISS), explores how men and women approach career decisions when work and family responsibilities collide.

Among surveyed men and women with fewer economic and professional resources, roughly six in 10 said the man’s career usually takes priority, a finding that suggests traditional gender expectations can persist even when couples frame their decisions around practical work obligations.

Who gets to put work first?

When work and family responsibilities conflict, 60.5% of men and 58.7% of women surveyed said the man’s career usually takes priority.

The study draws on a public opinion survey commissioned by KazISS and conducted from April 10 to May 10, 2026. It covered 8,000 respondents aged 18 and older across Kazakhstan’s 17 regions and the cities of Astana, Almaty and Shymkent.

Married respondents and those living with a partner were asked whose career typically took precedence when professional and family obligations clashed, including decisions involving overtime, business trips, relocation and promotions.

The difference became more pronounced among respondents with greater resources.

Researchers defined this group as respondents meeting at least two of three criteria: a university degree, a monthly income of at least 201,000 tenge (US$445) per family member, and employment as a manager, entrepreneur or self-employed person. Approximately one-quarter of adult respondents fell into this category.

Among men in this group, 64.6% said their careers took priority, compared with 51.1% of women, a 13.5-percentage-point difference in their responses.

Women with university degrees were less likely to identify the man’s career as the priority, while income alone did not produce a comparable difference. The findings point to a distinction between how families describe their arrangements and how they negotiate professional opportunities.

When attitudes and actions diverge

Around one in five women surveyed in Kazakhstan said they had turned down a career opportunity for family or household reasons in the past five years, regardless of their economic or professional resources.

Researchers found no significant difference between women with greater resources and those with fewer resources in their likelihood of reporting such decisions.

The finding points to a gap between attitudes toward career equality and women’s experiences. Although women with greater resources were less likely to report that men’s careers took priority in their households, they were just as likely to have forgone professional opportunities for family reasons.

This gap between attitudes and experiences raises a broader question: How much does a change in beliefs alter the actual distribution of responsibilities within a household?

Career decisions often involve competing demands, from childcare and household responsibilities to financial considerations and the requirements of a particular job. Yet when such adjustments repeatedly fall to women, the result can reinforce existing inequalities even without an explicit agreement that one career matters more.

When professional obligations reinforce gender inequalities

Gender inequality at home does not always involve explicit expectations about traditional family roles. It can also emerge through everyday decisions about work. A demanding schedule, an important business trip or responsibilities to employees may all be legitimate professional obligations. But when one partner’s commitments consistently take precedence, the other may be left to adjust their career plans.

In her analysis, Zabirova emphasizes that this language can make an unequal arrangement harder to challenge because they are often framed as practical necessities rather than questions of gender equality.

A husband does not have to oppose his wife’s promotion to become the person whose career takes precedence. He may simply point to his existing responsibilities, leaving his partner to reconsider her plans.

Employers can also influence these decisions. Requirements to work overtime, travel frequently or relocate may place additional pressure on households, particularly when one partner is expected to take on more family responsibilities to accommodate the other’s career.

From this perspective, the family becomes an important part of the broader discussion about professional equality. Workplace policies alone may not address inequalities that are reinforced by household expectations.

More education, persistent career trade-offs

Women in Kazakhstan are more likely than men to have higher education, with 53% holding university degrees compared with 44% of men, according to figures cited by Zabirova.

As more women gain university degrees and pursue professional careers, expectations about whose work should take priority may become increasingly contested. The study suggests that education can be associated with a different understanding of career equality, even when it does not eliminate the practical sacrifices women make for their families.

The findings, however, have limitations. Researchers surveyed individuals rather than couples, meaning differences between men’s and women’s responses do not necessarily reflect disagreements within the same households.

The survey also cannot, on its own, establish why women give up professional opportunities or determine how much of the decision results from gender expectations, income differences or personal preferences.

Equality beyond the workplace

The decisions that shape women’s careers are not always made at work. They also unfold at home, when a promotion requires relocation, business travel conflicts with childcare or one partner’s professional commitments take precedence over the other’s.

Changing that pattern requires more than agreeing that men and women should have equal opportunities. It also requires examining how families make decisions about relocation, childcare, working hours and career advancement.

Employers have a role to play as well. Flexible work arrangements, predictable schedules and family-friendly policies can help reduce the pressure on employees to resolve professional conflicts through sacrifices at home.

World.title: Tokayev’s Ambitious Construction Push Draws Optimism, Questions Over Implementation
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s announced plans for a sweeping infrastructure overhaul and long-term energy security have drawn reactions from Kazakh analysts, who see opportunities for economic growth alongside questions about how the government will turn ambitious proposals into lasting results.

In his Oct. 28 state-of-the-nation address, Tokayev outlined plans to allocate approximately 6.5 trillion tenge ($14.2 billion) from the National Fund through 2029 to modernize infrastructure, including new hospitals, schools, transportation networks and public utilities. He also proposed designating 2027 as a year of nationwide construction.

“Our country is entering a new historical cycle. At this turning point, we must critically reassess all national plans and strategies,” said Tokayev in his nearly one and half hour long address.

The address also called for considering a strategic uranium reserve to secure supplies for the country’s planned nuclear power plants for the next century.

Ambitious construction drive
