After learning that the trees were in Durban, Daily Maverick visited the AGL warehouse and photographed at least five baobabs. The trees lay on their sides on a paved surface. They appeared to have been left there in direct sunlight for two to three months.

Asked about the trees’ legal status, the company said such matters fell outside its responsibilities as a logistics provider. AGL also refused to disclose the client’s identity or contact details, citing confidentiality.

After Daily Maverick sent further questions to the DFFE, it emerged that no valid export licence had been issued for the trees. There was also no permit authorising their removal and relocation. According to available information, the baobabs came from the Waterberg District in Limpopo province.

Based on photographs, Jeff Nichols, a specialist in endemic plants, suggested that the trees could be more than 50 years old if they had been taken from the wild. If they had instead been grown under artificial conditions with irrigation, he estimated their age at 20 to 30 years.

The DFFE said the exporter applied for the required licence on 27 July 2026. The application covered the removal, possession, collection, transport, export and acquisition of five protected trees. However, the department rejected it on 31 July. “The application was rejected because a criminal investigation into the matter is under way. The department will not issue a licence retrospectively to legitimise actions that appear to have been unlawful,” the department said.

On 8 August, the exporter appealed against the decision. The department said the appeal was currently under review by the official responsible for such matters.

Asked whether the applicants had complied with the relevant regulations, the DFFE said they had failed to meet the requirements of the National Forests Act. According to the department, the trees came from the local municipality of Lephalale in Waterberg District, Limpopo province, and were intended for export to Georgia.

The department has launched criminal proceedings in the case. Under the law, the offence carries a fine or a prison sentence of up to three years.

The DFFE has not disclosed the names of those facing criminal proceedings, nor has it identified the owner of the trees or the exporter. The department explained that possessing, collecting, removing, transporting, exporting, buying or selling protected trees constitutes a Category 1 offence.

The plan to transport the baobabs to Georgia has also raised concerns among environmentalists. Dr Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, said that although it was technically possible to uproot baobabs and transplant them elsewhere, the record of their survival in Georgia was discouraging.

“Unfortunately, the survival rates of these trees in Georgia leave much to be desired,” Venter said.

The Kenyan case: eight baobabs transplanted to Georgia dried up and died

The investigation currently under way in South Africa echoes an earlier attempt to transport baobabs from Kenya to Georgia, an incident that attracted international attention in 2022.

On 24 October 2022, The Guardian reported that Kenyan farmers had sold baobabs growing on their land to a group led by Georgian national Giorgi Gvasalia. The plan involved uprooting eight trees and transporting them to Georgia.

In November that year, Kenya’s Ministry of Environment suspended a foreign company’s licence to uproot baobabs, citing several violations. The ministry also instructed the Kenya Forest Service to stop the trees from being moved.

The ministry said uprooting baobabs required the appropriate permit and a transparent process demonstrating how relocating the trees would benefit the public. It concluded that the established requirements had not been met in this case. In April 2023, the Environment Committee of Kenya’s National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the export of baobabs from the Kilifi region to Georgia.

The eight uprooted trees remained in that condition for almost two years and eventually died.

According to Georgia’s Dendrological Park, workers had uprooted the trees in 2021, but various obstacles delayed their transport to Georgia until October 2023. They planted the baobabs in the ground on 8 November 2023.

“These African giants spent almost two years uprooted, in natural conditions entirely unsuitable for them and without proper care. Unfortunately, the stress took its toll: six to seven months after they were planted in Georgia, all eight baobabs had died,” the park said.

Investigators in South Africa must establish who owned the trees and who arranged their removal from the country, under what circumstances these protected plants were uprooted, and who bears responsibility for the attempt to transport them to Georgia.

South Africa blocks shipment of baobabs to Georgia

World.title: Amnesty International, GYLA urge independent probe amid rising Georgian prison abuse claims
World.content:
Violence in Georgian prisons

International human rights organisation Amnesty International and the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) issued a joint statement calling on the Georgian authorities to ensure an independent investigation into reports of torture and other forms of ill-treatment in prisons, as well as to establish effective mechanisms to prevent violence.

According to the organisations, reports of torture and other forms of ill-treatment in Georgian penitentiary institutions have increased, including allegations of sexual violence, beatings and threats.

The organisations also expressed serious concern about the risk of reprisals against prisoners who speak out about such abuse.

In their joint statement, the organisations cited the cases of Giorgi Davitadze, Giorgi and Davit Peikrishvili, Lasha Chachanidze and other prisoners.

The authors of the statement also noted that the authorities’ hasty denials, in the absence of proper investigations, raised serious questions. The organisations urged the authorities to “break the vicious cycle of impunity and establish an oversight mechanism capable of effectively and independently preventing violence”.

Giorgi Davitadze case and allegations of sexual violence

On 2 October 2026, a recording of a court hearing emerged in the media in which prisoner Giorgi Davitadze alleged that he had been subjected to sexual violence by penitentiary service staff. According to him, on 21 December 2025, in a de-escalation room at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi, one of the officers inserted a finger into his anus.

The Special Penitentiary Service rejected the allegations and released CCTV footage. The service said that a forced search had been carried out in accordance with established procedures after the prisoner refused to undergo a search and began insulting staff.

The footage, which has no audio, shows several officers restraining Davitadze, placing him face down on a bed and positioning themselves behind him. As the officers partially obstruct the view of the prisoner, it is impossible to fully assess their actions.

According to his lawyers, the penitentiary service released only a short excerpt from footage lasting approximately 20 minutes. A second camera was installed in the room, but prosecutors did not obtain its recording. According to the Public Defender’s Office, Davitadze’s lawyers reported the alleged abuse on 26 December 2025, and prosecutors launched an investigation on 29 December. Prosecutors say dozens of witnesses have been questioned, while Davitadze refused to undergo a forensic medical examination on 12 January 2026.

His lawyers explained that the proposed examination was aimed solely at identifying physical injuries and did not involve investigating the alleged rape itself.

Amnesty International and GYLA said the published footage did not clarify what had happened in the room. The human rights organisations stressed that, in cases involving allegations of sexual violence, the authorities were obliged to promptly arrange independent medical and psychological examinations.

According to his defence team, Davitadze was repeatedly subjected to humiliation and threats: half of his hair was shaved off, the heating in his cell was deliberately switched off, and threats were made against him and his family members. On 13 October, his lawyers reported that two officers had verbally abused the prisoner and confiscated his television.

According to representatives of the human rights organisations, the prison administration had not restricted access to Davitadze for the officers he accused of abuse. They demanded that the investigation examine not only the events of December but also all allegations of repeated threats and humiliation.

Alleged reprisals against prisoners

The organisations also highlighted the cases of prisoners at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi who expressed solidarity with Davitadze. According to reports, after Davitadze’s allegations became public, some prisoners staged protests, including by making noise in their cells. They were reportedly subsequently subjected to beatings, placed in de-escalation cells (isolation cells) and transferred to other penitentiary institutions.

On 5 October, the lawyer representing Lasha Chachanidze said prison officers had physically assaulted his client and four other prisoners in response to their protest. According to the lawyer, Chachanidze was beaten with batons on 2 October, with officers striking his arms and legs. Visible injuries were documented on his body when he was transferred to Prison No. 3 in Batumi.

On 16 October, another prisoner, Beka Tsertsvadze, reported that prison officers had beaten and verbally abused him while transferring him to a de-escalation cell, after which he was moved to another facility.

The Special Penitentiary Service rejected the allegations of beatings. The service said that placing at least four prisoners in de-escalation cells was a lawful security measure. According to the service, the measure was taken in response to attacks on prison staff on 2 and 4 October and was unrelated to the protests.

The service also released video footage showing two incidents in which prisoners attacked prison officers.

Amnesty International and GYLA noted that prison authorities were obliged to protect both staff and prisoners from violence. However, they stressed that alleged misconduct by prisoners did not justify the use of violence in retaliation.

The use of force is permissible only when strictly necessary and must be proportionate to the situation. Furthermore, restrictive measures must not become a means of punishing prisoners who file complaints or express solidarity with others.

The statement also cited an assessment by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT). In a report published in February 2026, the committee expressed concern about the frequent and sometimes prolonged use of de-escalation cells in Georgian prisons. The CPT warned the authorities that, in practice, placing prisoners in such cells could amount to punishment. According to the committee, de-escalation cells should be used exclusively for prisoners who are agitated or displaying aggressive behaviour, for the shortest possible period and under medical supervision.

Davit Peikrishvili beating case

The case of Davit Peikrishvili has raised further concerns. On 20 October 2026, his lawyer, Paata Gogiashvili, reported that Peikrishvili had been repeatedly subjected to physical violence by fellow inmates at Gldani Prison No. 8 since 16 October.

According to the lawyer, the prisoner had been diagnosed with four fractured ribs, injuries to his skull and facial bones, and numerous bruises across his body. On 19 October, Peikrishvili was transferred to hospital, where medical staff confirmed that he had sustained multiple injuries.

On 19 October, the Special Penitentiary Service initially denied that Peikrishvili had been beaten. The following day, amid media reports and public criticism, the Justice Ministry announced the launch of a criminal investigation into his injuries. On 22 October, the Public Defender said that, according to Peikrishvili, prison officials had also participated in the beating. The Public Defender called on prosecutors to conduct an independent investigation.

On 26 October, prosecutors told journalists that the case had been transferred from the Justice Ministry’s General Inspectorate to the investigative department of Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office. Prosecutors also recommended the suspension of Giorgi Pataridze, director-general of the Special Penitentiary Service under the Justice Ministry.

Following the recommendation, Pataridze left his post, and a new head of the service was appointed.

According to human rights organisations, the developments surrounding Peikrishvili’s case have once again highlighted problems with the effective investigation of allegations of torture and other forms of ill-treatment in Georgia, as well as holding those responsible to account. They linked these concerns, in particular, to reports of violence against protesters detained since 2024.

Rights’ groups urge authorities to establish independent oversight mechanism

Amnesty International and GYLA insist that all credible allegations of torture and other forms of ill-treatment must be subject to prompt, thorough, independent and impartial investigations. They argue that the authorities must ensure that all relevant evidence is collected, victims of alleged abuse are protected, and those against whom there is sufficient evidence are held accountable.

The organisations also called on the authorities to review practices in penitentiary institutions, complaints procedures and mechanisms for protecting prisoners from ill-treatment.

“The Georgian authorities must break this vicious cycle of impunity by establishing an oversight mechanism genuinely capable of effectively and independently preventing violence, creating truly independent complaints procedures, and guaranteeing victims access to justice and compensation,” the organisations said in their joint statement.

World.title: Aliyev discusses peace, external threats and ‘double standards’ at Baku forum
World.content:
Aliyev’s speech at Baku Dialogue Forum

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev spoke at the opening of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku on 27 October. In his speech, he addressed peace efforts with Armenia, the role of international organisations, Azerbaijan’s foreign policy and security.

Aliyev said the country faced no internal threats, criticised “double standards” in international politics and proposed using Azerbaijan’s experience of transitioning from war to peace to help resolve other conflicts.

The World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue brings together representatives of governments, international organisations and experts from different countries to discuss intercultural and interfaith dialogue. The forum was first held in Baku in 2011 as part of the Baku Process initiative launched by Azerbaijan in 2008. It was originally intended to take place every two years. After a break caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the forum resumed in 2024. This year’s seventh edition takes place from 27 to 29 October under the theme “Dialogue for a Shared Future”.

Intercultural dialogue and national unity

Aliyev described Azerbaijan’s geographical position between Europe and Asia as an important factor in fostering intercultural ties. He said religious and ethnic tolerance, as well as traditions of multiculturalism, were among the foundations of the country’s stable development.

The president said members of different ethnic and religious groups in Azerbaijan enjoyed equal constitutional rights and lived in an atmosphere of mutual understanding. According to him, the idea of Azerbaijani identity united different ethnic groups, and this unity had been evident even during the most difficult periods in the history of independent Azerbaijan. As an example, he cited the participation of members of different ethnic and religious groups in the Second Karabakh War.

Aliyev recalled that October marked the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Azerbaijan’s independence. He stressed that, despite changes in political systems, the Azerbaijani people had managed to preserve their language, traditions and national identity. The president said the country’s achievements since independence were the result of the Azerbaijani people’s efforts and that its development had taken place without international assistance.

“All potential threats come from beyond our borders”

In the part of his speech devoted to security, Aliyev said Azerbaijani society demonstrated unity on all issues. In his assessment, the country faced no internal threats, while all potential risks came from abroad.

“All potential threats come from beyond our borders,” the president said.

He compared ideological risks to physical threats and stressed the need to remain vigilant to protect national identity, statehood, independence and the country’s way of life. However, Aliyev did not specify which countries or organisations might pose such threats.

Karabakh negotiations and military operations

Aliyev said that restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity had been the country’s main goal for most of its independence. The president criticised the years of negotiations over the Karabakh conflict, saying they had been aimed not at resolving the conflict but at freezing it.

He justified Azerbaijan’s military actions by citing the right to self-defence under the UN Charter.

According to the president, Azerbaijan restored its territorial integrity and sovereignty as a result of the 2020 war and the 2023 military operation, independently securing the implementation of UN Security Council resolutions adopted in 1993.

Peace with Armenia and experience of ending war

Speaking about relations with Armenia, Aliyev said that Azerbaijan had initiated peace efforts after the end of hostilities. According to him, the draft peace agreement initialled in the summer of 2025 had also been prepared by Baku.

The president stressed that Azerbaijan had not sought a protracted war and had decided not to continue the confrontation after achieving its military objectives. He noted that the desire for revenge could make war endless. In Aliyev’s view, it was important not only to achieve victory but also to know when to stop and offer peace.

The president suggested that parties involved in armed conflicts study Azerbaijan’s experience. He acknowledged that every conflict had its own characteristics but noted that ambition, aggression, the pursuit of superiority and a sense of impunity all played a role in their emergence.

UN resolutions, sanctions and “double standards”

Aliyev called for special attention to be paid to establishing a mechanism to ensure the implementation of UN Security Council decisions as part of discussions on UN reform. He criticised the failure to implement four resolutions on the Karabakh conflict for many years and the absence of sanctions against Armenia.

The president recalled that numerous sanctions had been imposed on countries to Azerbaijan’s north and south, describing the different approach towards Armenia as an example of “double standards”. He accused Armenia of occupying around 20% of Azerbaijan’s territory, carrying out ethnic cleansing and destroying religious and historical monuments. According to him, one million Azerbaijanis had been forced to flee their homes, while 65 mosques had been destroyed in Karabakh.

In criticising “double standards”, Aliyev addressed not only the international community’s response to wars. He also described attempts by other countries to dictate how Azerbaijan should live and what decisions it should make as unacceptable.

The president said Azerbaijan did not interfere in the internal affairs of other countries and expected the same treatment in return. According to him, displays of disrespect towards Azerbaijan and attempts to impose outside demands on the country had always met with firm resistance and would continue to do so. Aliyev also noted that relations based on mutual respect could help reduce the number of international conflicts.

Partnerships with US, China and Europe

Speaking about foreign policy, the president described Azerbaijan as a pillar of stability in an unstable region. He attributed the country’s stronger international standing to its independent policies, economic potential and role in the energy and transport sectors.

Aliyev highlighted strategic partnerships with China and the US, as well as strategic partnership agreements with ten EU member states. The president said Azerbaijan would host a summit of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation in 2027 and a summit of the European Political Community in 2028.

He also recalled the summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, held in Baku in October. According to him, Azerbaijan’s chairmanship of the organisation had been extended for another two years, and the country had been invited to become a full member of the Central Asian Consultative Format. Aliyev described these decisions as recognition of Azerbaijan’s growing role on the international stage.

External debt, energy and transport routes

Turning to economic issues, Aliyev said Azerbaijan’s external debt stood at just over 5% of GDP. He highlighted energy exports and international transport links as factors strengthening the country’s position.

In his view, Azerbaijan’s infrastructure and political ties, as well as its geographical location, played an important role in the development of international transport routes.

The president stressed that developing international transport links required maintaining good relations not only with neighbouring countries but also with their neighbours.

Peace agreement initialled in Washington and region’s future

Concluding his speech, Aliyev noted that both positive and negative developments had taken place around the world since the previous forum. He cited the outbreak of new wars in neighbouring regions as negative developments and the peace process with Armenia as a positive one.

The president recalled that the text of a peace agreement had been initialled in Washington in August 2025, with the participation of Donald Trump. Aliyev stressed that, at that stage, the agreement had only been initialled, not signed. The US president had, however, signed a trilateral declaration as a witness. According to Aliyev, this process marked a new chapter for the South Caucasus.

World.title: Tajikistan’s Khutalon hydropower plant to generate 2.5B kWh annually
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. The planned Khutalon (Shurob) Hydroelectric Power Plant in Tajikistan will have an installed capacity of 800 megawatts and an average annual electricity generation of more than 2.5 billion kilowatt-hours, the press service of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Energy and Water Resources reported following Minister Daler Juma’s visit to the proposed construction site on October 23.

The Khutalon hydropower plant is planned for the Vakhsh River, between two of Tajikistan’s major hydropower facilities - the Rogun hydropower plant upstream and the Nurek hydropower plant downstream.

The project is expected to contribute to increased electricity generation, more efficient use of the Vakhsh River’s water resources, and stronger energy independence for Tajikistan. The construction start date, project cost, and commissioning timeline have not been specified in the available information.

Trend estimates that the implementation of the Khutalon hydropower project could support further growth in Tajikistan’s electricity supply and strengthen the country’s capacity to meet rising domestic demand. If the plant achieves its projected annual generation level, its output could cover the annual electricity consumption of approximately 500,000–625,000 households, assuming average household consumption of 4,000–5,000 kWh per year. The actual number would depend on household consumption patterns and the share of electricity allocated to residential users rather than industry and other sectors.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s ferroalloy exports to South Korea fall 54% in Jan-Aug
World.content:
Photo: Kazakhstan's Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. Kazakhstan’s ferroalloy exports to South Korea fell by 54% year-on-year in volume terms in January-August 2026, totaling 22,518 tonnes compared with 48,906 tonnes in the same period of 2025, according to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan.

In value terms, exports to South Korea decreased by 51.5% year-on-year to $31.32 million from $64.60 million in the first eight months of 2025.

In August 2026, Kazakhstan shipped 758 tonnes of ferroalloys to South Korea, worth $1.18 million.

Overall, Kazakhstan exported 1.05 million tonnes of ferroalloys in January-August 2026, down 16.8% from 1.26 million tonnes in the same period of 2025. In value terms, total ferroalloy exports decreased by 6.16% year-on-year to $1.36 billion from $1.45 billion.

China remained the largest destination for Kazakh ferroalloys, importing 631,220 tonnes worth $704.5 million in the first eight months of 2026. Japan ranked second, with imports of 127,485 tonnes valued at $213.2 million.

Other major destinations by export value included the United States, which received 72,179 tonnes worth $135.7 million; Germany, with 28,042 tonnes worth $53.5 million; Russia, with 37,759 tonnes worth $47.7 million; Italy, with 20,716 tonnes worth $33.5 million; and South Korea, with 22,518 tonnes worth $31.3 million. Indonesia, Spain, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic were also among the main buyers.

In August 2026, Kazakhstan exported 102,127 tonnes of ferroalloys worth $145.49 million in total.

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover reached $102.96 billion in January-August 2026, up 12.8% in nominal terms compared with the same period of 2025.

Exports totaled $60.39 billion, an increase of 19.5% in nominal terms, while imports reached $42.57 billion, up 4.5%.

Crude oil and crude oil products obtained from bituminous minerals accounted for 49.8% of Kazakhstan’s exports in January-August 2026. Other major export commodities included refined copper and unwrought copper alloys (6.4%), radioactive chemical elements and radioactive isotopes (5.1%), copper ores and concentrates (4.4%), and ferroalloys (2.2%).

Passenger cars and other motor vehicles accounted for the largest share of imports, at 3.3%. Other major imported commodities included telephone equipment (2.7%), pharmaceutical products (2.5%), petroleum gases and other gaseous hydrocarbons (2.4%), and electric generating sets and rotary converters (2.2%).

Italy was Kazakhstan’s largest export destination, accounting for 18% of total exports. China ranked second at 17.6%, followed by Russia (8.5%), Türkiye (7.9%), France (6.1%) and the Netherlands (5.9%).

Russia was Kazakhstan’s largest import partner, accounting for 31% of total imports. China ranked second at 29.8%, followed by Germany (4.6%), the United States (3.9%), South Korea (2.5%) and Türkiye (2.1%).

World.title: Highly invasive weed threatening native flora and fauna at Uluru
World.content:
Uluru is arguably the nation's most recognised and revered landmark, but concerned tourism operators and rangers say the World Heritage site is facing a growing crisis.

Highly invasive buffel grass, which is known to choke native plants, destroy animal habitats and elevate fire risk, is blanketing the base of the sacred site and its neighbouring Kata Tjuta rock formations.

According to a handout from Parks Australia, which manages the Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, buffel grass was introduced in the late 70s "around the base of Uluru to reduce erosion from four-wheel drive vehicles".

"It now thrives in this area," it reads.

The NT government declared buffel grass a weed in 2024. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

Parks Australia says the weed has now infested about 2,650 hectares of the national park, equating to 2 per cent of its total area.

Tracey Guest has worked in and around the park for more than two decades, including as a Parks Australia manager, helping protect the natural and cultural values of the area before her recent retirement.

During that time, she was on the front line of the fight against the aggressive weed, including co-authoring papers and sitting on an NT government advisory committee about buffel.

Tracey Guest says buffel grass covers about 90 per cent of the land at the base of Uluru. (Supplied)

Ms Guest said buffel grass was "concentrated around the rock and Kata Tjuta", covering "maybe 90 per cent around the base of Uluru, except for where we've done some management".

"Buffel grass is the biggest threat to the World Heritage values, the cultural, natural values, of Uluru," she said.

"It's a very clever grass that has done a job way better than it was first anticipated and it's now become an environmental weed equal to the cane toad in Australia."

Native plants cannot compete

Ms Guest said this year had been one for the wildflower, a time when the local Aboriginal Anangu people say "country's really strong".

"But when you have the buffel grass covering all that, no one gets that sensation of the country and lifting your spirits and being exciting," she said.

"This year should be the year of the pretty flower; it should be amazing, yet we've got buffel grass where those sort of plants would grow.

Buffel grass is visible all around the base of Uluru. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"Nothing will come up around it because it just sends this toxin into the soil that's protecting itself from competition.

" It's just covering country and nothing else is able to compete against it. "

On the outskirts of the park, the Tjakura rangers work to care for the Katiti Petermann Indigenous Protected Area (IPA).

Part of their work is managing buffel grass alongside other park rangers, neighbouring Indigenous ranger groups and pastoralists, to prevent it from choking vital habitat.

Garth Forrester, an Anangu traditional owner, is the regional coordinator overseeing the IPA under the Central Land Council.

Mr Forrester said when buffel grass spreads, "it's indiscriminate, it takes over things".

Garth Forrester says the community is concerned about the spread of buffel grass. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"Looking around where we're standing now, you're just seeing spinifex, and you're seeing all the beautiful wildflowers and vegetation," he said.

"But if we drive away from here, just about 10 or 20 minutes down the road, you'll see where the buffel grass is starting to come in and impact.

"Our constituents are that worried about the buffel grass that we have acquired funding to get two brand new spray units to be able to combat the oncoming buffel grass."

Calls for action to avoid 'significant negative impacts'

Tourism Central Australia chief executive Danial Rochford said operators across the region were seeing the effect of buffel grass on the landscape, especially after recent weather created ideal conditions for the fast-growing weed to flourish.

"Most of our visitors aren't aware of buffel grass," he said.

Danial Rochford says there needs to be more resources made available to address buffel grass at Uluru. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"But what our members are seeing is its impact to the flora and fauna.

"This is a weed that is permeating through very sensitive parts of Central Australia.

"We will have significant negative impacts if we don't deal with buffel grass in the short term."

Mr Rochford said urgent investment was needed to tackle the problem head-on.

"We need to see resources flow through to manage this on the ground, otherwise we're just not going to be able to put the cat back in the bag," he said.

Uluru is sacred to the Anangu people of the region. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"We are not going to be able to eradicate buffel grass in totality; that's never going to happen, but there are places where we can draw a line in the sand.

" Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park is a perfect example of where we should be putting significant resources. "

In a statement, a Parks Australia spokesperson said buffel grass management was "specified as a priority" under its management plan and "a combination of mechanical removal, chemical treatment and drone technology" was used to monitor and manage buffel grass.

Solutions from the past

Ms Guest said a volunteer program and effort by parks staff in the early 2000s had helped to contain the weed.

"The park actually had a good program at that stage," she said.

"The conservation volunteers would come down and spend … the winter months digging out, paying to dig out, buffel grass around the rock.

Tracey Guest says in the 2000s buffel grass was better managed. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"And there was a lot of work done, and we were actually making headway through that time, and that program stopped in 2010.

"There wasn't enough follow-up."

Ms Guest said follow-up required vigilant, relentless work over extended periods.

"The follow-up is the most important element around managing buffel grass," she said.

"You can go and spray a big area, and if you don't do the follow-up, it'll be back again in 12 months."

The spread of buffel grass is negatively affecting the growth of native flowers, such as yellow billy buttons. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

She said reinstating a volunteer program or welcoming students undertaking a relevant TAFE or university course could also help.

"It is a no-brainer," she said.

"You need people that are bush regenerators, people that are physically able and interested in doing that sort of work and want to make a difference to the place," she said.

Art show highlights buffel grass devastation An art exhibition opening in Alice Springs today will shine a spotlight on the native plants driven out of Central Australia by buffel grass.

"You'd have a double whammy because you have cultural induction.

"So understanding how First Nations people look at the world so you get their view, and working alongside people is better than just having some class where someone talks at you."

She said new technology is also offering some light at the end of the tunnel.

"There's new things coming through that can help us manage buffel grass, and the more interest that we put on this, the more effort people will put into finding solutions," she said.

"If we do nothing, it's actually going to cost us way more. So we have to do something."

World.title: Police investigate motorhome fire as man remains in critical condition
World.content:
Police are investigating a suspicious motor home fire in Newcastle that left a man in a critical condition in hospital.

Emergency services were called to Bulkara Street at Wallsend shortly before 6am today following reports of a burning vehicle.

Police said a 69-year-old man was rescued from the blaze by a member of the public before officers arrived.

NSW Ambulance said he was treated for serious burns to his arms and legs before being taken to John Hunter Hospital in a critical condition.

He has since been transferred to the Royal North Shore Hospital.

In a statement, Fire and Rescue NSW said there had been reports of gas bottles involved in the fire.

"We are treating the matter as suspicious," Acting Superintendent Steven Benson said.

" I don't believe it's random … at this stage we do believe it was targeted. "

Fire and Rescue NSW said there are reports of gas bottles involved in the fire. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

Parked in the street

Resident Tom Eschebach said he was home when the fire broke out.

"I was lying in bed, and I heard a few odd noises … a minute later I heard a very loud bang which made me get out of bed," he said.

"I had a look out there and saw the motor home fully engulfed by fire."

Mr Eschebach said it had been parked in the street for more than 12 months and he believed the occupant was "doing it tough".

A 69-year-old man was rescued from the motorhome by a member of the public. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

"It's been sitting in that location for a bit over a year. It used to be around the corner," he said.

Mr Eschebach said complaints had been made to the council about the motor home.

"I know he's had several tickets and even had a green sticker on the window to say, 'You've got to move it, you're not a resident,'" he said.

" I hope it was an accident … because he was a very quiet old gentleman. "

Acting Superintendent Benson said that, as part of their inquiries, officers were looking into how long the motor home had been parked in the street and whether neighbours had complained about the vehicle.

Police have established a crime scene to determine the cause of the fire and are asking anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Rogue taxi drivers accused of exploiting passengers at Perth airport, casino
World.content:
Western Australia's transport minister says compliance checks will be ramped up in an attempt to weed out "bad apples" operating taxis in Perth, with a focus on the airport and the Crown Casino complex.

Rita Saffioti said "secret shopper" style checks and compliance blitzes had already taken place four times this year, and at least one driver was handed a fine.

Investigations were carried out in collaboration with WA Police and Australian Federal Police outside Perth Airport and the Burswood entertainment precinct — home to Perth Stadium and Crown Casino.

Perth Airport is one of the areas authorities are targeting in the compliance blitz. (ABC News: James Carmody)

Form of 'wage theft'

Perth taxi driver Jonathan Masih told the ABC illegal operators had found workarounds for compliance checks.

"A lot of drivers disappeared then because they got a network, they just ring each other up and then they don't show up," he told 102.5 ABC Perth.

Mr Masih said illegal taxi drivers taking fares from outside major hubs was a form of wage theft.

Protecting the reputation of legitimate taxi drivers is one of the minister's motivations. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

"Some of them are posing as a taxi, the other ones they've got private cars and they're just asking the customer to jump in," he said.

"They're just doing the work in front of the airport.

"I've been telling the airport authorities, federal police, Department of Transport, minister's office, but nothing changes."

Perth Airport chief warns of upheaval Perth Airport's chief executive has warned passengers the facility is set for major upheaval as it moves to consolidate its four terminals.

Mr Masih said he was worried about how illegal taxis would impact unknowing passengers.

"It's not really good for the customers, if there's an accident or anything bad happens there's going to be legal issues," he said.

Ms Saffioti said ensuring compliance was as much about protecting the reputation of legitimate drivers as it was stamping out "bad apples" in the industry.

"We want to make sure … all those hard-working taxi drivers continue to get clientele and aren't impacted by those that are abusing the system."

Data tracking leads to conviction

Ms Saffioti said investigations found evidence of "abuse".

Transport Minister Rita Saffioti says there need to be consequences for people exploiting the system. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Now we're able to go through and check data and check charges made compared to distance travelled and we've found some people are abusing that system," Ms Saffioti said.

"As a result, there's already been one fine imposed by the court and a number of other investigations are underway."

Ms Saffioti said there were a number of checks being made including car roadworthiness, driver authorisation and company authorisation.

"We need to make sure that those who are exploiting the system or not obeying the rules are dealt with," she said.

World.title: Breaking: Teen dies in hospital days after drive-by shooting south of Brisbane
World.content:
A Queensland teenager has died in hospital days after a drive-by shooting at a pub south of Brisbane.

Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau, 19, from Jimboomba was shot in the head and neck at Fitzys Loganholme on Saturday night.

She died at the Princess Alexandra Hospital.

Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau was shot in the neck and head. (Supplied)

She was one of four people shot by two masked men during a boxing event at the popular local nightspot.

Three men — Zachary Uchtman, Brodie Blackwood and Kane Barrett — were also hospitalised after being shot in the incident.

Logan District Detective Inspector Ian Galpin said the incident was now a homicide investigation.

"A 19-year-old woman in the prime of her life who was simply going out for a night out with friends has had her life taken from her in the most cowardly way," he said.

"We have not stopped and we will not stop until these people are identified and taken into custody."

Logan District Detective Inspector Ian Galpin said the matter is now a homicide investigation. (ABC News)

Detective Inspector Galpin appealed to anyone with information to be to come forward.

"There are people out there who know exactly who was involved in this offence and know exactly why it occurred.

"I'm asking those people to brave enough to come forward with that information and contact police."

With some 80 detectives working on the case, Detective Inspector Galpin said Queensland Police had not ruled out gang involvement in the shooting.

"We are keeping a very open mind to the involvement of gangs," he said.

"That said, our priority now is to identify the persons involved and the reasons for this offence occurring.

"The police have received a lot of information in the last few days.

"I encourage the community to keep that information coming in."

Detective Inspector Galpin said Ms Schuster-Togiatau's family were going through "an incredibly difficult time".

"We're in touch with the family and they're not doing well," he said.

"It's an incredibly difficult time. I can't imagine the hurt they're going through.

"We will continue to support the family in every way possible."

He confirmed that two of the other victims of Saturday's shooting have been released from hospital, with one remaining to receive more treatment.

World.title: Frances Crawford's son tells jury he was 'scared for her safety'
World.content:
The son of a woman who was allegedly killed by her husband at a rural southern Queensland property has told a jury none of her children "wanted her in an environment with my dad" and he was "scared for her safety".

Robert John Crawford is on trial in Brisbane, accused of murdering 49-year-old Frances Crawford in July 2024.

The former RAAF pilot, also aged 49, has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors allege he caused her death, before taking steps to make it look like she had a fatal ride-on mower accident at their Upper Lockyer home.

Frances Crawford, who was allegedly murdered by her husband in the Lockyer Valley in July 2024. (Supplied)

His defence team has rejected Ms Crawford was murdered.

The jury has already heard the couple had ongoing relationship issues, due to multiple instances of cheating carried out by Mr Crawford spanning several years.

In July 2023, after another revelation of infidelity, Mr Crawford was asked to leave the family home and Ms Crawford had the locks changed, the jury has heard.

In the days following, the jury has heard Mr Crawford forcefully entered the property, sparking a verbal altercation that resulted in police attending.

The house where Frances Crawford was found dead. (Queensland Police Service)

Two of the couple's children, Jessie and Jake Crawford, aged in their 20s, lived at the home at the time and gave evidence about this incident.

They also testified about the following period, when their parents were separated, and when they reconciled some months later.

Jessie Crawford told the jury she stopped speaking to her father after discovering he was unfaithful and initially grew closer to her mother, who was a "different person when she was away from him".

However, she said it was not long before her father returned to the home to help her mother with chores around the property.

Jessie Crawford (right) gave evidence at the trial. (ABC News: Talissa Siganto)

"At first, he started showing up just to try and speak with mum; she didn't want that … but he continued," she said.

"[Frances Crawford] said 'still don't want him here, but he's staying outside, he is doing something helpful, this doesn't change anything.'"

Jessie Crawford told the jury she noticed her parents speaking more frequently, and she believed her mother's "attitude started to change" at the end of December.

"She started to go on dates again [with Mr Crawford]," she said.

Jessie Crawford told the jury on Mother's Day in 2024, three months after leaving the family home, Ms Crawford revealed she had reconciled with Mr Crawford.

Members of Frances Crawford's family have attended the trial this week. (ABC News: Tara Cassidy)

She said her mother was "just that different person again" and she felt "quite hurt" she had been "pulled in again" by her father.

" She made promises she wouldn't let that happen again. "

Jessie Crawford told the jury she felt like Ms Crawford was "picking our abuser" over her and her siblings.

"All she really said was 'it's hard for me too,'" she said.

The court heard Frances Crawford stopped speaking to her husband after learning of his infidelity. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

Under cross-examination she accepted she told police she believed her parents got back together much earlier, despite her father failing a polygraph test in counselling, which was one of several rules Ms Crawford set for him.

The jury has already heard Mr Crawford told police he believed his wife died while he was asleep, after she attempted to move the mower before their sprinkler system turned on.

Jessie Crawford told the jury she never saw her mother using the mower, and never saw it parked anywhere other than in the shed, however she acknowledged she had lived elsewhere between 2021 and mid-2023.

She also said in a statement to police, if there was an issue with the sprinklers, she believed her mother would go to the panel to check them, not the physical sprinklers themselves.

The lawnmower police allege was used in Ms Crawford's death. (Queensland Police Service)

Her younger brother Jake Crawford told the jury during his parents' separation his mother had the house valued, and they had discussed moving.

"She was unsure if she could afford a house in Toowoomba that was big enough for the dogs or … for us to visit, she was quite worried about the financial situation," he said.

Jake Crawford also testified about seeing his father come to the house while they were separated and on one occasion he overheard Mr Crawford call Ms Crawford a "psychopath".

"For setting up the cameras and other things she did," he said.

Jake Crawford (middle) said he was scared for his mother's safety. (ABC News: Talissa Siganto)

When he found out their parents were back together, Jake Crawford told the jury he was "distressed for her" and "scared for her safety," he said.

"None of us kids wanted her in an environment with my dad," he said while getting emotional.

Jake Crawford also testified he never saw his mother mow the lawn, and his father would never leave it out "because he said it would kill the grass".

He also said his mother did not know how to use the sprinkler system properly which had been set up by their father.

The Triple Zero call made by Mr Crawford was played to the jury, in which he told the operator he had just found his wife "badly hurt" at the bottom of a retaining wall.

"I think the mower's rolled … I had to pull it off, I think she's still okay, I think, I need an ambulance ASAP," he said.

He told the operator his wife was not breathing, had a small amount of blood on her, and he was told to start CPR.

When asked when it happened Mr Crawford said he did not know as he had been sleeping, and the operator then asked why she was mowing late at night.

"She wasn't mowing … the sprinklers were on and I think she was moving it," he said.

"I went to bed, I think she was watching Netflix," he said.

While attempting to resuscitate her Mr Crawford said, "she's really cold".

At times during the call Mr Crawford cried and at one point said "come on Franny" and "Frances wake up".

The trial continues.

World.title: Less than a week from midterms, Trump is very, very unpopular in the US
World.content:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 US election against Kamala Harris, he pulled together a coalition of voters that don't have much history voting Republican.

Working class and lower income voters helped deliver him key swing states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, while Hispanic voters helped turn the sun belt states of Arizona and Nevada red.

Research from Pew found that Trump voters were markedly more racially and ethnically diverse in 2024 (20 per cent non-white) than they were in 2020 (14 per cent) and 2016 (10 per cent).

Virtually all demographic groups swung to Trump in 2024, but a New York Times analysis concluded the biggest shifts were among young Black and Hispanic voters.

At the time of that election, strategists wondered if Trump had catalysed a political realignment in the country that would continue to work in Republicans' favour.

But converting irregular voters into reliable members of the Republican base is not easy.

Two years on, as the cost of living bites, they don't appear to have stuck around, and the Hispanic voters that swung behind Trump have either swung right back to the Democrats, or are choosing to sit this election out.

The Republican Party appears almost certain to lose control of the House of Representatives in next week's midterm elections. Democrats also lead in polls in more than enough Senate races to be able to take control of that chamber as well (although many of those leads are within the margin of error).

US voters will have their say in the midterm elections in less than a week. (Reuters: Rebecca Cook)

Among the list of prizes that Democrats are hoping to pick up next week, the state of Texas glistens seductively.

Democrats haven't won a senate seat in the state since 1988, but this year, their candidate James Talarico is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in polling.

Republicans appear to be vulnerable in deep red states, and in recent weeks Trump has held rallies on Kansas, Iowa, Oklahoma and Alabama. That is not the strategy of a party that's feeling confident.

Donald Trump isn't on the ballot this year, but at rallies he has repeatedly asked voters to "pretend" he is.

"They say that Trump does great when he's on the ballot, but when he's not on the ballot … his people don't come and they don't vote for senators, congressmen," he said at a rally in South Carolina in August.

Loading...

Part of the Trump campaign's strategy in 2024 was to increase turnout rates among people who would usually stay home. Among the group of people who voted in that election but not in 2020, Pew estimated Trump had a 12 percentage point lead over Harris.

High turnout helped him two years ago. This year, it may be part of his undoing.

Trump wants voters to be thinking about him when they consider voting, because last time that drove lots of people to the polls.

The trouble is that, in 2026, the president is very unpopular.

Nobody's ever seen a president so disliked

American politicians are, as a general rule, held in much lower regard now than they used to be. But amidst an unpopular bunch, Donald Trump is reaching new depths.

YouGov and the Economist have been regularly tracking views on US presidents by asking voters whether they approve or disapprove of the job the leader is doing.

In his first term, Trump was into net negative territory effectively from the moment he took office. President Biden was in the negatives within seven months.

But in his second term, Trump has plummeted. A week out from polling day, the Economist recorded a net approval rating of -27, with 34 per cent of voters approving of the job he's doing and 61 per cent disapproving.

That is a lower net approval rating than any other president has recorded just before their midterm elections since World War II.

Given the president's party nearly always goes backwards in the House of Representatives, and that the Republicans only need to lose three seats to lose control of the House, it's not hard to see why forecasters are tipping a Democrat win.

If the midterms go as poorly for Republicans as opinion polls suggest, it could threaten Trump's command of the public's attention, as well as his authority over his party.

While he'll be in office for another two years, there's always an election around the corner in the US, and once the midterms are behind us attention will start to shift to the 2028 presidential election.

The results of these midterm elections will be an important moment in defining Trump's political legacy, as candidates start to position themselves for potential runs.

The current president regularly backs his preferred candidates in Republican primaries, and he believes his endorsement carries weight.

But will Republicans in the future be keen to embrace the Trump political project, or will they be keeping their distance the moment he's seen as a lame duck president?

World.title: Police uncover usernames allegedly directing Melbourne arson attacks
World.content:
Detectives have uncovered the usernames of several taskmasters suspected of orchestrating a wave of firebombings and extortions across Melbourne.

Armed Crime Squad detectives believe those behind the profiles were responsible for ordering attacks on bars, clubs and restaurants during the so-called "bar wars" earlier this year.

Figures instructing alleged foot soldiers under the online usernames "Onepercent", "Motion" and "Work" have become central to the investigation, which ramped up in April amid an almost daily onslaught of fires targeting venues, which were often located in busy CBD and inner-city precincts.

Detective Acting Inspector Simon Pengelly of the Armed Crime Squad said the investigation now relied on information from people who may have communicated with those usernames.

"The reality is, we can't do this without the help of the community. Police are only as good as the intelligence we have," he said.

"If you have any information on these handles — or have had any contact with them — you can play a critical role in helping us to curb this offending. We'd urge you to come forward and speak to police."

Police identified the alleged usernames of some of the crime figures orchestrating a wave of arson attacks on licensed venues. (Unsplash: Nic Chi)

Multiple underworld sources say those usernames were likely tied to "burner" or single-use accounts and devices and may no longer be active.

Social media and encrypted messaging apps have become preferred method of communication between criminals and underlings, who are often children, when planning alleged attacks.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Olivia Jenkins on Instagram at @by_oliviajenkins or on Signal at @oliviajenkins.22. If you're sharing sensitive information, read our tips on how to contact us confidentially.

Several youths are before the courts as they face charges for their alleged roles in some of the attacks, including a Pakenham home invasion and an alleged arson at Left Bank cocktail bar in Southbank.

In July, Operation Eclipse detectives charged 20-year-old Jesse Hadchiti with being a key middleman responsible for co-ordinating some of the attacks connected to bars and restaurants.

Detective Inspector Graham Banks said at the time that Mr Hadchiti painted himself as a high roller, allegedly used the handle "Commbank" on messaging platforms to allude to the amount of money he was making by working for the Hamad syndicate.

A 20-year-old Essendon man was arrested earlier this year and is alleged to have organised multiple violent crimes. (Victoria Police)

Police alleged he had up to 2,000 potential offenders at his disposal to commit crimes on behalf of the gang, believed to be run by Hamad's lieutenant, Ali al-Huseini, after Hamad was sentenced to life behind bars in Iraq for drug trafficking.

Before that, Hamad was widely believed to be responsible for Victoria's tobacco wars as he wrangled control of the black-market smoke trade from his alleged rivals, the Haddara family.

Mr Hadchiti has been behind bars since his arrest at his parents' Essendon home.

While the three organisers have been linked to the attacks on hospitality venues, police have previously said organised crime syndicates, particularly the dominant 313 gang run by exiled tobacco boss Kazem Hamad, operated across multiple criminal ventures such as illicit tobacco or drugs.

A more recent spate of arsons across Melbourne saw almost 20 cars, venues and homes targeted, with several of those attacks believed to be linked to illegal tobacco.

Victoria police are investigating multiple arson attacks which they allege were orchestrated via messaging apps. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration)

The ABC revealed that the alleged teenage arsonists who torched cars in Taylors Hill, which left a 13-year-old boy fighting for life, received their instructions on WhatsApp.

"Tasking criminal offences while hidden behind an online platform is not a faceless crime," Inspector Pengelly said.

"Arsons, extortions, kidnappings and other violent criminal offending is being used to intimidate, influence and impose and is putting the Victorian community at risk."

World.title: Club's social media post 'deeply troubling' after coach charged with rape
World.content:
The Northern Tasmanian Football Association says it is "deeply troubled" by a country football club's social media activity, after its former coach was charged with three counts of rape.

Former Bracknell Football Club coach Josh Adams is facing rape charges, with police confirming they charged a 44-year-old man with the offences, alleged to have occurred in April last year.

He is scheduled to appear in the Launceston Magistrates Court early next year.

An independent media outlet first reported the charges, and also detailed private messages exchanged between Bracknell Football Club president Nicole Jones and the mother of Mr Adams's alleged victim.

Ms Jones then apologised and resigned.

But the ABC has since seen copies of a post on the club's Facebook page calling for the club to stand together and saying "we must remember that people are more than headlines, allegations or one difficult chapter".

"We cannot let division tear apart something that has brought so many people together," the post also said.

" And we cannot allow this chapter to become the final chapter of something so special. "

AFL Tasmania said it was now reviewing related social media activity for potential breaches of the National Community Football Policy Handbook.

It said it would work with the Northern Tasmanian Football Association (NTFA) and the club to ensure these matters were appropriately addressed.

The NTFA said it was "deeply troubled" by the recent events involving Bracknell Football Club and subsequent social media activity.

It said it recognised the distress these circumstances may have caused, particularly to the alleged victim and others affected.

"The club has been asked to cease public commentary about this matter that may cause further distress or harm to those involved," it said.

'Safeguarding responsibilities' to be highlighted

The NTFA said it would engage directly with its member clubs to reinforce their safeguarding responsibilities, expected standards of conduct and obligations when responding to allegations of sexual violence and other serious misconduct.

Tasmanian football club coach charged with rape A former Tasmania football club coach has been charged with three counts of rape, and the club's president has resigned.

It also said it would engage "an appropriately qualified practitioner to provide practical guidance and education to clubs and their volunteers, particularly in responding to disclosures and allegations of sexual violence in a trauma-informed, respectful and accountable manner".

It said it had a pre-existing safeguarding framework, to which all clubs were required to commit.

"Community football should be an environment where everyone feels safe, supported and respected," it said.

"The NTFA is committed to maintaining those standards, strengthening safeguarding practices across its competition and holding its member clubs accountable to the expectations they have committed to uphold."

Association says it 'acted promptly'

The NTFA said it became aware Mr Adams was expected to face serious criminal charges on October 16.

It said it became aware of concerning messages attributed to Ms Jones days later on October 23.

It said it "acted promptly" referring the matter to the AFL for independent consideration and making clear its expectation that the president stand aside from all official club duties.

The president subsequently issued an apology and stood down.

"The NTFA also made clear that the former president was not to continue exercising any official responsibilities within the club while stood down," the NTFA said.

Neither the NTFA or AFL Tasmania said when they first became aware of the allegations about Mr Adams, but have said the circumstances surrounding the criminal allegations remain before the courts and a matter for the police.

The Bracknell Football Club has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Leaked letter reveals growing Labor rift over Kimberley fracking
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAThe Kimberley Leaked letter reveals growing Labor rift over Kimberley fracking Holly Thompson October 29, 2026 — 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A leaked letter written by a West Australian Labor MP has highlighted the schism growing between party members over leaving a small portion of the state open to oil and gas companies interested in fracking. Federal Member for Fremantle Josh Wilson has become the first Labor minister based in WA to reveal he has concerns over the possibility of fracking being undertaken in the Kimberley – the only region of the state where a moratorium on the practice is not in place. Labor MP Josh Wilson. Mark Naglazas And environment groups have said they have been made aware of more Labor MPs pushing for a ban internally. Wilson wrote to a member of his electorate on Wednesday after they called his office to discuss concerns about Black Mountain Energy’s Valhalla gas project proposal in the Kimberley, which includes plans to drill and frack up to 20 exploration wells.



“I share the sharp concern of many in our community when it comes to the significant risks that come with fracking in general,” Wilson wrote in his letter. “I am particularly concerned about fracking in the Kimberley, with the potential to impact on the Martuwarra/ Fitzroy River. “It is welcome that the WA government has established a moratorium that prevents fracking in 98 per cent of Western Australia – but clearly the Kimberley is the missing piece in terms of protecting the West Australian environment, water systems, and First Nations rights/ culture from this kind of intrusive and unnecessary method.” He also wrote that the WA Labor State Conference, held in November 2025, had passed a resolution calling for the moratorium to be extended to the Kimberley, and that he strongly supported that position. “While it’s important to note that the current proposal is limited to exploration and appraisal activities only … that doesn’t in any way diminish the serious concerns about the impacts of exploration drilling itself and concerns about the way in which an exploration approval could lead to a fracking operation in the Kimberley,” Wilson said.



He is the first WA Labor MP to provide strong opposition to fracking in the Kimberley. The process of hydraulic fracturing, known commonly as fracking, involves using water pressure down a pipe to fracture rock formations deep underground, to release the gas trapped inside. Back in May, Premier Roger Cook told the Australian Financial Review that WA could be forced to start fracking the Kimberley if Woodside’s Browse gas project was not developed – a stance he doubled down on in budget estimates that same day. “There are decisions coming for the state into the future. Our (Australian Energy Market Operator) projects a gas shortfall in the early 2030s and as a state, we need to come to a decision about what that means,” he told estimates. “If not Browse, then does something else make up that shortfall?”



WA’s environmental watchdog also green lit the Valhalla project, sparking more than 8000 appeals which are now under review. Lock the Gate WA coordinator Simone van Hattem said that decision from the Environmental Protection Authority had sparked one of the biggest grassroots campaigns in Australia. “Fracking in the Kimberley poses huge environmental risks ... that’s why fracking is already banned in huge parts of WA,” she said. “The widespread community opposition to fracking in the Kimberley is becoming impossible for Labor to ignore. “It’s clear that Labor is torn over this because they know it’s a vote loser and because they know opening the Kimberley to fracking makes no sense.”



She said whilst Wilson was the first MP to formally put it in writing, she claimed more than half a dozen MPs had told them they were also pushing for the ban internally. “Given how rarely Labor breaks ranks, [Wilson’s comment] speaks volumes,” she said. Wilson has been contacted for further comment.

World.title: Robert Pattinson’s sex-sting satire and a creepy-crawly horror, plus other new movies to watch this week
World.content:
(MA) 107 minutes

The US TV journalist Chris Hansen is closely associated with a particular kind of hidden camera sting, made famous in the 2000s on To Catch A Predator, his signature segment of the network current affairs show Dateline.

The target of the sting, always male, has been lured to a suburban home with the promise of sex with an underage girl or boy met online. Then the sharply dressed Hansen steps out of the shadows, proclaiming the truth like a press secretary for God: all of this has been a ruse, the cops are close at hand, and the target’s perverse desires will soon be put on show for the world to see.

Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen.

While this form of entrapment may not be especially edifying, it makes for gripping drama. It’s no wonder that the budding filmmaker Lance Oppenheim became fascinated with the show at a young age, setting him on a path that led to the making of Primetime, his first fiction feature after several offbeat documentaries (the screenplay is by Ajon Singh, also a first-timer). Robert Pattinson stars as Hansen, taking time out in between stints as The Batman, another preening vigilante with technology on his side.

World.title: ‘Decoy Dan’ dirty trick has sent Trump on the warpath in Alaska
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms ‘Decoy Dan’ dirty trick has sent Trump on the warpath in Alaska Michael Koziol October 29, 2026 — 3:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

New York: It may not be a quintessential October Surprise, but a bombshell news report on the unusual ballot situation in Alaska has rocked one of the closest contests in the US midterm elections, and sent Donald Trump and his Republicans into overdrive demanding justice. The situation is thus: voters in Alaska have four names on the ballot for the US Senate – including incumbent Republican senator Dan Sullivan, the Democratic challenger Mary Peltola and a second Dan Sullivan, who is unaffiliated. There is also another long-shot candidate named Gerald Heikes. Dan Sullivan, the Republican senator for Alaska, at a campaign rally with President Donald Trump. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson Republicans have tried and failed to keep the second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher, off the ballot, arguing he was a Democratic plant designed to confuse voters and suck votes from the Republican. Democrats had denied any involvement in his candidacy. But on Wednesday (US time), The New York Times released an investigation revealing that the Democrats had co-ordinated the ploy from the start.



Dan Sullivan (left) and Dan Sullivan (right) are both Republicans running for Senate in Alaska. AP Photo/Mark Thiessen; Becky Bohrer The Times reported that a staffer for Peltola received “unusual instructions from top campaign aides” in the summer of 2025 (July/August) asking them to find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska as possible. The investigation found that Peltola’s team worked with people trying to recruit these Sullivans to contest the election, including a “mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs”. A sample election ballot is displayed in Anchorage, Alaska. AP Photo/Haven Daley The initiative was called the “ballot composition project” and involved the Peltola campaign’s lawyers as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Times reported.



Related Article US midterms The death penalty is making headlines, but this might be its last gasp Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired in August, told the Times: “Alaskan voters need to know. There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions.” The Trump administration, through the Department of Justice, had already filed a legal complaint against the state of Alaska demanding that the election results not be certified if the Republican Sullivan lost and it were possible that he would have won if not for the other Sullivan. Trump had been publicly fuming about the situation before the Times story broke. On Wednesday, he seized on its revelations, insisting that Peltola and Sullivan should be struck off the ballot. “It was just determined that the Dumocrats in Alaska, despite their sworn statements to the contrary, put a man named Dan Sullivan on the Ballot in order to confuse the Public with respect to Highly Esteemed Senator Dan Sullivan,” he wrote on Truth Social.



Related Article US midterms ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans? “This is Voter Fraud at the Highest Level, and the Dumocrat Candidate, who was involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted - So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan. Nothing else will do! This behaviour in our Elections cannot be allowed to continue.” Speaking at a campaign function in Alaska on Wednesday, Peltola said the Times story was a diversion and a distraction, but did not deny the substance. “Anybody who’s working in our best interest isn’t going to talk about the nonsense,” she told reporters. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers, this is all stuff to get subscriptions. Nobody at The New York Times cares about affordability in Alaska.” On social media, Peltola has ignored the story completely, posting statements and video clips about other issues.



There is a great deal of irony in the fact this bombshell was dropped by the Times, a newspaper Trump regularly denigrates as “fake news”, and which he counts as among the most offensive news outlets in the US. But on Wednesday, he and other senior administration officials were only too happy to quote liberally from the Times’ story. Related Article Analysis

US midterms Trump’s election rallies are getting weirder and looser – and more racist “Even the New York Times admits that Mary Peltola is a total crook who tried to rig the Alaska senate race in her favour,” said Vice President JD Vance. There is no suggestion that what the Democrats have reportedly done is illegal. Alaska’s Supreme Court signed off on the “decoy” Dan Sullivan remaining on the ballot. His full name is shown as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr, and the papers clearly show the other candidate, Dan S. Sullivan, as the registered Republican incumbent.



Nonetheless, the tactic is clearly manipulative and designed to confuse voters for Democrats’ electoral gain. Sure, it pales in comparison to some of the things Trump and his allies have done to try to overturn legitimate election results. But that doesn’t excuse the Dems – especially since they appear to have lied about it in court. Related Article Opinion

US midterms Obama has never mocked Trump so personally. That comes with a big risk Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer At a time when voters are sick of political subterfuge, and wary of the grift and corruption encircling the Trump administration in Washington, why taint yourself by engaging in these kinds of dirty tricks? And why would you give Trump the ammunition to say, “Look, I was right all along, our elections are crooked.” The Times story was notable for its depth and rigour – it even had a former campaign aide quoted on the record. And yet Peltola’s instinct has been to dismiss it, ignore it and post through it. Clearly, in the Democrats’ view, you can just get away with this sort of stuff in modern US politics.



This is a disaster for the Democrats because at the very moment they should be identified by Americans as the party that wants to preserve this country’s great democracy, they have been shown to undermine it with tricky games, and then lie about it. Mary Peltola, whose campaign catchcry is “Fish, family, freedom”, is neck-and-neck in the polls with Dan Sullivan. AP Photo/Becky Bohrer And while Trump may find he has no legal leg to stand on, he will use this incident to his advantage if, as seems increasingly likely, he challenges the results of these elections – and not just in Alaska. As Lisa Murkowski, the other US senator from Alaska, and a Republican who frequently breaks with Trump, said on X: “While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments. By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong.”

A 19-year-old woman shot in the head during a drive-by shooting south of Brisbane on the weekend has succumbed to her injuries.
