World.title: They called him ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Now this Aussie coach has Beckham and Co. in his corner
World.content:
SportSoccerEngland They called him ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Now this Aussie coach has Beckham and Co. in his corner Vince Rugari October 29, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Peter Cklamovski has spent more time than anyone else riding shotgun with Ange Postecoglou - so for him, a rocky start to a new job is not just familiar terrain, but preferred. This time around, the rocks were extra jagged. Loading Being a self-proclaimed Postecoglou “disciple” was an advantage not so long ago. Now, post-Tottenham, and post-Nottingham, Postecoglou’s reputation in England has taken a battering, as unfair as that may be, to the point where even those who have worked with him are tainted by association. So when Cklamovski lost his first three matches in charge of English fourth-division club Salford City this season, some online critics swiftly settled on a nickname for him: ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Or ‘Temu Ange’, or any such derivative. The inference is clear, and it stings: he is a lesser version of a coach they don’t rate.



Cklamovski can only chuckle. “That’s modern-day football, modern-day society,” he tells this masthead. Peter Cklamovski and his long-time mentor, Ange Postecoglou, after a match between Shimizu S-Pulse and Yokohama F. Marinos. Getty “I’m proud of my connection with Ange, and I want to be a proud extension of his legacy. That’s how much I love the guy. Within that, there’s no secrets. They know, they’ve learned that I’m an Ange disciple, let’s say - so I guess there is a bit of a stigma to that, potentially. “But that’s all noise. If I do my job, and do it well, and do it the way I know I can, then that will be the way we can build something that we dream about. Stay humble, take the bullets when needed, no problem - but don’t let it knock you down.”



Such is the fickle nature of the game that those same supporters who wanted him gone a couple of months ago are probably now singing his name. Salford City are cruising on top of the table amid a club-record seven-game winning streak, and Cklamovski has just been named League Two’s manager of the month. It’s still early days - there are still 33 more games to be played this season - but they are hot favourites to be promoted, and some of the sport’s biggest names are swooning about the aggressive and relentless attacking football Cklamovski has them playing. Jorge Grant celebrates a goal for Salford City against Walsall. Getty Images Indeed, this is no ordinary club. Of all the teams in England’s Football League - the umbrella organisation for the three tiers below the Premier League - Salford City is arguably the best-placed to trace a similar arc as Wrexham and rise up the pyramid, powered by celebrity investment.



Actually, they kind of invented the concept of ‘doing a Wrexham’. In 2014, five members of Manchester United’s fabled Class of ’92 - Gary Neville, Phil Neville, Paul Scholes, Ryan Giggs and Nicky Butt - purchased the club, which is only a short drive from Old Trafford, and only a kilometre from where they used to train together. David Beckham later joined the ownership group, and their early efforts to lift the then-little-known club from the obscurity of England’s eighth division were captured in a fly-on-the-wall documentary by the BBC. Salford City co-owners Gary Neville and David Beckham. Salford City FC But after four promotions in five years, their progress stalled, and the ‘Ammies’ - a nickname taken from the club’s old name, Salford Amateurs - have been stuck in League Two for the past seven seasons. Most of the former players sold up as part of a recent ownership restructure which brought in fresh international capital - but Beckham and Gary Neville retained their shares, and their new ambition is to eventually bring Salford City into the Premier League.



The club has also gone back to its roots, reverting to its traditional orange colours this season and ditching the United-inspired red shirts introduced by the ex-players - a decision Gary Neville has since admitted was “quite selfish” and an error he was happy to rectify. League Two was not exactly top of Cklamovski’s list for his next job, but when the opportunity to join Salford City bobbed up while on holiday in England with his family, and he came to understand the scale of their project, he couldn’t say no. The initial approach was made by Gavin Fleig, a former City Football Group executive who now runs Salford City, and who knew Cklamovski from his time working under Postecoglou at Yokohama F. Marinos, a CFG partner club. Cklamovski, 48, was Postecoglou’s assistant in a variety of roles for more than a decade, but branched out on his own after lifting the Japanese title with Yokohama in 2019, and most recently was coach of the Malaysian national team.



Scholes no longer holds his 10 per cent stake, but remains at the club as chief football advisor. He was not alone in needing to look up Cklamovski’s name, but was blown away by his interview. “Peter was very impressive, right from the word go,” he said in a club feature on YouTube. Salford City chief football advisor Paul Scholes and coach Peter Cklamovski. Salford City FC Now Scholes watches the first team train most days, and acts as a valuable sounding board for Cklamovski. “He’s around for anything I need, really ... a really good eye for League Two because he’s been watching it for a decade or so, intimately,” Cklamovski says. “For me, that’s a depth of knowledge that I can always lean on.”



Other ex-United legends, including Roy Keane, routinely turn up for matches at their 2,246-seat home ground, Moor Lane, and more will jump on the bandwagon if their current form continues. After their most recent performance, a 4-2 victory over previously unbeaten Walsall, Gary Neville said he’d never seen Salford City play better football. With all the star power surrounding him, Cklamovski has to keep a deliberately narrow focus. ‘That’s a depth of knowledge that I can always lean on.’ Peter Cklamovski on working with Paul Scholes “There might be a bit of glitz and glamour in and around the club, but if I take my eye off what’s the most important thing, which is to get the football right, then I’m not doing my job,” he says. “The club has lofty ambitions, that’s for sure, and it’s being met with a solid plan. My job here is to put the foundation of the football in place ... build that identity of football for Salford City and, along with that, push hard and achieve success and get the club stepping up the English pyramid.“



For Cklamovski, that means doing what he has always done: trusting the process, even when it may feel like the walls are closing in on him. After those three first-up defeats, a fourth beckoned, and questions about his future would have surely followed. Salford were at home to Newport County and absolutely dominating - they finished with 31 shots to 4 - but it was one of those games when the ball just wouldn’t go in. Naturally, they went down 1-0 in the 71st minute, conceding a freakish long-range goal in which their goalkeeper was lobbed from 60 metres out. Peter Cklamovski. Getty Images “I’m thinking, ‘Oh no, not this again,’” Cklamovski says. “But there was a part inside me that was loving it. Seen it before, lived it before. I just knew that this is going to add to the story.”



Salford scored twice in the final 10 minutes, including a 90th-minute winner to prevail 2-1. Cklamovski looks back on it as the “circuit breaker” moment when his players were rewarded for refusing to abandon their principles - a familiar juncture for teams schooled in the ways of Angeball. Related Article Opinion

England The Ballon d’Or is everything football shouldn’t be. Thank goodness for Harry Kane Vince Rugari Reporter “I knew we were on track,” Cklamovski says. “I knew the boys were believing in the football, that the evidence was there on the pitch. They felt it. They saw it. They trained it.” The wins have flowed freely ever since, but there will be potholes in the road ahead. Cklamovski is encountering all the unique challenges of England’s lower professional leagues: the physicality is high, the stadiums almost uncomfortably intimate, the supporters fiercely passionate, while games can descend into disorder without warning. “There can be a lot of chaos in a game,” he says.



“It might be a referee call, it might be a tough away game, and the crowd get on top of you ... but chaos can get created very easily in this league. If we can control that chaos and play our football, then that control becomes a bit of a weapon.” It’s been a major change of pace for Cklamovski, who was accustomed to coaching in front of huge crowds in high-profile gigs in charge of FC Tokyo and Malaysia. Now he’s criss-crossing the heartlands of English football, working out of tiny grounds and falling for the peculiar romance of the lower leagues - all while trying to build something that he believes will one day find its way to a much bigger stage. “It’s humble beginnings right now,” he says. “But I’m sure in 12 months, 18 months, two years’ time - whether I’m here or not - the club will be a bigger brand, a bigger football club. You’ll see this place in a really innovative sort of spot where it’s building, and building something special. To be a small part of that, mate, it’s exciting.”

World.title: With COVID in the rearview mirror, Perth Festival pushes back against parochialism
World.content:
NationalWAPerth Festival With COVID in the rearview mirror, Perth Festival pushes back against parochialism Mark Naglazas October 29, 2026 — 3:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After a post-pandemic dip, Perth Festival is back doing what patrons want it to do: deliver the best in international arts and culture. Even though it’s been six years since COVID shut the world down, it has taken that long for the international arts touring scene to get back on track and for Perth Festival to be once again on global touring itineraries. Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece. Frances Andrijich During that period, successive Perth Festival artistic directors have been forced to call upon local companies and artists to make up the numbers. While it has provided opportunities for local practitioners, it also led to a rumbling among patrons, who complained the city’s premier arts festival was not doing its job.



That longing for large-scale world-class works will be satisfied in 2027, which will be a series of European blockbuster shows that hark back to Perth Festival’s glory days, such as Peter Brook’s nine-hour Mahabharata in the Boya Quarry (back in 1988), and Robert Lepage’s Seven Streams of the River Ota in 1998, transformative experiences that still burn bright in the memory. “Perth deserves to experience some of the best, most exciting artists and ideas from around the world.” Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece From Latvia comes trailblazing Polish director Łukasz Twarkowski’s ROTHKO, a four-hour time-shifting collision of cinema and theatre inspired by a famous art forgery; from Denmark comes Operation: Orfeo, a “hypnotic reimagining of the Greek myth of Orpheus and Eurydice told through extraordinary voices, light, architecture and illusion”; and from Greece comes Taverna Miresia – Mario, Bella, Anastasia, Mario Banushi’s wordless and visually stunning evocation of his Albanian childhood that recently won the Golden Lion at the Venice Biennale. Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece was unapologetic about the pivot to the international for next year’s late-summer arts jamboree. “We are an international arts festival, and we should be proud of that. It is also our point of difference within the local scene,” Reece said ahead of Thursday’s program unveiling at the East Perth Power Station, which the Festival has brought back from the dead in the past two years.



“Over the past couple of years we’ve worked really hard to create a distinct identity for Perth Festival. “We have created new spaces for Perth people to gather and experience art, such as the Power Station and The Embassy Ballroom in the Perth Town Hall. Perth Festival will again take over the East Perth Power Station this year. Jessica Wyld Photography “These are now familiar gathering points that are critical for the Festival. “With those foundations in place we are ready to expand our international ambition again. Perth deserves to experience some of the best, most exciting artists and ideas from around the world.”



Reece said Perth Festival’s re-embracing of its international ambition, upon which it built its reputation, did not mean local practitioners would be overlooked. Editor's pick Marine life Where have the calves gone? The troubling shift in Australia’s whale highways “A great international arts festival should expand our sense of what’s possible at the same time as strengthening our commitment to WA artists. The two make each other stronger,” she said. “There were a number of local commissions last year and there will be another wave 2028. “It has to do with the cycles and the time it takes to complete work.



“International work challenges us and it challenges our local artists. It broadens our perspective and connects our city to conversations happening far beyond our borders.” Reece is reluctant to dive back into COVID – “it’s boring,” she laughs – but emphasised the damage the pandemic did to arts festivals around the world. Łukasz Twarkowski’s ROTHKO. “The knock-on effect of COVID has been enormous,” she said. “Everything stopped. It meant you couldn’t tap into the tours of European companies.



“If you wanted the work, they had to come back together and rehearse it. The global pipeline dried up. “Perth Festival over the years has hosted some of the great masters, such as Robert Lepage. This year we are introducing local audiences to the next generation of superstars, such as Łukasz Twarkowski and Mario Banushi. It’s incredibly exciting.” Perth Festival runs from February 5 to 28. Tickets for all shows are on sale from November 2. Lotterywest Films begins on November 23 with Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut.

World.title: ‘It hurts just thinking about it’: But this is why Radley will consider leaving the Roosters
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘It hurts just thinking about it’: But this is why Radley will consider leaving the Roosters Christian Nicolussi October 29, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victor Radley is eager to strike a new deal with the Roosters, but has conceded that he will entertain offers from NRL rivals – and even the Super League – for the first time in his career so he can look after his young family. Amid the exodus of stars including Mark Nawaqanitawase, Daly Cherry-Evans, Angus Crichton and Spencer Leniu that followed the Roosters’ premiership win, and this week’s headlines surrounding Sam Walker’s messy contract situation, it is easy to forget Radley will hit the open market for the first time on Sunday. Victor Radley trains with the England team in Wollongong on Thursday. Peter Keleman/SWpix.com The 28-year-old enforcer has spent a decade in the NRL, winning three premierships with the Roosters, and has never felt the need to explore what might be out there beyond the eastern suburbs – until now. Radley is in no rush to sort his future as he finalises his departure from long-time agent Sam Ayoub before joining a new management team.



The hard-hitting forward’s preference is to finish a one-club player, but said it was important his next contract was one that looked after his fiancée Taylah and two young boys, Vinnie and Cruze. If Radley, a local junior, cannot agree to a new deal with the Roosters, he is open to linking with an NRL rival – including the PNG Chiefs – or even a move to England, the country he will represent in the World Cup on Friday night against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong. Victor Radley with fiancée Taylah and sons Vinnie and Cruze after the Roosters’ grand final win earlier this month. Instagram “The Roosters are everything I’ve ever known,” Radley told this masthead. “I love the club so much. They’ve done right by me for years. “It hurts me inside just thinking about playing elsewhere, but I need to look at all my options now. The days are gone where I’m living in a two-bedroom unit, having a good time. I have two kids, a fiancée, and a house that needs paying off.



“Like everyone in Australia, you have your struggles with interest rates. People will laugh at that and say, ‘He’s been on good money’. But I’ve got a decent mortgage. “I also copped some financial pain at the end of last year [The Roosters hit Radley with a $150,000 penalty for bringing the club into disrepute during a Sunshine Coast golf trip]. “It hurts me inside just thinking about playing elsewhere, but I need to look at all my options now. I have two kids, a fiancée, and a house that needs paying off.” Victor Radley “I’m open to everything. I love new experiences, that might even include living in England and playing in the Super League. It’s something I’d be interested in.” Radley’s immediate focus, though, is finalising his management situation. “I’m joining a new company run by my fiancée’s uncle [Paul Williams] who has brought on board my good friend Max Muddle. I’m excited about that. We’ll sit down on Monday and work out what we want to do moving forward.”



Radley has a long history of head knocks but insisted there was no cause for prospective new clubs to be alarmed. He only missed one through game concussion in 2026 after a desperate tackle in the 80th minutes against the Wests Tigers saw him come off second best. Related Video Video icon 2:13 Kangaroos stars dragged into Walker saga “I understood what happened to me at the start of last year – I was in that state of chronic fatigue, which is why I kept getting those concussions,” Radley said. “I worked hard with the staff to make sure I never get into that state of fatigue again, and the proof has been in the pudding with just the one [head knock this year].” Radley backed Dolphins star and England teammate Herbie Farnworth to join the Roosters, a move which has been the subject of heavy speculation for most of this year.



“He’s a quality player,” Radley said. “I’ve said it since 2022 [when I first met him with England]. When you see how hard he works at training, he’ll be a quality player for any team – and hopefully it’s us.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: King Charles dances in the Bahamas as calls for slavery reparations grow louder
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaRoyal family King Charles dances in the Bahamas as calls for slavery reparations grow louder Michael Holden and Isabel Infantes October 29, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. London/Nassau: King Charles danced in the street with a troupe of dancers in the Bahamas on Wednesday, the second day of a royal visit to the Caribbean that has been somewhat overshadowed by increasingly vocal demands for Britain to pay reparations for its role in the slave trade. Wielding a pair of cowbells in the colours of the flag of the Bahamas, Charles took part in a traditional Junkanoo – a carnival event celebrating the island’s culture. King Charles shakes traditional cowbells at the head of the Bahamian Junkanoo. AP Dressed in a suit and sunglasses, the King cut a dapper figure at the front of the parade among the feathered headdresses and colourful costumes of the dancers, and was met with cheers by the crowd. He began the day by paying respects to fallen members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force, laying a wreath at the Flamingo Monument, and later visited the Bahamas Boxing Academy, where he was presented with a T-shirt bearing an image of himself wearing a champion’s belt.



Loading Arriving in the Bahamas on Tuesday for his first visit as King, Charles acknowledged the injustices of slavery, saying Commonwealth leaders would discuss the issue at their summit next week. Charles meets a young boxer at the Bahamas Boxing Academy in Nassau. Getty Images Speaking in the Bahamian capital Nassau at the start of a three-day trip, the King said it was “only right” to acknowledge “the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond”. Charles added that some of what was “best” in Bahamian culture today – “the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright” – was “born out of darkness”.



His remarks come before the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda next week, where regional leaders are expected to press demands for reparations for slavery and colonialism. Jamaica recently took its claim for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the UK’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. The British government, however, has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations. ‘Pay us what you owe us’ In Nassau, members of the islands’ Rastafarian community and others staged a demonstration near Clifford Park, where the King met local students, demanding reparations. “Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against black people.” Members of the Ethiopian African Black International Congress stage a demonstration in downtown Nassau. AP



Charles will visit Guyana next before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda where he will be joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the biennial summit of the Commonwealth which comprises 56 nations, mostly former British colonies. Related Article Analysis

International affairs King underlines peacemaker role as row hangs over Commonwealth summit The issue of reparations has gathered momentum across the Caribbean recently. Last month, CARICOM, the regional bloc, said it wanted the matter on the agenda at the summit. “The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” CARICOM Secretary-General Carla Barnett said last month. Buckingham Palace had indicated that the King would address the issue during the tour, but not offer a formal apology, in line with British government policy, which also rules out financial reparations.



Charles inspects an honour guard of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force. AP A palace spokesperson said the visit would focus mainly on “modern partnerships and opportunities for the future” in the region, but added that for Charles it was also part of “a lifelong” effort to engage with and educate about “the most shameful aspects of our past”. Campaigners and some Caribbean leaders have called on Britain to go further, including through an apology, reparations in the form of financial compensation and the return of cultural artefacts. From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations. World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAThe Kimberley Leaked letter reveals growing Labor rift over Kimberley fracking Holly Thompson October 29, 2026 — 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A leaked letter written by a West Australian Labor MP has highlighted the schism growing between party members over leaving a small portion of the state open to oil and gas companies interested in fracking. Federal Member for Fremantle Josh Wilson has become the first Labor minister based in WA to reveal he has concerns over the possibility of fracking being undertaken in the Kimberley – the only region of the state where a moratorium on the practice is not in place. Labor MP Josh Wilson. Mark Naglazas And environment groups have said they have been made aware of more Labor MPs pushing for a ban internally. Wilson wrote to a member of his electorate on Wednesday after they called his office to discuss concerns about Black Mountain Energy’s Valhalla gas project proposal in the Kimberley, which includes plans to drill and frack up to 20 exploration wells.



“I share the sharp concern of many in our community when it comes to the significant risks that come with fracking in general,” Wilson wrote in his letter. “I am particularly concerned about fracking in the Kimberley, with the potential to impact on the Martuwarra/ Fitzroy River. “It is welcome that the WA government has established a moratorium that prevents fracking in 98 per cent of Western Australia – but clearly the Kimberley is the missing piece in terms of protecting the West Australian environment, water systems, and First Nations rights/ culture from this kind of intrusive and unnecessary method.” He also wrote that the WA Labor State Conference, held in November 2025, had passed a resolution calling for the moratorium to be extended to the Kimberley, and that he strongly supported that position. “While it’s important to note that the current proposal is limited to exploration and appraisal activities only … that doesn’t in any way diminish the serious concerns about the impacts of exploration drilling itself and concerns about the way in which an exploration approval could lead to a fracking operation in the Kimberley,” Wilson said.



He is the first WA Labor MP to provide strong opposition to fracking in the Kimberley. The process of hydraulic fracturing, known commonly as fracking, involves using water pressure down a pipe to fracture rock formations deep underground, to release the gas trapped inside. Back in May, Premier Roger Cook told the Australian Financial Review that WA could be forced to start fracking the Kimberley if Woodside’s Browse gas project was not developed – a stance he doubled down on in budget estimates that same day. “There are decisions coming for the state into the future. Our (Australian Energy Market Operator) projects a gas shortfall in the early 2030s and as a state, we need to come to a decision about what that means,” he told estimates. “If not Browse, then does something else make up that shortfall?”



WA’s environmental watchdog also green lit the Valhalla project, sparking more than 8000 appeals which are now under review. Lock the Gate WA coordinator Simone van Hattem said that decision from the Environmental Protection Authority had sparked one of the biggest grassroots campaigns in Australia. “Fracking in the Kimberley poses huge environmental risks ... that’s why fracking is already banned in huge parts of WA,” she said. “The widespread community opposition to fracking in the Kimberley is becoming impossible for Labor to ignore. “It’s clear that Labor is torn over this because they know it’s a vote loser and because they know opening the Kimberley to fracking makes no sense.”



She said whilst Wilson was the first MP to formally put it in writing, she claimed more than half a dozen MPs had told them they were also pushing for the ban internally. “Given how rarely Labor breaks ranks, [Wilson’s comment] speaks volumes,” she said. Wilson has been contacted for further comment.

World.title: Robert Pattinson’s sex-sting satire and a creepy-crawly horror, plus other new movies to watch this week
World.content:
(MA) 107 minutes

The US TV journalist Chris Hansen is closely associated with a particular kind of hidden camera sting, made famous in the 2000s on To Catch A Predator, his signature segment of the network current affairs show Dateline.

The target of the sting, always male, has been lured to a suburban home with the promise of sex with an underage girl or boy met online. Then the sharply dressed Hansen steps out of the shadows, proclaiming the truth like a press secretary for God: all of this has been a ruse, the cops are close at hand, and the target’s perverse desires will soon be put on show for the world to see.

Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen.

While this form of entrapment may not be especially edifying, it makes for gripping drama. It’s no wonder that the budding filmmaker Lance Oppenheim became fascinated with the show at a young age, setting him on a path that led to the making of Primetime, his first fiction feature after several offbeat documentaries (the screenplay is by Ajon Singh, also a first-timer). Robert Pattinson stars as Hansen, taking time out in between stints as The Batman, another preening vigilante with technology on his side.

World.title: ‘Decoy Dan’ dirty trick has sent Trump on the warpath in Alaska
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms ‘Decoy Dan’ dirty trick has sent Trump on the warpath in Alaska Michael Koziol October 29, 2026 — 3:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

New York: It may not be a quintessential October Surprise, but a bombshell news report on the unusual ballot situation in Alaska has rocked one of the closest contests in the US midterm elections, and sent Donald Trump and his Republicans into overdrive demanding justice. The situation is thus: voters in Alaska have four names on the ballot for the US Senate – including incumbent Republican senator Dan Sullivan, the Democratic challenger Mary Peltola and a second Dan Sullivan, who is unaffiliated. There is also another long-shot candidate named Gerald Heikes. Dan Sullivan, the Republican senator for Alaska, at a campaign rally with President Donald Trump. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson Republicans have tried and failed to keep the second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher, off the ballot, arguing he was a Democratic plant designed to confuse voters and suck votes from the Republican. Democrats had denied any involvement in his candidacy. But on Wednesday (US time), The New York Times released an investigation revealing that the Democrats had co-ordinated the ploy from the start.



Dan Sullivan (left) and Dan Sullivan (right) are both Republicans running for Senate in Alaska. AP Photo/Mark Thiessen; Becky Bohrer The Times reported that a staffer for Peltola received “unusual instructions from top campaign aides” in the summer of 2025 (July/August) asking them to find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska as possible. The investigation found that Peltola’s team worked with people trying to recruit these Sullivans to contest the election, including a “mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs”. A sample election ballot is displayed in Anchorage, Alaska. AP Photo/Haven Daley The initiative was called the “ballot composition project” and involved the Peltola campaign’s lawyers as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Times reported.



Related Article US midterms The death penalty is making headlines, but this might be its last gasp Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired in August, told the Times: “Alaskan voters need to know. There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions.” The Trump administration, through the Department of Justice, had already filed a legal complaint against the state of Alaska demanding that the election results not be certified if the Republican Sullivan lost and it were possible that he would have won if not for the other Sullivan. Trump had been publicly fuming about the situation before the Times story broke. On Wednesday, he seized on its revelations, insisting that Peltola and Sullivan should be struck off the ballot. “It was just determined that the Dumocrats in Alaska, despite their sworn statements to the contrary, put a man named Dan Sullivan on the Ballot in order to confuse the Public with respect to Highly Esteemed Senator Dan Sullivan,” he wrote on Truth Social.



Related Article US midterms ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans? “This is Voter Fraud at the Highest Level, and the Dumocrat Candidate, who was involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted - So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan. Nothing else will do! This behaviour in our Elections cannot be allowed to continue.” Speaking at a campaign function in Alaska on Wednesday, Peltola said the Times story was a diversion and a distraction, but did not deny the substance. “Anybody who’s working in our best interest isn’t going to talk about the nonsense,” she told reporters. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers, this is all stuff to get subscriptions. Nobody at The New York Times cares about affordability in Alaska.” On social media, Peltola has ignored the story completely, posting statements and video clips about other issues.



There is a great deal of irony in the fact this bombshell was dropped by the Times, a newspaper Trump regularly denigrates as “fake news”, and which he counts as among the most offensive news outlets in the US. But on Wednesday, he and other senior administration officials were only too happy to quote liberally from the Times’ story. Related Article Analysis

US midterms Trump’s election rallies are getting weirder and looser – and more racist “Even the New York Times admits that Mary Peltola is a total crook who tried to rig the Alaska senate race in her favour,” said Vice President JD Vance. There is no suggestion that what the Democrats have reportedly done is illegal. Alaska’s Supreme Court signed off on the “decoy” Dan Sullivan remaining on the ballot. His full name is shown as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr, and the papers clearly show the other candidate, Dan S. Sullivan, as the registered Republican incumbent.



Nonetheless, the tactic is clearly manipulative and designed to confuse voters for Democrats’ electoral gain. Sure, it pales in comparison to some of the things Trump and his allies have done to try to overturn legitimate election results. But that doesn’t excuse the Dems – especially since they appear to have lied about it in court. Related Article Opinion

US midterms Obama has never mocked Trump so personally. That comes with a big risk Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer At a time when voters are sick of political subterfuge, and wary of the grift and corruption encircling the Trump administration in Washington, why taint yourself by engaging in these kinds of dirty tricks? And why would you give Trump the ammunition to say, “Look, I was right all along, our elections are crooked.” The Times story was notable for its depth and rigour – it even had a former campaign aide quoted on the record. And yet Peltola’s instinct has been to dismiss it, ignore it and post through it. Clearly, in the Democrats’ view, you can just get away with this sort of stuff in modern US politics.



This is a disaster for the Democrats because at the very moment they should be identified by Americans as the party that wants to preserve this country’s great democracy, they have been shown to undermine it with tricky games, and then lie about it. Mary Peltola, whose campaign catchcry is “Fish, family, freedom”, is neck-and-neck in the polls with Dan Sullivan. AP Photo/Becky Bohrer And while Trump may find he has no legal leg to stand on, he will use this incident to his advantage if, as seems increasingly likely, he challenges the results of these elections – and not just in Alaska. As Lisa Murkowski, the other US senator from Alaska, and a Republican who frequently breaks with Trump, said on X: “While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments. By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong.”

World.title: They called him ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Now this Aussie coach has Beckham and Co. in his corner
World.content:
SportSoccerEngland They called him ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Now this Aussie coach has Beckham and Co. in his corner Vince Rugari October 29, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Peter Cklamovski has spent more time than anyone else riding shotgun with Ange Postecoglou - so for him, a rocky start to a new job is not just familiar terrain, but preferred. This time around, the rocks were extra jagged. Loading Being a self-proclaimed Postecoglou “disciple” was an advantage not so long ago. Now, post-Tottenham, and post-Nottingham, Postecoglou’s reputation in England has taken a battering, as unfair as that may be, to the point where even those who have worked with him are tainted by association. So when Cklamovski lost his first three matches in charge of English fourth-division club Salford City this season, some online critics swiftly settled on a nickname for him: ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Or ‘Temu Ange’, or any such derivative. The inference is clear, and it stings: he is a lesser version of a coach they don’t rate.



Cklamovski can only chuckle. “That’s modern-day football, modern-day society,” he tells this masthead. Peter Cklamovski and his long-time mentor, Ange Postecoglou, after a match between Shimizu S-Pulse and Yokohama F. Marinos. Getty “I’m proud of my connection with Ange, and I want to be a proud extension of his legacy. That’s how much I love the guy. Within that, there’s no secrets. They know, they’ve learned that I’m an Ange disciple, let’s say - so I guess there is a bit of a stigma to that, potentially. “But that’s all noise. If I do my job, and do it well, and do it the way I know I can, then that will be the way we can build something that we dream about. Stay humble, take the bullets when needed, no problem - but don’t let it knock you down.”



Such is the fickle nature of the game that those same supporters who wanted him gone a couple of months ago are probably now singing his name. Salford City are cruising on top of the table amid a club-record seven-game winning streak, and Cklamovski has just been named League Two’s manager of the month. It’s still early days - there are still 33 more games to be played this season - but they are hot favourites to be promoted, and some of the sport’s biggest names are swooning about the aggressive and relentless attacking football Cklamovski has them playing. Jorge Grant celebrates a goal for Salford City against Walsall. Getty Images Indeed, this is no ordinary club. Of all the teams in England’s Football League - the umbrella organisation for the three tiers below the Premier League - Salford City is arguably the best-placed to trace a similar arc as Wrexham and rise up the pyramid, powered by celebrity investment.



Actually, they kind of invented the concept of ‘doing a Wrexham’. In 2014, five members of Manchester United’s fabled Class of ’92 - Gary Neville, Phil Neville, Paul Scholes, Ryan Giggs and Nicky Butt - purchased the club, which is only a short drive from Old Trafford, and only a kilometre from where they used to train together. David Beckham later joined the ownership group, and their early efforts to lift the then-little-known club from the obscurity of England’s eighth division were captured in a fly-on-the-wall documentary by the BBC. Salford City co-owners Gary Neville and David Beckham. Salford City FC But after four promotions in five years, their progress stalled, and the ‘Ammies’ - a nickname taken from the club’s old name, Salford Amateurs - have been stuck in League Two for the past seven seasons. Most of the former players sold up as part of a recent ownership restructure which brought in fresh international capital - but Beckham and Gary Neville retained their shares, and their new ambition is to eventually bring Salford City into the Premier League.



The club has also gone back to its roots, reverting to its traditional orange colours this season and ditching the United-inspired red shirts introduced by the ex-players - a decision Gary Neville has since admitted was “quite selfish” and an error he was happy to rectify. League Two was not exactly top of Cklamovski’s list for his next job, but when the opportunity to join Salford City bobbed up while on holiday in England with his family, and he came to understand the scale of their project, he couldn’t say no. The initial approach was made by Gavin Fleig, a former City Football Group executive who now runs Salford City, and who knew Cklamovski from his time working under Postecoglou at Yokohama F. Marinos, a CFG partner club. Cklamovski, 48, was Postecoglou’s assistant in a variety of roles for more than a decade, but branched out on his own after lifting the Japanese title with Yokohama in 2019, and most recently was coach of the Malaysian national team.



Scholes no longer holds his 10 per cent stake, but remains at the club as chief football advisor. He was not alone in needing to look up Cklamovski’s name, but was blown away by his interview. “Peter was very impressive, right from the word go,” he said in a club feature on YouTube. Salford City chief football advisor Paul Scholes and coach Peter Cklamovski. Salford City FC Now Scholes watches the first team train most days, and acts as a valuable sounding board for Cklamovski. “He’s around for anything I need, really ... a really good eye for League Two because he’s been watching it for a decade or so, intimately,” Cklamovski says. “For me, that’s a depth of knowledge that I can always lean on.”



Other ex-United legends, including Roy Keane, routinely turn up for matches at their 2,246-seat home ground, Moor Lane, and more will jump on the bandwagon if their current form continues. After their most recent performance, a 4-2 victory over previously unbeaten Walsall, Gary Neville said he’d never seen Salford City play better football. With all the star power surrounding him, Cklamovski has to keep a deliberately narrow focus. ‘That’s a depth of knowledge that I can always lean on.’ Peter Cklamovski on working with Paul Scholes “There might be a bit of glitz and glamour in and around the club, but if I take my eye off what’s the most important thing, which is to get the football right, then I’m not doing my job,” he says. “The club has lofty ambitions, that’s for sure, and it’s being met with a solid plan. My job here is to put the foundation of the football in place ... build that identity of football for Salford City and, along with that, push hard and achieve success and get the club stepping up the English pyramid.“



For Cklamovski, that means doing what he has always done: trusting the process, even when it may feel like the walls are closing in on him. After those three first-up defeats, a fourth beckoned, and questions about his future would have surely followed. Salford were at home to Newport County and absolutely dominating - they finished with 31 shots to 4 - but it was one of those games when the ball just wouldn’t go in. Naturally, they went down 1-0 in the 71st minute, conceding a freakish long-range goal in which their goalkeeper was lobbed from 60 metres out. Peter Cklamovski. Getty Images “I’m thinking, ‘Oh no, not this again,’” Cklamovski says. “But there was a part inside me that was loving it. Seen it before, lived it before. I just knew that this is going to add to the story.”



Salford scored twice in the final 10 minutes, including a 90th-minute winner to prevail 2-1. Cklamovski looks back on it as the “circuit breaker” moment when his players were rewarded for refusing to abandon their principles - a familiar juncture for teams schooled in the ways of Angeball. Related Article Opinion

England The Ballon d’Or is everything football shouldn’t be. Thank goodness for Harry Kane Vince Rugari Reporter “I knew we were on track,” Cklamovski says. “I knew the boys were believing in the football, that the evidence was there on the pitch. They felt it. They saw it. They trained it.” The wins have flowed freely ever since, but there will be potholes in the road ahead. Cklamovski is encountering all the unique challenges of England’s lower professional leagues: the physicality is high, the stadiums almost uncomfortably intimate, the supporters fiercely passionate, while games can descend into disorder without warning. “There can be a lot of chaos in a game,” he says.



“It might be a referee call, it might be a tough away game, and the crowd get on top of you ... but chaos can get created very easily in this league. If we can control that chaos and play our football, then that control becomes a bit of a weapon.” It’s been a major change of pace for Cklamovski, who was accustomed to coaching in front of huge crowds in high-profile gigs in charge of FC Tokyo and Malaysia. Now he’s criss-crossing the heartlands of English football, working out of tiny grounds and falling for the peculiar romance of the lower leagues - all while trying to build something that he believes will one day find its way to a much bigger stage. “It’s humble beginnings right now,” he says. “But I’m sure in 12 months, 18 months, two years’ time - whether I’m here or not - the club will be a bigger brand, a bigger football club. You’ll see this place in a really innovative sort of spot where it’s building, and building something special. To be a small part of that, mate, it’s exciting.”

World.title: With COVID in the rearview mirror, Perth Festival pushes back against parochialism
World.content:
NationalWAPerth Festival With COVID in the rearview mirror, Perth Festival pushes back against parochialism Mark Naglazas October 29, 2026 — 3:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After a post-pandemic dip, Perth Festival is back doing what patrons want it to do: deliver the best in international arts and culture. Even though it’s been six years since COVID shut the world down, it has taken that long for the international arts touring scene to get back on track and for Perth Festival to be once again on global touring itineraries. Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece. Frances Andrijich During that period, successive Perth Festival artistic directors have been forced to call upon local companies and artists to make up the numbers. While it has provided opportunities for local practitioners, it also led to a rumbling among patrons, who complained the city’s premier arts festival was not doing its job.



That longing for large-scale world-class works will be satisfied in 2027, which will be a series of European blockbuster shows that hark back to Perth Festival’s glory days, such as Peter Brook’s nine-hour Mahabharata in the Boya Quarry (back in 1988), and Robert Lepage’s Seven Streams of the River Ota in 1998, transformative experiences that still burn bright in the memory. “Perth deserves to experience some of the best, most exciting artists and ideas from around the world.” Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece From Latvia comes trailblazing Polish director Łukasz Twarkowski’s ROTHKO, a four-hour time-shifting collision of cinema and theatre inspired by a famous art forgery; from Denmark comes Operation: Orfeo, a “hypnotic reimagining of the Greek myth of Orpheus and Eurydice told through extraordinary voices, light, architecture and illusion”; and from Greece comes Taverna Miresia – Mario, Bella, Anastasia, Mario Banushi’s wordless and visually stunning evocation of his Albanian childhood that recently won the Golden Lion at the Venice Biennale. Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece was unapologetic about the pivot to the international for next year’s late-summer arts jamboree. “We are an international arts festival, and we should be proud of that. It is also our point of difference within the local scene,” Reece said ahead of Thursday’s program unveiling at the East Perth Power Station, which the Festival has brought back from the dead in the past two years.



“Over the past couple of years we’ve worked really hard to create a distinct identity for Perth Festival. “We have created new spaces for Perth people to gather and experience art, such as the Power Station and The Embassy Ballroom in the Perth Town Hall. Perth Festival will again take over the East Perth Power Station this year. Jessica Wyld Photography “These are now familiar gathering points that are critical for the Festival. “With those foundations in place we are ready to expand our international ambition again. Perth deserves to experience some of the best, most exciting artists and ideas from around the world.”



Reece said Perth Festival’s re-embracing of its international ambition, upon which it built its reputation, did not mean local practitioners would be overlooked. Editor's pick Marine life Where have the calves gone? The troubling shift in Australia’s whale highways “A great international arts festival should expand our sense of what’s possible at the same time as strengthening our commitment to WA artists. The two make each other stronger,” she said. “There were a number of local commissions last year and there will be another wave 2028. “It has to do with the cycles and the time it takes to complete work.



“International work challenges us and it challenges our local artists. It broadens our perspective and connects our city to conversations happening far beyond our borders.” Reece is reluctant to dive back into COVID – “it’s boring,” she laughs – but emphasised the damage the pandemic did to arts festivals around the world. Łukasz Twarkowski’s ROTHKO. “The knock-on effect of COVID has been enormous,” she said. “Everything stopped. It meant you couldn’t tap into the tours of European companies.



“If you wanted the work, they had to come back together and rehearse it. The global pipeline dried up. “Perth Festival over the years has hosted some of the great masters, such as Robert Lepage. This year we are introducing local audiences to the next generation of superstars, such as Łukasz Twarkowski and Mario Banushi. It’s incredibly exciting.” Perth Festival runs from February 5 to 28. Tickets for all shows are on sale from November 2. Lotterywest Films begins on November 23 with Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut.

World.title: ‘It hurts just thinking about it’: But this is why Radley will consider leaving the Roosters
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘It hurts just thinking about it’: But this is why Radley will consider leaving the Roosters Christian Nicolussi October 29, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Victor Radley is eager to strike a new deal with the Roosters, but has conceded that he will entertain offers from NRL rivals – and even the Super League – for the first time in his career so he can look after his young family. Amid the exodus of stars including Mark Nawaqanitawase, Daly Cherry-Evans, Angus Crichton and Spencer Leniu that followed the Roosters’ premiership win, and this week’s headlines surrounding Sam Walker’s messy contract situation, it is easy to forget Radley will hit the open market for the first time on Sunday. Victor Radley trains with the England team in Wollongong on Thursday. Peter Keleman/SWpix.com The 28-year-old enforcer has spent a decade in the NRL, winning three premierships with the Roosters, and has never felt the need to explore what might be out there beyond the eastern suburbs – until now. Radley is in no rush to sort his future as he finalises his departure from long-time agent Sam Ayoub before joining a new management team.



The hard-hitting forward’s preference is to finish a one-club player, but said it was important his next contract was one that looked after his fiancée Taylah and two young boys, Vinnie and Cruze. If Radley, a local junior, cannot agree to a new deal with the Roosters, he is open to linking with an NRL rival – including the PNG Chiefs – or even a move to England, the country he will represent in the World Cup on Friday night against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong. Victor Radley with fiancée Taylah and sons Vinnie and Cruze after the Roosters’ grand final win earlier this month. Instagram “The Roosters are everything I’ve ever known,” Radley told this masthead. “I love the club so much. They’ve done right by me for years. “It hurts me inside just thinking about playing elsewhere, but I need to look at all my options now. The days are gone where I’m living in a two-bedroom unit, having a good time. I have two kids, a fiancée, and a house that needs paying off.



“Like everyone in Australia, you have your struggles with interest rates. People will laugh at that and say, ‘He’s been on good money’. But I’ve got a decent mortgage. “I also copped some financial pain at the end of last year [The Roosters hit Radley with a $150,000 penalty for bringing the club into disrepute during a Sunshine Coast golf trip]. “It hurts me inside just thinking about playing elsewhere, but I need to look at all my options now. I have two kids, a fiancée, and a house that needs paying off.” Victor Radley “I’m open to everything. I love new experiences, that might even include living in England and playing in the Super League. It’s something I’d be interested in.” Radley’s immediate focus, though, is finalising his management situation. “I’m joining a new company run by my fiancée’s uncle [Paul Williams] who has brought on board my good friend Max Muddle. I’m excited about that. We’ll sit down on Monday and work out what we want to do moving forward.”



Radley has a long history of head knocks but insisted there was no cause for prospective new clubs to be alarmed. He only missed one through game concussion in 2026 after a desperate tackle in the 80th minutes against the Wests Tigers saw him come off second best. Related Video Video icon 2:13 Kangaroos stars dragged into Walker saga “I understood what happened to me at the start of last year – I was in that state of chronic fatigue, which is why I kept getting those concussions,” Radley said. “I worked hard with the staff to make sure I never get into that state of fatigue again, and the proof has been in the pudding with just the one [head knock this year].” Radley backed Dolphins star and England teammate Herbie Farnworth to join the Roosters, a move which has been the subject of heavy speculation for most of this year.



“He’s a quality player,” Radley said. “I’ve said it since 2022 [when I first met him with England]. When you see how hard he works at training, he’ll be a quality player for any team – and hopefully it’s us.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: King Charles dances in the Bahamas as calls for slavery reparations grow louder
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaRoyal family King Charles dances in the Bahamas as calls for slavery reparations grow louder Michael Holden and Isabel Infantes October 29, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London/Nassau: King Charles danced in the street with a troupe of dancers in the Bahamas on Wednesday, the second day of a royal visit to the Caribbean that has been somewhat overshadowed by increasingly vocal demands for Britain to pay reparations for its role in the slave trade. Wielding a pair of cowbells in the colours of the flag of the Bahamas, Charles took part in a traditional Junkanoo – a carnival event celebrating the island’s culture. King Charles shakes traditional cowbells at the head of the Bahamian Junkanoo. AP Dressed in a suit and sunglasses, the King cut a dapper figure at the front of the parade among the feathered headdresses and colourful costumes of the dancers, and was met with cheers by the crowd. He began the day by paying respects to fallen members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force, laying a wreath at the Flamingo Monument, and later visited the Bahamas Boxing Academy, where he was presented with a T-shirt bearing an image of himself wearing a champion’s belt.



Loading Arriving in the Bahamas on Tuesday for his first visit as King, Charles acknowledged the injustices of slavery, saying Commonwealth leaders would discuss the issue at their summit next week. Charles meets a young boxer at the Bahamas Boxing Academy in Nassau. Getty Images Speaking in the Bahamian capital Nassau at the start of a three-day trip, the King said it was “only right” to acknowledge “the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond”. Charles added that some of what was “best” in Bahamian culture today – “the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright” – was “born out of darkness”.



His remarks come before the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda next week, where regional leaders are expected to press demands for reparations for slavery and colonialism. Jamaica recently took its claim for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the UK’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. The British government, however, has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations. ‘Pay us what you owe us’ In Nassau, members of the islands’ Rastafarian community and others staged a demonstration near Clifford Park, where the King met local students, demanding reparations. “Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against black people.” Members of the Ethiopian African Black International Congress stage a demonstration in downtown Nassau. AP



Charles will visit Guyana next before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda where he will be joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the biennial summit of the Commonwealth which comprises 56 nations, mostly former British colonies. Related Article Analysis

International affairs King underlines peacemaker role as row hangs over Commonwealth summit The issue of reparations has gathered momentum across the Caribbean recently. Last month, CARICOM, the regional bloc, said it wanted the matter on the agenda at the summit. “The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” CARICOM Secretary-General Carla Barnett said last month. Buckingham Palace had indicated that the King would address the issue during the tour, but not offer a formal apology, in line with British government policy, which also rules out financial reparations.



Charles inspects an honour guard of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force. AP A palace spokesperson said the visit would focus mainly on “modern partnerships and opportunities for the future” in the region, but added that for Charles it was also part of “a lifelong” effort to engage with and educate about “the most shameful aspects of our past”. Campaigners and some Caribbean leaders have called on Britain to go further, including through an apology, reparations in the form of financial compensation and the return of cultural artefacts. From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations. World.title: Port of Tauranga reports weaker Q1 cargo volumes
World.content:
Port of Tauranga's (POT) first quarter trading update at its Annual Shareholders' Meeting highlighted weaker cargo volumes than the strong prior year period.

Total trade tonnage was down -4.8 percent in 1Q27 against the prior year (which was up +5.9 percent) with containers down -2.6 percent (1Q26 +9 percent).

Management suggests the decline in total tonnage reflects "the continued impact of elevated fuel costs on the export log market".

Statistics NZ log export data shows Port of Tauranga's log volumes declined -11 percent in the first quarter, with September particularly weak.

The company has retained FY27 NPAT guidance of NZ$160 million-NZ$175m, but with consensus expectations already above the top end, earnings risk at this stage appears more to the downside.

On its ongoing Stella Passage resource consent saga, POT expects to confirm an urgent court hearing date "any day now".

World.title: Dunedin councillor found to breach code of conduct for a third time
World.content:
Controversial Dunedin councillor Benedict Ong has been found to have breached the code of conduct for a third time.

Ong has already been suspended from some duties and been asked to resign following two upheld complaints over his behaviour.

In June, deputy mayor Cherry Lucas complained, alleging he had publicly posted confidential information and criticised the council's chief executive on social media.

The Dunedin City Council met behind closed doors on Thursday to discuss the complaint.

Councillor Andrew Simms, who chaired the item, said the council accepted the findings that he had materially breached the code in a public and deliberate manner.

Simms said he had been suspended from all council committees and subcommittees for nine months until July 2027.

He received a similar nine-month suspension in May after an independent report found he was likely deliberately and repeatedly leaking information that could potentially jeopardise the council's commercial interests.

The suspension was not expected to affect him for long.

Last month, he announced plans to stand as an independent candidate in the Dunedin electorate.

He has since confirmed on social media that he would resign on 31 December regardless of whether his tilt was successful.

This was at odds with his previous declarations that he would never resign after his colleagues asked him to in the wake of the first code of conduct complaint.

"It's becoming a cliché - Never. I have been asked many times, I'm going to be asked again. I think it's just too clichéd. I should have t-shirt that just says 'never'," he told media at the time.

Ong has been embroiled in controversy since he was elected, including being trespassed from the University of Otago grounds and buildings following student complaints about [. https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/community/1340300/dunedin-councillor-benedict-ong-trespassed-from-the-university-of-otago inappropriate and unwanted behaviour].

Ong has claimed he has been subject to "false, malicious co-ordinated political attacks" since he was elected last October.

He posted on social media that this had made his ongoing public role as a councillor "untenable to hold".

Andrew Simms said the suspension did not impact Ong's attendance at full Council meetings.

World.title: 'Large damaging hail': Severe thunderstorm warning issued for Canterbury
World.content:
Large and damaging hail could hit parts of Canterbury as severe thunderstorms sweep up part of the South Island.

MetService has issued a severe thunderstorm warning for Selwyn, Ashburton and Christchurch City for Thursday evening.

"These thunderstorms are expected to be accompanied by large hail," MetService said.

"Large hail can cause significant damage to crops, orchards, vines, glasshouses and vehicles, and make driving conditions hazardous."

A weather radar detected the storms near Leeston shortly after 5pm on Thursday, and they were forecast to land near Lincoln, Leeston, Lake Ellesmere, Springston and Tai Tapu at 5.45pm.

The severe thunderstorms were expected to reach near Christchurch, Lyttelton and Banks Peninsula at 6.15pm.

MetService has a severe thunderstorm watch in force for Christchurch and the Canterbury Plains until 8pm.

"They could be severe and accompanied by large damaging hail, larger than 20mm diameter," MetService said.

The National Emergency Management Agency advised people to take shelter indoors away from windows, avoid sheltering under trees, get back on land if anyone was on the water, move cars under cover or away from trees, secure any loose items around their home, check their gutters and drains were clear, and be ready to slow down or stop if they were driving.

World.title: RNZ to release accounts after election following finance chief's unexpected exit
World.content:
RNZ will reveal the state of its finances several days after the election and more than a month on from the unexpected resignation of its chief financial officer.

In a statement, an RNZ spokesperson confirmed the annual report would be released on Monday 9 November, two days after the close of voting.

The board approved the report this week, on condition that independent checks of its accounts were completed by accounting firm EY on behalf of the Auditor-General.

The spokesperson said the report would set out RNZ's financial result, along with its response, but would not discuss those figures before then.

Hilary Parker resigned on Friday 2 October and left immediately, triggering an emergency board meeting and the appointment of RNZ director Richard Dellabarca as interim CFO.

Board chair Brent Impey previously declined to explain her departure, except to say she had resigned of her own accord and there was no suggestion of criminality.

In its latest statement, RNZ said Dellabarca had been working with its finance team and EY to finish the accounts ahead of the 31 October deadline.

"RNZ will be meeting this deadline," the spokesperson said.

Once RNZ received EY's audit report, the public broadcaster had 15 working days to give its yearly report to the government.

The spokesperson said RNZ would give the report to ministers and "relevant stakeholders" on 9 November and publish it that same day, "well before" deadline.

World.title: About 40 TVNZ staff picket over stalled pay negotiations
World.content:
Some staff at TVNZ have briefly walked off the job on Thursday in protest over stalled pay negotiations.

About 40 staff members from the E Tū and PSA unions picketed outside of the broadcaster's downtown Auckland offices for about an hour.

Some signs noted their service might be free, but the workers still needed pay, others took aim at highly paid chief executive Jodi O'Donnell, while some referenced famous TVNZ characters Goodnight Kiwi and Chris Warner.

RNZ / Rowan Quinn

One staff member said they had initially sought a five percent pay rise but talks were now stalled at 2.5 percent.

E Tū union said annual inflation was at 3.7 percent which meant the pay offer of 2.5 percent was effectively a cut.

Some TVNZ workers were struggling to afford basics, and that was not fair, it said.

National secretary Rachel Mackintosh said TVNZ did an important job for the whole country.

"Whether it's breaking news, current affairs, or local drama, TVNZ tells our stories. The reporters, camera operators, producers, and technicians who make that happen should be able to pay their rent," she said.

Staff in Wellington and Christchurch also downed tools for the hour.

A TVNZ spokesperson said it had been in constructive bargaining discussions with the unions since July.

World.title: Part of State Highway 1 and trainline in Canterbury blocked after two vehicle crash
World.content:
A major highway and a trainline in mid Canterbury are blocked following a serious two vehicle crash.

The crash on the Rakaia Highway north of Ashburton happened about 3.10pm.

Two people have been injured, including one critically.

Motorists are being diverted through Wilkinson and Hatfield-Overdale roads.

New Zealand Transport Agency said State Highway 1 was closed near the Chertsey Line Road turn-off and could be closed for several hours.

World.title: RLWC 2026: Pride on the line as Pacific teams battle for semifinal spots
World.content:
The Pacific dream at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) comes down to this weekend's final round of group games.

Only the Australians have secured their semifinal spots in both the men's and women's categories of the competition.

Everything is on the line for the Pacific Island teams that have set themselves in the running for top two finish.

In the men's Group A, New Zealand and Fiji will play off for a spot in the semifinals on the Gold Coast on Saturday.

Both sides won a game each, and lag behind the defending champions Australia, which is two out of two, but have Cook Islands in their last game this weekend.

The combine Groub B and C is more complicated, with four teams fighting for a top-two finish on the combined table.

Currently, Samoa and Tonga have two wins each, while Papua New Guinea and England have one each to their names.

It is win or go home on Friday night at WIN Stadium when England face the PNG Kumuls.

Whoever wins that clash stands a chance of getting into the top two, but will then have to wait for the result of the Samoa v Tonga clash.

Sunday night's showdown between fierce Pacific rivals Tonga and Samoa at a sold-out CommBank Stadium will decide who tops the combine Pool B and C.

In the women's competition, New Zealand and Fiji are chasing wins to secure a top-two finish in Pool B.

Fiji has won one out of two and face France in their last match.

New Zealand takes on the Papua New Guinea Orchids.

In Pool B, England and Samoa will play-off for a semifinal berth at WIN Stadium on Friday night.

A win for Samoa will see them join Australia in the final four.

Kick off: Friday, 30 October, 10:05pm

PNG Kumuls head coach Jason Demetriou has made several changes to his line-up ahead clash against England.

Some of the changes made are positional, while others reflect the recovery of previously injured players.

The match could also be the last for captain Rhyse Martin, who is retiring after the world cup.

The equation for the Kumuls to progress further is simple, beat England and hope Samoa defeats Tonga by a big margin to keep their semi-finals hopes alive.

The Kumuls are currently 88 points behind Tonga on for and against and a Tonga victory will end PNG's dreams.

World.title: Aussie captain most expensive player at WPL auction
World.content:
Australia captain Sophie Molineux has proved the most expensive buy in India's Women's Premier League auction, and she'll suit up for a UP Warriorz side captained by former national team skipper Meg Lanning.

With many of the world's top players having already been retained for the 2027 edition of the lucrative Indian league, Molineux's signature was the most coveted one still left and the Lucknow-based franchise captured the T20 World Cup-winning skipper for the biggest price, INR 1.1 crore ($A164,000).

The spinning all-rounder won't be leading the team in the January 14-February 7 tournament, though.

Instead, Molineux will be playing under the captaincy of 34-year-old Lanning, the inspirational figure who skippered Australia when she first came into the side, in a T20I in India eight years ago.

Big life changes for WBBL winning duo A lot has changed since Nicola Carey and Elyse Villani lifted the WBBL trophy last year, as the Hobart Hurricanes prepare to defend their title.

Molineux's base price in the auction in Kochi was 50 Lakh ($A75,000) but she eventually went for over twice that price as a bidding battle began between Royal Challengers Bengaluru and the Warriorz.

With their superior budget, UP also snapped up big-hitting all-rounder Grace Harris going for $45,000, meaning that the side will have four Australians in their ranks with Phoebe Litchfield already on board.

Intriguingly, national skipper Molineux has been bought for less than both Lanning and Litchfield and four others among the 14-strong Australian contingent in the league.

The most expensive Australian in the league — each of the five teams has at least one Aussie World Cup winner in its ranks — will be Ash Gardner, captain of the Gujarat Giants, who was retained for $523,000 in a side that also includes four Aussies.

Gardner is the joint most-lucrative retention, alongside Royal Challengers Bengaluru captain Smriti Mandhana and Mumbai Indians' England skipper Nat Sciver-Brunt.

Of the 11 Australians up for grabs in Wednesday's auction, only three were sold.

Heather Graham, Tayla Vlaeminck, Tess Flintoff, Charli Knott, Samantha Bates, Maitlan Brown, Maddie Penna and Milly Illingworth were the ones to miss out.

World.title: Gold Coast Suns AFLW finals feat faces home-ground headache
World.content:
The Gold Coast Suns have earned their place in the AFLW finals — but their reward could be a home final away from home.

After back-to-back seasons near the bottom of the ladder, the Suns have surged into fourth spot with eight wins, booking their first finals appearance since 2023.

A victory over GWS on Sunday would strengthen their grip on a double chance, guaranteeing a home final during the series.

But there's a catch.

Carrara Stadium is unavailable for weeks two, three and four of the finals series, due to Australia's T20 clash with England, leaving the Suns and the AFL searching for an alternative venue.

Springfield, home of Queensland rivals the Brisbane Lions and an hour's drive up the highway, and Southport's Fankhauser Reserve are among the alternatives being considered.

Southport however comes with a significant caveat — any final would need to be played during the day, when November temperatures average around 28 degrees and humidity can hover around 70 per cent.

A spokesperson for the club said it is "working with all stakeholders on home venues for each week of the finals" where Carrara is not available.

"Our playing group and staff have been resolute all season in their efforts to play anywhere, anytime, across eight different venues and we know they'll take that attitude into any scenario that presents throughout the post-season campaign," the spokesperson said.

Despite this, coach Rhyce Shaw said on Tuesday the club is embracing the excitement of a long-awaited finals campaign.

Michael Voss Oval in Springfield is being considered as one option for an alternative venue. (Supplied: Brisbane Lions)

"I took [my son] Henry to swimming the other day and all the staff were getting behind us," Shaw said.

"It is exciting for our footy club … It's been a bit of a tough year all round, but for our girls to pick up the slack a little bit and get going and make finals is really, really cool."

"We've got a big job against the Giants and then we'll think of finals after that."

If the Suns were to fall to GWS on Sunday, there is the potential for them finish as low as seventh on the ladder.

However, a fifth or sixth place finish would mean they would earn a home final next weekend and the ABC can confirm Carrara Stadium would be available in this instance.

Rhyce Shaw, Senior Coach of the Suns, says it's been a "tough year" for the club. (Getty Images: Maya Thompson)

ABC Sport AFLW expert Chyloe Kurdas said regardless of the ladder outcome, the lack of venue certainty is an unwanted distraction.

"I think it is such a valuable home ground advantage [finishing in the top four] but it's also not just that, it's the distraction of this conversation right now that happens in the lead up to," she said.

"It occupies bandwidth and it occupies energy from the playing group and the coaching group and the staff."

Kurdas said not being able to play at Carrara, a venue the side has won their last three games at, would be a missed opportunity.

"I think there's a real sweet spot right now with the number of talented kids that are Gold Coast born and raised … that are now playing at the Suns," Kurdas said.

"Fan engagement is going to be such an important part of this Gold Coast Suns women's team journey … they're so talented."

The Suns have had a 75 per cent increase in AFLW memberships for this season.

A familiar problem

The Suns aren't the only club caught in a scheduling squeeze.

Second-placed Geelong, one win away from securing a top-two finish, also faces a venue clash, with Kardinia Park unavailable next weekend due to the AUSX Supercross Championship.

While, the AFLW Grand Final, should it be played in Melbourne, has already been locked in for Princes Park — with a capacity of 13 thousand that has sold out for the showpiece game within hours in recent seasons.

Docklands Stadium, with a 53,343-capacity is unavailable, with Harry Styles booked across the weekend, despite players calling for a bigger venue.

The Geelong Cats are facing a similar venue problem. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Grand Final has also been scheduled for Friday night, November 27, to avoid a clash with the Victorian State Election.

It's a familiar problem that's haunted the competition since it started in 2017.

In the inaugural season, the Brisbane Lions earned the right to host the Grand Final but were forced to play at Carrara, with the Gabba unavailable due to cricket.

Now in its 11th season, the debate continues about where the AFLW competition belongs in the sporting calendar.

The AFL is reportedly considering an earlier start to align the women's season with the end of the men's competition.

"You do your due diligence and you look at where is there likely to be these kind of clashes," Chyloe Kurdas said.

"But ultimately, whenever you choose to play it, you then have to live and die by those decisions."

She says clubs and the AFL must also be prepared to make commercial decisions that put their women's programs first.

" You can't just buy in when it suits you. "

The AFL and Stadiums Queensland were contacted for comment.

World.title: WBBL winning duo on eve of big life changes
World.content:
A lot has changed since Nicola Carey hit the winning runs for the Hobart Hurricanes in last year's WBBL final.

Cricket-wise, her partner Elyse Villani retired and handed over the captaincy.

Life-wise, they're building a house together and are expecting their first child.

"Now that you've pointed it out, I am a bit overwhelmed," Carey joked.

"We've got a bit going on, don't we?
